## The Chronicle of Gotama Buddha

Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## The Gem of the Saṅgha
## Chapter 43
## Section on the Therāpadāna
I shall now set forth the Therāpadāna—the life stories and practices of the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) who were endowed with the nine attributes of the Ariya Saṅgha, such as being well-practiced (suppaṭipannatā), and who attained the distinguished titles of Etadagga. This account will begin with the story of the Venerable Koṇḍañña, based primarily on the commentary to the Etadaggavagga of the Ekakanipāta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
2:
2
## (1) The Story of Venerable Koṇḍañña
In presenting the life story (Therāpadāna) of this great elder, I shall write according to the commentaries, focusing on these four points: (a) Past Aspiration, (b) Circumstances of Ordination in the final life, (c) Attainment of the Special Dhamma, and (d) Appointment to the Etadagga position.
## (a) The Past Aspiration of the Great Elder
Counting backward from this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), one hundred thousand aeons ago, the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world. (The reason for His name 'Padumuttara' has already been described on page 396 of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume One, Part Two).
After the Buddha Padumuttara appeared prominently among the three classes of beings, He traveled on a journey (cārika) through villages, market towns, and royal capitals to compassionately uplift the masses, accompanied by one hundred thousand monks. Eventually, He arrived at the golden city of Haṃsāvatī (His birthplace). His father, King Ānanda, hearing the good news of his son's arrival, went out to welcome Him along with the citizens and the royal host. When the Buddha Padumuttara preached the Dhamma to the assembly led by King Ānanda, at the conclusion of the sermon, some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some reached the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala).
The royal father invited the Buddha for the next day's meal. On the following day, having announced the mealtime, he offered a great donation to the Buddha Padumuttara and His retinue of one hundred thousand monks in his golden palace.
3:
3
After the Buddha Padumuttara had given the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, He returned to the monastery. In the same manner, on the next day, the citizens offered a great donation (Mahādāna). On the following day, King Ānanda offered a Mahādāna. Thus, the King and the citizens took turns offering great donations for a long period.
At that time, the future Venerable Koṇḍañña was born into a wealthy family of great householders (Gahapati Mahāsāla) in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī. One day, while the Buddha was preaching, he saw the people of Haṃsāvatī carrying flowers, scents, and other offerings, going to hear the Dhamma where the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—resided. He then followed those people to the place of the sermon.
At that time, the Buddha Padumuttara appointed a certain monk, who was the first in His Sāsana to realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation, to the foremost and highest position of Etadagga in the rank of Rattaññū (those of long standing/seniority). The noble youth, the future Koṇḍañña, heard this and thought: "This monk is truly great and noble. Aside from the Buddha Himself, there is no other monk who realized the Four Noble Truths before him. If only I, too, could become a noble monk in the Sāsana of a future Buddha, capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths first, just like this monk!"
4:
4
Having entered into this noble thought, after the sermon ended, he approached the Buddha and invited Him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my meal offering tomorrow." The Buddha Padumuttara accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing well that the Buddha had accepted, the noble youth paid his respects with great devotion and returned home. Throughout the night, he decorated the place where the Buddha and the monks would sit with garlands of scents and flowers. He prepared exquisite food and delicacies. When the night had passed and the next day arrived, he offered the Buddha Padumuttara and His retinue of one hundred thousand monks a donation of extraordinary gruel and delicacies, along with fragrant Sāli rice of excellent flavor. After the meal, he laid out at the Buddha's feet brand-new, soft, and thick cloths from the Vaṅga country, sufficient to sew three robes. He then reflected: "I am not one who seeks a minor position in the Sāsana; I am one who seeks a great position related to the Sāsana. It is not possible to aspire for such a high rank by performing a Mahādāna for only one day. Therefore, I shall offer a great Mahādāna for seven consecutive days and then make my aspiration."
That noble youth continued to offer Mahādāna in this manner for seven days. When the meal ceremony was concluded on the seventh day, he had his cloth granaries opened and placed soft, exquisite cloths at the Buddha's feet.
5:
5
After offering sets of three robes (Ticīvara) to the one hundred thousand monks, he approached the Buddha and said: "Exalted Buddha, seven days ago from today, Your Exalted Self praised and appointed a monk to the position of Etadagga. May I, like him, be one who is capable of penetrating and realizing the Four Noble Truths first, after ordaining in the Sāsana of a Buddha who will appear in the future." Having said this, he remained prostrate at the Buddha's feet in respectful salutation.
The Buddha Padumuttara, hearing the words of the noble youth's aspiration, considered with His Golden Knowledge of the Future (Anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa): "This noble youth has performed a great act of merit (adhikāra). Will this noble youth's current aspiration be fulfilled or not?" He then saw clearly: "It will certainly be fulfilled."
Indeed, for the Buddhas, when they reflect upon the past, the future, or the present, there are no obstacles or hindrances. Past events separated by many hundreds of millions of aeons, future events, or present events separated by thousands of world systems, are all connected simply to their reflection and attention. (As soon as they reflect and attend, it becomes clear and known.) Thus, with His unhindered knowledge, the Buddha Padumuttara saw: "One hundred thousand aeons from now, the Buddha Gotama will appear prominently among the three classes of beings. At that time,
6:
6
this noble youth's aspiration will be fulfilled." Knowing this, the Buddha Padumuttara spoke these words of prophecy (byādita) to the noble youth, the future Koṇḍañña: "Young man, one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will appear prominently among the three classes of beings. When that Buddha Gotama preaches the first sermon, the Dhamma-cakka, you will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) together with eighteen crores of Brahmas, endowed with a thousand methods, at the conclusion of the Te-parivaṭṭa-dhammacakkappavattana Sutta."
Later, after the Buddha Padumuttara had passed into Parinibbāna (as described in the Section on the Twenty-four Buddhas, Volume One, Part Two, page 403), when the people built a great Stupa (Sarīra-cetiya) seven yojanas high, this noble merchant, the future Koṇḍañña, built and donated a jewel chamber inside the Stupa. Furthermore, he erected and donated a thousand jewel archways surrounding the Stupa.
## The Story of the Brothers Mahākāla and Cūḷakāla
That noble merchant, the future Koṇḍañña, performed meritorious deeds such as dāna for a hundred thousand years. Upon passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. While he circled between the celestial and human realms, ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and nine (99,909) great aeons passed. (This means that for 99,909 aeons, he did not fall into the lower realms but only traveled back and forth between the celestial and human worlds). After this long period had passed, counting backward from this Bhadda-kappa,
7:
7
ninety-one aeons ago, this noble youth, the future Koṇḍañña, was born into a householder's family in a village near the royal city of Bandhumatī, and was named Mahākāla. His younger brother was named Cūḷakāla.
At that time, the Bodhisatta Vipassī passed away from the Tusita heaven and was conceived in the womb of Queen Bandhumatī, the chief consort of King Bandhuma in the royal city of Bandhumatī. (As described in the Section on the Twenty-four Buddhas below), He eventually attained Omniscient Buddhahood. When the Great Brahma requested Him to preach the Dhamma, He reflected: "To whom should I preach the Dhamma first?" He perceived that His younger brother, Prince Khaṇḍa, and the chaplain's son, the young man Tissa, were capable of penetrating and realizing the Four Noble Truths first. He decided: "I shall preach the Dhamma to them, and I shall also uplift my royal father." Thus, He traveled from the Mahābodhi seat through the air and descended at the Migadāya (Deer Park) named Khema. He then sent for Prince Khaṇḍa and the young man Tissa to come to His presence and preached the Dhamma to them. At the conclusion of the sermon, both of them, along with eighty-four thousand beings, were established in the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala).
Then, the eighty-four thousand noblemen who had followed the Bodhisatta and ordained when He renounced the world, heard this news and—
8:
They came to the presence of the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and were established in the fruit of Arahatship. In that very Khema Deer Park, the Blessed One Vipassī appointed the Elder Khaṇḍa as the chief disciple on the right and the Elder Tissa as the chief disciple on the left.

King Bandhumā also heard of this and, thinking, "I shall go and pay homage to my son, the Buddha," went to the park. Having heard the Dhamma and being established in the three refuges, he invited the Blessed One Vipassī for the next day's meal, paid his respects, and departed. Upon returning to the royal palace, while sitting in his noble mansion, the King reflected: "My eldest son has renounced the world and become a Buddha. My second son has become the chief disciple on the right. Tissa, the son of the royal chaplain, has become the chief disciple on the left. These remaining eighty-four thousand monks who follow him were also his retinue when they were laymen. Therefore, this Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is my responsibility alone, both in the past and now. I alone shall attend to the Buddha and the monks with the four requisites; I shall not give others the opportunity to serve them."

With this thought, he had a fence of khadir wood built on both sides of the path from the monastery gate to the palace gate. He had it covered with cloth and hung with flower garlands the size of palm trunks, adorned with golden stars. He had a canopy spread above and the ground below covered with exquisite carpets. On both sides within the path, he placed water pots amidst flower bushes, and placed flowers among perfumes and perfumes among flowers so that the entire path would be fragrant.
9:
He then sent word that it was time for the Blessed One to come for the meal. The Blessed One Vipassī, surrounded by the assembly of monks, proceeded to the royal palace within the screened enclosure, partook of the meal, and returned to the monastery along the same path. Not a single other person had the opportunity even to behold him. How then could they have the chance to offer food or make offerings? No one at all received such an opportunity.

Then the citizens of the city deliberated and consulted among themselves:

"It has now been seven years and seven months since the Blessed One appeared in the world. Yet, we have not even had the chance to behold the Blessed One. What need is there to mention offering food, making offerings, or hearing the Dhamma? (It is certain we have no opportunity). The King, thinking 'The Buddha is my Buddha, the Dhamma is my Dhamma, the Saṅgha is my Saṅgha,' cherishes and serves the Triple Gem alone. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is for the benefit of the world of beings, including devas and Brahmās. He did not appear for the benefit of the King alone. Indeed, the fires of hell do not burn for the King alone while appearing like blue lotuses to others. Therefore, let us address the King: 'It would be good if you grant us the opportunity to serve the Blessed One. If you do not grant it, we shall wage war against the King, take possession of the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna).'

There is a special reason: the citizens alone would not be able to do this. Therefore, let us secure a leader to head our cause."

Having consulted thus, they went to the Commander-in-Chief and spoke to him openly, asking directly, "O General, will you be on our side or on the King's side?"
10:
Then the General said, "I will be on your side. However, I have a special request: you must grant me the privilege of serving the Saṅgha on the first day." The citizens agreed to this condition.

The General went to the King and reported, "Great King, the citizens are angry with you." The King asked, "Friend General, why are the citizens angry with me?" "They say that only the King serves the Blessed One and they do not get the opportunity. Great King, it is not too late. If they are granted the opportunity to serve now, they will not be angry. But if they do not get it, they wish to wage war against you," the General reported candidly. Then the King said, "Friend General, I will rather fight a war, but I will never give up the Saṅgha of monks."

The General then spoke pressingly, "Great King, your subjects say they will fight against you. Whom will you call upon to fight the war?" The King tried to win him over, saying, "Are you not my Commander-in-Chief?" The General replied, "Great King, I cannot fight if I am separated from the citizens."

Then the King realized, "The citizens are very powerful, and the General is on their side."
11:
He then requested, "Friends, if that is the case, grant me the privilege of supporting the Saṅgha for another seven years and seven months." The citizens did not accept or agree. The King gradually reduced his request to six years, five years, and so on, finally asking for just seven days. Then the citizens consulted and agreed, "It is not proper to remain stubborn and compete with the King when he asks for only seven days at the end." Thus, they granted the King's request for seven days.

King Bandhumā prepared for the seven days of offerings with the same magnitude as he would have for seven years and seven months. For the first six days, he made the offerings while not a single citizen could see. On the seventh day, he invited the citizens, showed them the grand scale of the offerings, and tested them, saying, "Friends, will you be able to make such a grand offering as this?" The citizens countered, "Great King, is it not because of us that these offerings of yours are possible?" and declared, "We are able to do so."
12:
King Bandhumā, wiping away tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Venerable Blessed Son, your father had resolved to support the Buddha and the 168,000 monks with the four requisites for the rest of his life without sharing the responsibility with others. However, as I can no longer hold out, I have now granted the citizens the opportunity to serve. It is true, the citizens are angry with me, saying 'We do not get the opportunity to make offerings.' Venerable Blessed Son, starting from tomorrow, please show compassion and favor to those citizens."

Thus, he spoke these sorrowful words of relinquishment. Then, on the second day, the General gave a great offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, according to the original agreement. (Here, I shall briefly present the story of Saddhāsumanā from the Manorathapūraṇī, Vol. 3, p. 13):

## The Story of Saddhāsumanā
On that first day, which was the General's turn, he organized a great offering and issued an order: "For today, guards must be stationed to ensure that no other person has the opportunity to offer even a single spoonful of alms-food." He placed soldiers and royal attendants all around as guards. On that day, the widow of a wealthy treasurer in the city of Bandhumatī was deeply grieved (because they did not get the chance to offer food on the first day) and lamented loudly.
13:
When her daughter returned from playing with five hundred maiden companions, the mother said to her, "Dear daughter, if your father were alive, I would have been the first to offer alms-food to the Blessed One this very day." She spoke these words of weakness and complaint. The treasurer's daughter encouraged her mother, saying, "O mother, do not be troubled by various thoughts. I will arrange it so that the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha receives and partakes of my alms-food first."

Then the treasurer's daughter filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with pure milk-rice, enriched it with ghee, honey, and sugar, covered it with another golden bowl, and wrapped the two bowls with garlands of jasmine (sumanā) flowers until it resembled a large ball of flowers. When the Blessed One entered the city, she carried it on her head and left the house, surrounded by many attendants.

Upon reaching the road, the treasurer's daughter and the guards exchanged words:

Guards: "Daughter, do not come this way."

Treasurer's Daughter: "Uncles, why do you not allow me to pass?" (Those with merit speak endearing words, and others are unable to refuse them).

Guards: "The General has issued a strict order that no other person is to be allowed to offer any food or provisions, and he has stationed us as guards, daughter."
14:
Treasurer's Daughter: "Uncles, do you see any food or provisions in my hand that you should forbid me?"

Guards: "We only see a large ball of flowers, daughter."

Treasurer's Daughter: "What is this? Has your General forbidden even the offering of flowers?"

Guards: "He has given permission for the offering of flowers, daughter."

Then the treasurer's daughter said to the guards, "If that is so, move aside; do not block me, uncles." She approached the Blessed One and requested, "Venerable Blessed One, please accept this offering of a ball of flowers." The Blessed One looked at one of the guards and had him take the ball of flowers. The treasurer's daughter paid homage to the Blessed One and made an aspiration:

"Venerable Blessed One, in whatever life I am born in the round of rebirths, may I never have to live in longing or anxiety. Like this jasmine (sumanā) flower, may I be loved by all in every life throughout saṃsāra, and may I be known only by the name Sumanā."

Having made this prayer, the Blessed One responded, "May you be happy in both body and mind."
15:
The merchant's daughter, filled with joy, paid her respects to the Buddha and departed. The Buddha arrived at the General's house and sat on the prepared seat. The General brought gruel (yāgu) and approached the Buddha. The Buddha covered his bowl with his hand. Thinking that the Buddha was not accepting the offering because all the monks had not yet arrived, the General said, "Venerable Sir, all the monks of the Saṅgha have arrived and are seated." The Buddha replied, "We already have a meal-set that we received on the way." When the jasmine flowers covering the top were removed, milk-rice (pāyāsa) was seen emitting steam. Then, the young man, a disciple of the General who had carried the golden bowl, said, "O Lord General, the woman deceived me by saying it was a 'flower ball'." The milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, starting with the Buddha. After offering the gruel and milk-rice, the General offered the other gifts he had prepared. When the Buddha had finished his meal, he gave a discourse of blessing and departed.

After the Buddha had left, the General asked his disciples, "What is the name of that woman who offered the meal?" When the disciples replied, "Lord General, she is the daughter of a merchant," the General praised her, saying, "She is indeed a wise woman. If such a wise woman manages a household, for the master of the house,
16:
it will not be difficult to attain the bliss of the heavenly realms." He then took the merchant's daughter as his wife and placed her in the position of the chief lady.

That merchant's daughter managed and administered the wealth of both her father's house and the General's house. Throughout her life, she performed meritorious deeds and gave offerings to the Buddha. When she passed away from that life, she was reborn in the Kāmāvacara deva realm. At the very moment of her birth, a rain of jasmine flowers fell, covering the entire deva realm to the depth of one's knees. The devas said, "This goddess has brought her own name with her," and they named her "Sumanā Devī" (Jasmine Goddess).

That Sumanā Devī wandered through the deva and human realms for ninety-one aeons, remaining free from the lower realms. In every place she was born, there was a rain of jasmine flowers, and she was known only as "Sumanā Devī" or "Sumanā Kumārī". In the era of the current Buddha's dispensation, this Sumanā Devī was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Kosala. On that same day, five hundred daughters of various ministers and others were also conceived. All these girls were born from their mothers' wombs on the same day as Princess Sumanā. At that moment, a rain of jasmine flowers fell, reaching the depth of one's knees.

Seeing this phenomenon, King Kosala thought, "This daughter of mine must be one who has performed exceptional merit in the past."
17:
With a heart full of delight and joy, he said, "My daughter is one who has brought her own name," and he had her named Sumanā. Reflecting that "My daughter will not have been born alone," he ordered a search throughout the city. Upon hearing the news that five hundred other girls were born, the King himself took responsibility for their care and upbringing. He also issued an order that "Every month, those five hundred girls must be brought and shown to my daughter."

When Princess Sumanā reached the age of seven, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had completed the construction of the Jetavana Monastery and sent a messenger to invite the Buddha. The Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks, traveled to the city of Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika went to King Kosala and said, "Great King, the Buddha's arrival in our city of Sāvatthī is a great blessing for Your Majesty and for us. Therefore, I would like Princess Sumanā, together with her five hundred companions, to be sent to welcome the Buddha, carrying full water pots, perfumes, flowers, and so on." King Kosala agreed, saying, "Very well, Great Merchant," and arranged everything as Anāthapiṇḍika had requested. Princess Sumanā, following her father's command, went to welcome and pay respects to the Buddha. After honoring him with perfumes and flowers, she stood in a suitable place.
18:
The Buddha preached the Dhamma to Princess Sumanā while still on the road. Princess Sumanā, along with her five hundred companions, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Furthermore, another five hundred young women, five hundred older women, and five hundred laymen also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry at that same teaching session. Thus, on the day of the Buddha's arrival, two thousand noble ones (Ariyas) who were Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) emerged even before reaching the monastery.

When Princess Sumanā reached maturity, her father King Kosala gave her five hundred chariots and various honors so that she could travel with her five hundred companions. In that era, there were three women who received five hundred chariots and such honors from their parents: (1) Princess Cundī, the daughter of King Bimbisāra; (2) Visākhā, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya; and (3) Princess Sumanā, the daughter of King Kosala, who has just been described. This is the story of Sumanā.

As previously mentioned, on the day after the King had the opportunity to serve the Buddha Vipassī and the assembly of monks, the General gave a great donation. Following this, the citizens of the city performed offerings even greater than the King's and gave a grand donation (Mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. In this way, when the sequence of meal offerings for the whole city was completed, the people living at the city gates got their turn and arranged to perform their offerings.
19:
At that time, the householder Mahākāla said to his younger brother Cūḷakāla, "Tomorrow is our turn to perform an offering to the Buddha. What kind of offering shall we make?" The younger brother Cūḷakāla replied, "Brother, you yourself should consider what is appropriate." Then the elder brother Mahākāla said, "Dear brother, if you will follow my wish, the rice in our sixteen-pe (a measure of land) field is now full of grain and ripening. Shall we break open those rice husks, take the grain, and cook suitable milk-rice for the Buddhas?" Cūḷakāla replied, "Brother, doing this will not benefit anyone. Therefore, I do not like or agree with this plan."

Then the householder Mahākāla said, "Dear brother, if you cannot follow or agree to this, I wish to take what is my rightful share as my own property." He then divided the sixteen-pe field in the middle, marking off eight pe. From his own portion, he extracted the young rice grains (in the milk stage), had them cooked with pure milk, added the four sweet ingredients (catumadhū), and offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Remarkably, at every spot where Mahākāla had extracted the young grain, the rice husks filled up again and returned to their original state. (This was the 1st offering: the offering of the first young grain).
20:
When the rice was suitable for making parched rice, the householder Mahākāla similarly made the 2nd offering: the first parched rice. When the crops matured along with those of the other villagers, he made the 3rd offering: the first of the harvest. In the same way, when the crops were reaped, he took the first handfuls and made the 4th offering: the first of the reaping. When the sheaves were bound, he took the first bound sheaves and made the 5th offering: the first of the sheaves. When the sheaves were piled together, he took the first portion and made the 6th offering: the first of the stack. When they were taken from the stack and threshed, he took the first portion and made the 7th offering: the first of the threshing. When the threshed grain was winnowed and piled on the threshing floor, he took the first portion and made the 8th offering: the first of the grain pile. When the grain was moved from the threshing floor into the granary, he took the first portion and made the 9th offering: the first of the granary. Thus, for every single planting of rice, the householder Mahākāla made nine foremost offerings (aggadāna). The grain he extracted and offered never decreased; it only increased and became more abundant than before. This was (a) the meritorious deed of the Elder's past aspiration.

## (b) Becoming a Monk in the Final Life
The virtuous householder Mahākāla, the future Venerable Koṇḍañña, performed such meritorious deeds as long as the Buddha lived and as long as he himself lived. When he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the deva realm. Wandering through the deva and human realms, he enjoyed heavenly and human bliss for a period of ninety-one aeons.
21:
21
After our Buddha had enjoyed [his previous lives] and was about to appear in the world, he was born into a wealthy Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla family in the Brahmin village of "Doṇavatthu" near the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day of his naming, the young Brahmin was given the name "Koṇḍañña." As Koṇḍañña grew up, he studied the three Vedas and reached the further shore of mastery in the science of the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa).

At that time, our Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and was conceived in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, the chief consort of King Suddhodana of Kapilavatthu. On the day the Bodhisatta was to be named, one hundred and eight Brahmins were honored with gifts of brand-new clothes and fed with pure, undiluted milk-rice. From among those one hundred and eight Brahmins, eight Brahmin scholars of sharp wisdom were specifically selected and seated in order on the upper terrace of the golden palace. The infant Bodhisatta prince, adorned with all ornaments, was laid upon a white cloth and brought before the Brahmins so they could examine his marks.

Among the eight Brahmin scholars, the one seated in the first place raised two fingers and predicted, "If he remains in the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he renounces the world, he will surely and certainly become a Buddha in the three worlds." In the same manner, the seven senior Brahmin scholars in succession raised two fingers. Among those eight Brahmin scholars, the young Koṇḍañña...
22:
22
...was the youngest of all. When it was his turn to make a prediction, he carefully and meticulously examined the Bodhisatta's perfection in all the marks of a Great Man. (Reflecting that since the mark of a Universal Monarch was present on the soles of his feet, it is not fitting for such a mark to be on the feet of one who would merely become a Cakkavatti), he raised only one finger and boldly predicted, "There is no reason at all for this Bodhisatta prince to remain in the midst of a household; this Bodhisatta will surely and certainly become a Buddha."

Afterward, when the Brahmin scholars returned to their respective homes, they called their sons and gave them this instruction: "Dear sons, we are now aged. Whether we will live to see Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana, attain the state of Omniscient Buddhahood, we do not know. If Prince Siddhattha attains Omniscient Buddhahood, you should renounce the world and become monks in his Dispensation (Sāsana)."

King Suddhodana also arranged for nurses and provided great protection, attendants, and ceremonies for his son, the Bodhisatta, allowing him to grow up in comfort. When the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen, he enjoyed the glory of the golden palace, which was like celestial bliss. Upon reaching the age of twenty-nine and having matured in wisdom, he saw the faults in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. On the day Prince Rāhula was born, accompanied by his co-natal courtier Channa and mounting the royal horse Kanthaka...
23:
23
...he departed on the Great Renunciation through the city gate opened by the devas. In that single night, he passed through the three kingdoms of Kapilavatthu, Koliya, and Devadaha. He became a monk on the banks of the Anomā River, donning the robes and requisites brought and offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma. With a most inspiring deportment, like a great elder of sixty rains and eighty years of age, he arrived at the city of Rājagaha. After wandering for alms in that city and partaking of his meal in the shade of the Paṇḍava Hill, he was invited by King Bimbisāra to accept the kingship of his realm, but he refused and rejected that invitation. Proceeding on his journey, he reached the forest of Uruvelā. Reflecting, "Oh, this ground is truly delightful; this is the most suitable place for a man of good family who wishes to strive in the work of meditation (padhāna)," he began the practice of great austerities (dukkharacariyā) and remained in that forest.

When the Bodhisatta thus renounced the world, the seven other Brahmin scholars, apart from the Brahmin Koṇḍañña, had already passed away. Only the youngest, the Brahmin Koṇḍañña, remained in good health. When Koṇḍañña heard the news that "the Bodhisatta has renounced the world," he went to the sons of those seven deceased Brahmin scholars and said, "Prince Siddhattha has renounced the world. That prince will surely and certainly become a Buddha without a doubt. If your fathers were still alive today, they would have renounced the world and...
24:
24
...become monks. If you also wish to renounce the world, come; let us follow that Great Man and become monks." Not all seven could reach a consensus to renounce; three were unable to do so. Only the remaining four, with the Brahmin Koṇḍañña as their leader, became monks.

After these five monks of the group (Pañcavaggiyā) had renounced the world, they wandered for alms through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, eventually reaching the presence of the Bodhisatta. For six years, while the Bodhisatta was engaged in the Great Striving (Mahāpadhāna), these five monks lived and moved near him, attending to him with great expectation, thinking, "He will become a Buddha very soon; he will become a Buddha very soon."

When the six years had passed, although the Great Being spent his time in exhaustion by consuming only a single grain of rice or a single sesame seed, he realized that the attainment of the Noble Path and Fruit (Ariya Magga Phala) was not possible through the practice of austerities. (As mentioned in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 2, pages 262-263), he wandered for alms in Senānigama and partook of whatever coarse food, rice, or cakes he received. At that time, the five monks of the group, prompted by the nature of things, became weary and discouraged with the Bodhisatta. They abandoned the Great Being and went to the Isipatana Migadāya forest.

After the five monks had thus departed, the Bodhisatta, by partaking of whatever coarse food, rice, or cakes he received...
25:
25
...restored his skin, flesh, and blood to their normal state within two or three days. On the full moon day of Kason (the day he was to become Buddha), he partook of the noble milk-rice offered by the merchant's wife Sujātā. After floating the golden bowl in the Nerañjarā River, he made the resolution: "Today, I shall surely and certainly become a Buddha." In the evening, being joyfully praised by the Dragon King Kāla with various eulogies, he ascended the terrace of the Mahābodhi. Seated cross-legged on the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita Pallanka) at the immovable site, facing the eastern quarter, he resolved upon the energy endowed with four factors (caturaṅga-vīriya). Before sunset, he dispelled Māra the deity; in the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa); in the middle watch, he attained the divine eye (Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). When the dawn approached, he applied his wisdom to the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda). Contemplating the twelve factors of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order (as described in the section on attaining Buddhahood) with the Great Diamond-like Insight (Mahāvajira-vipassanā), he realized the unique Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) attained by all Buddhas and reached Buddhahood. He then remained on that same Mahābodhi throne, entering the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti) for seven days.

In this way, after the Blessed One had stayed at the seven locations (as described below), and following the request of Sahampati Brahma, he reflected, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" He realized that the great teachers Āḷāra and Uddaka had already passed away. He then continued to reflect...
26:
26
"The five monks of the group (Pañcavaggiyā) have been very helpful to me. These five monks attended to me while I was engaged in the Great Striving. It would be well if I were to preach the Dhamma first to the five monks." Such a thought is the custom (dhammatā) of all Buddhas. In truth, apart from the Brahmin Koṇḍañña, there was not a single person in this Buddha's Dispensation who was capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths first. That Brahmin Koṇḍañña had performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) for a hundred thousand aeons to be able to realize the Four Noble Truths first; furthermore, as mentioned before, he had offered the special gift of the nine first-fruits to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.

## (c) How the Elder Attained the Special Dhamma

Then the Blessed One took his bowl and robe and proceeded in stages to the Isipatana Migadāya forest, approaching the place where the five monks were staying. The five monks saw the Blessed One coming and, although they had previously made a pact not to perform any major or minor duties for him, as he drew closer, they were unable to maintain their original pact. One went to receive his bowl and robe, one prepared the seat, one set out water for washing the feet, one washed his feet, and one brought a palm-leaf fan and fanned him, each performing their respective duties.

Thus, after the five monks had performed their duties and were seated near the Blessed One, the Blessed One...
27:
The Buddha preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, characterized by the three rounds (tiparivaṭṭa), primarily addressing the Venerable Koṇḍañña in His presence. In that assembly of Dhamma, the human audience consisted only of the five monks of the group of five (pañcavaggiya), while the audience of devas and Brahmas was immeasurably large. At the conclusion of the Dhammacakkra discourse, the Venerable Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen crores (180,000,000) of Mahā Brahmas, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

## The Naming of Aññāsikoṇḍañña
At that time, the Blessed One reflected, “This monk Koṇḍañña has first understood the noble Four Noble Truths, which I have carried and borne through thousands of difficulties; therefore, this monk shall be named ‘Aññāsikoṇḍañña’.” Wishing to call the Elder by that name, He uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna): “Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño, aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño,” meaning, “Oh, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! Oh, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!” According to this inspired exclamation, the name of the Venerable Koṇḍañña became known as “Aññāsikoṇḍañña” from that time onwards.

## (d) Receiving the Title of Ratthaññū Etadagga
Thus, the Venerable Koṇḍañña was established in the fruit of Stream-entry on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era (the year the Buddha attained Enlightenment). Subsequently, the Venerable Bhaddiya on the 1st day after the full moon, the Venerable Vappa on the 2nd day, the Venerable Mahānāma on the 3rd day, and the Venerable Assaji on the 4th day were established in the fruit of Stream-entry in succession. Then, on the 5th day after the full moon,
28:
at the conclusion of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta discourse, all five monks of the group of five were established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). At that time, there were six Arahants in the world: the Blessed One and the five monks of the group of five.

From that time onwards, the Blessed One led many groups of people to the attainment of the Noble Path and Fruit, including the fifty-five youths led by the merchant's son Yasa, then the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes in the Kappāsika forest, and then the one thousand former matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila) on the stone plateau of Gayāsīsa. On the full moon day of Phussa in the year 103 of the Great Era, He arrived at the city of Rājagaha and established 110,000 brahmin householders, led by King Bimbisāra, in the fruit of Stream-entry, and 10,000 brahmin householders in the Three Refuges. Thus, throughout the island of Jambudīpa, He caused the Dhamma to blossom and bear fruit—the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the threefold training (sikkhā) and the eight wonderful qualities. He made the entire expanse of Jambudīpa radiant with the glow of saffron robes and caused the surrounding air to be stirred by the movement of noble monks. Later, on another occasion, while He was staying at the Jetavana monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, He sat upon the decorated Buddha-seat and Dhamma-throne in the midst of the Saṅgha. Wishing to show that “Among the monks who first understood the Four Noble Truths, my eldest son Koṇḍañña is the most excellent and foremost,” He addressed the monks regarding the Venerable Koṇḍañña:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ rattaññūnaṃ yadidaṃ aññāsikoṇḍañño = Monks,
29:
among my monk disciples who are of long standing (rattaññū), Aññāsikoṇḍañña is the foremost.”

With these words of praise, He appointed him to the position of Etadagga in the rank of Rattaññū.

(In this context, “Rattaññū = one who knows the divisions of the nights” means one who has known a long duration of nights since the time of ordination. Since there was no one in this Dispensation who was ordained before the Venerable Koṇḍañña, he is a Rattaññū person who has known a long duration of nights since ordination. According to this view, Rattaññū refers to the person with the greatest seniority in monkhood.)

Alternatively, because the Venerable Koṇḍañña was the very first among all disciples to understand the Four Noble Truths, he is a Rattaññū person because he has known the divisions of the nights since that long-ago time of realization. (According to this view, Rattaññū refers to the earliest person to understand the Four Noble Truths.)

Alternatively, since the divisions of night and day are clear to every Arahant, they are called Rattaññū. Because the Venerable Koṇḍañña was the first to become an Arahant, he is the most excellent and foremost among the Rattaññū Arahants who know the divisions of night and day.)

## After Becoming an Arahant
## The Story of the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña
The Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña became an Arahant on the 5th day after the full moon of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era. In that same year, the Blessed One arrived at the city of Rājagaha on the full moon day of Phussa, and on the 1st day of the waxing moon of Māgha,
30:
the two Chief Disciples (Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna) were ordained. On the 7th day of the waxing moon, Venerable Moggallāna became an Arahant, and on the full moon day of Māgha, Venerable Sāriputta became an Arahant. When the Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, and ordinary disciples had thus fully appeared in the Dispensation, all disciples went for alms according to their seniority at the time of alms-round. When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, He would sit on the decorated Buddha-seat and Dhamma-throne in the center, with the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), Venerable Sāriputta, sitting on His right side, and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sitting on His left side.

Behind those two Chief Disciples, a seat was prepared for the Venerable Koṇḍañña. The remaining monks sat surrounding the Venerable Koṇḍañña. The two Chief Disciples held great respect for the Venerable Koṇḍañña because he was the first to realize the Four Noble Truths in the Dispensation and because of his advanced age. They regarded the Elder as if he were a Great Brahma, a great bonfire, or a venomous serpent with potent venom. Although they had to sit in the front seats, they felt hesitant and lacked confidence; they felt shy and deferential toward him. At that time, the Venerable Koṇḍañña reflected: “The two Chief Disciples have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappa) for the sake of the front seats. Now, although these two Chief Disciples are sitting in the front seats, they are hesitant and lack confidence; they feel shy and deferential toward me.
31:
I will act in such a way that these two Chief Disciples can live comfortably.” This was one reason.

Furthermore, the Venerable Koṇḍañña was a Great Disciple of immense merit. Just like the fame of the Buddha’s virtues, the fame of the Elder’s virtues spread among the humans of this universe and the devas and Brahmas living in the ten thousand world systems. Thus, after devas and humans went to the Blessed One to make offerings of perfumes, flowers, and so on, they would immediately visit and make offerings to the Venerable Koṇḍañña, saying, “The Great Elder is the Great Disciple who first realized the extraordinary Four Noble Truths.” According to the traditions of the Dispensation, there was also the duty to give a suitable Dhamma talk or engage in detailed conversation with those who came into his presence. However, the Elder was one who placed great importance only on living comfortably in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), also known as the noble dwelling (ariyavihāra). Therefore, for the Elder, having to give suitable Dhamma talks or engage in detailed conversations with those visitors became like an excessive and burdensome task. This was another reason.

Due to these two aforementioned reasons, the Venerable Koṇḍañña wished to depart from the vicinity of the Buddha and live elsewhere. He reflected and saw that “My nephew, the young Puṇṇa, son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī, will ordain and become a noble Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) in the Dispensation.”
32:
Having realized this, he went to the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu, ordained his nephew Puṇṇa, and thought, “This nephew of mine, the monk Puṇṇa, will remain in the presence of the Buddha.” After making his nephew Puṇṇa a resident pupil (antevāsika) of the Buddha, he approached the Blessed One and said, “Exalted Blessed One, a monastery near a village is not suitable (sappāya) for me. I am unable to live comfortably while mixed with the four classes of people. Therefore, I ask permission to go and live at Lake Chaddanta.” The Blessed One granted him permission to go and live there.

Having received permission from the Buddha, the Venerable Koṇḍañña put away his bedding, took his bowl and robes, and went to the banks of the Mandākinī pond near Lake Chaddanta. In that region of Lake Chaddanta, eight thousand elephants, who were endowed with great power and long-lived like devas, and who were already accustomed to serving and attending to Paccekabuddhas in the past, saw the Elder and were filled with joy, thinking, “A great fertile field for our merit has arrived.” They cleared the ground with their hooves to make a path for walking meditation (caṅkama) free of grass, removed tree branches that would obstruct the Elder’s walking path, and cleaned the area where the Elder resided. All eight thousand elephants then consulted together, saying:

“Friends, if we think, ‘This elephant will perform the duties for the Elder,’
33:
“If we remain expectant, thinking ‘this elephant will do it’ or ‘that one will do it,’ the Venerable Elder will have to return to the monastery with his bowl as empty as when he set out, like a monk arriving at a village where he has many relatives [but no one offers]. Therefore, let us serve the Venerable Elder in turns so that there is no neglect. Especially, when it is one elephant's turn, the other elephants must also remain mindful and assist, rather than being indifferent thinking it is not their turn.”

Having discussed thus, they established a rotation. The elephant whose turn it was would prepare the water for washing the face and the tooth-sticks for the Venerable Elder early in the morning. The method of preparation was as follows: the elephant on duty would rub pieces of dry wood that ignite easily, such as pine or divine wood, against each other to start a fire. In that fire, they would heat stones and rocks, then roll those stones with sticks into large stone water-vessels. After testing to ensure the water was hot, they would prepare tooth-sticks made of Naga-creeper (Kaṃkaw-nway). Then, that elephant would sweep both the inside and outside of the small meditation hut where the Venerable Elder resided using tree branches, and perform great and small duties by offering food in the following manner.

## Maṇḍākinī Lake

The Maṇḍākinī Lake, where the Venerable Koṇḍañña resided, was fifty leagues (yojanas) wide. In the center of that lake, for an area of twenty-five leagues, there were no weeds or algae at all; there was only water as clear as crystal. Beyond that central water, in water that was waist-deep, there was a belt of
34:
white lotus forest about half a league wide, surrounding the fifty-league lake. Beyond that white lotus forest, there was a red Paduma lotus forest of the same width of half a league. Beyond that red Paduma lotus forest, a red Kumuda lotus forest of half a league. Beyond that red Kumuda lotus forest, a white Kumuda lotus forest of half a league. Beyond that white Kumuda lotus forest, a blue lotus forest of half a league. Beyond that blue lotus forest, a red lotus forest of half a league. Beyond that red lotus forest, a forest of fragrant red Sāli rice of half a league. Beyond that rice forest, there were vast forests of sweet-tasting climbing fruits such as cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins, each half a league wide. Beyond those fruit forests, a sugarcane forest half a league wide surrounded the lake. In that sugarcane forest, the stalks were as thick as betel nut trees.

Beyond that sugarcane forest, a banana forest half a league wide surrounded the lake. If humans were to eat about two ripe bananas from this forest, they would become so full and bloated that they would suffer greatly. Beyond that banana forest, on the outer side, was a jackfruit forest with fruits the size of large water jars. Beyond that jackfruit forest, a rose-apple forest; beyond that, a mango forest; beyond that, a wood-apple forest, and so on. To summarize, it cannot be said that any edible fruit was missing from the vicinity of Maṇḍākinī Lake; indeed, all varieties were present.

When the flowers bloomed, the wind would blow the pollen from those flowers and deposit it upon the lotus leaves in the Paduma lotus forest. Then, water droplets would fall onto those lotus leaves. Thereafter,
35:
it would be cooked by the heat of the sun and settle like thickened milk curds. This is called 'lotus honey' (paduma-madhu). The elephants on duty would collect and offer this lotus honey to the Venerable Elder.

The lotus roots were as thick as the head of a plow; the elephants would also take these and offer them to the Elder. The lotus fibrous stalks were as large as the body of a great drum; in each joint of these stalks, there was about one measure (nāḷi) of lotus milk. The elephants would take this lotus milk and offer it to the Venerable Elder.

The elephants would also mix the lotus fibers with honey and offer them to the Venerable Elder. They would place sugarcane stalks, which were as thick as betel nut trees, on stone slabs and crush them with their feet. The sugarcane juice would flow out, filling small stone bowls and hollows, and after being cooked by the sun's heat, it would become molasses as solid as stone-sugar (goda-pāsāṇa). The elephants would take these pieces of molasses and offer them to the Venerable Elder.

A deity named Nāgadatta lived on Mount Kelāsa in the Himavantā. From time to time, the Venerable Elder would go to the entrance of that deity's celestial mansion. The deity would offer a bowl full of pure milk-rice, unmixed with water, and blended with fresh ghee and lotus honey powder. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, this deity had offered fragrant ghee and milk as 'ticket-food' (salāka-bhatta) for twenty thousand years. Due to that merit, this pure milk-rice mixed with ghee and lotus honey powder became his food and sustenance.
36:
Thus, the Venerable Koṇḍañña resided near the Chaddanta Lake and Maṇḍākinī Lake for twelve years. When he reviewed his life-span (āyu-saṅkhāra), he saw that the continuity of his life was coming to an end. He reflected, “Where should I attain Parinibbāna?” Then he considered, “These eight thousand elephants who have served me for twelve years have done what is difficult to do. Their gratitude is very great. I shall go to the presence of the Blessed One to ask permission for Parinibbāna, and then I shall enter Parinibbāna right here in this meditation hut near these elephants.”

Having made this decision, he traveled through the air to the presence of the Blessed One, who was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. He bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, kissed the Blessed One's feet with his mouth, and massaged them firmly with his hands. He announced his name, saying, “O Blessed One of great glory, I am Koṇḍañña. O Blessed One who speaks words of excellence, I am Koṇḍañña.”

(In this regard: The reason Venerable Koṇḍañña announced his name in this way was that among the monks present near the Blessed One at that time, some senior elders knew him, but the junior monks did not. Under such circumstances, the Venerable Elder thought: “Those junior monks who do not know me might have corrupted thoughts and offend me, thinking, ‘Who is this old monk with white hair, a bent back, and missing teeth, who is now engaging in friendly conversation with the Blessed One?’ Those junior monks who commit such an offense would go to the states of loss (apāya). If I announce my name to the Blessed One, those junior monks who did not know me before will come to know me. Both the senior and junior monks—these two types of fellow practitioners—will then think, ‘He is indeed a great disciple as famous as the Blessed One throughout the ten thousand world-systems,’ because they either knew me before or have just come to know me. They will be filled with faith and devotion, and all those who have such a clear and devoted mind will go to the heavenly realms.” Thinking thus, he announced his name to the Blessed One because he wished to close the path to the states of loss and open the path to heaven for all beings.)
37: At that time, a thought arose in the mind of Venerable Vaṅgīsa: “This Venerable Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña has come to visit the Blessed One after a very long time of twelve years. He has bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, kissed them with his mouth, and massaged them firmly with his hands. He has announced his name, saying, ‘O Blessed One of great glory, I am Koṇḍañña. O Blessed One who speaks words of excellence, I am Koṇḍañña.’ It would be well if I were to praise Venerable Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña in the presence of the Blessed One with suitable verses.” After this thought, Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, and raising his joined palms in reverence toward the Buddha, he said, “O Blessed One of great glory, inspired verses (paṭibhāna) occur to my mind. O Blessed One who speaks words of excellence, inspired verses occur to my mind.”
38:
Then the Blessed One said, “Dear Vaṅgīsa, let the inspired verses occur to your mind as you wish.” Having received permission, Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised Venerable Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña in the presence of the Blessed One with these suitable verses:

1. Buddhānubuddho so thero,
Koṇḍañño tibbanikkamo.
Lābhī sukhavihārānaṃ,
vivekānaṃ abhiṇhaso.

That great Elder, known by the name of Koṇḍañña of the royal lineage, who has arrived to pay homage to the Blessed One, is a 'Buddhānubuddha' (one who awakened after the Buddha) because he was the very first to deeply realize the four Noble Truths following the Buddha's own enlightenment. He possesses supreme and intense energy in Right Effort (sammappadhāna). He is one who constantly attains the three kinds of seclusion (viveka), which are the causes for living in coolness and bliss in this very life.

2. Yaṃ sāvakena pattabbaṃ,
satthusāsanakārinā.
Sabbassa taṃ anuppattaṃ,
appamattassa sikkhato.
39:
Whatever should be attained through wisdom by a noble disciple (ariya-saṅgha) who follows the instructions of the Great Teacher—such as the four Paths, the four Fruits, and the various analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—all of that has been attained by this glorious and eminent Venerable Koṇḍañña. By holding fast to the practice of diligence (appamāda) and by cultivating the three trainings (sikkhā), he has reached the goal before many other disciples and elders, excelling in his extraordinary spiritual perfections.

3. Mahānubhāvo tevijjo,
cetopariyakovido.
Koṇḍañño buddhadāyādo,
pāde vandati satthuno.

The great Elder named Koṇḍañña of the royal lineage, who possesses great psychic power, who is endowed with the three knowledges (tevijja), who is a master of the supernormal knowledge of knowing others' minds (cetopariya-abhiññā), and who was the first to receive the ninefold supramundane inheritance of the Blessed One, is now bowing down, kissing, and clasping with his hands the lotus-like feet of the Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and men.
40:
40
After praising the Buddha with these verses, the assembly remained very silent and peaceful. Knowing that the assembly was silent and peaceful, the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña, after exchanging pleasantries with the Buddha, addressed Him: "O Blessed One, my life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) is exhausted; I shall now attain Parinibbāna, O Lord," thus he requested permission.

Then the Blessed One asked, "Dear Koṇḍañña, in which place will you attain Parinibbāna?"

The Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña replied, "O Blessed One, the herd of elephants who have served and attended to me for twelve years have performed what is difficult to do. Therefore, I shall attain Parinibbāna at Lake Chaddanta, in the vicinity of those elephants, O Lord."

The Blessed One gave His permission by remaining silent.

(In this regard: When the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña informed the Buddha of his intent to attain Parinibbāna, if the Blessed One had said, "Dear son, do not attain Parinibbāna yet," it would have been as if He were telling him to continue delighting in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) within the three realms (tebhūmaka), which the Buddha Himself taught to be weary of. If He had said, "Dear son, attain Parinibbāna," it would have been as if He were encouraging death. Therefore, to avoid both extremes, the Blessed One asked a neutral question: "Dear son, in which place will you attain Parinibbāna?")

Thereafter, the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña paid his respects to the Blessed One and said, "O Blessed One, there was the first time I beheld You when You were practicing austerities (dukkharacariyā) in the past. Alternatively, there was the beholding in the Migadāvana forest. That was the first time I beheld You, O Lord. This present beholding is
41:
41
the last time I shall behold You, O Lord." After saying this, while the crowd of people was weeping, he paid homage to the Blessed One and departed from His presence. Standing at the gateway, he exhorted the people, saying, "Do not worry, do not weep. Whether it be the Buddhas or their disciples, there is no such thing as conditioned things (saṅkhāra) that do not perish as soon as they arise." Having thus admonished the crowd, while they were still watching, he flew into the sky and descended on the shore of Lake Mandākinī. After bathing in the lake, he properly dressed and robed himself, put away his lodgings and bedding from the monastery, and spent the three watches of the night in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). (This means he remained in phalasamāpatti throughout the night.) At the break of dawn, he entered the Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna) and was extinguished.

At the very moment the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña attained Parinibbāna, all the trees in the Himavanta forest blossomed and bore fruit from top to bottom and bowed down. The elephant whose turn it was to serve the Elder, not knowing that the Elder had attained Parinibbāna, prepared the water for washing and the tooth-sticks early as usual. After performing his major and minor duties, he brought fruits for the Elder to eat and stood at the end of the walkway (caṅkama). That attendant elephant, not seeing the Elder come out even after sunrise, thought, "In the past, the Elder would come out to the walkway very early. He would wash his face. But today, he has not come out of the leaf-hut even though the sun has risen. What could be the reason for this?" Reflecting thus, he slightly opened the door of the leaf-hut just enough to see inside. When he looked in, he saw the Elder sitting still.
42:
42
Seeing the Elder, the elephant extended his trunk and touched him to investigate whether there was any inhalation or exhalation. Realizing that both inhalation and exhalation were no longer present and that "The Elder has attained Parinibbāna," he put his trunk into his mouth and trumpeted loudly. The sound echoed throughout the entire Himavanta forest.

Eight thousand elephants gathered together in unison. They placed the remains (utujarūpakalāpa) of the Elder on the frontal globes (uṇhīsa) of the largest elephant. Each holding well-blossomed branches, they surrounded the elephant king carrying the body and circumambulated the entire Himavanta forest repeatedly in worship. Then they carried the remains back to their own place at Lake Chaddanta.

At that time, Sakka, the King of Devas, called the celestial architect Vissakamma and commanded, "Friend Vissakamma, our elder brother, the Venerable Koṇḍañña, has attained Parinibbāna. Let us perform an act of worship and honor. Friend, create a gabled pavilion (pāsāda) nine leagues in size, made of the seven kinds of jewels and topped with a pinnacle."

Vissakamma did as Sakka commanded, and after placing the remains of the Elder in that pavilion, he handed it over to the elephants.

The herd of elephants together lifted the pavilion and circumambulated the entire Himavanta forest, which is three thousand leagues wide, many times in worship. From the hands of the elephants, the terrestrial devas (ākāsasoṭṭha) took it and celebrated with a festival of honor (sādhukīḷana). Thereafter, the Vassa-valāhaka devas, the Sīta-valāhaka devas, the Uṇha-valāhaka devas,
43:
43
the Cātumahārājika devas, and the Tāvatiṃsa devas—in this manner, the pavilion carrying the remains reached as far as the Brahma realm. Again, the Brahmas handed it back to the devas. In this way, it was handed back down in succession until it reached the hands of the elephants.

Each deva and brahma brought two pieces of sandalwood, each about four finger-breadths in size. The great pyre of sandalwood (thin-ka-lar) was nine leagues high. Then they placed the pavilion containing the remains upon the sandalwood pyre. Five hundred monks arrived through the air and spent the entire night chanting the Dhamma. The Venerable Elder Anuruddha preached the Dhamma at that assembly, and many hosts of devas realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

During that night, the fire element (tejo-dhātu) consumed the body. At dawn the next morning, they extinguished the sandalwood pyre. The white relics (dhātu), which had the appearance of jasmine buds, were placed into a water-strainer until it was full. The monks then carried them and handed them over to the Blessed One, who was waiting at the gateway of the Veḷuvana monastery.

## The Earth-born Stupa
The Blessed One, holding the water-strainer containing the relics in His hand, delivered a discourse on the sense of urgency (saṃvega) appropriate for the occasion. Then He extended His hand toward the great earth. At that very moment, a great stupa, shaped like a large silver bubble, emerged from the great earth. The Blessed One, with His own hand,
44:
44
enshrined the relics of the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña in that stupa. It is said that this stupa remains prominent to this day.

This is the account of the Venerable Elder Koṇḍañña.
