## (2-3) The Account of the Two Chief Disciples
In this Dispensation, the Venerable Elder Sāriputta and the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna are known as the Two Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka). Since these two elders mostly fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) together and, in their final existence, also renounced the world and were ordained together, their accounts are explained together in the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries. Accordingly, in this text, the account of these two Chief Disciples shall be presented together.

## (a) The Past Aspiration of the Two Elders
Counting backward from this Bhadda-kappa, one asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons ago, the future Venerable Sāriputta was born into a wealthy Brahmin family and was named Sarada the youth. The future Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was born into a wealthy householder family and was named Sirivaḍḍhana the householder. Both of them were close childhood friends who played together in the dust.
45:
45
When Sarada the youth's father passed away, he managed the vast family wealth that had been handed down through generations. One day, he reflected: "I know only this present life. I do not know the state of the hereafter. For every living being that is born, death is as certain as a strike upon the ground. Therefore, it is proper that I should become an ascetic of some kind and seek the Dhamma that leads to liberation from the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra)."

Sarada the youth went to his friend, Sirivaḍḍhana the householder, and asked, "Friend Sirivaḍḍhana, I shall become an ascetic and seek the Dhamma for liberation from saṃsāra. Will you be able to become an ascetic with me?" Sirivaḍḍhana the householder replied, "Friend, I am not able to become an ascetic. You alone should become an ascetic." Then Sarada the youth reflected: "Those who go to the next world do not take friends, relatives, or companions with them. Only the good and evil deeds one has performed are truly one's own property."

Thereafter, Sarada the youth had the treasuries of wealth and jewels opened and gave great alms to the orphaned, the poor, travelers, and beggars. Then he went to the foot of a mountain and became an ascetic. Following his example, one, two, three, and so on, a total of seventy-four thousand (74,000) matted-hair ascetics were ordained. Sarada the ascetic himself developed the five mundane superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti).
46:
46
After attaining these, he taught the seventy-four thousand disciple ascetics the method of practicing the kasina preliminaries. All those disciple ascetics also developed the five mundane superknowledges and the eight attainments.

At that time, the Buddha Anomadassī appeared in the world. (The details of that Buddha's city, etc., have been described in the first volume, second part, pages 369-370 of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas.) One day, at dawn, the Buddha Anomadassī arose from the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and surveyed the world of beings. Seeing the ascetic Sarada, He reflected: "Today, if I go to the ascetic Sarada, there will be a great preaching of the Dhamma. That ascetic Sarada will aspire for the position of the Right-hand Chief Disciple. His friend, Sirivaḍḍhana the householder, will aspire for the position of the Left-hand Chief Disciple. At the conclusion of the discourse, his seventy-four thousand matted-hair disciple ascetics will attain Arahatship. Therefore, it is proper that I should go to the foot of the mountain where the ascetic Sarada resides." Having thus decided, He took His bowl and robes Himself and, without informing anyone else, traveled alone like a lion king. While Sarada's disciples were away searching for large and small fruits, the Buddha resolved, "Let the ascetic Sarada know of My state as the Omniscient Buddha." While Sarada was watching, the Buddha descended from the sky and stood upon the ground.

The ascetic Sarada, having beheld the Buddha's power and the glory of His physical form (rūpakāya),
47:
Upon examining the treatises on physiognomy, he thought, "Anyone endowed with these marks will either become a Universal Monarch if he remains in the household life, or an Omniscient Buddha if he renounces the world. This Great Man who has arrived now is undoubtedly the Omniscient Buddha." Having gained unwavering faith and knowledge, he went out to welcome Him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and prepared a seat. After the Buddha Anomadassī sat upon the prepared seat, the hermit Sarada also took a suitable seat for himself and sat at a respectful distance.

At that time, his seventy-four thousand resident pupils returned to their teacher, bringing large and small fruits that were exceptionally good and rich in essence. Upon seeing the Buddha and the place where their teacher was sitting, they said, "Teacher, we have wandered with the belief that there is no one superior to you in this world. Yet, this Great Man seems to be far more noble and superior than you."

Then the hermit Sarada said, "Disciples, what are you saying? You are trying to compare a tiny mustard seed with Mount Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand (168,000) yojanas in depth. My dear sons, do not make a comparison or an analogy between me and the Omniscient Buddha." When he spoke these words of restraint, the resident pupils said to one another, "If this person were of an inferior or lowly nature, our teacher would not have used such an analogy. This man must indeed be extremely noble."
48:
All the resident pupils then prostrated themselves at the feet of the Buddha and paid homage with their heads in great reverence.

Afterward, the teacher Sarada said to his disciples, "My sons, we do not have offerings suitable for Buddhas. The Buddha has come to our place at the foot of this mountain during his alms-round. Let us offer whatever we can according to our ability. Disciples, bring the best large and small fruits you can find." Having said this and had them brought, the teacher Sarada himself washed his hands and offered the fruit-alms into the Buddha's bowl. As soon as the Buddha accepted the fruits, the devas added divine essence (ojā) to them. Sarada himself also filtered drinking water and offered it. After the Buddha had finished the fruit-meal and washed his hands, and was sitting peacefully, Sarada gathered all his disciples and spoke words to the Buddha that were worthy of lifelong remembrance.

The Buddha Anomadassī then resolved and willed, "Let the two Chief Disciples, along with the assembly of monks, come to me here at the foot of this mountain." Knowing the Buddha's will, the two Chief Disciples (the Elder Nisabha and the Elder Anoma), surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahant elders, arrived in an instant. They paid homage to the Buddha and stood at a suitable place.

Then the hermit Sarada called his disciples and said, "My sons, the seat currently prepared for the Buddha is too low."
49:
"There are also no seats yet for the one hundred thousand monks. My sons, today you should perform a noble act of Buddha-pūjā (veneration). Bring flowers of beautiful color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain." Even as he was speaking, it seemed as if a long time had passed; the range of psychic power of those with such powers is indeed inconceivable and wondrous. Thus, in an instant, those resident pupils brought flowers of beautiful color and fragrance by psychic power and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddha measuring one yojana. The flower-seat prepared for the two Chief Disciples was three gāvutas, the flower-seats for the remaining monks were half a yojana (two gāvutas), and even the flower-seat for the most junior monk (saṅghanava) was as large as one usabha.

When the seats had been thus prepared, the hermit Sarada stood upright before the Buddha with palms joined in reverence and said, "Venerable Sir, for my long-term benefit and happiness, please ascend and sit upon this flower-seat." The Buddha Anomadassī ascended the flower-seat and remained there for seven days, entering the Attainment of Cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). After the Buddha was seated, the two Chief Disciples and the remaining monks also sat in their respective places. Knowing that the Buddha had entered the Attainment of Cessation, all the monks also entered the attainment.
50:
The hermit Sarada held a large flower parasol and stood shading the Buddha. While the Buddha remained in the Attainment of Cessation for seven days, the resident pupils, when it was time to seek food, searched for and consumed forest roots and fruits; for the rest of the time, they stood with palms joined in homage to the Buddhas. As for the hermit Sarada, he did not even go to search for fruit-food, but spent the seven days sustained by the food of rapture and bliss (pīti-sukha) while holding the flower parasol.

When the Buddha emerged from the Attainment of Cessation, he addressed the Elder Nisabha, the Right-hand Chief Disciple sitting on his right, saying, "Dear Nisabha, give a Dhamma talk of appreciation (anumodanā) regarding the flowers to the hermits who have performed this act of veneration." The Elder Nisabha, with a heart full of great joy like a great warrior who has received a grand reward from a Universal Monarch, stood firm in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) and delivered the flower-appreciation Dhamma talk. When the Elder Nisabha finished his talk, the Buddha addressed the Elder Anoma, the Left-hand Chief Disciple, saying, "My son, you also give a Dhamma talk." The Elder Anoma reflected on the words of the Buddha from the Tipitaka and delivered a Dhamma talk.

Despite the Dhamma talks by the two Chief Disciples, not a single hermit attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths. Thereafter, the Buddha Anomadassī, standing in his incomparable Buddha-domain, delivered a Dhamma talk. At the conclusion of the discourse, all seventy-four thousand matted-hair hermits, except for their teacher Sarada, attained Arahantship.
51:
The Buddha stretched out his right hand and gave the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' call, saying, "Etha Bhikkhave" (Come, monks). At that very moment, the hair and beards of all those hermits disappeared, and they were instantly robed and equipped with the eight requisites, becoming monks.

## Sarada Hermit's Aspiration for Chief Discipleship

One might ask why the hermit Sarada, despite being the teacher, did not reach Arahantship and was left behind. The answer is: because his mind was distracted. To elaborate—within the mind of the teacher Sarada, from the moment the Right-hand Chief Disciple Nisabha began his Dhamma talk, the thought repeatedly arose: "How good it would be if I, too, could obtain the position attained by this noble Chief Disciple in the dispensation of a Buddha who will appear in the future!" Because of this thought, the teacher Sarada was unable to penetrate the Path and Fruition (magga-phala).

After his disciples had become Ehi Bhikkhu monks, the hermit Sarada paid homage to the Buddha and, standing before Him, asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the title in Your dispensation of the monk who sits in the seat immediately next to You?" The Buddha replied, "That monk, who is able to follow me in turning the Jewel of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) that I have turned, who has reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, and who stands having penetrated the sixteen types of knowledge, is the Right-hand Chief Disciple in my dispensation, named the Elder Nisabha."
52:
Upon hearing this, the hermit Sarada made his aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the merit of the act of veneration I have performed by holding the flower parasol over You for seven days, I do not desire the status of Sakka or Brahma. Instead, may I truly become the Right-hand Chief Disciple of a future Buddha, just like this noble Elder Nisabha."

The Buddha Anomadassī directed his Knowledge of the Future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) to see if this man's aspiration would be fulfilled. Seeing that it would be fulfilled after the lapse of one asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons (kappa), He said to the hermit Sarada, "This aspiration of yours will not be in vain. Indeed, in the future, after one asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons, the Buddha Gotama will appear in the three worlds. The mother of that Buddha Gotama will be Queen Mahāmāyā, the father will be King Suddhodana, the son will be Prince Rāhula, and the second Chief Disciple on the left will be named the Elder Moggallāna. You shall be the Right-hand Chief Disciple of that Buddha Gotama, named the Elder Sāriputta." Having delivered this prophecy and a Dhamma talk, the Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks, flew up into the sky.

The hermit Sarada then approached the elders who had been his resident pupils and sent a message to his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana: "Venerable Sirs, please tell my friend Sirivaḍḍhana: 'Your friend, the hermit Sarada, has made an aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassī for the position of Right-hand Chief Disciple in the dispensation of the future
53:
Buddha Gotama. You, householder, should also make an aspiration for the position of the second Chief Disciple on the left.'" After giving this message, the hermit Sarada traveled quickly by a side path ahead of the monks and stood at the door of the householder Sirivaḍḍhana's house.

The householder Sirivaḍḍhana thought, "Oh, my master has come after a long time," and invited the hermit Sarada to sit on a seat. He himself sat on a lower seat and asked, "Venerable Sir, your assembly of resident pupils is not seen?" The hermit Sarada replied, "Yes, friend. The Buddha Anomadassī came to our hermitage. We performed acts of veneration for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha according to our ability. The Buddha preached the Dhamma to all of us. At the end of the discourse, except for me, the remaining seventy-four thousand (74,000) resident pupils reached Arahantship and became monks." Upon hearing this, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana asked again, "But why did you not become a monk, Venerable Sir?" The hermit Sarada said, "I saw the Buddha's Right-hand Chief Disciple, the Elder Nisabha, and I have made an aspiration for the position of Right-hand Chief Disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha Gotama. Friend, you should also make an aspiration for the position of the (second) Left-hand Chief Disciple in that same dispensation of the Buddha Gotama."
54: When the ascetic Sarada spoke these words of encouragement, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana replied, "Venerable Sir, I am not accustomed to conversing with Buddhas." Sarada the ascetic then encouraged him, saying, "Let the responsibility of conversing and making requests to the Buddhas be mine; you should only manage the performance of this great adhikāra (extraordinary merit)." After listening to the encouragement of Sarada the ascetic, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana had an area of about eight karīsas at the entrance of his house leveled and spread with white sand. He then scattered flowers with roasted rice as the fifth element, and had a large pavilion constructed, covered with blue lotuses. He prepared a seat for the Buddha and also arranged seating for the remaining monks. After properly preparing the great offerings, he gave a signal to Sarada the ascetic to invite the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Hearing the householder's word, Sarada the ascetic invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and arrived at the householder Sirivaḍḍhana's home. The householder Sirivaḍḍhana went out to welcome them, took the alms-bowl from the Buddha's hand, and respectfully escorted the Buddha into the pavilion. When the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha were seated on the prepared seats, he offered the water of donation, served them with excellent food, and when the meal was finished, he offered very valuable cloth for robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He then addressed the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, this renewal of my merit is..."
55: "...not for the sake of a minor position. Therefore, please show your compassion and favor by accepting this for seven days in this same manner." The Buddha accepted by remaining silent. The householder Sirivaḍḍhana performed this great almsgiving (mahādāna) for seven days in that manner. Then, after respectfully paying homage to the Buddha, he stood with palms joined and made a wish to the Buddha Anomadassī: "Venerable Sir, my friend Sarada the ascetic has made a wish to become the right-hand chief disciple of the Buddha Gotama. I, too, wish to become the left-hand chief disciple of that same Buddha Gotama." The Buddha looked into the future and, seeing that the householder Sirivaḍḍhana's wish would be fulfilled, prophesied: "After one asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand kappas from this world-cycle, you will become the second disciple, the left-hand chief disciple, of the Buddha Gotama." Upon hearing the Buddha's prophecy, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana was greatly delighted and joyful. The Buddha, after delivering a discourse of appreciation for the meal, returned to the monastery together with his retinue of monks. From that time on, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and when he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial world of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara deva loka). Sarada the ascetic developed the four brahmavihāras and was reborn in the Brahma realm.
56: ## (b) Becoming Monks in Their Final Life After the lives as Sarada the ascetic and Sirivaḍḍhana the householder, the Commentaries do not describe the details of the meritorious deeds performed by these two noble ones during the intervening period, but only describe the events of their final life (pacchima bhava). The description is as follows: Long before our Buddha appeared, the Great Being who was to become the Venerable Sāriputta, and who had been Sarada the ascetic, was conceived in the womb of the brahmin lady Rūpasārī in the village named Upatissa, near the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, the Great Being who was to become the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and who had been the householder Sirivaḍḍhana, was also conceived in the womb of the brahmin lady Moggallī in the village named Kolita, also near Rājagaha. Both of these great families had been friendly and intimate households for seven generations. For these two youths who were conceived as future chief disciples, pregnancy protection was provided on the same day. When they were born after ten months, sixty-six nurses each were provided to care for the two youths. On the naming day, the son of the brahmin lady Rūpasārī was named "Upatissa" because he was the son of the leading family in Upatissa village. The son of the brahmin lady Moggallī was named "Kolita" because he was the son of the leading family in Kolita village. Both of these youths...
57: ...as they grew up, reached the pinnacle of mastery in all arts. Regarding the retinue and ceremonies of the youth Upatissa, whenever he went on a trip for amusement to the river, the garden, or the mountain, he was always accompanied by five hundred golden palanquins and a retinue. For the youth Kolita, he was always accompanied by five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. Both friends had a retinue of five hundred youths each. Every year in the city of Rājagaha, the Mountain-top Festival (Giragga-samajja) was held. For these two friends, a couch was prepared and spread in the same place. Both friends sat together and watched the festival, laughing when it was time to laugh, being stirred when it was time to be stirred, and giving rewards when it was time to give rewards. In this way, they had watched the festival many times. One day, while watching the festival, because their wisdom had matured, they no longer laughed when it was time to laugh, nor were they stirred when it was time to be stirred, nor did they give rewards as they had on previous festival days. Both friends thought, "What is there worth seeing in this festival? All these people, both the performers and the spectators, will surely perish and disappear before reaching a hundred years. Therefore, it is proper that we seek a teaching for liberation from Saṃsāra." Reflecting on this thought of urgency (saṃvega) repeatedly, they remained seated.
58: Then the friend Kolita asked the friend Upatissa, "Friend Upatissa, today you do not seem pleased and satisfied as on other days. What are you considering, my friend?" The youth Upatissa replied, "Friend Kolita, there is not the slightest essence in watching these festivals. This enjoyment of festivals is fruitless and vain. Therefore, I am sitting here thinking that one should only seek the teaching for one's own liberation from Saṃsāra." Then he asked, "Friend Kolita, why are you also looking unhappy and dissatisfied?" The friend Kolita replied in the same way. Knowing then that Kolita's intention was exactly the same as his own, the youth Upatissa said to the youth Kolita, "Friend Kolita, both our thoughts are well-conceived. Especially for those seeking the teaching for liberation from Saṃsāra, it is proper to obtain the state of a monk. Under whom shall we become monks?" At that time, the great wanderer (paribbājaka) Sañjaya was living in Rājagaha as a great teacher with a large following of wanderers. The two friends, the youth Upatissa and the youth Kolita, agreed, "Let us become monks under that teacher Sañjaya," and they ordained under the teacher Sañjaya together with their five hundred followers. From the time the youth Upatissa and the youth Kolita ordained, the teacher Sañjaya...
59: ...became one who reached the pinnacle of gains, offerings, retinue, and fame, surpassing others. Within two or three days, the two wanderers, Upatissa and Kolita, learned and mastered all the doctrines of the teacher Sañjaya. They asked, "Teacher, is the doctrine you know only this much, or is there more to be learned further?" When the teacher Sañjaya said, "The doctrine I know is only this much; you two have already known our entire doctrine," the two friends thought: "If this is so, practicing the holy life (brahmacariya) under this teacher Sañjaya is in vain. We left the household life to seek the teaching for liberation from Saṃsāra. It is impossible by any means to realize that teaching for liberation from Saṃsāra, which we seek, under this teacher Sañjaya. The island of Jambudīpa is very vast. If we wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals in search, we will surely find a teacher who will preach the teaching for liberation from Saṃsāra." Thus they planned and consulted. From then on, the wanderers Upatissa and Kolita went to various places where they heard there were wise monks and brahmins, and they engaged in questioning and discussing the Dhamma related to liberation from Saṃsāra. There were no other monks or brahmins claiming to be wise who were able to answer the questions asked by these two. In fact, it was only the two friends, the wanderers Upatissa and Kolita, who answered the questions of those monks and brahmins claiming to be wise.
60:
60
They had to solve the problem. After traveling and searching throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, they found no one worthy of being their teacher. Thus, the wandering ascetics Upatissa and Kolita returned to their own ascetic monastery and made a mutual pact: "Friend, whichever of us first attains and realizes the Deathless (Amata) shall inform the other."

It was about the 1st day of the waxing moon of Tabodwe, approximately half a month after the Blessed One had arrived in the city of Rājagaha. (O virtuous readers of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, please refer back to pages 2 to 25 at the beginning of the third volume of the Maha Buddhavamsa. By reviewing those pages, you will clearly understand (b) how the two Chief Disciples, along with their retinue of wandering ascetics, became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks in the presence of the Blessed One, and (c) how they reached the pinnacle of the Knowledge of a Disciple (Sāvaka-ñāṇa). Here, I shall omit those details with an ellipsis.)

## (d) Attaining the Titles of Etadagga

In the year the Blessed One attained Buddhahood, He spent the rainy season (vassa) in the Migadāvana forest. From there, He proceeded to the Uruvelā forest, where He converted the one thousand hermits led by the three Kassapa brothers, establishing them in the Fruit of Arahantship through the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. On the full moon day of Pyatho, He arrived at the city of Rājagaha accompanied by those one thousand monks. About half a month after arriving in Rājagaha, on the 1st day of the waxing moon of Tabodwe, the wandering ascetic Upatissa met the Arahant Elder Assaji, one of the group of five (Pañcavaggiya), in Rājagaha. Upon hearing the verse beginning with "Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā," he became a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer). Having heard that same verse from the wandering ascetic Upatissa...
61:
61
...the wandering ascetic Kolita also became a Sotāpanna. Subsequently, the two friends, now Sotāpanna ascetics, along with their retinue of wandering ascetics, became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks in the presence of the Blessed One. As for the disciples, they listened to the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One before becoming Ehi Bhikkhu monks and attained Arahantship at that very moment. However, the two Elders who were to be the Chief Disciples did not become Arahants at that time because the Knowledge of the Perfection of a Chief Disciple (Aggasāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) is exceedingly great and noble. The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna attained Arahantship seven days after his ordination, and the Venerable Sāriputta attained Arahantship fifteen days after his ordination, on the full moon day of Tabodwe. (The detailed account should be sought from the beginning of the third volume of this Maha Buddhavamsa up to page 25.)

In this manner, while the Blessed One was residing in Rājagaha, both great Chief Disciples reached the pinnacle of the Knowledge of the Perfection of a Chief Disciple. However, at a later time, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in the city of Sāvatthī, He declared:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mahāpaññānaṃ yadidaṃ sāriputto = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess great wisdom, Sāriputta is the foremost.

Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ iddhimantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahāmoggallāno = Monks, among my disciple monks who are endowed with psychic powers, Mahā Moggallāna is the foremost."
62:
Praising them in this way, the Buddha declared Venerable Sāriputta foremost among those of great wisdom and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna foremost among those of great psychic power.

From the time they became monks, these two great elders practiced for the welfare of the world of beings for a period of forty-four rainy seasons (vassa). The teachings preached by these great elders are numerous within the five Nikāyas of the Piṭaka. They are so abundant that it is impossible to extract and describe them all. In particular, the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, the Mahāniddesa Pāḷi, and the Cūḷaniddesa Pāḷi are the Dhamma teachings preached by the great elder Venerable Sāriputta. The Sāriputtatheragāthā is like a great storehouse of Dhamma for the great elder Venerable Sāriputta, and the Mahāmoggallānatheragāthā is like a great storehouse of Dhamma for the great elder Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Let those who desire to do so extract and study them from the respective Pāḷi and Burmese translations. In this book, however, I shall only describe the circumstances of their entry into Parinibbāna after they had practiced for the welfare of the world of beings for forty-four rainy seasons.

## (a) Venerable Sāriputta
## The Circumstances of His Parinibbāna

The Blessed One spent his final and forty-fifth rainy season at the small village of Veḷuva near the city of Vesālī. Upon departing from there, he set out from the small village of Veḷuva following the same route he had come (as described in the section on the Parinibbāna of the Buddha), and while traveling on his final journey...
63:
63
He arrived at the city of Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana Monastery. The Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), paid his respects to the Blessed One and went to his place of day-rest. After the disciple monks had performed their duties and departed, the great Elder swept the place of day-rest, spread out his leather mat (cammakhaṇḍa), washed his feet, sat down cross-legged, and entered the Attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti).

Then, at the designated time, having emerged from the Attainment of the Fruit (Phala-samāpatti), a reflection arose in the Elder's mind: "Do the Buddhas enter Parinibbāna first, or do the two Chief Disciples enter Parinibbāna first?" Then, he realized, "It is the custom for the two Chief Disciples to enter Parinibbāna first." He then examined his own life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) and knew, "My life-force will last for only seven more days." He further reflected, "In what place shall I enter Parinibbāna?"

Then he considered, "The Elder Rāhula has entered Parinibbāna in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña has entered Parinibbāna at the Chaddanta Lake. Where should I enter Parinibbāna?" As he reflected repeatedly, he remembered his mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī (the wife of a wealthy man). The way he remembered her was:

"Oh, my mother is indeed the mother of seven Arahants, yet she is one who does not have faith in the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha."
64:
64
"Does my mother possess the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit, or not?"

Reflecting thus, he saw that she possessed the supporting condition of past merit to attain the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). He then further reflected, "By whose Dhamma teaching will the realization of the Four Noble Truths occur?"

He realized, "The realization of the Four Noble Truths and the liberation of my mother will occur only through my own Dhamma teaching; it will not occur through the Dhamma teaching of another person. If I were to remain indifferent and not make an effort to convert my mother, people would say: 'The Venerable Sāriputta is indeed a refuge for others. Truly, on the day the great Elder preached the Samacitta Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1, page 64), one hundred thousand crores of devas and brahmās reached the Fruit of Arahantship. The devas and brahmās who reached the lower three Paths were countless. In other instances, many were seen to realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. Not only that, the number of families who, out of faith and devotion to the great Elder, were reborn in the deva realms is eighty thousand (80,000). Yet now, that Venerable Sāriputta is unable even to remove the wrong view of his own mother.' Such words of blame and criticism would surely arise. Therefore, after I have converted my mother from her wrong view...
65:
65
...I shall enter Parinibbāna in the very chamber where I was born."

Having made this resolution, he thought, "I shall inform the Blessed One and obtain permission today, and then depart from the Jetavana Monastery." He then called his younger brother, the Venerable Cunda, and instructed him: "Friend Cunda, give a signal to our retinue of five hundred disciple monks, saying, 'Friends, prepare and take your bowls and robes; the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, wishes to go to his birthplace, the village of Nālaka.'" The Venerable Cunda went around and informed the five hundred disciple monks exactly as the great Elder had instructed.

The five hundred disciple monks put away their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and assembled before the great Elder in unison. The great Elder put away his own lodging, swept his place of day-rest, and standing at the doorway of that place, he looked at it and thought, "This looking is now the final look. There will be no more returning again." Then, surrounded by the five hundred disciple monks, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and requested permission: "Exalted Buddha, may the Fortunate One grant me permission. May the Well-Spoken One grant me permission. The time has come for my Parinibbāna; I have relinquished my life-force."
66:
66
(In this context: In the Pali passage beginning with "Anujānātu me bhante bhagavā," the translation of "Anujānātu" as "Please grant me permission" is a conventional linguistic translation. If translated according to the underlying grammatical sense, it should be rendered as: "Anujānātu = Please consider and realize that I am about to enter Parinibbāna." The intended meaning is: "I have already realized that I must enter Parinibbāna; may the Exalted Buddha also be aware of this.")

It is the custom of Buddhas that when Arahant disciples come to inform them and seek permission for Parinibbāna, if they were to say, "Enter Parinibbāna," those with wrong views would criticize them, saying, "They praise the virtue of death." If they were to say, "Dear son, do not enter Parinibbāna yet," they would be criticized, saying, "The Buddha praises the virtue of the round of suffering (vaṭṭa-dukkha)." Therefore, it is not the custom of Buddhas to speak either of those two ways. Thus, the Blessed One asked the Venerable Sāriputta, "Dear Sāriputta, in what place will you enter Parinibbāna?" When Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Exalted Buddha, there is my birth chamber in Nālaka village, within the region of Magadha. I shall enter Parinibbāna in that chamber, Lord," the Blessed One said, "Dear Sāriputta, you yourself now know the time for your Parinibbāna. However, for the monks who are your elder and younger brothers, it will certainly be difficult to see a monk like you again. Therefore, dear Sāriputta, give a final discourse to your elder and younger brothers."

The Great Elder, knowing the Buddha's intention, thought, "The Blessed One desires and wishes for a discourse preceded by my display of extraordinary psychic powers."
67:
67
Having understood the Buddha's wish, he paid respectful homage to the Blessed One. Then, he ascended into the sky to the height of one palm tree, descended from the sky, and paid homage at the Blessed One's feet. Again, he ascended into the sky to the height of two palm trees, descended, and paid homage at the Blessed One's feet once more. In this manner, he sequentially ascended to the heights of three, four, five, six, and seven palm trees, performing hundreds of psychic miracles and delivering the Dhamma. A summary of his manner of teaching is as follows:

He taught the Dhamma while making his body visible. He taught while making his body invisible. He taught while making the upper part of his body visible and the lower part invisible, and vice versa. Sometimes he manifested the form of the moon's mansion. Sometimes he manifested the form of the sun's mansion. Sometimes he manifested the form of a great mountain, and sometimes the form of a great ocean. Sometimes he became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), sometimes the Great King Vessavaṇa, sometimes the King of Devas Sakka, and sometimes the Great Brahmā. Thus, displaying hundreds of psychic miracles, he taught the Dhamma. The entire city of Sāvatthī gathered together. After the Great Elder had preached the Dhamma to their heart's content, preceded by the display of psychic miracles, he descended from the sky, paid respectful homage at the Blessed One's feet, and stood firm and upright like a golden pillar.
68:
68
Then the Blessed One asked, "Dear Sāriputta, what is the name of this Dhamma discourse?" When Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Exalted Buddha, it is the Sīhavikkīḷita (Lion's Play) discourse," the Blessed One approvingly said, "Dear Sāriputta, it is indeed the Sīhavikkīḷita discourse. Dear Sāriputta, it is truly the Sīhavikkīḷita discourse."

## Final Homage to the Buddha
The Venerable Sāriputta spread his hands, which were as red as lac-dye, and firmly grasped the Blessed One's feet—which resembled golden tortoises—at the ankles, and said:

"Exalted Buddha, I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas) in order to be able to behold these two feet of Yours. That heart's desire of mine has now reached its pinnacle and success. From this time forward, there will be no more meeting or joining with You, Lord, in any other existence by way of rebirth. All intimacy and familiarity associated with this life have been completely severed. Now, I shall enter the city of Nibbāna—the place where hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have entered, which is free from aging, free from death, free from enemies, peaceful, cool, and safe. Lord, if there have been any physical or verbal actions of mine that were displeasing to You,"
69:
69
"...if such faults were evident, please forgive them, Lord. It is now time for me to go."

Thus he spoke, requesting forgiveness and permission to depart. The Blessed One replied, "Dear Sāriputta, I forgive you. There is not even a single physical or verbal action of yours that was displeasing to my mind. Dear Sāriputta, you yourself now know the time for your departure; your going shall be according to your own will."

Immediately after the Blessed One had given permission, the Venerable Sāriputta massaged the Blessed One's feet with all his strength and paid homage. As he rose from that spot, as if to say, "Though I can bear Mount Meru, the Cakkavaḷā mountains, the Himavantā, and the seven surrounding mountain ranges (Sattarabbhan), I can no longer bear this mass of gratitude today," the great earth shook violently to the edge of the waters, echoing and roaring. The entire sky resounded with heavy thunder. Great clouds arose in an instant, causing the Pokkharavassa rain to fall abundantly.

The Blessed One thought, "Sāriputta has already paid homage to my sitting physical body (rūpakāya). Now, I shall let Sāriputta pay homage once more to my standing physical body." Having so reflected, He rose from the Buddha-seat (buddhāsana) where He had been teaching and walked toward the Gandhakuti, standing upon a slab adorned with precious gems.
70:
70
Standing there, the Venerable Sāriputta circumambulated the Blessed One three times and paid homage from the four directions—front, back, left, and right—and said:

"Exalted Buddha, one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons ago, prostrating at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassī, I made an aspiration to behold You. That aspiration of mine is now fulfilled. I have beheld You to my heart's content. While making that prayer, hearing the words of prophecy from the Buddha Anomadassī and beholding You with wisdom was my first beholding. This present beholding is my last. There will be no further opportunity to behold You again, Lord."

Having made this final statement, he raised his joined palms, which were beautiful and bright with ten fingernails like lotus petals. He walked backward as long as the Blessed One remained in sight, paying homage, and then departed together with five hundred disciple monks. Once again, the great earth, unable to bear the essence of his virtues, shook to the edge of the waters.

The Blessed One said to the monks standing around Him, "Dear sons, go and see your elder brother off." At that moment, the entire fourfold assembly left the Blessed One alone at the Jetavana monastery and followed him without exception. The citizens of Sāvatthī also came out, saying, "Venerable Sāriputta has asked permission from the Blessed One to enter Parinibbāna and has departed from the Jetavana monastery. Let us behold the Great Elder for the last time."
71:
71
The people came out in such crowds that there was no room to move through the city gates. Carrying perfumes, flowers, and the like, with their hair disheveled, they lamented and cried, "Lord, now that the Great Elder is departing, whom shall we ask, 'Where does the Great Wise Sāriputta Thera dwell? Where does the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) Sāriputta Thera dwell now?' To whom should we go? In whose hands has the Great Elder entrusted the Blessed One before departing?" Thus wailing, they followed closely behind the Elder.

Venerable Sāriputta, being one established in great wisdom, exhorted the crowd briefly: "This path ending in death for all beings is a path that no being can escape." He then told them, "Friends, you must stay behind. Do not be heedless regarding the Blessed One." He also sent the assembly of monks back and proceeded toward Nālaka village with his own followers. To the people who followed him wailing, "In the past, the Venerable One went on a journey from which he would return; this journey is not for the sake of returning again," he gave the exhortation on heedfulness (appamāda), saying, "O lay disciples, remain as those who hold fast to the practice of heedfulness. Conditioned things (saṅkhāras), both mental and physical, are of such a nature: having arisen, they end in death and dissolution." Having thus advised them, he sent them back.
72:
Then the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, without lingering at any place along the way, spent one night at each stop, bestowing blessings upon the people for seven days during the journey. Eventually, he arrived at Nālaka village in the evening and rested at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate.

At that time, a youth named Uparevata, who was the Elder's own nephew, came out of the village. Seeing the Elder, he approached, paid homage, and stood nearby. The Elder asked his nephew, the youth Uparevata, “Uparevata, is your grandmother at home?” The youth Uparevata replied, “She is, Bhante.” The Elder then instructed him, “Go then, and tell her that we have arrived at this village. If your grandmother asks, ‘Why has he come?’, tell her, ‘He will stay in the village for this one day. Please clean and prepare the chamber where my uncle was born. Also, prepare places for five hundred monks.’”

The youth Uparevata went to his grandmother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī (the wealthy merchant's wife), and said, “O Grandmother, my uncle (Upatissa) has arrived.” The grandmother asked, “Where is he now?” When Uparevata replied, “At the village gate,” she asked again, “Is he alone, or is there anyone else with him?” Uparevata answered, “There are others; five hundred monks are with him.” The grandmother asked once more, “For what reason has he come?” Uparevata then
73:
conveyed the message given by the Elder to his grandmother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī. The lady thought to herself, “Oh, why does my eldest son have the places cleaned and prepared for so many as five hundred monks? I suppose having ordained in his youth, he now wishes to become a layman in his old age.” Thinking thus, she had the birth chamber cleaned and prepared, arranged seating for the five hundred monks, lit the lamps, and sent someone to invite the Elder.

The Elder, together with the five hundred monks, ascended the mansion, entered his birth chamber, and sat down. He then dismissed the monks, saying, “Go to your respective places.” As soon as the monks had left, a severe and violent illness arose in the Elder's body. Painful dysentery, which would end only in death, occurred incessantly. Vessels were brought in and carried out in constant rotation. The mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī, thinking, “The condition of my son is not pleasing,” stood leaning against the door of her own room.

At that time, the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā) looked out, wondering, “Where is the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, staying now?” Seeing that “The Elder is lying on his deathbed in the birth chamber of Nālaka village to attain Parinibbāna; let us go to pay our final respects and attend to him,” they consulted each other and then came to the Elder, paid homage, and stood there. When the Elder asked, “Who are you?”, they replied, “We are the Great Kings, Bhante.”
74:
When they replied thus, the Elder asked again, “Why have you come?” They answered, “We have come to serve as your attendants, Bhante.” The Elder then said, “Let it be; there is an attendant monk. You may return,” and dismissed them. After the Four Great Kings had departed, Sakka, the King of Devas, arrived in the same manner. When Sakka departed, Mahābrahmā arrived. To both Sakka and Mahābrahmā, the Elder spoke words of dismissal in the same way and sent them back.

The mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī, seeing the deities and Brahmās coming and going, wished to know, “Who are those who paid homage to my son and departed?” She went near the door of the Elder's chamber and asked, “Dear Cunda, what has happened?” The younger brother, Venerable Cunda, explained to his mother about the Elder's illness and then informed Venerable Sāriputta, “The great lay devotee (his mother) has arrived, Bhante.” The Elder asked, “Lay devotee, why have you come at an improper time?” The mother replied, “Dear son, I have come to see you,” and continued, “Dear son, who were those who first came to you?” The Elder said, “Lay devotee, those who first arrived were the Four Great Kings.” The mother then asked, “Dear son, are you more noble and superior even to the Four Great Kings?”
75:
The Elder replied, “Lay devotee, those Four Great Kings are like the temple guards of my sons. From the moment our teacher, the Buddha, took conception, they have protected him, holding swords in their hands.” When he said this, the mother asked further, “Dear son, who was it that came after the Four Great Kings had left?” The Elder replied, “It was Sakka, the King of Devas.” The mother asked again, “Dear son, are you more noble and superior even to Sakka, the King of Devas?”

The Elder replied, “Lay devotee, that Sakka is like a young novice who carries the bowl and requisites of my sons. When our teacher, the Buddha, descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the human world after preaching the Abhidhamma, Sakka followed, carrying the bowl and robes.” When he said this, the mother asked again, “Dear son, who was it that came with such a radiant aura after Sakka had left?” The Elder replied, “Lay devotee, that last visitor was Mahābrahmā, whom you regard as your god and teacher.” The mother then asked, “Dear son, are you more noble and superior even to my god, Mahābrahmā?”

Then the Venerable Elder said to his mother, “Yes, it is so, lay devotee. These Mahābrahmās, on the day our teacher, the Buddha, was born, not just one but
76:
four Mahābrahmās came and received the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, with a golden net.” Thus he explained.

## The Mother Attains the Special Dhamma

At that moment, the mother thought, “The power I see now is only the power of my son. What then must be the power of my son's teacher, the Buddha? It must be beyond imagination!” As she reflected thus, the five kinds of joy (pīti) arose repeatedly and spread throughout her entire body. The Elder thought, “Now joy and gladness have arisen in my mother's mind; this is the most suitable time to preach the Dhamma to her.” He then asked, “Lay devotee, what are you thinking about?” The mother replied, “Dear son, I am reflecting that the power I see now is only the power of my son. What then must be the power of my son's teacher, the Buddha? It must be beyond imagination!”

The Elder then said to her, “Lay devotee, when my teacher, the Buddha, was born, when he renounced the world, when he attained Enlightenment, and when he preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka, the ten thousand world systems shook and trembled. In terms of the virtues of morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana), there is no one in the world equal to our teacher, the Buddha. That teacher of ours, for these and these reasons,”
77:
“is the Worthy One (Araham), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).” In this manner, he preached the Dhamma discourse concerning the virtues of the Buddha in detail.

At the end of the discourse by her beloved eldest son, the mother was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). She then spoke words of reproach to her son, the Elder, “Dear Upatissa, why did you not give me this noble, deathless bliss for such a long time? Why did you act in this way?” The Elder thought, “I have now repaid the great debt of my birth to my mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī. This much, the Fruit of Stream-entry, is sufficient for her.” He then said, “You may go, lay devotee,” and dismissed her. After that, he asked his younger brother, Venerable Cunda, “Cunda, what time is it now?” Venerable Cunda replied, “It is near the break of dawn, Bhante.” The Elder then said, “Assemble the monks.” When Cunda replied, “The monks are already assembled, Bhante,” the Elder said, “Cunda, help me up and let me sit.” He sat up with assistance.

The Elder then addressed the assembly of monks, “Friends, for forty-four rains (vassa), you have traveled and lived together with me. If there has been any bodily or verbal action of mine that was displeasing to you, please forgive those actions.” Thus he spoke words of apology. The monks replied, “Bhante, during these forty-four rains,”
78:
The disciples, who had been living and traveling with the Venerable, never leaving him like his own shadow, said: "Venerable Sir, for us who have lived under your guidance, there is not even a single unpleasing deed of body or word toward you. Indeed, it is only you, Venerable Sir, who should forgive us." After they had spoken these words of apology and reverence, the Great Elder gathered his outer robe, covered his face, and lay down on his right side. He then entered the nine successive meditative attainments (samāpatti) in both forward and reverse order, just as the Buddha did. Then, entering from the first jhāna up to the fourth jhāna, and immediately after emerging from that fourth jhāna, he passed away into the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), causing the great earth to echo.

His mother, the wealthy lady Rūpasārī, thinking, "What has happened to my son? He says nothing at all," rose from her seat and felt the tops of the Elder's feet. Realizing that he had attained Parinibbāna, she cried out in a loud voice, prostrated at the Elder's feet, and lamented: "O my son, until this time, your mother did not know your virtues. Now, I no longer have the opportunity to invite and offer food to hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of monks in this house, with you at the head. I no longer have the opportunity to offer sets of robes. I no longer have the opportunity to build hundreds and thousands of monasteries." In this manner, she wept until dawn. As soon as the sun rose, the mother called for the goldsmiths.
79:
She summoned them, ordered the treasuries to be opened, and had the gold bars and nuggets weighed on large scales. She said, "Friends, use these gold bars and nuggets to construct five hundred golden mansions and five hundred golden pavilions," and handed them over.

Sakka, the King of Gods, also called the celestial architect Vissakamma and commanded, "Friend Vissakamma, the Marshal of the Dhamma, Sāriputta Thera, has attained Parinibbāna. Create five hundred golden mansions and five hundred golden pavilions with arched entrances." Vissakamma, according to Sakka's command, created them in an instant. Thus, there were one thousand golden mansions and pavilions made by the mother, and one thousand created by Vissakamma, totaling two thousand golden structures.

Afterward, a large and sturdy pavilion was built in the center of Nālaka village. The largest golden mansion was placed in the center of that pavilion, surrounded by the other mansions as attendants, and the funeral festival (sādhukīḷana) was celebrated. During that festival, devas moved among humans and humans among devas, crowded together in solemn worship.

## The Story of the Woman Revatī
A female lay follower named Revatī, a disciple of the Great Elder, thought, "I shall make an offering to the Great Elder." She had three golden flower pots made and came to the place where the cremation ceremony was being held. At that time,
80:
with the intention of making an offering to the Great Elder, Sakka, the King of Gods, descended to the human world accompanied by twenty-five million celestial nymphs. Seeing that Sakka had descended, the crowd of people moved back to make way. In that assembly, the lay follower Revatī also moved back like the others, but because she was pregnant, she was unable to move away to a safe place in time and stumbled among the people. The people, not seeing Revatī, trampled over her. The lay follower Revatī died right there and was reborn in a golden mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At the moment of her rebirth, the celestial body of the goddess Revatī was about three gāvutas in size, like a mass of precious jewels. Her celestial ornaments were equivalent to the load of sixty carts, and she was surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs.

Then, the attendant nymphs placed a celestial full-length mirror before the goddess Revatī. When she saw her great splendor and wealth, she reflected, "This wealth is vast and magnificent. What kind of meritorious deed did I perform?" She then realized, "I made an offering of three golden flower pots at the place where the Elder Sāriputta attained Parinibbāna. The crowd of people trampled me, and I died there, being reborn here in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. I shall now go and speak clearly to the humans about the benefits of the merit obtained by relying on the Great Elder."
81:
Thinking thus, she descended to the human world along with her great golden mansion.

The multitude of people saw the golden mansion from afar and looked on in wonder, asking, "What is this? Have two suns risen?" As the great mansion gradually drew closer, it appeared in the shape of a golden palace. Then the people said, "This object is not the sun; it is a golden mansion." Even as the people were speaking, that golden mansion reached the vicinity in an instant and came to a halt in the sky above the pile of scented wood prepared for the cremation of the elder’s physical remains. The goddess Revatī left the great golden mansion in the sky and descended to the ground. When the people asked, "Lady, who are you?", the goddess Revatī replied, "Do you not know me? I am the woman named Revatī. Having made an offering to the great elder with three golden flower pots, I was trampled by the crowd and, upon passing away, I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Look at my splendor and prosperity! You too should give alms now. Furthermore, perform other meritorious deeds." After speaking these words on the virtues of performing meritorious deeds, she circumambulated the elder’s pyre of scented wood to the right, paid her respects, and returned to her own abode in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. (This is the story of the woman Revatī).

## Bringing the Relics to Sāvatthī by Venerable Cunda

The multitude of people also celebrated the funeral festival (sādhukīḷana) for seven days, and then they set fire to the pile of various scented woods...
82:
The funeral pyre was ninety-nine cubits high. They placed the Elder's physical remains upon the pyre and ignited it with flowers, scents, and bundles of grass. Throughout the night of the cremation ceremony, a great Dhamma discourse was held. At dawn, the Venerable Anuruddha extinguished the funeral pyre with various kinds of scented water. The Venerable Cunda, the biological younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta, placed the relics in a water-strainer and reflected, "I cannot remain here in this Nālaka village now. I shall go and inform the Blessed One of the passing of my elder brother, the Marshal of the Dhamma, Sāriputta Thera." Taking the water-strainer containing the relics and the Elder's requisites such as his bowl and robes, he departed for the city of Sāvatthī. He traveled without staying two nights at any single stop, resting only for one night at each place, until he reached Sāvatthī.

Then, the Venerable Cunda bathed in the pond near the Jetavana monastery, came ashore, dressed properly, and thought: "The Buddhas are supreme individuals who are revered like a great stone parasol. They are difficult to approach, like a cobra with its hood raised, or like lions, tigers, and elephants in rut. I do not dare go directly to the Buddha to report this. To whom should I go?" He then considered, "My preceptor, the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, was a very close and noble
83:
friend of my elder brother. I shall go to the Venerable Ānanda, explain the situation, and then, after inviting him, I will report it to the Blessed One." Having reflected thus, he went to the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He then informed the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained Parinibbāna. These are the bowl and robes of the Venerable Sāriputta; this is the water-strainer containing the relics." (It should be noted here that because Venerable Cunda had great respect for both the Buddha and his preceptor Ānanda, he did not go directly to the Buddha but went first to the Venerable Ānanda.)

Then the Venerable Ānanda said, "Friend Cunda, this is a matter to be presented to the Blessed One. Come, Friend Cunda, let us go. Let us approach the Blessed One and report this matter to Him." Taking Venerable Cunda with him, they went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Venerable Ānanda then said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, this Venerable Cunda, who is known as a novice (samaṇuddesa), says: 'Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained Parinibbāna. These are the bowl and robes of the Venerable Sāriputta; this is the water-strainer containing the relics.'"

So saying, he presented the water-strainer containing the relics of the Venerable Sāriputta into the hands of the Blessed One.
84:
The Blessed One stretched out His hand, received the water-strainer with the relics, and placing it upon His palm, addressed the monks:

"Monks, fifteen days ago, after performing many miracles, the Venerable Sāriputta asked my permission to enter Parinibbāna. Now, only these bodily relics of Sāriputta, as white as a polished conch, remain.

Monks, this monk Sāriputta is one who fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons. This monk Sāriputta is the one who followed me in turning the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakka) that I set in motion. This monk Sāriputta is the one who properly attained the second position after me.

This monk Sāriputta is the one who beautifully filled the assembly of disciples (sāvaka-sannipāta). (This was said in reference to the assembly that occurred on the day Sāriputta became an Arahant). Excluding me, there is no one equal to him in the quality of wisdom throughout the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth.

This monk Sāriputta is one of great wisdom, wide wisdom, bright wisdom, quick wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrating wisdom. This monk Sāriputta is one of few wishes, easily satisfied, secluded from the hindrances,"
85:
85
He is one who avoids socializing with people, possesses ardent effort, is capable of admonishing by pointing out faults, and is one who censures evil and those who do evil without partiality.

"Dear monks, that monk Sāriputta (a) was one who renounced great wealth and entered the monkhood for a period of five hundred lives. (b) That monk Sāriputta was a person of great patience, like the great earth, within my Dispensation. (c) That monk Sāriputta was very humble, like a bull with broken horns. That monk Sāriputta was also one with a humble mind, like the son of an outcaste."

"Dear monks, behold the relics of Sāriputta, who possessed great wisdom. Monks, behold the relics of Sāriputta, who possessed wide wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and wisdom capable of penetrating the defilements; who had few wishes, was easily satisfied, was secluded from the hindrances, avoided socializing with people, possessed ardent effort, was capable of admonishing by pointing out faults, and censured evil and those who do evil without partiality."

(After speaking thus in prose)—

Yo pabbajī jātisatāni pañca,
Pahāya kāmāni manoramāni.
Taṃ vītarāgaṃ susamāhitindriyaṃ,
Parinibbūtaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ. (1)

Bhikkhave = O dear monks. Yo sāriputto = That noble monk known as Sāriputta...
86:
86
...the noble monk. Manoramāni = Sensual pleasures that can make the heart joyful and delighted. Pahāya = Having renounced them completely without lingering. Pañcajātisatāni = For a period of five hundred lives. Pabbajī = He entered the monkhood with faith. Vītarāgaṃ = Who is now entirely free from lust and craving. Susamāhitindriyaṃ = Who also possesses well-stabilized faculties of concentration. Parinibbūtaṃ = Who has attained Parinibbāna, ceased, and ended the cycle of suffering. Taṃ sāriputtaṃ = That noble monk known as Sāriputta. Vandatha = Bow down and pay homage with faith and humility, subduing all pride.

Khantibalo pathavisamo na kuppati,
Na cāpi cittassa vasena vattati.
Anukampako kāruṇiko ca nibbuto,
Parinibbūtaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ. (2)

Bhikkhave = Dear monks. Yo sāriputto = That noble monk known as Sāriputta. Khantibalo = Being one who has the strength of extreme patience (adhivāsana-khanti). Pathavisamo = Being like the great earth. Na kuppati = Does not get angry at an opponent. Cittassa = Of the unstable mind. Vasena = By its will and nature. Na cāpi vattati = Never follows at any time. Anukampako = He protects and supports beings with loving-kindness. Kāruṇiko ca = He is also compassionate and merciful. Nibbuto = He is one who is cooled, not smeared by the heat of defilements. Parinibbūtaṃ = Who has attained Parinibbāna, ceased, and ended the cycle of suffering.
87:
87
Taṃ sāriputtaṃ = That noble monk known as Sāriputta. Vandatha = Bow down and pay homage with faith and humility, subduing all pride.

Caṇḍālaputto yathā nagaraṃ paviṭṭho,
Nīcamano carati kaḷopihattho.
Tathā ayaṃ vicarati sāriputto,
Parinibbūtaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ. (3)

Bhikkhave = O dear monks. Nagaraṃ paviṭṭho = Entering into a town to seek food. Caṇḍālaputto = The son of a very poor outcaste. Kaḷopihattho = Holding a worn-out basket made of bamboo in his hand. Nīcamano = With a humble mind, without pride. Vicarati yathā = Just as he wanders and goes about. Tathā = In the same way. Ayaṃ sāriputto = This noble monk known as Sāriputta. Nīcamano = With a humble mind, without pride. Vicarati = Is accustomed to wandering and going about. Parinibbūtaṃ = Who has attained Parinibbāna, ceased, and ended the cycle of suffering. Taṃ sāriputtaṃ = That noble monk known as Sāriputta. Vandatha = Bow down and pay homage with faith and humility, subduing all pride.
