Aheṭhayanto carati purantare vane.
Tathā ayaṃ viharati sāriputto,
Parinibbūtaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ. (4)

Bhikkhave = O dear monks. Chinnavisāṇako usabho = A bull with broken horns. Purantare = Within the town. Vane = Or in the forest. Aheṭhayanto = Without harming...
88:
88
...or oppressing anyone at all. Carati yathā = Just as he wanders and lives. Tathā = In the same way. Ayaṃ sāriputto = This noble monk known as Sāriputta. Aheṭhayanto = Without harming or oppressing anyone at all. Viharati = Is accustomed to living gracefully in the four postures: lying, sitting, standing, and walking. Parinibbūtaṃ = Who has attained Parinibbāna, ceased, and ended the cycle of suffering. Taṃ sāriputtaṃ = That noble monk known as Sāriputta. Vandatha = Bow down and pay homage with faith and humility, subduing all pride.

In this manner and others, the Blessed One praised the virtues of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta with five hundred verses.

As the Blessed One praised the Elder's virtues in various ways, the Venerable Elder Ānanda became increasingly distraught, finding no ground to stand on; he was trembling incessantly like a chicken in the mouth of a cat. Therefore, the Venerable Elder Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, because I have heard that 'Venerable Sāriputta has attained Parinibbāna,' my body feels especially heavy and rigid; the directions are not clear to me, and the teachings (Dhamma) do not appear to me (= meaning, he had no heart to learn the scriptures not yet learned, or to recite and chant the scriptures already learned)."
89:
89
Thus he spoke. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to comfort the Venerable Elder Ānanda, said:

"Dear Ānanda, did Sāriputta take away your mass of virtue (sīla) and attain Parinibbāna? Did he take away your mass of concentration (samādhi), your mass of wisdom (paññā), your mass of liberation (vimutti) known as Path and Fruition, or your mass of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) known as reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) and attain Parinibbāna?"

Then, the Venerable Elder Ānanda replied to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, Venerable Sāriputta did not take away my mass of virtue and attain Parinibbāna. He did not take away my mass of concentration, my mass of wisdom, my mass of liberation, or my mass of knowledge and vision of liberation and attain Parinibbāna.

Indeed, Venerable Sir, Venerable Sāriputta admonished me; he made me enter into the Dhamma. He made me know the Dhamma. He made me establish the Dhamma. He made me ardent in practicing the Dhamma. He made me joyful. He took great care in preaching the Dhamma; he was one who supported his fellow practitioners. Venerable Sir, we constantly remember that Dhamma-essence, those Dhamma-requisites, and that support through the Dhamma of Venerable Sāriputta."

Then, the Blessed One, perceiving that "This monk Ānanda is greatly distressed,"
90:
90
and wishing once again to comfort him, said:

"Dear Ānanda, have I not already taught you that there is separation from all those who are dear and beloved (nānābhāva), parting from them (vinābhāva), and their becoming otherwise (aññathābhāva)? Dear Ānanda, in this matter, how can it be obtained according to one's wish: 'May that which is born, come into being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration, not disintegrate'? There is no such possibility.

Dear Ānanda, just as when a great tree possessed of heartwood is standing, its largest branch might break; even so, while the great community of monks possessed of heartwood remains, Sāriputta has attained Parinibbāna. Dear Ānanda, in this matter, how can it be obtained according to one's wish: 'May that which is born, come into being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration, not disintegrate'? There is no such possibility.

Dear Ānanda, therefore, dwell as islands unto yourselves, as refuges unto yourselves, not depending on others; dwell with the Supramundane Dhamma as your island, with the Supramundane Dhamma as your refuge, not depending on any other teaching.

Dear Ānanda, how does a monk dwell as an island unto himself, as a refuge unto himself, not depending on others; how does he dwell with the Supramundane Dhamma as his island, with the Supramundane Dhamma as his refuge, not depending on any other teaching?"
91:
91
"Dear Ānanda, in this Dispensation, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful (etc.); contemplating the mind in the mind (etc.); contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief regarding the world.

Dear Ānanda, in this way, a monk dwells as an island unto himself, as a refuge unto himself, not depending on others. He dwells with the Supramundane Dhamma as his island, with the Supramundane Dhamma as his refuge, not depending on any other teaching.

Dear Ānanda, those monks who, either now or after my passing, shall dwell as islands unto themselves, as refuges unto themselves, not depending on others; who shall dwell with the Supramundane Dhamma as their island, with the Supramundane Dhamma as their refuge, not depending on any other teaching—all those monks shall truly become the highest among those monks who desire the three trainings (i.e., they shall become Arahants)."

Having spoken thus, he comforted Venerable Ānanda. Afterward, the Blessed One had a cetiya built for the relics of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta in the city of Sāvatthī.

This is the account of the Parinibbāna of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta.
92:
## The Parinibbāna of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna

As previously mentioned, after the Buddha had the relics of the Venerable Sāriputta enshrined in a stupa (dhātu-cetiya) in Sāvatthī, he gave notice to the Venerable Ānanda of his intention to travel to Rājagaha. The Venerable Ānanda then informed the monks, saying, "The Blessed One will be journeying to Rājagaha." Surrounded by a large company of monks, the Buddha departed from Sāvatthī and arrived at Rājagaha, where he resided and found delight in the Veḷuvana Monastery.

(Note: The Buddha attained Enlightenment on the full moon day of Kasun in the year 103 of the Great Era. On the 1st day of the waxing moon of Tabodwe in that same year, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were ordained. On the seventh day after his ordination, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Arahantship, and on the fifteenth day—the full moon of Tabodwe—the Venerable Sāriputta attained Arahantship.

In the year 148 of the Great Era, after the Buddha had completed 45 vassa (rains retreats) and the two Chief Disciples had completed 44 vassa each, the Venerable Sāriputta entered Parinibbāna on the full moon day of Tazaungmon in his birthplace, the village of Nālaka. On the new moon day of that same month of Tazaungmon, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna entered Parinibbāna at the Kāḷasilā rock on the slopes of Mount Isigili in Rājagaha—this should be noted in brief. The account of the Parinibbāna of the Venerable Sāriputta has already been described; now follows the account of the Parinibbāna of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.)

While the Buddha was thus residing and finding delight in the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna
93:
was staying at the rock known as Kāḷasilā on the slopes of Mount Isigili.

Because the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had reached the pinnacle of psychic power, he would travel to the celestial realms and the Ussada hells. Having personally witnessed the great splendor enjoyed by the disciples of the Buddha in the heavens, and the immense suffering endured by the disciples of the sectarians (titthiyas) in the Ussada hells, he would return to the human world and preach to the people: "Such and such male and female lay devotees have been reborn in such and such celestial realms and are enjoying great bliss. Among the disciples of the sectarians, such and such men and women have been reborn in the hell of such a name."

Consequently, people gained great faith in the Dispensation (Sāsana) and avoided the sectarians. Great offerings and honor accrued to the Buddha and his disciples, while the offerings and honor for the sectarians diminished and declined day by day.

Therefore, the sectarians harbored a grudge against the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, thinking, "If this monk Moggallāna continues to live, our supporting lay devotees will be ruined day by day, and our offerings and honor will also diminish and decline. Let us have this monk Moggallāna killed." Having reached this agreement, they gave a thousand pieces of silver to a bandit chief named Samaṇaguttaka to kill the Elder.

That bandit chief Samaṇaguttaka, intending to kill the Elder, set out with a large following of bandits
94:
towards the place where the Kāḷasilā rock was located. When the Elder saw the bandit chief Samaṇaguttaka approaching, he used his psychic power to fly into the sky and escaped. Not finding the Elder that day, the bandit chief returned, and on the following day, he went again in the same manner. The Elder also escaped as before. In this way, six days passed.

On the seventh day, however, a past unwholesome kamma (aparāpariya kamma) of the Elder, committed long ago, found the opportunity to bear fruit. To clarify the nature of that past unwholesome kamma:

In a past life, when he was young, the Elder had wrongly listened to the divisive words of his wife and, wishing to kill his parents, he took them to the forest in a small carriage. Pretending to be a group of attacking bandits, he beat his parents. Because both parents were blind and could not see, they did not recognize their own son and truly believed they were being attacked by bandits. Crying out only for their son's safety, they said, "Dear son, these bandits are beating us. You, dear son, must flee to safety!"

The son thought, "Oh, even though it is I who am beating my mother and father, they cry out in great anxiety only for me. I have committed a most improper deed." Feeling remorse, he comforted his parents, made it appear as though the bandits had fled, and then massaged his parents' limbs, saying, "O mother and father, do not be afraid; the bandits have run away."
95:
After saying this, he led his parents back to their home.

That evil deed, that unwholesome kamma, had not yet had the opportunity to bear fruit for all this time, remaining like embers covered by ash. Now, in this final existence (pacchima-bhava), it pursued and caught up with his physical body. To use a worldly simile, just as when a hunter sees a deer and releases a dog, that dog pursues the prey and bites it wherever it catches it, so too did the unwholesome kamma committed by the one who was to become the Venerable Moggallāna bear fruit in the very existence where it found the opportunity. There is no one who can escape from kamma that has found its opportunity to ripen.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, well aware that his past unwholesome kamma had caught up with him, did not attempt to escape to another place by psychic power on that seventh occasion. Due to the consequence of that unwholesome kamma, he was no longer able to fly into the sky. The psychic power of the Elder, which was capable of taming the Naga king Nandopananda and making the Vejayanta Palace tremble and shake, became weakened by the power of that unwholesome kamma.

The bandit chief Samaṇaguttaka surrounded and captured the Elder. He pounded and crushed the Elder's bones until they were the size of broken rice grains. Having performed the torture known as palālapīṭhika (crushing all bones into a pulp like a bundle of straw), he threw the body onto a bush with the perception that he was dead, and then departed with his followers.
96:
The Elder regained consciousness and reflected, "I shall enter Parinibbāna only after I have seen the Blessed One." He bound his crushed body firmly with the 'cloth' of meditative absorption (jhāna) and supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). Then, flying through the air, he went into the presence of the Buddha. After prostrating, he spoke back and forth with the Blessed One as follows:

(Venerable Moggallāna:)
"Venerable Sir, I have relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra). I shall now enter Parinibbāna, Lord."

(The Buddha:)
"Will you now enter Parinibbāna, my son Moggallāna?"

(Venerable Moggallāna:)
"I shall enter it, Lord."

(The Buddha:)
"My son Moggallāna, where will you go to enter Parinibbāna?"

(Venerable Moggallāna:)
"Venerable Sir, I shall go to the Kāḷasilā rock and enter Parinibbāna there."

(The Buddha:)
"My son Moggallāna, if that is so, preach the Dhamma to me before you go. For now, there will be no further opportunity to see a disciple like you again."

When the Buddha spoke thus, the Elder replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I shall do so." Having respectfully prostrated to the Buddha, he flew into the sky to the height of one palm tree, two palm trees, and so on, up to seven palm trees. On this, the day of his Parinibbāna, just like the Venerable Sāriputta,
97:
the Elder performed various psychic miracles and preached the Dhamma. After respectfully prostrating to the Buddha, he proceeded to the forest where the Kāḷasilā rock was located and entered Parinibbāna.

At that very moment, a great commotion arose simultaneously throughout the six celestial realms of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). The devas and brahmas said to one another, "Our teacher, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, has entered Parinibbāna." They brought celestial perfumes, flowers, scents, incense, and sandalwood powder, as well as various fragrant celestial woods. The pile of sandalwood funeral wood was ninety-nine cubits high. The Buddha himself, along with the monks, went there and stood majestically near the remains of the Elder, supervising and directing the cremation ceremony.

For a distance of one yojana around the cremation site, a rain of flowers fell. At that funeral ceremony, humans moved among the devas, and devas moved among the humans. In succession, Yakkha deities stood among the devas, Gandhabbas among the Yakkhas, Nāgas among the Gandhabbas, Garuḍas among the Nāgas, and Kinnaras among the Garuḍas. Among the Kinnaras were parasols; among the parasols were golden yak-tail whisks; among the whisks were cylindrical banners; and among the cylindrical banners were flat banners. Devas and humans celebrated the festival of honor (sādhukīḷana) for seven days.
98:
The Buddha had the relics of the Elder brought and caused a stupa (dhātu-cetiya) to be built near the main gate of the Veḷuvana Monastery.

## The Punishment of the Killers

The news that "the Venerable Moggallāna has been killed by bandits" spread throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. King Ajātasattu sent out spies in all directions to find and capture the bandits. While those killers were drinking liquor in a tavern, one killer struck the drinking cup out of the hand of another killer to provoke him. The one who was provoked threatened him in various ways, saying, "You fool, who is hard to discipline! Why did you strike my drinking cup and make it fall to the ground?"

The provocateur replied, "Hey, you wicked fool! What of it? Did you not dare to be the first to strike, stab, and beat the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to death?" The one who was provoked, not wanting to be outdone, retorted, "You fool! Do you not know that it was I who struck and stabbed him?"

In this manner, as the killers were boasting to one another, saying, "I struck and killed him," and "I struck and killed him," the king's spies heard them. They arrested all the killers and reported the matter to King Ajātasattu. King Ajātasattu then [questioned] the killers.
99: When they were summoned before him and asked, "Did you kill the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna?", the assassins confessed, saying, "Yes, your majesty, we killed him." When King Ajātasattu further asked, "Who ordered you to kill him?", the assassins gave their statement, saying, "Your majesty, the naked ascetics (Acelaka Titthiyas) gave us money and ordered us to kill him." King Ajātasattu had the five hundred naked ascetics arrested and, together with the five hundred assassins, buried them all in pits as deep as the navel in the palace courtyard. He then had them covered with straw and set on fire. After knowing that they were all burnt, he had them plowed over repeatedly with plows fitted with iron shares, cutting them all into pieces. (Note: The account of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's parinibbāna is extracted from the commentary on the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka in the Cattālīsanipāta (Jā-a 5.133, 134, 135); the account of the assassins' punishment is extracted from the story of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the Dhammapada Commentary (Dhp-a 2.43)). Regarding the funeral rites of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, which the Buddha himself supervised, the monks in the Dhamma Hall began a discussion: "Friends, Venerable Sāriputta did not pass away near the Buddha and thus did not receive such great honor and reverence from the Buddhas. However, Venerable Moggallāna passed away near the Buddha and has received great honor and reverence."
100:
They were engaged in this conversation. Then the Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When the monks reported the matter, the Blessed One said, "Monks, Moggallāna has not only received cherished care from the Buddha in this life; he received it in the past as well." He then preached the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka from the Cattālīsannipāta to the monks. (That Sarabhaṅga Jātaka should be studied in detail from the 550 Jātaka stories).

Not long after the two Chief Disciples had entered Parinibbāna, the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of monks, traveled on a journey through the Mahāmaṇḍala region and arrived at the city of Ukkacela. After wandering for alms in that city, he preached the Ukkacelā Sutta to the monks on the sandy banks of the Ganges River. (The details of that Sutta should be studied in the Burmese translation of the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta, pages 146, 147, 148).

This is the account of the two Chief Disciples.
