## (4) The Story of Venerable Mahākassapa
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

One hundred thousand aeons ago, the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world. While he was residing in the Khema Migadāyona (Deer Park) near the royal city of Haṃsāvatī, a wealthy man named Vedeha, who possessed eighty billion (koti) in wealth (the future Venerable Mahākassapa), finished his fine morning meal and...
101: having observed the Uposatha and taking perfumes, flowers, and so on, went to the monastery. After honoring and worshipping the Buddha, he sat in a suitable place. At that time, the Buddha Padumuttara placed the Elder named Mahānisabha, who was his third disciple, in the position of Etadagga (foremost), declaring: "Monks, among my disciple monks who personally practice the noble dhutaṅga (ascetic) practices and also preach, demonstrate, and advise their fellow practitioners in the Saṅgha to practice the noble dhutaṅga practices, the monk Nisabha is the best and foremost." Hearing these words, the lay devotee Vedeha was filled with faith and devotion. After the Dhamma talk was over and the crowd had departed, he respectfully worshipped the Buddha and said, "Blessed One, please accept my alms-food for tomorrow." When the Buddha Padumuttara said, "Layman, the company of monks is very large," he asked, "Blessed One, how many monks are there?" When the Buddha Padumuttara replied, "Layman, there are six million eight hundred thousand," the lay devotee Vedeha boldly requested, "Blessed One, please accept my alms-food together with all the monks, without leaving even a single novice behind in the monastery." The Buddha Padumuttara accepted Vedeha's invitation by remaining silent. Knowing well that the Buddha had accepted, the lay devotee Vedeha returned home and,
102: having prepared a great offering, sent word the next morning that it was time for the Buddha to come for the meal. The Buddha, taking his bowl and robes and surrounded by the company of monks, went to the house of the lay devotee Vedeha and sat on the prepared seat. When the libation ceremony was completed, he accepted the gruel and other offerings, and partook of the meal. The lay devotee Vedeha sat near the Buddha, his faith and devotion increasing. During that time, the Elder Mahānisabha arrived at that path while wandering for alms. Seeing the Elder, the lay devotee Vedeha rose from his seat, worshipped the Elder, and requested, "Venerable Sir, please grant me your bowl." The Elder handed the bowl to the layman. When the layman said, "Venerable Sir, please enter the house; the Buddha is also sitting inside the house," the Elder replied, "Layman, it would not be appropriate to enter and stay inside the house." The lay devotee Vedeha filled the Elder's bowl with alms-food and offered it to him. After seeing the Elder off and returning, he sat near the Buddha and asked, "Blessed One, although I told the Elder Mahānisabha that the Buddha was sitting inside the house, he did not wish to enter. Does that Elder possess virtues superior to yours?"
103: In the nature of the Buddhas, there is absolutely no envy regarding the praise or virtues of others (vaṇṇamacchariya). Therefore, immediately after the lay devotee Vedeha had asked his question, the Buddha said: "Layman, we sit in houses waiting for alms-food. The monk Nisabha, however, does not sit like this waiting for alms-food at all. We reside in monasteries near villages. The monk Nisabha resides only in forest monasteries. We reside in monasteries with roofs. The monk Nisabha resides only in the open air. In this way, these and those are the special virtues of the monk Nisabha." Thus, he preached the virtues of the Elder in detail, like adding more water to the great ocean. The lay devotee Vedeha, whose faith and devotion were already strong, became even more inspired, like pouring oil onto a burning lamp. He thought and resolved: "What benefit is there for me in other human or divine pleasures? In the future, under a Buddha, I shall make an aspiration to become an Etadagga (foremost) person among the dhutavāda monks—those who personally practice the noble dhutaṅga practices and also preach, demonstrate, and advise their fellow practitioners in the Saṅgha to practice them." The lay devotee Vedeha again invited the company of monks headed by the Buddha for the next day and offered alms-food. In this manner, for seven days,
104: he gave a great offering. On the seventh day, after offering triple robes (ticīvara) to the large company of monks headed by the Buddha, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and said: "Blessed One, there is this mass of merit from my offering of a great gift while performing loving-kindness through bodily, verbal, and mental actions for seven days. Because of this mass of merit, I do not desire any divine pleasures, the pleasures of Sakka, the pleasures of Māra, or the pleasures of Brahmā. Indeed, may this merit of mine be the merit that surely brings to fulfillment the attainment of the position reached by the noble Elder Mahānisabha under a future Buddha—to be the best and foremost among those who practice the thirteen dhutaṅga practices." The Buddha Padumuttara thought, "This lay devotee Vedeha has made an aspiration for a very great thing; will it be fulfilled or not?" Looking into the future with his golden knowledge (Anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), he saw that it would surely be fulfilled and said: "Layman, you have made an aspiration for a delightful position. In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world. Under that Buddha Gotama,
105:
He will be the third disciple of the Buddha, named Mahākassapa."

Upon hearing this prophecy, the lay devotee Vedeha, knowing that "there is no double-speech (uncertainty) in the words of the Buddhas," rejoiced, regarding the attainment of the position of the third disciple as if it were a fortune to be received the very next day. The lay devotee Vedeha gave various kinds of alms throughout his life, observed the precepts, and performed other meritorious deeds. When he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm.

## Life as Mahāekasāṭaka Brahmin

From that time on, while enjoying prosperity in the celestial and human worlds, ninety-one aeons ago from this present aeon, the Buddha Vipassī appeared in the world. While he was residing in the Khema Migadāyona near the royal city of Bandhumatī, this noble being, the future Venerable Mahākassapa, passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn into an obscure and poor Brahmin family.

In particular, at that time, the Buddha Vipassī held a special Dhamma festival every seven years and preached the Dhamma. When such a Dhamma festival was held, he set a time so that every being could hear the Dhamma; during the day, he preached in the evening, and during the night, he preached throughout the entire night. As the Dhamma festival drew near, there was a great commotion, and the devas also...
106:
“The Buddha will preach the Dhamma!”—this announcement was proclaimed throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

The Brahmin who was to become the future Venerable Mahākassapa heard this news. This Brahmin, in particular, possessed only a single lower garment; likewise, his wife, the Brahmin lady, also had only one lower garment. Between the two of them, they had only one upper garment. For this reason, the Brahmin was well-known throughout the city as “Ekasāṭaka Brahmin,” meaning the Brahmin who has only one garment. If there was a meeting of Brahmins for some business, the Brahmin himself would go to the meeting, leaving his wife at home. If there was a meeting of Brahmin ladies, the Brahmin himself had to remain at home, and the Brahmin lady would go, wearing that single upper garment.

On the day when the Buddha Vipassī was to preach the Dhamma, the Great Ekasāṭaka Brahmin asked his wife, “O lady, how shall it be? Will you go to listen to the Dhamma at night, or will you go during the day?” The Brahmin lady replied, “We womenfolk are unable to listen to the Dhamma at night. I will listen to the Dhamma during the day.” Having said this, she left the Brahmin at home, and wearing that upper garment, she went during the day with other female lay devotees (upāsikās). After paying homage to the Buddha and sitting in a suitable place to listen to the Dhamma, she returned home together with her companions. Then, the Brahmin took his turn, and leaving his wife at home, he wore that garment and went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma at night.
107: At that time, the Buddha Vipassī was seated upon the magnificent Dhamma-throne in the midst of the assembly. Holding a decorative fan, he preached the Dhamma like one descending and swimming in a celestial river, or like a man vigorously churning the great ocean using Mount Meru as a churning stick. As the Great Ekasāṭaka Brahmin sat at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, five types of joy (pīti) arose repeatedly, pervading his entire body even during the first watch of the night. The Brahmin folded the upper garment he had brought and thought, “I shall offer this to the Buddha.” After he had this thought, a thousand faults were presented to him, and stinginess (macchariya) arose repeatedly, making him unwilling to give. When stinginess arose, the Brahmin thought, “My wife and I have only this one upper garment between us. There is not a single other upper garment to change into. Without wearing it, one cannot go about outside the house.” Thinking and worrying in this way, he again became one who was completely unwilling to give. Then, when the first watch had passed and the middle watch arrived, the five types of joy arose in the Brahmin’s mind just as before. The Brahmin thought in the same way as before and again became unwilling to give. Then, when the middle watch had passed and the dawn watch arrived, the five types of joy arose in the Brahmin’s mind once more. This time, the Brahmin did not allow the unwholesome state of stinginess to arise. He made a firm decision, thinking, “If I am to be free from death, let it be so; if death must come, let it come. I will think about the matter of clothing later.”
108:
Folding that upper garment, he placed it at the feet of the Buddha and offered it generously. Then, bending his left arm and striking it with his right hand three times in a gesture of triumph, he shouted boldly three times, “I have won! I have won!”

At that time, King Bandhuma was sitting behind a curtain behind the Dhamma-throne, listening to the Dhamma. For a king who wished to be the only winner, the sound “I have won” was an unpleasant sound. Therefore, the King sent a royal attendant, saying, “Friend, go at once. Ask that man what he is saying.” The royal attendant went to the Ekasāṭaka Brahmin and asked the reason. The Brahmin replied:

“O young man, other people, including kings, ride on elephant-vehicles and horse-vehicles, and holding swords, shields, and armor, they conquer enemy armies. That victory is not surprising. As for me, like a man who strikes the head of a wild and fierce bull that is jumping and chasing him to gore him with a club and makes that fierce bull flee, I have suppressed the mind of stinginess and have successfully offered my upper garment to the Buddha. I have conquered that stinginess which is difficult to conquer.”

The royal attendant returned and reported this matter to the King.
109:
King Bandhuma said, “Friends, we do not know what is appropriate for the Buddha; the Brahmin knows,” and he ordered a pair of garments to be sent to the Brahmin. The Brahmin said, “This King did not give anything to me when I remained silent at first, but gave only after I spoke of the Buddha’s virtues. What use have I for this set of garments obtained by relying on the Buddha’s virtues?” and he offered that set of garments to the Buddha as well.

The King asked his attendants, “What did the Brahmin do with the garments I gave?” and upon hearing that “The Brahmin offered those garments to the Buddha as well,” he sent two more pairs of garments to the Brahmin. The Brahmin offered those two pairs to the Buddha as well. The King then sent four pairs of garments to the Brahmin. The Brahmin offered those four pairs to the Buddha as well. In this manner, the King increased the gift step by step until he sent thirty-two pairs. Then, the Great Ekasāṭaka Brahmin thought, “Giving away everything I receive without keeping anything for myself is like receiving more and more,” and from those thirty-two pairs, he took out two pairs—one for himself and one for the Brahmin lady—and offered the remaining thirty pairs to the Buddha. From that time on, the Brahmin became an intimate and close devotee of the Buddha.

Later, one day when it was very cold, the King saw the Brahmin listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha.
110:
Seeing this, the King gave the Brahmin his own red woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand and said, “From now on, wear this blanket while listening to the Dhamma.” The Brahmin reflected, “What benefit is there for me to wear this blanket on this foul corpse of a body?” and he offered it as a canopy to be spread above the couch where the Buddha resided within the Gandhakuti, and then returned home.

One day, the King went to the monastery early and sat near the Buddha inside the Gandhakuti. At that time, the six-colored rays of the Buddha struck the red woolen blanket that was spread as a canopy, making the red blanket exceedingly beautiful. When the King saw the blanket, he recognized it and said, “Venerable Sir, this blanket is mine. I gave this blanket to the Ekasāṭaka Brahmin to wear when listening to the Dhamma.” The Buddha replied, “Great King, you have honored the Brahmin, and the Brahmin has honored me.” The King thought, “The Brahmin knows what is suitable and appropriate, but we do not know so,” and with great faith and devotion, he made an offering called the Sabbatthaka, consisting of sixty-four of every kind of human necessity, and appointed the Great Ekasāṭaka Brahmin to the position of Chaplain (Purohita).

The Great Ekasāṭaka Brahmin, the Chaplain, reflected, “The term ‘Attha-atthaka’ (eight times eight) means sixty-four,”
111:
and having considered this, he established a regular offering of sixty-four sets of ticket-food (salāka-bhatta) daily. He gave alms and observed the precepts throughout his life, and when he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm.

## Life as a Householder

Passing away from the celestial realm, during the interval between the two Buddhas, Buddha Konāgamana and Buddha Kassapa, in this Bhadda-kappa, he was reborn in the house of a wealthy man in the city of Bārāṇasī. When that wealthy man grew up and lived as a householder, one day he went for a walk in the forest to stretch his legs. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was sewing a robe near a riverbank, and as he did not have enough cloth for the border, he was preparing to fold and put away the robe he was sewing.

The wealthy man saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, “Venerable Sir, why are you folding and putting away the robe?” The Paccekabuddha replied, “Lay follower, there is not enough cloth for the border, so I am folding it away.” The wealthy man then said, “Venerable Sir, please make the border with this cloth,” and after offering his own cloth, he made an aspiration: “In whatever life I am born in Saṃsāra, may I never experience any deficiency in any kind of necessity.”

Later, at the wealthy man’s house, while his sister and his wife were quarreling with each other, a Paccekabuddha arrived for alms.
112: Then, the householder's sister, having offered alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, made an aspiration referring to the householder's wife: "May I be a person who can avoid such a foolish woman even from a hundred yojanas away." The householder's wife, standing at the door of the house, heard those words and thought, "May this Paccekabuddha not enjoy the alms-food offered by this woman." She took the bowl, threw away the food, filled it with mud, and gave it back. Seeing this, the householder's sister rebuked her, saying, "O foolish woman, if you wish to abuse me, then abuse me; if you wish to strike me, then strike me. But it is not proper to throw away the food from the bowl of such a Paccekabuddha, who has fulfilled the perfections for two asaṅkheyyas, and to give it back filled with mud." At that moment, the householder's wife regained her sense of propriety and pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please wait a moment." She threw away the mud, washed the bowl until it was clean, rubbed it with scented powder, and filled it with catumadhura. On top of that, she poured ghee as white as a lotus stalk, making it shine brilliantly. She then offered the bowl into the hands of the Paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: "Just as this alms-food shines brilliantly, may my body also be radiant." The Paccekabuddha gave his blessing and flew into the sky. That husband and wife performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives, and when they passed away from that existence, they were reborn in the celestial realm.
113:
## Life as a Wealthy Merchant in Bārāṇasī
When they passed away from the celestial realm, the householder became the son of a merchant with eighty crores of wealth in the city of Bārāṇasī during the time of Kassapa Buddha. The householder's wife also became the daughter of another merchant with eighty crores of wealth on that same night. When the merchant's son reached maturity, that merchant's daughter was brought to his house to be his wife. Due to the power of the unwholesome karma she had previously committed, which had not yet yielded its full result, as soon as she entered the house of her lord and husband and stood within the threshold, a foul odor like that of an opened latrine emanated from her entire body. The merchant's son asked, "Whose smell is this?" and when he learned, "It is the smell of the merchant's daughter who has just arrived," he said, "Take her out!" and sent her back to her parents' house with the same ceremonial retinue she had come with. In this manner, she was sent back to her parents' house from seven different places because of the foul odor that arose as soon as she reached the threshold of the house. Unwholesome karma is indeed fearsome. At that time, as Kassapa Buddha had attained Parinibbāna, the people began to build a great cetiya one yojana high for the Buddha, using red-gold bricks worth a hundred thousand each, cast from pure gold. While the cetiya was being built, the merchant's daughter thought, "I am one who has been sent back from seven places. What is the use of my living a long life?"
114: She sold all her ornaments and belongings, and with the money obtained, she had a brick cast that was one cubit long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths thick. Then, the merchant's daughter took that golden brick along with orpiment, realgar, and eight lotus flowers, and went to the site where the cetiya was being built. At that moment, a layer of golden bricks was being laid around the great cetiya, and one golden brick was needed to complete the connection. The merchant's daughter said to the master mason, "Master, please place this golden brick of mine in the spot where one brick is needed." The master mason kindly granted permission, saying, "O lady, you have come at a good time. You yourself may place this golden brick." The merchant's daughter climbed up to that spot, mixed oil with powdered orpiment and realgar, and having fixed her golden brick with that adhesive, she offered the lotus flowers on top of the brick. She paid homage respectfully and made an aspiration: "In every existence throughout the round of rebirths, may the scent of sandalwood emanate from my body and the scent of blue lotuses from my mouth." After paying her respects to the cetiya, she returned to her home. At that very moment, the merchant's son who had first sent her back felt a constant longing and remembrance for the merchant's daughter. A festival was then being celebrated in the city of Bārāṇasī. The merchant's son asked his men, "There was a merchant's daughter who was brought to my house some time ago. In which house is that young lady living now?" The merchant's son's men replied, "Lord Merchant, that young lady is still at her parents' house."
115: When they said this, the merchant's son sent them, saying, "Friends, go and fetch that young lady. We shall enjoy the festival together with her." The merchant's son's men went to the young lady, paid their respects, and stood there. When the young lady asked, "Friends, for what reason have you come?" they explained the matter. The young lady said, "Friends, I have offered all my ornaments and belongings to the cetiya. I have no finery left to wear." When she said this, the merchant's son's men returned and told the merchant's son. The merchant's son replied, "Just bring the young lady. She will receive ornaments." Upon his word, those men brought the young lady to the merchant's house. As soon as the young lady entered the house, the entire house became filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and blue lotuses. The merchant's son asked her, "When you first came to this house, a foul odor emanated from your body. But now, the fragrance of sandalwood comes from your body and the fragrance of blue lotuses from your mouth. What is the reason for this?" When the young lady recounted the story of the meritorious deed she had performed from the beginning, the merchant's son, filled with faith and devotion, exclaimed, "Oh, how the teaching of the Buddha truly leads one out of the suffering of the round of rebirths!"
116:
Filled with even greater devotion, he covered the great golden cetiya, which was one yojana high, with a woolen shroud, and decorated it beautifully with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels at various places. The hanging golden stems and petals of those golden lotuses were about twelve cubits in size. 

## Life as King Nanda
That husband and wife, having performed meritorious deeds diligently in that life, lived out their lifespan and were reborn in the celestial realm. When they passed away from the celestial realm, the merchant's son was reborn into a minister's family in a place one yojana away from Bārāṇasī, and the merchant's daughter became the eldest princess in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī. When they both reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the minister's son, Nanda, lived. The young Nanda said to his mother, the minister's wife, "O Mother, give me clothes; I shall enjoy the festival." When his mother gave him a set of clothes that had been washed and smoothed, Nanda said, "O Mother, these clothes are too coarse and thick. Give me another set." When he rejected them, his mother gave him another set. When he rejected those too as being coarse and thick, his mother exchanged them again. After several such exchanges, his mother said, "Dear son, we are born into such a minister's family. In this house, we do not have the merit to obtain clothes finer than these."
117: When she said this, the young Nanda replied, "O Mother, if that is so, I shall go to a place where I can obtain clothes finer than these." His mother said, "O dear son, this very day I wish for you to obtain the kingship in the city of Bārāṇasī," speaking these auspicious words of blessing. The young Nanda paid respects to his mother and said, "O Mother, I am leaving." His mother gently replied, "Dear son, go." In her mind, she thought, "Where else will my son go? He has no other place to go; he will just stay here and there around my house," and thus she gave him permission so easily. However, driven by the impulse of his meritorious karma, Nanda left his village and went to the city of Bārāṇasī, where he lay down on the auspicious stone slab in the royal garden, covering himself even over his head. That day was the seventh day after the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away. The ministers, having performed the king's funeral rites, assembled in the palace courtyard and discussed, "The Great King had only one daughter. No son was born to him. A kingdom without a king is not proper. Who shall be the king?" They began to defer to one another, saying, "You become the king," "You become the king." Then the Chaplain (Purohita) said, "We should not just look at each other..."
118:
“It is not appropriate. We shall release the Phussa chariot—the auspicious chariot used to find the heir to the throne,” they decided. The ministers all agreed, hitched four Sindh horses with the color of white water lilies, placed the five royal regalia upon the chariot, and released the auspicious Phussa chariot. They followed the chariot with the fourfold army, playing the five kinds of musical instruments.

The auspicious Phussa chariot exited through the eastern gate of the city and headed towards the royal garden. Some people said, “The chariot is heading towards the garden out of habit. Shall we turn it back?” The Chief Chaplain (Purohita) forbade them, saying, “Do not turn it back.” The Phussa chariot entered the royal garden, circled the youth Nanda clockwise, and stood ready for him to mount. The Chief Chaplain lifted the edge of the cloth Nanda was wearing, inspected the soles of his feet, and remarked, “Let alone this Jambudīpa; this future king is worthy of ruling all four great islands along with their two thousand surrounding small islands with radiant glory.” He then ordered, “Play the musical instruments again! Play the musical instruments again!” and had the music played three times.

Then, the youth Nanda opened his eyes, looked around, and exchanged words with the ministers:

(Nanda)
“For what purpose have you come?”

(Ministers)
“Your Majesty, the kingship of Bārāṇasī has reached you.”
119:
(Nanda)
“Where is the sovereign king?”

(Ministers)
“He has passed away, Your Majesty.”

(Nanda)
“How many days have passed since the sovereign king passed away?”

(Ministers)
“Today marks the seventh day.”

(Nanda)
“Did the late king have no son or daughter?”

(Ministers)
“Your Majesty, there is only one daughter. There is no son.”

When the ministers reported this, the youth Nanda accepted, saying, “If that is so, I shall take up the kingship of Bārāṇasī.” At that moment, the ministers constructed a consecration pavilion, dressed the princess in full regalia, and brought her to the garden. They then performed the royal consecration (Abhiṣeka) by pouring the ceremonial water on the youth Nanda and elevated him to the kingship of Bārāṇasī.

After the royal consecration, they offered King Nanda a set of robes worth a thousand pieces. King Nanda asked, “Friends, what kind of cloth is this?” The ministers replied, “Your Majesty, it is a set of robes for you to wear.” King Nanda then asked, “Friends, are these robes not very thick and coarse? Are there no other softer robes besides these?” The ministers replied, “Your Majesty, among the clothes used by humans, there are no clothes softer than these.”
120:
When they replied thus, King Nanda asked, “Did your late sovereign king wear such robes?” The ministers replied, “Yes, Your Majesty.” King Nanda then said, “It seems your late sovereign king was not one of great merit. Bring a golden pitcher; we shall obtain very soft clothing.” The ministers brought and offered the golden pitcher.

King Nanda rose from his seat, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his palms, and sprinkled it towards the eastern direction. At that moment, eight wish-fulfilling trees (Kalpavriksha) emerged, breaking through the solid great earth. When he took water again and sprinkled it towards the south, west, and north in order, eight wish-fulfilling trees emerged in each direction. Thus, thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees emerged in the four directions. King Nanda wore one divine robe and draped another over his shoulders. He then commanded, “Let it be proclaimed by drum throughout the kingdom of King Nanda that women who spin cotton should no longer do so.” Then, with the white parasol raised and adorned in full regalia, he rode upon the back of an elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great royal bliss.

After King Nanda had enjoyed this great royal bliss for some time, one day the Chief Queen...
121:
...looking at King Nanda's great royal bliss, showed a sign of pity, thinking, “Alas, how meager it is if no new merit is performed.” When the King asked, “My Queen, why do you show such pity?” the Queen replied, “Your Majesty, your bliss is indeed great. It is certain that in the past, you performed good deeds with faith in the Buddhas. However, now you are not performing any meritorious deeds for the sake of future happiness.”

“To whom shall we give? There are no virtuous recipients of alms,” the King said. The Queen boldly replied, “Your Majesty, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants. Your Majesty, simply prepare the offerings. I, your servant, will find a way to invite the worthy recipients of offerings.”

The next day, the King had offerings prepared at the eastern gate of the city. The Queen, having observed the Uposatha precepts early in the morning, prostrated herself on the palace roof facing the east and made an invitation, saying, “If there are Arahants in this eastern direction, may they come tomorrow and accept our alms-food.” Since there were no Arahants in the east, none came. Those offerings were then given to the poor and beggars. The next day, offerings were prepared at the southern gate, and the same was done. The following day, offerings...
122:
...were prepared at the western gate, and the same was done. Since there were no Arahants in the south or west, none came.

On the fourth day, when offerings were prepared at the northern gate and the Queen made the invitation as before, the Great Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, the eldest among the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Queen Padumavatī living in the Himalayas, addressed the other Paccekabuddhas, “Venerable Paccekabuddhas like myself, King Nanda has invited you. Please accept King Nanda's invitation.” Those Paccekabuddhas accepted, and the next day, after washing their faces at Lake Anotatta, they traveled through the air and descended to the earth at the northern gate of the city.

The townspeople went to the King and reported, “Your Majesty, five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived.” The King, together with the Queen, went to welcome them, paid homage, took their bowls, and invited the five hundred Paccekabuddhas up to the golden palace. After offering a great feast to the five hundred Paccekabuddhas in the palace, when the meal was over, the King prostrated at the feet of the eldest Elder, and the Queen prostrated at the feet of the youngest monk, saying, “If your reverences stay in our garden, you will live comfortably with the four requisites without hardship. We, too, will prosper in merit without decline. Therefore, in our garden in this city of Bārāṇasī...”
123:
“...please give us your word to reside here.” Having requested and received their promise, they fully prepared five hundred leaf-huts, five hundred walkways, and other necessary lodgings in the auspicious garden. They had the five hundred Paccekabuddhas reside in that garden and looked after them with the four requisites so that they would not be troubled or weary.

After they had been cared for in this way for some time, the border regions of the King's country became restless and rose in rebellion. The King told the Queen, “My Queen, I shall go to the border regions to quell the rebel threat. Do not be negligent in caring for the Paccekabuddhas.” He then departed.

The Queen, as the King had instructed, looked after the Paccekabuddhas with the four requisites without negligence. After some days of such care, before the King returned, the life-span (āyu-saṅkhāra) of the Paccekabuddhas came to an end. Thus, the eldest, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, entered meditative absorption (jhāna) for all three watches of the night, and at dawn, while leaning against a door-plank, passed into Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna) while still standing. In this manner, the remaining Paccekabuddhas also passed into Parinibbāna.

The next day, the Queen had the Paccekabuddhas' living quarters smeared with cow dung, scattered flowers, and offered incense. While she sat waiting for the arrival of the Paccekabuddhas, she saw no sign of them. Therefore, she said to a palace attendant, “Dear son, go and investigate.”
124:
The messenger was sent with the words, "Go and see if there is any discomfort or illness for the Venerable Ones."

The man went to the park and opened the door of the monastery of the Venerable Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha. Not seeing him in the monastery, he went to the walkway (caṅkama) and found him standing there, leaning against the support board. He paid homage and invited him, saying, "It is time for the meal, Bhante." How could the physical body (utujarūpa) of one who has attained Parinibbāna respond? It remained silent. The man thought, "He must be sleeping," and approaching, he felt the top of the feet with his hand. Realizing from the coldness and stiffness of the feet that the Paccekabuddha had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the second Venerable One, and in the same manner, to the third. Having investigated in this way and realizing that all the Paccekabuddhas had attained Parinibbāna, he returned to the palace. When the Queen asked, "Young man, where are the Venerable Paccekabuddhas?", the man replied, "Your Majesty, the Venerable Paccekabuddhas have entered Parinibbāna."

The Queen wept and lamented loudly, and leaving the city with the citizens, she went to the park. After performing the funeral rites (sādhukīḷana) for the bodies of the Paccekabuddhas, she took the relics and had a stupa enshrined. 

When the King, having pacified the border regions at the edge of the kingdom, returned to the country—
125:
—and saw the Queen who had come to welcome him, he immediately asked, "My Queen, did you look after the Venerable Paccekabuddhas without negligence? Are the Venerable Ones free from illness?" The Queen replied, "Your Majesty, they have entered Parinibbāna." Upon hearing this, the King was struck with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and reflected, "Even in the continuity of the aggregates (khandha) of such wise ones, death still occurs. How can there be any escape from death for us?"

The King did not go to the city but entered the park. He summoned his eldest son, handed over the sovereignty of the throne, and he himself ordained as a monk (like a monk within the Sasana). The Queen also reflected, "If the King ordains, what business do I have left? = None at all," and she too ordained as a nun in that very park. Both of them developed the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), and when they passed away from that life, they were reborn in the Brahma realm.

## (b) Renunciation in the Final Life

While those two were residing in the Brahma realm, the time arrived for the appearance of our Blessed Buddha. At that time, the youth Pippali, who was to become the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera, was conceived in the womb of the chief wife of the wealthy Brahmin named Kapila, in the Brahmin village of Mahātittha within the kingdom of Magadha. The woman who was the future Bhaddā Kāpilānī was conceived in the womb of the chief wife of a wealthy Brahmin of the Kosiya clan, in the city of Sāgala within the kingdom of Madda.
126:
As those two grew up in due course, the youth Pippali reached the age of twenty, and the young woman Bhaddā Kāpilānī reached the age of sixteen. The mother and father of the youth Pippali, seeing that their son had come of age, urged and persuaded him to marry, saying, "Dear son, you have reached the age to marry. One must ensure the continuity of the lineage."

Because Pippali had come from the Brahma realm, he said, "Do not speak such words in my presence. While my mother and father are alive, I will look after them. When they have passed away, I will leave the household life and become a monk." When two or three days had passed, the parents urged him again. Pippali refused as before. When they urged him yet again, he still refused. From that time on, his mother, the wealthy Brahmin lady, urged him constantly.

After being told many times, Pippali thought, "I will make my mother clearly understand my desire to ordain." He gave a thousand nikkhas of pure gold to goldsmiths and had them cast a golden statue of a woman. When the golden statue was finished and polished, he had it dressed in red garments and adorned with brilliant flowers and ornaments. He then summoned his mother and said, "O mother, if I can find a beautiful woman like this golden statue,
127:
I will stay at home. If not, I will not remain in the household life."

His mother, being a wise woman, thought, "My son is one of great merit, one who has given gifts, and one who has made noble aspirations in the past. When he performed meritorious deeds, he would not have done them alone. Surely, there must be a noble woman as beautiful as a golden statue who performed meritorious deeds together with my son." She summoned eight Brahmins, honored them greatly, and placed the golden statue on a carriage. She sent them off with the instruction, "Go, sirs. If you find a young woman in a family equal to ours in caste, lineage, and wealth who resembles this golden statue, give this statue as a betrothal gift (guarantee)."

The eight Brahmins accepted, saying, "This is a task for us wise men to perform." They left the village and consulted among themselves, "Where would it be best for us to go?" They unanimously agreed, "The kingdom of Madda is a land where beautiful women abound in this world. Therefore, let us go to the kingdom of Madda." They traveled to the city of Sāgala in Madda, placed the golden statue at the bathing ghat, and sat down nearby to observe.

At that time, the head nurse of the wealthy Brahmin's daughter, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, had bathed and adorned Bhaddā,
128:
and after leaving her in the auspicious chamber, she came to the bathing ghat to bathe. Seeing the golden statue, she thought, "My mistress has come to this bathing ghat before me." She spoke threateningly, saying, "Hey, you difficult-to-discipline girl! Why have you come to this bathing ghat alone?" and raising her hand to slap her, she said, "Go back home quickly!" and struck the back of the statue. The nurse's entire palm felt as if it had struck a stone slab, and it became very painful and shaken. Stepping back, she exclaimed, "Oh! Even though I see this large-necked woman who is so hard to the touch, I mistook her for my mistress. This person is not even fit to be the one who holds the clothes for my mistress!"

Then the eight Brahmins surrounded the nurse and asked, "Is your mistress really this beautiful?" The nurse replied, "What is this statue compared to her? My mistress is a hundred times, a thousand times more beautiful than this. If my mistress sits in a chamber twelve cubits long, there is no need to light a lamp; her natural radiance alone can dispel the darkness." The eight Brahmins said, "If that is so, let us go," and taking the nurse with them, they placed the golden statue on the carriage and stood at the gate of the house of the wealthy Brahmin of the Kosiya clan, making their arrival known.

The wealthy Brahmin of the Kosiya clan, after showing hospitality to the visiting Brahmins, asked, "From where
129:
have you come?" The Brahmins replied, "We have come from the house of the wealthy Brahmin Kapila in the village of Mahātittha in Magadha." When asked for the reason for their visit, the Brahmins explained their purpose. The wealthy Brahmin of the Kosiya clan said, "Sirs, this is a good thing. The wealthy Brahmin Kapila is equal to us in caste, lineage, and wealth. I will give my daughter." He then accepted the golden statue as the betrothal gift. The Brahmins sent word back to the wealthy Brahmin Kapila, saying, "We have obtained the maiden; please make all the necessary arrangements."

## Two Letters

Hearing this news, the servants of the youth Pippali joyfully told him, "Master, a maiden who can be compared to the golden statue has been found for you." Pippali thought, "I thought they would not find one. But these people say, 'A maiden has been found.' Since I am one who has no desire for this, I will send a letter to Bhaddā." He went to a secluded place and wrote a letter:

"Sister Bhaddā should marry another person who is suitable in caste, lineage, and wealth. As for me, I am one who will leave the world to become a monk. I do not want you to be unhappy later."

He then had the letter sent secretly to Bhaddā.
130: The wealthy young lady Bhaddā Kāpilānī also heard the news, "My parents wish to give me in marriage to the young man Pippali, the son of the wealthy Brahmin Kapila of Mahātittha village in the Magadha kingdom." Just like him, she went to a secluded place and wrote a letter to be sent secretly to the young man Pippali: "Brother Pippali, I wish for you to take another wife who is suitable to your caste, lineage, and wealth. As for me, I am one who will go forth into the forest and become a nun. I do not want you to be unhappy in the future." When the messengers from both sides met on the road, Bhaddā's people asked, "Friends, from whom and to whom is this letter you are carrying?" Pippali's people replied honestly, "This is a letter sent by our master, the wealthy son Pippali, to the wealthy daughter Bhaddā." Then Pippali's people asked, "Friends, from whom and to whom is the letter you are carrying?" Bhaddā's people also confessed straightforwardly, "This is a letter sent by our mistress, the wealthy young lady Bhaddā, to the wealthy son Pippali." When the people from both sides agreed to open and read the two letters, they understood the meaning of the letters, which were filled with an amazing and intense sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). They said, "Look at the actions of this young man and young lady!"
131:
They spoke thus and, tearing up both letters, discarded them in the forest. They then wrote two new letters expressing mutual agreement and joy and sent them to the bridegroom and the bride. In this way, although the merchant's son Pippali and the merchant's daughter Bhaddā had no desire for the household life, they reached the time of marriage according to the arrangements of their parents and intermediaries.

## The Unfading Garlands

On the very day of the wedding, the merchant's son and daughter each took a garland of flowers and placed them on their respective sides in the middle of the bed. After dinner, they both came to the bedchamber together to retire. The merchant's son Pippali got onto the bed from the right side, and the young merchant's daughter Bhaddā got onto the bed from the left side. She then made a vow, saying, "Let it be recognized that lust has arisen in the mind of the one whose flowers fade. Let no one touch these garlands."

Because both of them were afraid of touching each other's bodies, they spent the entire three watches of the night without sleeping, and the flowers did not fade. During the day, they lived like brother and sister, without even a smile of greed or lust.

## Great Wealth of the Merchant

Both the merchant's son and daughter did not involve themselves at all in the attachment to sensual pleasures known as worldly bait (loka-āmisa). They did not even consider the business of the household until their mother and father...
132:
passed away; only then did they manage the household business. The wealth of the young merchant Pippali was immense. His gold and silver amounted to eighty-seven billion (koti). Every day, the gold dust rubbed off from his body and discarded could fill about twelve Magadhan measures (kummāsa) if collected. There were sixty large reservoirs equipped with machinery. The area of his farmland was twelve yojanas wide. There were fourteen large villages for the servants and workers (each the size of Anurādhapura in Sri Lanka), fourteen elephant corps, fourteen cavalry corps, and fourteen chariot corps.

## Spiritual Urgency of the Merchant and His Wife

One day, the great merchant Pippali rode his well-adorned horse to the fields. While standing at the edge of the field, he saw crows and other birds picking out and eating earthworms and insects from the soil turned up by the plows. He asked, "Friends, what are these crows and birds eating?" When the servants replied, "Master, they are eating earthworms and insects," the great merchant Pippali asked, "Friends, whose demerit (akusala kamma) is this evil deed committed by these crows and birds?" The servants replied, "Master, since they are plowing the fields for you, this evil demerit is yours." Upon hearing this, the great merchant Pippali was struck with great spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and...
133: "If this evil demerit committed by these crows and birds is indeed my evil demerit, what benefit is there for me in eighty-seven koṭis of gold and silver? It is of no benefit. What benefit is there in the wealth of twelve yojanas of farmland, sixty large reservoirs with machinery, and fourteen villages of workers? It is of no benefit. Therefore, I shall hand over all this wealth to the mistress Bhaddā Kāpilānī, go forth into the forest, and become a monk," he reflected deeply. At that same moment, the mistress Bhaddā Kāpilānī was sitting surrounded by her nurses, having spread sesame seeds from three large pots on mats to dry in the sun within the house compound. Seeing crows pecking and eating the sesame insects, she asked the nurses, "Mothers, what are these crows eating?" When the nurses replied, "O Mistress, they are eating sesame insects," the mistress Bhaddā asked again, "Mothers, whose evil demerit is this demerit caused by the crows pecking and eating the sesame insects?" The nurses replied, "O Mistress, since it is being done for you, this evil demerit is your demerit." Then the mistress Bhaddā Kāpilānī reflected deeply, "Oh, for me, four cubits of cloth for clothing and one measure of rice for food would be sufficient. I cannot wear more than four cubits of cloth,
134:
I cannot wear more than this, nor can I eat more than one measure of cooked rice. If the evil demerit committed by so many people were to be my own, I would certainly not be able to lift my head from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) even in a thousand lives. As soon as my lord returns, I will hand over all the wealth to him, leave the household, and become a nun." Thus she reflected deeply.

## Both Renounce the World

When the merchant Pippali returned home, he took a bath and went up to the palace, sitting on the merchant's couch worthy only of noble ones. Then, a great meal suitable for universal monarchs was prepared and served to the merchant. The merchant Pippali and his wife, the lady Bhaddā Kāpilānī, ate together. When the attendants had left, they went to a secluded place and sat quietly in a peaceful spot.

Then, the merchant Pippali and his wife Bhaddā Kāpilānī consulted each other:

(Pippali)
"Lady Bhaddā, how much wealth did you bring when you came to this house?"

(Bhaddā)
"My lord, I brought wealth amounting to fifty-five thousand cartloads."

(Pippali)
"All this wealth you brought, as well as the eighty-seven billion existing in this house, and the large reservoirs equipped with machinery..."
135: and all other wealth and possessions. I give them all to you alone." (Bhaddā) "O Lord, where then will you go?" (Pippali) "Mistress Bhaddā, as for me, I shall become a monk." (Bhaddā) "O Lord, I too have been waiting for the time of your return. I too shall become a nun." Thus they consulted each other. For these two who had fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), the three worlds of existence—the sensual realm (Kāma), the fine-material realm (Rūpa), and the immaterial realm (Arūpa)—appeared like three leaf-roofed huts engulfed in blazing fire. Therefore, the two great beings had robes and alms-bowls brought from the market, shaved each other's hair, and declared, "Our renunciation is dedicated to the Arahants who are worthy of the highest offerings in the world." They put on the monastic robes, placed their bowls in their respective bags, slung them over their left shoulders, and descended from the palace. Not a single maidservant, manservant, or worker in the house recognized the two noble ones. Then, as the two noble ones left the Mahātittha Brahmin village and passed through the gate of the workers' village, the villagers recognized them by their appearance and demeanor as their two masters. They wept bitterly, prostrated at their feet, and said, "Lords, why
136:
"Why do you leave us helpless?" they lamented. The two noble ones replied, "Friends, we have gained great spiritual urgency (saṃvega), realizing that the three realms of existence are like a hut made of leaves engulfed in a blazing fire. If we were to work to free each of you from the state of being servants to the king, even a hundred years would not suffice. You yourselves must wash your heads, free yourselves from the state of being servants to the king, and live your lives." Having said this, they departed while the servants were weeping and wailing.

## The Two Noble Ones Parting Ways
While walking ahead, the Elder Pippali looked back and reflected: "This beautiful lady, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, whose worth is equal to the whole of Jambudīpa, is following behind me. If someone were to think wrongly, 'These two cannot part from each other; they are doing what is unbecoming for monastics,' there is a reason for such wrong thoughts. Furthermore, if someone were to have a corrupt mind towards us and consequently reach the lower realms, they might indeed go there. Therefore, it is only fitting and proper that I part from this beautiful lady Bhaddā Kāpilānī."

Thus he reflected.
137:
As the Great Elder continued his journey, he encountered a fork in the road and stood at the point where the path divided into two. Bhaddā Therī, following behind, also arrived, paid homage to the Great Elder, and stood there. Then, the Great Elder said to Bhaddā Therī, “O Bhaddā, if people see a beautiful woman like you following me, they might wrongly think, ‘Even after ordaining, these two cannot part from one another.’ If they harbor such corrupt thoughts and commit an offense against us, the multitude of people would be headed for the four woeful states. Therefore, choose whichever of these two paths you prefer; I shall take the other path which you do not desire.”

Bhaddā Therī replied, “Indeed, Bhante, for monks, womankind is an impurity. People will surely blame us, saying, ‘Even after ordaining, they cannot part from one another.’ Please, Bhante, take one path, and I shall take the other; let us two part ways.” Having said this, she circumambulated him three times, keeping him to her right. She paid respect with the five-point prostration at the four directions—front, back, left, and right. Then, raising her joined palms in reverence, she said, “The friendship and intimacy we have shared since a hundred thousand aeons ago ends today.” She continued, “Venerable sirs are of the right-hand nature; therefore, the right-hand path is suitable and proper for you. We women are of the left-hand nature; therefore, the left-hand path is suitable and proper for us.” After saying this and paying homage, she departed along the left-hand path.
138:
When those two noble ones parted and went their separate ways, this Great Earth quaked violently, resonating with a great echo as if to say, “Though I can bear the weight of the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Meru, I am no longer able to bear the weight of the virtues of you two noble ones.” In the sky, there was a sound like a thunderclap. The Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Meru rose higher and higher (due to the earthquake).

## The Meeting of the Buddha and the Great Elder
At that time, the Buddha had arrived at Rājagaha after his first rainy season retreat and was dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery (this was during the same year he attained Buddhahood, before he had traveled to Kapilavatthu). While the Buddha was staying in the Gandhakuṭī chamber within the great Veḷuvana Monastery, he heard the sound of the Great Earth quaking and contemplated, “For whom does this Great Earth tremble?” Upon reflection, he realized, “The young man Pippali and the lady Bhaddā Kāpilānī have renounced immeasurable wealth for my sake and entered the monkhood. This earthquake occurred at the place where they parted due to the power of the virtues of them both. It is proper that I should go and show them favor and support.” Having considered this, he departed from the Gandhakuṭī chamber, taking only his bowl and robes. Without calling any of the eighty great disciples to follow him, he traveled alone for a distance of three gāvutas.
139:
The Buddha went to welcome him and sat cross-legged at the foot of a banyan tree named Bahuputtaka, located between Rājagaha and Nālandā.

In particular, the Buddha did not sit there inconspicuously like an ordinary monk practicing the Pāṃsukūla dhutaṅga. Instead, to increase the faith of Venerable Mahākassapa, who had never seen the Buddha before, he sat without concealing his natural Buddha-glory, which was radiant with the major and minor marks. He emitted solid Buddha-rays that shone brilliantly for a distance of eighty cubits. At that moment, the Buddha-rays—some the size of a leaf-umbrella, some the size of a chariot wheel, and some the size of a pinnacled palace—flashed here and there, making the entire forest glow as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen simultaneously. Thus, the whole forest became exceedingly beautiful, like the sky sparkling with stars or a body of water filled with blooming five-colored lotuses, due to the splendor of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Although the trunk of a banyan tree is naturally white, its leaves naturally dark green, and its mature leaves naturally reddish, on that day, because they were suffused with the continuous Buddha-rays, the entire Bahuputtaka banyan tree with its many branches appeared brilliantly golden.
140:
Venerable Mahākassapa thought, “This noble one must indeed be my teacher, the Exalted Buddha. It is for the sake of this very Buddha that I have renounced the world.” From the moment he saw the Buddha, he approached while bowing repeatedly. He paid homage with deep respect at three points: once from afar, once from a middle distance, and once when he reached the Buddha’s presence. Then, he formally accepted discipleship by declaring three times: “Satthā me bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmi—Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple. Satthā me bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmi—Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple.”

Then the Buddha said to Venerable Mahākassapa, “Kassapa, if you were to show such extreme reverence to this Great Earth, it would not be able to bear it. However, such extreme reverence shown by you, who knows the greatness of the virtues of the Buddha who has come rightly like the Buddhas of the past, is not even able to stir a single hair of mine. Sit down, Kassapa; I shall give you your inheritance.” (This is the explanation found in the Commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Ekakanipāta, Etadaggavagga, AA. i. 142, and the Commentary to the Theragāthā, Cattālīsanipāta, Mahākassapattheragāthā, ThagA. ii. 443).
141:
In the Nidānavagga 5, Kassapa Saṃyutta, 11. Cīvara Sutta (Burmese Pitaka Translation, page 409), it is stated that when Venerable Mahākassapa had thus solemnly declared his discipleship three times, the Buddha said to him: “Kassapa, if anyone were to say ‘I know’ without knowing, or ‘I see’ without seeing such a disciple who is endowed with a wholehearted devotion, his head would fall off. Kassapa, because I know, I say ‘I know’; because I see, I say ‘I see.’”

(The meaning here is: If such a disciple, full of faith and devotion with a wholehearted mind, were to show such extreme reverence—as Venerable Mahākassapa is doing now—to any outside teacher (bāhiraka) who claims to know and see without actually knowing and seeing, that outside teacher’s head would fall from his neck like a ripe palmyra fruit falling from its stalk; it would split into seven pieces.

To clarify the Buddha’s intended meaning: If Venerable Mahākassapa were to show this extreme reverence with such mental devotion to the great ocean, the waters of the ocean would vanish like a drop of water placed on a red-hot iron plate. If he were to show it to the Cakkavāḷa mountain, it would crumble and be destroyed like a handful of chaff. If he were to show it...
142:
...to Mount Meru, it would be destroyed and scattered like a lump of dough pecked at by a crow’s beak. If he were to show it to the Great Earth, the Great Earth would be scattered like a heap of ashes blown by the wind. The reverence of the Great Elder, which possesses such power, cannot even stir a single hair on the Buddha’s feet. Let alone Venerable Mahākassapa, even if a thousand or a hundred thousand monks similar to the Great Elder were to manifest such reverence, they would not be able to cause even a single hair on the Buddha’s feet to tremble or change, nor could they stir a single thread of the pāṃsukūla robe worn by the Blessed One. Such is the greatness of the Buddha’s power.)

## Granting Ordination by Acceptance of Exhortation
As mentioned before, the Buddha said to Venerable Mahākassapa, “Sit down, Kassapa; I shall give you your inheritance.” (As stated in the Nidānavagga 5, Kassapa Saṃyutta, 11. Cīvara Sutta, Burmese Pitaka Translation, page 409):

“Kassapa, therefore, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will establish a keen sense of shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa) toward all monks, whether they be seniors, juniors, or of middle standing’ (1).

Kassapa, therefore, you should train yourself thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma I hear that is connected with what is wholesome, I will listen to all that Dhamma with respect, paying attention, applying my whole mind to it, and lending an attentive ear’ (2).”
143:
143

“Kassapa, therefore, in this Dispensation, you should train yourself thus: ‘Mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by joy, shall not desert me.’” (3)—

The Buddha gave these three instructions of exhortation. The Elder Mahākassapa also respectfully accepted these three exhortations. These three instructions themselves constituted the admission to the Order and the higher ordination for the Venerable Mahākassapa. In this Dispensation, only the Elder Mahākassapa received this type of ordination, which is known as the *ovādapaṭiggahaṇa upasampadā* (ordination by accepting exhortation).

(In this context: The Blessed One granted the status of a monk to the Elder Mahākassapa through these three exhortations. Regarding the first exhortation (1), the meaning is: “Dear Kassapa, you must first and foremost arouse and maintain intense shame (*hiri*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) towards all three types of fellow practitioners: those senior to you in age and seniority, those junior to you, and those of middle seniority equal to you.” This first exhortation was taught to the Elder Mahākassapa to abandon the pride of birth (*jātimāna*), as he was of the Brahmin caste.

Regarding the second exhortation (2), the meaning is: “Dear Kassapa, while listening to the faultless Dhamma, you must not let your mind wander elsewhere, but must listen respectfully, applying both the ear of wisdom and the physical ear throughout the beginning, middle, and end.” This second exhortation was taught to the Elder Mahākassapa to abandon the pride of being a person of great learning (*bahussuta*), which can lead to self-conceit.

Regarding the third exhortation (3), the meaning is: “Dear Kassapa, you must strive and exert yourself so that the first jhāna, which is accompanied by the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) arising from mindfulness directed to the body and the object of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), does not depart from your mental continuum.”
144:
144

This was the intended meaning. This third exhortation was taught to the Elder Mahākassapa to abandon the greed and craving (*taṇhā-lobha*) for his own body that might arise based on his physical perfection (*upadhi*), as he was a person endowed with a handsome appearance.)

After the Blessed One had granted the *ovādapaṭiggahaṇa* ordination to the Elder Mahākassapa at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree as described, He departed from the foot of that banyan tree and continued His journey, making the Elder His attendant monk. The Blessed One was adorned and beautiful with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa*), while the Elder Mahākassapa was appropriately beautiful, adorned with seven of the marks of a Great Man. The Elder followed closely behind the Blessed One, like a small golden boat following a large golden boat. After traveling some distance, the Blessed One stepped off the main road and indicated His intention to sit at the foot of a certain tree. The Elder, realizing that “the Blessed One wishes to sit,” folded his outer robe (*dukuṭa*), which was very soft, into four layers and spread it out, then addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, the Fortunate One, sit here. Such sitting by the Blessed One will be for my long-term benefit and happiness.”

## The Exchange of Robes

The Blessed One sat upon the seat made of the four-layered robe and then, with His golden hand which had the color of a Paduma lotus, He touched the edge of the four-layered robe and praised it, saying:
145:
145

“Dear Kassapa, this old cloth robe of yours, this *dukuṭa* robe, is very soft indeed.”

(In this context: If it is asked, “Why did He speak such words of praise?”, the answer is: “He spoke these words of praise because He wished to exchange robes with the Elder.”

If it is asked, “Why did He wish to exchange robes?”, the answer is: “He wished to exchange them because He wanted to place the Elder in His own position.”

One might ask, “Were Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna not there to be placed in His position?” The answer is: It is not that they were not there; they were. However, this thought occurred in the Blessed One’s mind: “These two, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will not remain for long; they will attain Parinibbāna before Me. But Kassapa will live for a long life of one hundred and twenty years. Four months after My Parinibbāna, he will reside in a cave where the *carayī* tree grows, and after conducting the Council (*Saṅgāyana*) for both the Dhamma and Vinaya, he will ensure that My Dispensation can continue and endure for five thousand years.” Because He saw this, He considered that if He placed the Elder in His own position, the monks would show respect and humility toward the Elder. This was the primary reason He wished to place the Elder in His position. Because He wished to place the Elder in His position, He desired to exchange robes. And because He desired to exchange robes, He spoke those words of praise.)

It was the natural character of the Elder that if anyone spoke of the virtues of his alms-bowl or his robes, he would offer them, saying, “Venerable Sirs, please accept this bowl or this robe for yourselves.”
146:
146

Therefore, the Elder, perceiving the hint, thought, “The Blessed One is praising the softness of my *dukuṭa* robe, my double-layered robe; He must wish to wear it.” He then addressed the Buddha: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, the Fortunate One, wear this *dukuṭa* robe.” The Blessed One asked, “Dear Kassapa, what robe will you wear?” When the Elder Mahākassapa replied, “Venerable Sir, if I may receive the robe that the Blessed One wears, I shall wear it,” the Blessed One said: “Dear Kassapa, will you be able to wear this rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) which has become worn out by My wearing it? Indeed, on the day I took up this rag-robe, this great earth (*Mahāpathavī*) shook, extending to the limits of the waters. This robe which has been used and worn out by the Buddhas cannot be worn by a person of little merit; it is only worthy of being accepted by a person who is a natural bearer of rag-robes (*jāti-paṃsukūla*) and who is capable of fulfilling the practice (*paṭipatti*).” Saying this, He exchanged robes with the Elder Mahākassapa. In this way, after exchanging robes, the Blessed One wore the robe that the Elder had worn, and the Elder wore the robe of the Blessed One. At that moment, this great earth, though having no consciousness, shook violently as if to say, “Venerable Sir, You have done what is difficult to do; there has never been a case before where a robe worn by the Buddha was given to a disciple; I am unable to bear the weight of Your virtues,” and it trembled to the limits of the waters.
147:
## (c) The Great Elder Attaining the Special Dhamma and Receiving the Title of Etadagga

The Venerable Mahākassapa, thinking, "I have now received the robes used by the Buddhas; what else is there for me to do for the sake of the higher Paths and Fruits? There is nothing more," did not become conceited just by receiving the robes. Instead, in the presence of the Buddha, he wholeheartedly accepted and undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). While striving and cultivating the recluse's Dhamma, he remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days. At dawn on the eighth day, he attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa).

Taking the Venerable Mahākassapa as an example, the Buddha preached many discourses found in the Kassapa Saṃyutta of the Nidānavagga. (Please refer to the Burmese translation of the Nidānavagga, Kassapa Saṃyutta).

The Buddha praised the Great Elder through many suttas, such as the Candūpama Sutta, saying: "Kassapo, bhikkhave, candūpamo kulāni upasaṅkamati — Monks, like the moon, Kassapa withdraws his body and mind; being always like a guest, he approaches the four classes of families without any harshness in body, speech, or mind." Later, based on the Great Elder's practice of dhutaṅga as recorded in the Kassapa Saṃyutta, the Buddha declared:

"Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhutavādānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākassapo — Monks, among my monk disciples who advocate the ascetic practices, the foremost is Mahākassapa."
148:
148

among my monk disciples who themselves practice the noble ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) which shake off the defilements, and who also teach, demonstrate, and advise others to do so, Mahākassapa is the best and the foremost.”

This is the account of the Elder Mahākassapa.
