## (5) The Account of the Elder Anuruddha

## (A) The Elder’s Past Aspiration

One hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time when the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world, the future Elder Anuruddha was a wealthy man whose name was not well-known. One afternoon, he followed a group of people who were going to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. The wealthy man paid respect to the Buddha with devotion, stood at the edge of the assembly, and listened to the Dhamma. After the Buddha Padumuttara had preached the Dhamma discourse in its proper sequence, He placed a certain monk in the position of *Etadagga* for being foremost among those who possess the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).

At that time, the thought occurred to the wealthy man: “The Blessed One Himself has placed this monk in the position of *Etadagga* for possessing the divine eye; therefore, this monk is truly superior and noble. It would be well if I, too, in the Dispensation of a future Buddha, could become the best and foremost among the monks who possess the divine eye.”
149:
After having this thought, he went to the Buddha amidst the assembly, invited the Buddha along with the community of monks, and on the following day, after providing a great offering to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, he reflected, "I have aspired to a very great position." In that same manner, he invited them daily, saying, "Please come for the sake of merit today, please come for the sake of merit tomorrow," and for seven consecutive days, he performed a great offering. Then, he offered excellent robes to the Buddha and the accompanying monks and made an aspiration:

"Venerable Sir, I have not performed this act of worship to attain celestial bliss, nor have I performed it to attain human bliss. Indeed, seven days ago, you placed a certain monk in the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). May I also, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become the foremost among monks who possess the divine eye, just like this monk."

Having made this prayer, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet. The Buddha, looking into the future and seeing that the householder's wish would be fulfilled, declared: "Lay disciple, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will appear in the world. In the dispensation of that Buddha, you will be the one named Anuruddha Thera, the foremost among monks who possess the divine eye."
150:
After giving this prophecy and delivering a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, the Buddha returned to the monastery. 

The householder also performed meritorious deeds as long as the Buddha was alive. After the parinibbāna of Padumuttara Buddha, when a great golden stupa seven leagues (yūjanā) high had been built, he approached the community of monks and asked, "Venerable sirs, what is the preliminary meritorious act for attaining the divine eye?" The community of monks replied, "Lay disciple, it is proper to give the gift of lamps." Saying, "Very well, venerable sirs, I shall perform the gift of lamps," he first had one thousand large lamp-trees made, each containing a thousand lamps, and offered them. Following those one thousand large lamp-trees, he had medium-sized lamp-trees made and offered them, and following those, he had small lamp-trees made and offered them. In this way, he offered thousands of lamp-trees, and the remaining lamps were so numerous they could not be counted.

## Offering Lamps to the Stupa of Kassapa Buddha

Thus, the future Venerable Anuruddha, that householder, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandering through the realms of devas and humans. After one hundred thousand aeons had passed, during the time of Kassapa Buddha in this Bhadda-kappa, he was born as a householder in the city of Bārāṇasī. After the Buddha's parinibbāna, when a great stupa one league high had been built,
151:
he had many golden bowls cast, filled each golden bowl with clarified butter, placed a lump of molasses in the center of the golden bowls, and lit them. He offered the lamps by placing the golden bowls around the stupa so that their rims touched. Furthermore, he had a very large golden bowl cast for himself, filled it with clarified butter, and lit one thousand wicks around its rim. For the central wick, he wrapped it with coarse cloth and lit it. Carrying this large golden bowl with a thousand lit lamps on his head, he circumambulated the one-league-high stupa in worship throughout the three watches of the night. In this manner, he performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived in that life, and when he passed away from that existence, he was reborn in the deva realm.

## The Life as Annabhāra

Again, before our Buddha appeared, he took rebirth in a poor family in the city of Bārāṇasī and lived depending on a wealthy merchant named Sumana. The name of that poor man was "Annabhāra." The merchant Sumana gave a great offering daily at his gate to the destitute, travelers, and beggars.

One day, a Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana. Upon emerging from that attainment, he reflected, "Whom should I favor today?" Generally, Paccekabuddhas are very compassionate toward the poor. Thus, the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha
152:
thought, "Today, I should favor the poor man Annabhāra." Knowing that "Now Annabhāra will be returning home from the forest," he took his bowl and robes, ascended into the sky from Mount Gandhamādana, and stood directly in front of Annabhāra at the village gate.

Annabhāra, seeing the Paccekabuddha coming with an empty bowl (without alms-food), paid respect and asked, "Venerable Sir, did you receive alms-food?" When the Paccekabuddha replied, "I shall receive it, lay disciple," Annabhāra said, "Venerable Sir, please wait here for a moment." He went quickly and asked his wife at home, "O wife, is there a portion of rice kept for me, or is there none?" When the wife replied, "It is there, my lord," he returned from that spot, took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, and upon reaching home, said, "O wife, because we did not perform meritorious deeds in previous lives, we have to live in longing for food. Even when we have the intention to give, we often lack the objects to give. Even when we have objects to give, we often do not find a recipient. Today, I have met the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha, and my portion of rice is also available. Pour my portion of rice into this bowl."
153:
"The very wise wife thought, "Since my lord is offering his portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha, I too should be a sharer in this merit." Considering this, she also added her own portion of rice into the bowl of the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha. Annabhāra took the bowl and offered it into the hands of the Paccekabuddha, making a prayer: "Venerable Sir, may we be swiftly liberated from such a life of poverty and hardship." The Paccekabuddha also gave a blessing, saying, "O meritorious lay disciple, may it be as you have prayed."

Annabhāra spread his upper garment in a certain place and said, "Venerable Sir, please sit here and partake of the meal." The Paccekabuddha sat on the place spread by Annabhāra and partook of the meal while reflecting on the nine aspects of loathsomeness (1. going for alms - gamana, 2. seeking - pariyesana, 3. consuming - paribhogha, 4. the secretions such as phlegm, bile, blood, and pus - āsaya, 5. the stomach as the receptacle - nidhāna, 6. undigested food - aparipakka, 7. digested food - paripakka, 8. the primary result - phala [and] the consequences that ooze and seep here and there - nissanda, 9. the smearing - makkhana). 

(In this context, if the primary result - phala and the consequence - nissanda are taken separately, there are ten aspects. The manner of reflecting on the loathsomeness through these nine or ten aspects should be studied in the commentary to the Visuddhimagga on the perception of loathsomeness in food [āhāre paṭikūlasaññā], and especially in the section on meditation in the Paramatthasaruūpabhedanī [Bhedanī 2, page 372] written by the Most Venerable Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw.)
154:
After the Paccekabuddha had finished the meal, Annabhāra offered water for washing the bowl. When the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha had completed the meal, he performed the act of appreciation (anumodanā):

Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, sabba-meva samijjhatu.
Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā.

Tuyhaṃ = for you; icchitaṃ = what is desired; patthitaṃ = what is aspired; sabba-meva = all entirely; samijjhatu = may it be fulfilled. Pannaraso cando yathā = like the full moon on the fifteenth day of the waxing fortnight; tuyhaṃ = for you; sabbe = all entirely; saṅkappā = all noble thoughts and intentions; pūrentu = may they be fulfilled.

After giving this blessing, he continued on his journey.

## The Goddess Gives Praise

At that time, the goddess guarding the parasol of the merchant Sumana uttered a cry of praise three times: "Aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ, Upariṭṭhe su-patiṭṭhitaṃ = Oh, what a supreme gift, well-established in the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha!" The merchant Sumana asked, "Hey goddess, have you not seen me giving alms for such a long time?" The goddess replied, "O merchant, I did not give the 'Sādhu' praise for your gift. I gave the 'Sādhu' praise because I was so delighted with the faith of the poor man Annabhāra for the alms-food he offered to the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha."
155:
“Oh, how wonderful! Although I have given alms for such a long time, I have not been able to make the devas cry out 'Sādhu' in approval. This poor man Annabhāra, though he lives depending on me, has obtained a worthy recipient and, by offering just one meal, has made them cry out in praise. It is proper that I give this poor man Annabhāra suitable wealth and make the meal he offered mine.” Having thought thus, he sent for Annabhāra and asked, “Did you give anything as an offering to anyone today?” The poor man Annabhāra replied, “I did, my lord merchant. I gave my own portion of rice to the Noble Uparitṭha Paccekabuddha.” Then the great merchant Sumana requested, “Come, Annabhāra, take this. Take one kahāpaṇa and give that meal you offered to me.”

When the poor man Annabhāra refused, saying, “My lord merchant, I cannot give it,” the great merchant Sumana increased the offer up to a thousand kahāpaṇas. However, the poor man Annabhāra continued to refuse, saying, “I cannot give it even for a thousand kahāpaṇas.” Then the great merchant Sumana, giving up on the purchase, requested again, “Friend Annabhāra, if you cannot give that meal, let it be. Accept these thousand kahāpaṇas and give me the share of the merit of that alms-offering.” Annabhāra replied, “I do not clearly know whether I should or should not give this share of merit. However, I will ask the Noble Uparitṭha Paccekabuddha, and if he says I should give it, I will.”
156:
He ran after the Noble Paccekabuddha and, upon catching up, he addressed him: “Venerable Sir, the great merchant Sumana has offered me a thousand kahāpaṇas and is asking for the share of merit from the meal I offered to you. Should I give it or not, Venerable Sir?” Then the Noble Paccekabuddha said:

“Wise man, I shall give you a simile. Suppose in a village of a hundred houses, only one house has a lamp lit. If the people from the other ninety-nine houses come with their own oil and wicks, light them from that lamp, and take them away, does the light of the original lamp remain as it was, or does it diminish and disappear?”

When asked thus, Annabhāra replied, “Venerable Sir, it does not diminish. The light increases even more than before.” Then the Noble Paccekabuddha said:

“Wise man, it is just the same. Whether it be a single portion of gruel or a single portion of rice, when the donor shares the merit of their offering with others, whether they give it to a hundred people or a thousand, the merit increases for as many people as they share it with. Now, in your offering of alms, you have offered only one meal. If you share the portion of merit with the great merchant Sumana, for you, the alms-offering...
157:
(the original) becomes one, and for the great merchant Sumana, the alms-offering (the increased merit) becomes another. In this way, there will be two alms-offerings.”

Thus he explained clearly. The poor man Annabhāra, his doubts cleared and feeling satisfied, respectfully paid homage to the Noble Paccekabuddha. He then went to the great merchant Sumana and joyfully shared the merit, saying, “My lord merchant, please take the share of merit from my alms-offering.” Thereafter, the great merchant Sumana and the poor man Annabhāra exchanged the following words:

(Merchant)
“Come, friend, take these thousand kahāpaṇas.”

(Annabhāra)
“My lord merchant, I am not selling the meal. Indeed, out of great faith, I share the portion of merit with you.”

(Merchant)
“Friend, you share the portion of merit with me out of great faith. As for me, I wish to honor your virtue, so I give you these thousand kahāpaṇas. Please accept them, friend.”

When he said this, Annabhāra replied, “Very well, let it be so, my lord merchant,” and accepted the thousand kahāpaṇas. Then the great merchant Sumana spoke further, inviting him: “Friend, from the time you have received these thousand kahāpaṇas...
158:
you no longer have the need to work with your own hands (meaning: you are no longer a poor laborer as before). Build a house on the main road and live there. I will have whatever items you desire brought to you; I will give them to you. Therefore, just have the items you desire brought from my house.”

## Becoming a Great Wealthy Merchant on That Very Day
An offering given to a Paccekabuddha who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) yields results in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya). Therefore, although the great merchant Sumana had not taken Annabhāra to the royal palace on other days, on that day, due to the power of the merit of the alms-offering that gives results in this life, he took Annabhāra with him to the golden palace.

When they arrived at the palace, because of Annabhāra’s merit, the King did not look at the merchant Sumana but gazed intently only at Annabhāra. Then the merchant Sumana and the King questioned and spoke to each other as follows:

(Merchant)
“Your Majesty, why do you gaze so intently at this man?”

(King)
“I look at him, great merchant, because I have never seen this man on other days.”

(Merchant)
“Your Majesty, this man is indeed one worthy of being gazed at intently.”

(King)
“Great merchant, what is the virtue of this man that makes him worthy of being gazed at intently?”
159:
(Merchant)
“Your Majesty, this man did not eat his own portion of rice today but offered it to the Noble Uparitṭha Paccekabuddha, and thus he is one who has received a thousand kahāpaṇas from my hand.”

(King)
“What is this man’s name?”

(Merchant)
“His name is Annabhāra, Your Majesty.”

(King)
“Since he has already received a thousand kahāpaṇas from your hand, he is also worthy of receiving a thousand from mine. I, too, shall honor this man.”

Saying this, the King also gave Annabhāra another thousand kahāpaṇas.

After that, the King said to his men, “Friends, find a house for this Annabhāra to live in.” The men replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and while they were clearing an old house site, they were amazed to find jars of jewels and gold touching each other at the rims at every spot they dug with their hoes. They reported this to the King. The King ordered, “Friends, if that is so, go and dig them up.” But as the men were digging, the jars of jewels and gold sank deeper and deeper. When they reported this to the King again, the King commanded once more, “Friends, do not dig in my name, but...
160:
dig according to the instructions of Annabhāra.” The men went to that place and, saying that it was according to Annabhāra’s instructions, they dug. At every spot they dug with hoes and spades, jars of jewels and gold appeared in abundance like mushroom buds.

The men gathered all that gold, silver, and treasure and piled it up near the King. The King assembled his ministers and asked, “In this city of Bārāṇasī, who else besides Annabhāra possesses such vast wealth?” The ministers replied, “Your Majesty, no one else possesses such vast wealth.” Then the King issued a royal decree: “Friends, if that is so, let this Annabhāra be the royal merchant in my capital of Bārāṇasī, with the title ‘Dhana-seṭṭhī’.” On that very day, Annabhāra received the white umbrella of a merchant from the King and became the great merchant in the King's service, known as Mahādhana-seṭṭhī.

## (b) Becoming a Monk in the Final Life
From the time he became the royal merchant named Dhana-seṭṭhī, Annabhāra performed meritorious deeds until the end of his life. When he passed away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. That noble being, the future Venerable Anuruddha, wandered through the celestial and human realms for a very long time. During the time when our Buddha was to appear, he took conception in the palace of Sukkodana the Sakyan in the royal city of Kapilavatthu.
161:
On the day of his naming, he was given the name “Prince Anuruddha.” This Prince Anuruddha was the son of Sukkodana the Sakyan, the paternal uncle of the Buddha, and the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan. He was extremely delicate and possessed great merit.

After the Buddha first visited the city of Kapilavatthu and while he was staying at the Anupiya Grove on his return journey, Prince Anuruddha came to the presence of the Buddha together with Prince Bhaddiya, Prince Ānanda, Prince Bhagu, Prince Kimbila, Prince Devadatta, and Upāli the barber, and they were ordained as monks. (The details of this account have already been presented in Volume 3, pages 145 to 160 of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas. Please refer back to those passages here.)

## How Venerable Anuruddha Became an Arahant
After the six Sakyan princes, together with Upāli the barber, went to the Anupiya Grove and were ordained in the presence of the Buddha, among those seven monks, Venerable Bhaddiya attained the fruit of Arahantship—becoming an Arahant—within that very rainy season. Venerable Anuruddha developed the higher knowledge of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). Devadatta developed the eight mundane attainments and also attained mundane higher knowledges. Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Venerable Bhagu and Venerable Kimbila attained the fruit of Arahantship at a later time. The stories of the past aspirations and meritorious deeds of these elders will be evident in their respective places.
162:
In particular, after his ordination, the Venerable Anuruddha attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) within that very first rains retreat. He also developed the supernormal knowledge of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), which enabled him to see a thousandfold world system. One day, the Venerable Anuruddha went to the Venerable Sāriputta and said:

“Friend Sāriputta, with the Divine Eye, which is purified and surpasses the human eye, I can see a thousandfold world system (1). My energy is unflagging, my mindfulness is established without forgetfulness, my body is calm and tranquil, and my mind is well-concentrated on a single object (2). Yet, despite this, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging (3).”

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the Venerable Anuruddha:

“Friend Anuruddha, the thought ‘I can see a thousandfold world system with the Divine Eye, which is purified and surpasses the human eye’—this very thought is conceit (māna) in you (1).

“Friend Anuruddha, the thought ‘My energy is unflagging, my mindfulness is established without forgetfulness, my body is calm and tranquil, and my mind is well-concentrated on a single object’—
163:
this very thought is restlessness (uddhacca) in you (2).

“Friend Anuruddha, the thought ‘Yet, despite this, my mind is not yet liberated from the taints through non-clinging’—this very thought is worry (kukkucca) in you (3).

“I urge and request you: it would be good if the Venerable Anuruddha would abandon these three states (conceit, restlessness, and worry), and instead of attending to them, direct your mind toward the Deathless element (Nibbāna).”

After receiving this meditation instruction, the Venerable Anuruddha took his leave of the Buddha and traveled to the Ceti country. There, he stayed in the Eastern Bamboo Grove (Pācīnavaṃsadāya). While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, he meditated for half a month (fifteen days) without sleeping, practicing walking meditation. Because he had exerted himself so intensely in his meditation practice, his body became exhausted, and he sat down for a brief rest under a bamboo thicket. At that moment, the following Great Thoughts of a Great Person (Mahāpurisavitakka) arose clearly in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha. They arose as follows:
164:
(1) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one with few wishes (appiccha), not for one with many wishes.
(2) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one who is contented (santuṭṭha), not for one who is discontented.
(3) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one who is secluded (pavivitta), not for one who delights in company.
(4) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one who is energetic (āraddhavīriya), not for one who is lazy.
(5) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness (upaṭṭhitasati), not for one who is unmindful.
(6) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one with a concentrated mind (samāhita), not for one who is unconcentrated.
(7) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one who is wise (paññavanta), not for one who is unwise.

Thus, these thoughts clearly arose.

(A special note here: Regarding the person with few wishes, there are four types: (a) Paccaya-appiccha = one with few wishes regarding the four requisites; (b) Adhigama-appiccha = one who hides their attainment of the Paths and Fruits from others; (c) Pariyatti-appiccha = one who hides their extensive scriptural knowledge from others; (d) Dhutaṅga-appiccha = one who hides their practice of the ascetic duties (dhutaṅga).
165:
Thus, there are four types of persons with few wishes (appiccha).

(a) Among these four, the person with few wishes regarding requisites (paccaya-appiccha) accepts only a little even if much is offered; if a little is offered, they accept even less than that, and they do not accept everything.

(b) The person with few wishes regarding attainments (adhigama-appiccha) lives in seclusion, hiding their attainment of the Paths and Fruits from others, like the Elder Majjhantika. (A brief summary of Elder Majjhantika’s story: He was a great Arahant. However, his bowl and robes were worth only a single pāda (a quarter of a kahāpaṇa). On the day King Asoka dedicated his monastery, the Elder was the senior-most monk (Saṅghamahāthera). Seeing his bowl and robes were very poor, worn, and old, the people thought he was an insignificant monk and told him, “Venerable Sir, please step outside for a moment.” Only then did the Elder think, “If an Arahant like me does not support the King, who will?” He then dived into the earth and reappeared to receive the first offering of alms intended for the senior monk while others were unaware. Thus, although he was an Arahant, he did not wish for people to know him as such.)

(c) The person with few wishes regarding learning (pariyatti-appiccha) is one who, despite being proficient in the Tipitaka, does not want others to know of their great knowledge, like the Elder Tissa who lived in Sāketa.

A brief summary of his story: When monks requested him to teach the Pali texts and commentaries, he declined, saying he had no time. The monks then criticized him, saying, “Venerable Sir, if that is the case, you won't even have time to die.”
166:
Because of this criticism, he left his own group and monastery and went to the Kaṇikāravālika-samudda Monastery. There, he stayed for the three months of the rains retreat (living like an ordinary, unlearned elder), performing duties for the senior, junior, and middle-ranking monks, being of great service to them. On the full moon day of Mahāpavāraṇā at the end of the retreat, when a Dhamma assembly was held, he preached so profoundly that the gathered crowd was moved to horripilation, shouted “Sādhu,” and threw their turbans in the air in appreciation. To those who were not present, the news spread, causing a stir as they asked, “How can we hear the Dhamma from this Elder?” Fearing that people would recognize him as the one who preached that night, and due to his fewness of wishes regarding learning (pariyatti-appicchatā), he returned to his original residence before the people could find him.

(d) The person with few wishes regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-appiccha) does not want others to know that they observe ascetic practices, like the elder of two brother monks.

A brief summary of the elder brother’s story: Two brother monks lived on Cetiya Mountain. A supporter sent a piece of sugarcane for the elder brother. The younger brother brought it to the elder, explained the situation, and said, “Please enjoy this, Venerable Sir.” It was the time when the elder brother had finished his meal and was washing up. When the elder brother said, “Friend, that is enough,” the younger brother asked, “Why, Venerable Sir? Do you observe the practice of eating at one sitting (ekāsanika-dhutaṅga)?” The elder brother then said, “Friend, bring the sugarcane,” and
167:
although he had observed the ekāsanika-dhutaṅga for fifty years, because he wished to keep his practice secret, he consumed the sugarcane. After washing up, he re-undertook the ekāsanika-dhutaṅga and departed.

(The details of these four types of appiccha persons are taken from the Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 3, p. 226, while the stories are taken from the Majjhima Commentary, Vol. 2, pp. 45-46. From Majjhima Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 45 onwards, there are detailed explanations of the three types of desires, four types of fewness of wishes, twelve types of contentment, three types of seclusion, five types of association, etc. If desired, one should extract and note them from those commentaries and sub-commentaries.)

While the Venerable Anuruddha was reflecting on these seven Great Thoughts of a Great Person, the Buddha was staying in the Bhesakaḷā Grove (a sanctuary) near the city of Sumsumāragira in the Bhagga country. Between the Bhesakaḷā Grove and the bamboo grove where Anuruddha stayed, the Bhesakaḷā Grove was to the west and the bamboo grove was to the east. Therefore, that bamboo grove is called Pācīnavaṃsadāya—the Eastern Bamboo Grove relative to the Bhesakaḷā Grove where the Buddha was staying.

After reflecting on the seven Great Thoughts of a Great Person mentioned earlier, the Venerable Anuruddha moved to the next stage but was exhausted while trying to reflect on the eighth Great Thought. Indeed, for disciples, after reflecting on these qualities—fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), seclusion (paviveka), energy (vīriyārambha), established mindfulness (upaṭṭhitasatitā), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—as he moved higher to reflect on one more Dhamma...
168:
It is natural for it to be burdensome and tiring to consider and reflect upon. For disciples, it is natural to remain at the end of the Dhamma only through wisdom. For this reason, after Venerable Anuruddha had contemplated and reflected on the seventh Great Thought of a Great Man (Mahāpurisavitakka) concerning wisdom, he was weary in continuing to contemplate and reflect on the eighth Great Thought of a Great Man.

At that time, while staying in the Bhesakaḷā forest, the Blessed One realized, “Anuruddha is weary while reflecting on the eighth Great Thought of a Great Man.” He then thought, “I shall fulfill the wish and thought of Anuruddha,” and through his psychic power, he arrived before Venerable Anuruddha in an instant. Sitting on the prepared seat, he said:

“Excellent, Anuruddha! Excellent! Anuruddha, you have rightly reflected on the thoughts of a Great Man, thinking: ‘(1) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one with few wishes, not for one with many wishes... (7) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for the wise, not for the foolish.’

Anuruddha, if that is so, you should also reflect on this eighth thought of a Great Man: ‘(8) This ninefold supramundane Dhamma is for one who delights and rejoices in Nibbāna, which is free from the proliferation (papañca) of craving, conceit, and views that expand the cycle of rebirth. It is not for one who delights and rejoices in proliferation.’"
169:
“...It is not for one who delights and rejoices in proliferation.”

Thus, the Buddha completed the eighth Great Thought of a Great Man which was missing. After completing it, the Blessed One continued to teach Venerable Anuruddha that by contemplating these eight Great Thoughts of a Great Man, one can easily attain and dwell in the mundane first, second, third, and fourth jhānas. He also taught in detail that by contemplating these eight Great Thoughts and easily attaining the four mundane jhānas, one would easily achieve the four practices of the Lineage of the Noble Ones (Ariyavaṃsa-paṭipadā), namely: (1) Cīvarasantosa = contentment with robes, (2) Piṇḍapātasantosa = contentment with alms-food (note specifically that contentment with medicinal requisites is included here), (3) Senāsanasantosa = contentment with lodgings, and (4) Bhāvanārāmatā = delight in meditation. (The details of this teaching can be found starting from page 64 of the third volume of the Burmese translation of the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

After teaching this, the Blessed One considered, “In which lodging would the meditation subject be suitable (sappāya) for Anuruddha?” He knew well that staying in that very bamboo grove would be suitable.

“Anuruddha, therefore (since staying in this bamboo grove is suitable), you, dear son, should also spend the rainy season retreat right here in this bamboo grove in the Ceti country in the future.”
170:
Having said this, the Buddha ascended into the air and returned to the Bhesakaḷā forest. There, he taught the Dhamma of these eight Great Thoughts of a Great Man in detail to the monks again. (The details should be noted from page 66 of the third volume of the Burmese translation of the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

As soon as the Blessed One had departed, Venerable Anuruddha practiced the Dhamma of a recluse with great effort. Before long (during the following rainy season), he became an Arahant, free from taints and endowed with the Three Knowledges (tevijjā: recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of taints). He joyfully reflected, “Oh, the Blessed One, knowing my mind, came and completed the eighth Great Thought of a Great Man for me. My heart's desire has now reached its pinnacle.” Focusing on the Buddha's teaching and the supramundane Dhamma he had attained, he recited these verses of solemn utterance (Udāna):

(a) Knowing my thought,
the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world,
came to me through his psychic power
with a mind-made body.

In the world = in the three realms. Unsurpassed = peerless and most noble. The Teacher = the Buddha, the teacher of gods and men. My = of me, the Elder Anuruddha. Thought = the thought arising in the mind. Knowing = having known clearly and distinctly. With a mind-made body = with a body that moves swiftly and instantly due to the mind of supernormal knowledge. Through psychic power = with incomparable
171:
psychic power, he arrived in my presence in an instant.

(b) Just as my thought was,
he taught even beyond that.
The Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation,
taught non-proliferation.

My = of me, the Elder Anuruddha. Just as = in the manner of the seven thoughts. Thought = the thought of a Great Man. Was = had occurred. Beyond that = the eighth thought to be above those seven thoughts I had contemplated. Taught = he taught with compassion. (How did he teach?): Delighting in non-proliferation = the Blessed One, known as the Omniscient Buddha, who delights in the unconditioned Nibbāna—the true escape from the three types of proliferation that expand the cycle of rebirth—and dwells in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Non-proliferation = he taught the unconditioned Nibbāna, the true escape from the three types of proliferation that expand the cycle of rebirth, with compassion.

(c) Having understood his Dhamma,
I dwelt delighting in the Teaching.
The Three Knowledges have been attained;
the Buddha's Teaching is done.

I = I, the Elder Anuruddha. His = of that Blessed One known as the Omniscient Buddha, the pinnacle of the world. Dhamma = the teaching he spoke and revealed.
172:
Having understood = having reached the knowledge of the fruition of Arahantship. In the Teaching = in the Sasana of the threefold training. Delighting = being constantly delighted and rejoicing through the attainment of fruition. Dwelt = I have been able to live with the happiness of the present life. I = I, the Elder Anuruddha. The Three Knowledges = the three knowledges (recollection of past lives, divine eye, and destruction of taints). Attained = have been reached at the moment of the fruition of Arahantship. The Buddha's = of the Blessed One known as the Omniscient Buddha, the pinnacle of the world. Teaching = the Sasana of the threefold training. Done = has been fully practiced and accomplished upon reaching the fruition of Arahantship.

## Receiving the Foremost Title (Etadagga)

Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery, during an assembly to confer titles of foremost (Etadagga) upon various monks, he praised Venerable Anuruddha, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dibbacakkhukānaṃ yadidaṃ anuruddho = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), Anuruddha is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed him to the position of Etadagga in the matter of possessing the divine eye.

(Here, a question may arise: “Since other Arahants with the Three Knowledges and Arahants with the Six Supernormal Knowledges also possess the divine eye, why did the Buddha specifically appoint Venerable Anuruddha as the foremost in possessing the divine eye?” The answer is: While it is true that other Arahants with the Three Knowledges and Six Supernormal Knowledges also possess the divine eye, those Elders did not
173:
...they do not enter [the attainment]. As for the Venerable Anuruddha, except for the time he goes for alms and partakes of his meal, he spends most of his time expanding the light kasiṇa (āloka-kasiṇa) and viewing beings with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Thus, because the Venerable Anuruddha possessed greater mastery (vasībhāva) and practice in the divine eye both day and night compared to other elders, the Buddha appointed him to the foremost position (Etadagga) in 'attaining the divine eye.' This is the answer.

Alternatively, it can be explained that because the Venerable Anuruddha had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made aspirations for this position of Etadagga in the divine eye for a hundred thousand aeons, in this final life where his perfections (pāramī) were fulfilled, he habitually entered and practiced the divine eye more exceedingly than other Arahant elders, in accordance with his past tendencies (vāsanā). Therefore, the Buddha appointed the Venerable Anuruddha to the foremost position in 'attaining the divine eye.' This is the answer.

## The Venerable Anuruddha Receiving the Pāṃsukūla Robe Offered by a Deity
(Extracted from Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, 387-8)

While the Buddha was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha, one day the Venerable Anuruddha, having worn-out robes, was searching for refuse-rag (pāṃsukūla) cloth in places like dust heaps. His former wife from three lives ago had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a goddess named Jālinī.

The goddess Jālinī, seeing the Great Elder searching for coarse pāṃsukūla cloth, [prepared] for the Elder a piece of cloth thirteen cubits long and four cubits wide...
174:
three celestial cloths, thirteen cubits long and four cubits wide. She thought, “If I offer these celestial cloths to the Elder in this form, he will not accept them.” So, she placed them in a rubbish heap in front of the Elder who was searching for coarse rag-robes, making only the fringes and edges of those celestial cloths visible.

When the Elder came along that path searching for rag-robes, he saw only the fringes and edges of those celestial cloths. He picked them up right there, thinking, “These cloths are excellent rag-robes,” and after seeing the three celestial cloths mentioned, he took them and departed.

Later, on the day the Elder was making his robes, the Blessed One, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to Venerable Anuruddha's dwelling where the robes were being made and sat down. The Elders belonging to the group of the eighty Great Disciples also sat in that same dwelling where the robes were being made. To sew the robes, Venerable Mahā Kassapa sat at the head (the beginning part), Venerable Sāriputta sat in the middle, and Venerable Ānanda sat at the end, and they sewed the robes. The community of monks twisted the thread and provided it. The Blessed One threaded the needles and provided them. Venerable Mahā Moggallāna traveled about to obtain whatever materials were needed for that robe-making ceremony.

The goddess Jālinī also entered the city and said, “O people! To make robes for our master, Venerable Anuruddha, the Blessed One is sitting in the monastery together with five hundred monks, surrounded by the eighty Great Disciple Arahants. Go to the monastery taking rice gruel and other offerings.”
175: Women were encouraged and established to bring gruel and alms-food. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also brought large clusters of rose-apples (jambu) before the mealtime. Five hundred monks could not finish those rose-apples. Sakka, the King of Devas, created a smooth and level ground at the place where robes were being sewn; thus, the ground for sewing robes appeared as if it had been poured with lac-dye. The gruel, snacks, and alms-food left over by the monks remained in a large heap. At that time, the monks criticized, saying: "What is the use of so much gruel, snacks, and alms-food for this many monks? (In truth,) should they not have told the relatives and lay supporters, 'Bring only this much,' after taking note of the measure? It seems the Venerable Anuruddha wishes to make known that he has many relatives and lay supporters." Then, the Blessed One asked those monks, "Bhikkhus, what talk are you engaging in?" When the monks replied, "We are talking about such and such, Bhante," the Blessed One asked, "Bhikkhus, do you think that Anuruddha caused these gruel, snacks, and alms-food to be brought?" When the monks replied, "Yes, Bhante, we think the Venerable Anuruddha caused them to be brought," the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, my son Anuruddha does not speak such words of requesting the four requisites..."
176: "...does not speak such words. Indeed, Arahants do not speak with emphasis on words related to the four requisites. This alms-food, however, arose through the power of a deity." Having said this, and wishing to connect the preceding and following words to preach the Dhamma, He uttered this verse: "Yassāsavā parikkhīṇā, āhāre ca anissito. Suññato animitto ca, vimokkhā yassa gocaro. Ākāseva sakuntānaṃ, padaṃ tassa durannayaṃ." (Bhikkhave = O monks). Yassa = In whose (an Arahant's) continuity. Āsavā = The four taints (āsavas) of sensual desire, existence, wrong view, and ignorance. Parikkhīṇā = Have been completely exhausted, leaving not even a trace. Yo = That Arahant. Āhāre ca = Also in nutriment. Anissito = Is not attached at all by means of craving and wrong view. Suññato vimokkho ca = Nibbāna, which is called the 'void liberation' because it is empty of greed, hatred, and delusion, and is liberated from all conditioned things. Animitto vimokkho ca = Nibbāna, which is called the 'signless liberation' because there are no signs of greed, hatred, and delusion, and it is liberated from those signs. (Appaṇihito vimokkho ca = Nibbāna, which is called the 'undirected liberation'...
177:
...Nibbāna, and [the word 'ca' connects them]. Yassa = of which Arahant. Gocaro = the range of constant practice through the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), which is also the village for alms. Ākāse = in the open sky. Sakuntānaṃ = of the many birds that go. Padaṃ = the track made by treading with feet, or the place reached by striking with chest, head, or wings. Durannayaṃ iva = just as it is impossible to know. Tassa = of that Arahant. Padaṃ = the state of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) reached after death. Durannayaṃ = is difficult for ordinary people to know.

At the end of the discourse, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

This is the story of Ven. Anuruddha.

## (6) About Ven. Bhaddiya
In this section on the Jewel of the Saṅgha, there are two Elders named Bhaddiya: the present Ven. Bhaddiya (No. 6) and Ven. Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya who will be described in No. 7. Among these two, the Ven. Bhaddiya to be described now is the one who ordained from the status of Prince Bhaddiya, one of the six Sakyan princes mentioned earlier in the story of Ven. Anuruddha. The mother of this Ven. Bhaddiya was a Sakyan princess named "Kāḷigodhā." Therefore, this Ven. Bhaddiya is recognized as "Kāḷigodhāputta Bhaddiya = Bhaddiya, the son of the Sakyan princess Kāḷigodhā."
178: ## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration. This Venerable Bhaddiya, in the past, one hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time when the Padumuttara Buddha appeared, was a son of a wealthy merchant in a family of great wealth (mahābhoga). According to the method mentioned (in the story of Venerable Anuruddha), he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. On that day, seeing the Padumuttara Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of high birth, he reflected: "It would be well if I too, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become a monk who is the best and most excellent among monks of high birth, receiving the title of Etadagga, just like this monk." He then invited the Buddha and performed a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days. He then aspired, "Bhante, by the merit of this gift, I do not desire any other wealth; but indeed, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, may I become the best and most excellent monk among those of high birth, receiving the title of Etadagga." He then lay prostrate at the feet of the Buddha. The Buddha, looking into the future and seeing that the merchant son's aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy: "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled. At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from this aeon, the Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. At that time, you will become the best and most excellent monk among those of high birth in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, receiving the title of Etadagga." Having given the prophecy and preached the Dhamma of appreciation for the meal, He returned to the monastery.
179:
After receiving that prophecy, the merchant's son inquired about meritorious deeds that lead to birth in a noble family. He then had Dhamma-seats (pulpits) made and donated them. He had coverings made for those seats and donated them. He also donated fans for the use of Dhamma-preachers when they preached, offered honor and respect to the venerable Dhamma-preachers, and donated lamps outside the Uposatha halls and ordination halls (sīma). 

Thus, having performed many meritorious deeds throughout his life, when he passed away from that life, he wandered between the celestial and human realms. In the interval between the time of Kassapa Buddha and our Gotama Buddha, he was reborn as a merchant's son in a merchant's house in the city of Bārāṇasī.

At that time, many Paccekabuddhas came from Mount Gandhamādana and sat to eat their alms-food at a pleasant place by the banks of the Ganges River in Bārāṇasī. The future Ven. Bhaddiya, the merchant, knowing that those Paccekabuddhas always ate their alms-food at that spot, offered eight large stone slabs for them to sit on and served the Paccekabuddhas for the rest of his life.

## (b) Ordaining in the Final Life
Thereafter, during the interval between Kassapa Buddha and Gotama Buddha—the period of a Buddhantara—he wandered only in the celestial and human realms without falling into the lower states. In the time of this Buddha, he was born into the Sakyan royal clan in the city of Kapilavatthu. His parents named the prince Bhaddiya.
180:
When Prince Bhaddiya reached maturity (as mentioned in the section on the six Sakyan princes ordaining along with Upāli the barber in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, pages 145 to 160), he was one of the leading princes. While the Buddha was staying at the "Mango Grove Monastery" near the city of Anupiya, he ordained in the presence of the Buddha and attained Arahantship within that very rainy season.

(After becoming an Arahant, Ven. Bhaddiya lived happily in the attainment of fruition and exclaimed the solemn utterance, "Aho sukhaṃ, aho sukhaṃ! = Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" Ordinary monks, not knowing this and thinking he was exclaiming out of longing for his former royal splendor, reported this to the Buddha. This account can be found in the Burmese translation of the Udāna Pāḷi, Khuddaka Nikāya, page 90).

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title
Later, while the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, during an assembly to confer Etadagga titles upon the monks, he praised Ven. Bhaddiya, saying:

"Bhikkhus, among my monk disciples who are of noble birth, Bhaddiya, the son of the Sakyan princess Kāḷigodhā, is the foremost."

Thus, he was appointed to the position of Etadagga in being "Uccākulika = of noble birth."
181:
(In this regard, the original name of the Elder's mother, the Sakyan princess, was "Godhā." Because her complexion was slightly dark, she was called "Kāḷigodhā, the Sakyan princess." Being her son, the Arahant Ven. Bhaddiya was called "Kāḷigodhāputta Bhaddiya = Ven. Bhaddiya, the son of the Sakyan princess Kāḷigodhā."

The Sakyan princess Kāḷigodhā was the eldest among all Sakyan princesses. By the time the Bodhisatta became the Buddha, his father King Suddhodana had reached the age of over ninety (this can be inferred upon careful consideration). At that time, King Suddhodana no longer had the strength to lead the country as the primary ruler as he did in his youth. Therefore, King Suddhodana likely remained only as the great leader (nāyaka) of the Sakyans. Thus, at that time, when a suitable ruler was chosen from among the Sakyans according to the lineage of seniority, Prince Bhaddiya, being of the noblest and eldest lineage, was chosen and appointed as the leading king. Prince Bhaddiya was one who renounced the position of the leading Sakyan king which was already in his hands to ordain. Therefore, when the Etadagga title was conferred, he was given the title of "foremost among those of noble birth."

Alternatively, due to the power of his past aspirations, this Ven. Bhaddiya had been born into royal families and became king for five hundred consecutive lives. Therefore, he received the Etadagga title of Uccākulika. This is a special point to be noted).

This is the story of Ven. Bhaddiya.

## (7) About Ven. Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
This Ven. Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya also lived in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha...
182: Born into a wealthy merchant family (Mahābhoga), as a son of a merchant, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma following the same manner described in the story of Ven. Anuruddha. At that time, he saw the Blessed One appointing a monk with an exceptionally sweet voice to the foremost position (Etadagga). He thought to himself, "It would be wonderful if I too could become the foremost among monks with sweet voices in the dispensation of a future Buddha." He then invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, offered a great donation (Mahādāna) for seven days, and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this donation, I do not desire any other wealth. Indeed, I wish to become the monk who is foremost among those with sweet voices in the dispensation of a future Buddha." Having said this, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, looking into the future, saw that the merchant son's aspiration would be fulfilled and gave the prophecy: "Your aspiration will be fulfilled. One hundred thousand aeons from now, Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. At that time, you will become the monk who is foremost among those with sweet voices in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha." After giving this prophecy, the Buddha returned to the monastery.
183: ## The Life as a Cittapatta Cuckoo After receiving the prophecy, the merchant's son performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. Upon passing away, he wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was reborn as a cuckoo named "Cittapatta" living in the Khema Migadāyuna forest. One day, he went to the Himālayas, picked up a sweet mango with his beak, and while returning, he saw the Blessed One surrounded by a group of monks. He thought, "On other days, I have seen the Buddha without any offering. Today, I have brought this ripe mango for my young ones. I will bring other fruits for my children; it is proper that I offer this mango to the Blessed One." He descended from the sky but did not land on the ground, hovering in the air instead. Vipassī Buddha, knowing the cuckoo's intention, looked at his attendant, Ven. Asoka. Ven. Asoka took the alms-bowl from its bag and placed it in the Buddha's hand. Then, the cuckoo placed the mango he had carried in his beak into the Buddha's bowl. The Blessed One sat right there and consumed the mango. The Cittapatta cuckoo, with a heart full of faith and devotion, reflected on the Buddha's virtues as much as he knew, paid homage, and returned to his nest. For seven days, he did not go out to search for food, spending his time in joy and happiness (pīti-sukha).
184:
In that existence as a cittapatta cuckoo bird, he performed such wholesome deeds; due to this wholesome kamma, the Elder's voice became exceedingly sweet and melodious.

## Life as a Master Carpenter

During the time when Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world, the future Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya became a master carpenter. After the Parinibbāna of Kassapa Buddha, when the people were consulting and planning to build a single great stupa for the single collection of bodily relics, the primary problem was: "What should be the size of the great stupa?" Some suggested building a great stupa seven yojanas in size. Others suggested, "This seven yojanas is too large; (it might not be completed). Let us build a great stupa six yojanas in size." Others suggested, "This six yojanas is also still too large. (It might not be completed). Let us build a great stupa five yojanas in size... (etc.)... four yojanas, three yojanas, two yojanas in size."

When these suggestions were made, the future Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, the master carpenter, being a key decision-maker in that assembly, gave the final decision, saying: "O friends, come! No matter who says what, it is only proper to build a stupa that will be easy to repair in the future." Taking a measuring line and circling the area for the stupa, he stood at a distance of one gāvuta and said: "Let each side of the stupa be one gāvuta. If built thus, the four sides combined—"
185:
—will have a circumference of one yojana and a height of one yojana."

All those people abided by the master carpenter's decision and built a great Dhatu-stupa (relic stupa) that was one gāvuta on each side (each entrance), totaling one yojana in circumference for the four sides (four entrances), and one yojana in height. In this way, that master carpenter determined and spoke of the dimensions for the stupa of the Buddha, the possessor of incomparable virtues.

## (b) Ordaining and Becoming an Arahant in the Final Life

Due to the kamma of determining and speaking of the dimensions for the stupa of the Buddha, the possessor of incomparable virtues, the future Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was born with a body that was shorter and smaller than others in every subsequent existence. In this present final life, during the time our Buddha appeared, he was born in Sāvatthī into a wealthy merchant family (mahābhoga-seṭṭhi). His parents and relatives named him "Bhaddiya."

When the young merchant Bhaddiya reached maturity, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, he went to the monastery, heard the Dhamma, and developed great faith. He entered the monkhood as a servant of the Sāsana, learned meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Buddha, and practiced Vipassanā, through which he attained the Fruit of Arahatship.
186:
## Teachings Related to Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

(In this section, I shall briefly present the Sutta teachings related to Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya that are worthy of note and devotion.)

## The Sutta on the Great Elder Becoming an Arahant

After becoming a monk, Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya learned meditation subjects from the Buddha and practiced Vipassanā, first attaining the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). At that time, many Sekha monks (those who are Stream-winners, Once-returners, or Non-returners) used to approach Venerable Sāriputta to request meditation instructions for the higher paths, to request Dhamma discourses, or to ask questions. The Venerable Sāriputta, fulfilling the wishes of those monks who requested and asked, explained the method of practicing meditation, gave Dhamma discourses, and answered their questions. As those monks continued to strive diligently in their monastic practice, some attained the Fruit of Once-returning, some the Fruit of Non-returning, some the Fruit of Arahatship, some the Three Knowledges (tevijja), some the Six Supernormal Powers (chalabhiññā), and some the Four Analytical Insights (paṭisambhidā).

Seeing those monks, Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, being a Sotāpanna Noble One himself and knowing the proper time, reflected on his own mental fortitude and the attenuation of his defilements. He approached Venerable Sāriputta, exchanged polite and friendly greetings, and requested him to preach the Dhamma. Venerable Sāriputta then preached a Dhamma discourse that was in accordance with the inclination and disposition of Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.
187: Ven. Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya practiced insight meditation, following the sequence of the teaching given by Ven. Sāriputta. Due to the power of Ven. Sāriputta's discourse and the perfection of his own past merits, his insight matured, and he attained the fruit of Arahatship. Knowing this clearly, the Blessed One at that time uttered this inspired verse (Udāna): "Uddhaṃ adho sabbadhi vippamutto, Ayaṃhamasmīti anānupassī. Evaṃ vimutto udatāri oghaṃ, Atiṇṇapubbaṃ apunabbhavāya." (He who is released above, below, and everywhere, who does not perceive 'This I am.' Thus released, he has crossed the flood never crossed before, for the sake of no more rebirth.) The meaning is: That Arahat who is completely released from the Rūpa and Arūpa realms (above), the Kāma realm (below), and from all conditioned things (everywhere) through the three types of liberation—Vikkhambhana-vimutti, Samuccheda-vimutti, and Paṭipassaddhi-vimutti. That Arahat no longer wrongly perceives the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness) as "This is I" through wrong view (diṭṭhi) or conceit (māna). Thus, the Arahat who is completely released from the ten fetters and all unwholesome states has crossed the flood (ogha) of the fourfold whirlpool of Saṃsāra, which he had never crossed before attaining the Noble Path...
188:
...which he had never crossed even in dreams. Oghaṃ = the fourfold flood of the whirlpool of saṃsāra. Apunabbhavāya = so as not to be reborn in a new existence. Udatāri = he has crossed over beautifully and stands safely on the other shore through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbāna).

(This is an excerpt from the Udāna Pali, 7. Cūḷavagga, 1. First Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Sutta, Khuddaka Nikāya 1, page 170).

## Venerable Sāriputta Continuing to Preach to Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, Mistaking Him for a Trainee (Sekha)

The Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya attained Arahatship while sitting, through the first exhortation he received (from Venerable Sāriputta), according to the procedure mentioned in the aforementioned first sutta. However, the Venerable Sāriputta, not realizing (as he did not reflect upon it) that Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya had attained Arahatship, mistook him for a trainee (sekha). Like a generous donor who, out of a great desire for merit, gives more than what is requested, Sāriputta repeatedly and extensively preached the Dhamma for the sake of Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya's attainment of Arahatship. Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, without thinking, "I have already completed the task of a monk; what benefit is there in this advice?" continued to listen respectfully as before, out of respect for the Dhamma (dhamma-gārava).

Seeing this, the Buddha, while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī of the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, through his divine power, [perceived] the exhaustion of Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya's defilements...
189:
189
He uttered this inspired solemn utterance (Udāna) so that the Venerable Sāriputta might know:

Acchecchi vaṭṭaṃ byagā nirāsaṃ,
visukkhā saritā na sandati.
chinnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ na vattati,
esevanto dukkhassa.

(The meaning is:) Yassa = in which Arahant whose taints are exhausted; vaṭṭaṃ = the cycle of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa); acchecchi = has been completely cut off (know that when the cycle of defilements is cut, the cycle of karma is also cut). Yo = which Arahant whose taints are exhausted; nirāsaṃ = to the bliss of Nibbāna, the state free from craving; byagā = has specifically reached, attaining the fruit of Arahantship. Yassa = in which Arahant whose taints are exhausted; visukkhā = has been completely dried up by the appearance of the fourth sun of the Path of Arahantship, just as the five great rivers dry up when the fourth sun appears at the end of an aeon; saritā = the great river of defilements, namely craving, which flows continuously (since craving is the root cause of suffering, the Truth of the Origin, when that craving is abandoned, all defilements are abandoned; therefore, the Buddha taught specifically highlighting craving); na sandati = it no longer flows in any way. Chinnaṃ = being severed like a tree cut at the root; vaṭṭaṃ = the cycle of karma (kammavaṭṭa); na vattati = no longer revolves. (Know that when the cycle of karma is cut, the cycle of results (vipākavaṭṭa) that would occur in the future is also cut). Eseva = only this, the non-arising of the cycle of results in the future due to the cutting of the cycles of defilements and karma...
190:
...because it is cut off, the non-arising of the round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa) in the future is indeed. Dukkhassa = of the suffering of the whirlpool of saṃsāra. Anto = the end, the complete destruction.

(This is an excerpt from the Udāna Pali, 7. Cūḷavagga, Second Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Sutta, Khuddaka Nikāya 1, pages 170-71).

## The Buddha Manifestly Revealing the Virtues of Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

On one occasion, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, many monks came to the presence of the Buddha. At that time, the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, having gone for alms in a certain village together with many monks and having finished his meal, cleaned his bowl, placed it in its bag, and hung it on his shoulder. He folded his upper robe, placed it on his left shoulder, and with an inspiring manner of moving forward, retreating, looking straight, looking aside, bending, and stretching, he walked towards the Buddha with downcast eyes, endowed with proper deportment. As if clearly demonstrating the abundance of his mindfulness and wisdom, he cultivated mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) well, treading with his hind foot upon the track of his forefoot with a composed mind.

While walking thus, he went behind the many monks without mingling with them. The reason was that he was accustomed to dwelling alone (ekacārī). Alternatively, some worldling monks, such as the Chabbaggiya monks, used to mock, tease, and disparage his short (pukwa) and unsightly physical form. The Great Elder, considering this, thought, "These worldling monks..."
191:
191
...increase unwholesome states on account of me," and so he followed behind those many monks. Thus, the many monks and the Elder reached Sāvatthī, entered the Jetavana Monastery, and approached the place where the Buddha was.

The Buddha saw from afar the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya following behind the many monks with an inspiring sense of restraint. He thought, "These monks do not know the great power of my son. Therefore, some worldling monks mock and look down upon my son. Such behavior will lead to their lack of benefit and to their suffering for a long time. Now, I shall manifestly reveal the virtues of this son of mine to the monks, to free them from the danger of mocking and looking down upon my son." Having thus reflected, he asked the monks, "Monks, do you see that monk following behind the many monks, who is unsightly, difficult to look at, and dwarfish, and who is being mocked and looked down upon by some worldling monks?"

When the monks replied, "We see him, Bhante," the Buddha said:

"Monks, this monk is one of great psychic power (iddhi) and great majesty (ānubhāva). There is almost no attainment (samāpatti) belonging to disciples that this monk has not entered. (This means he has entered all attainments belonging to disciples, such as the fine-material attainments, immaterial attainments, the divine abodes, the attainment of cessation, and the attainment of fruition...
192:
192
...By this statement, his great psychic power is shown). In this very life, he has realized for himself through direct knowledge, attained, and dwells in the fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of the matchless holy life, the primary goal for which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. (This means he is a monk who frequently enters the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. By this statement, his great majesty is shown. Indeed, in this context, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is called majesty (ānubhāva) because it is enjoyed and experienced by the Elder.)"

Having spoken thus, he also uttered this inspired solemn utterance (Udāna) revealing the Elder's virtues:

Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattati ratho.
Anīghaṃ passa āyantaṃ, chinnasotaṃ abandhanaṃ.

Nelaṅgo = the chariot of the body of my breast-born son Bhaddiya, which has the wheel of the primary factor of virtue of the fruit of Arahantship that is free from flaws. Setapacchādo = which has the white canopy and furnishings of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. Ekāro = which has the single axle of the mindfulness of the fruit of Arahantship. Ratho = the chariot of the physical body of Bhaddiya. Vattati = it rolls along beautifully without needing oil. Āyantaṃ = who is following behind the many monks. Anīghaṃ = who is entirely free from the distress and suffering of defilements.
193:
Chinnasotaṃ = one in whom the ever-flowing stream of craving has been cut off. Abandhanaṃ = one who does not have even a single cord of the ten types of fetters (saṃyojana). (Imaṃ = this chariot which is the physical body of this son of mine, Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya). Passa = passāhi = behold and look closely. (In this context, the Buddha was so delighted by the Elder's virtues that he even used the exhortation "Behold!" regarding himself [his son]).

(This is an excerpt from the Udāna Pāḷi, 7. Cūḷavagga, 5. Apara Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Sutta [Khuddaka Nikāya 1, page 172].)

Furthermore, the stories and Dhamma teachings related to Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya should be extracted and noted from the Dhammapada Commentary, Theragāthā Commentary, Apadāna Commentary, and so forth.

## (c) Receiving the Distinguished Title of Etadagga

At a later time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, during an assembly to confer distinguished Etadagga titles upon the monks, he declared regarding this Arahant Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mañjussarānaṃ yadidaṃ lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess a sweet and melodious voice, Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya is the foremost."
194:
Thus praising him, the Buddha placed him in the position of Etadagga in the category of "Mañjussara = possessing a sweet and melodious voice."

This is the account of Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.

## (8) The Account of Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

The future Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was born into the species of lions and lived roaming at the foot of a mountain. One day, when Padumuttara Buddha surveyed the world of sentient beings at dawn, he saw that the lion was endowed with the conditions to attain the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. After wandering for alms in the city of Haṃsāvatī, in the afternoon when the lion went out to search for food, the Buddha entered the lion's cave, sat cross-legged in the air, and remained there having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

After finding its prey, the lion returned and stood at the mouth of the cave. It saw the Buddha sitting wonderfully in the air inside the cave and thought: "No other being is capable of coming to my place and sitting here. This noble person must indeed be one worthy of great honor and worship. Because he is so worthy of worship, he is able to sit cross-legged in the air inside the cave. The radiance of this noble person's body is also spreading and shimmering all around. I have never seen such a wonder before."
195:
195
This noble person must be the most excellent and supreme among those worthy of worship in this world. It is only proper that I should pay homage and make offerings to this noble person to the best of my ability." Thinking thus, he brought various land and water flowers from the forest and arranged a floral seat from the ground up to the level in the air where the Buddha was sitting cross-legged. For three watches of the night, he stood in front of the Buddha, paying homage and making offerings. The next day, he discarded the old flowers and similarly arranged a seat with fresh flowers as an offering.

In this manner, for seven days, he arranged the floral seat, feeling great joy and delight, and remained at the mouth of the cave as a guardian. On the seventh day, the Buddha emerged from the attainment of cessation and stood at the mouth of the cave. Then the lion king circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage at the four directions—front, back, left, and right—and then stepped back and stood there.

The Buddha reflected, "This mass of merit is now sufficient to be a supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits for this lion." He then flew up into the air and returned to the monastery.

## Life as the Son of a Mahāsāla Treasurer

That lion, suffering great mental distress due to being separated from the Buddha, passed away and was reborn in the city of Haṃsāvatī in the family of a Mahāsāla treasurer. When he reached the age of maturity, one day, together with the city dwellers...
196:
While going to listen to the Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appointing a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who are "Sīhanādika" (those who speak the bold Lion's Roar regarding the Path and Fruit). Following the method described in the stories of the elders of the past, he performed a great offering (mahādāna) for seven days and aspired for that same position.

The Buddha, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, delivered a prophecy (vyākaraṇa). After receiving the prophecy, that son of a wealthy mahāsāla family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. Upon passing away from that life, he did not fall into the four woeful states for a hundred thousand eons, but wandered between the celestial and human realms.

## (b) Renouncing in the Final Life
Having thus wandered up and down between the celestial and human realms, during the time this Buddha appeared, he was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha and was named "Bharadvāja."

## How he came to be named Piṇḍola Bharadvāja
When the youth Bharadvāja reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and lived as a teacher, wandering about and teaching the Vedic texts to five hundred Brahmin youths. Because this teacher, the Brahmin youth Bharadvāja, was a teacher himself, he would take charge of the food for everyone at places where they were invited for meals and would take it for himself. This teacher, the Brahmin youth Bharadvāja, had a nature that was somewhat fickle and greedy regarding food.
197:
Together with his five hundred students, he would wander about, preoccupied and searching only for gruel, rice, and snacks, asking, "Where can we get gruel? Where can we get rice?" Because this teacher, the Brahmin Bharadvāja, lived and wandered about waiting primarily for food wherever he went, he became known as "Piṇḍola Bharadvāja" (Bharadvāja the Brahmin who primarily seeks food).

## Even when he became a monk
## How he was still named Piṇḍola Bharadvāja
At a later time, the Brahmin Piṇḍola Bharadvāja encountered the danger of losing his wealth and fell into a state of poverty. One day during that time, when the Buddha arrived at the city of Rājagaha and preached the Dhamma, the Brahmin Piṇḍola Bharadvāja heard the teaching, gained faith, and entered the Order as a monk.

Those who enter the Sasana are usually known by names related to their lineage. Thus, this monk Piṇḍola Bharadvāja should have been known simply as "Bhikkhu Bharadvāja," yet he did not become known by that name, but rather as "Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera." The reason for being so named is that the Elder used to carry a very large bowl, and he would drink a full bowl of gruel. He would also eat a full bowl of cakes and consume a full bowl of alms-food. At that time, the monks reported his great appetite to the Buddha.
198:
The Buddha did not allow a bowl-bag for that Elder. Consequently, the Elder's bowl had to be kept upside down under his couch. When the Elder placed the bowl under the couch, he had to push it in while it rubbed against the floor, and when he took it out, he had to pull it out in the same manner. After a long time, due to frequent rubbing, the edges of the bowl (the large vessel) wore away, and the bowl, which was originally the size of a large vessel, became a bowl that could only hold a single portion of food. When the monks reported this matter to the Buddha, only then did the Buddha allow the use of a bowl-bag for the Elder. Thus, because the Elder seemed to have become a monk out of hardship for the sake of alms-food (Piṇḍola), and because he was of the Bharadvāja lineage, these two names were combined, and even after becoming a monk, he was known as "Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja."

At a later time, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera practiced the development of the faculties (indriya-bhāvanā) with great effort, attained the Fruit of Arahatship, and became an Arahat.

Immediately after attaining the Fruit of Arahatship, the Elder took a key and went from one monastery to another, from one precinct to another, declaring boldly without fear like a lion's roar: "Let any monk who has doubts regarding the Path and Fruit question me!" (The details of this account can be found in...)
199:
...the Burmese translation of the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi, pages 202-203; 4-Indriya Saṃyutta, 5-Jarā Vagga, 9-Piṇḍolabhāradvāja Sutta).

One day, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera, using his psychic powers, took a sandalwood bowl that a merchant of Rājagaha had suspended in the air at a height of sixty cubits by erecting successive bamboo poles. Surrounded by a crowd of people offering praise, he went to the Veḷuvana Monastery and placed the bowl in the hands of the Buddha. Although the Buddha already knew, He asked, "Dear Bharadvāja, where did you get this bowl?" When the Elder reported the circumstances, the Buddha rebuked him in many ways, saying, "Dear Bharadvāja, you have displayed to the public the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)—the jhānas, Paths, and Fruits—which are superior to the ten wholesome courses of action of humans. You have done what should not be done." After this, He laid down a training rule (sikkhāpada) prohibiting the display of psychic powers. (The details of this account should be read again in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 1, Part 2, pages 487 to 500).

Later, among the assembly of monks, three types of praise arose concerning the virtues of Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera: "(1) The Lion-Roarer Elder: Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who is accustomed to speaking boldly, declared in the midst of the Sangha on the very day he attained Arahatship, 'Let any monk who has doubts regarding the Path and Fruit question me.' (2) He also declared his attainment of Arahatship in the presence of the Buddha, while other disciples remained silent.
200:
(3) Because the Elder himself is accustomed to speaking boldly, he inspired faith in the people, flew into the sky, and brought back the sandalwood bowl of the Rājagaha merchant." The monks combined these three virtues of the Elder and reported them to the Buddha.

Since it is the custom of Buddhas to criticize what is blameworthy and praise what is praiseworthy, in this instance, the Buddha took only the praiseworthy qualities of Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera and said:

"Monks, through the development and frequent practice of three faculties, the monk Bharadvāja declares the Fruit of Arahatship, saying: 'I know that birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further to be done for the sake of the Path.'

Which three? It is through the development and frequent practice of the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Monks, through the development and frequent practice of these three faculties, the monk Bharadvāja declares the Fruit of Arahatship, saying: 'I know that birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further to be done for the sake of this Path.'

Monks, what is the end of these three faculties? Their end is destruction.

Destruction of what is their end?
201:
The destruction of birth, aging, and death is their end. Monks, because he clearly perceives that birth, aging, and death are exhausted, the monk Bharadvāja declares the Fruit of Arahatship, saying: 'I know that birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further to be done for the sake of this Path.' (From the Burmese translation of Mahāvagga Saṃyutta, page 203)."

In this manner, the Buddha spoke words of praise for the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera.

It was this same Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera who preached the Dhamma to King Udena of Kosambī, leading him to become a lay follower (upāsaka) established in the Three Refuges. (The details of this account should be sought in the Burmese translation of the Bhāradvāja Sutta, starting from page 322 of the Saḷāyatanavagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi).

## (c) Receiving the Foremost Title
At a later time, when the Buddha held an assembly to confer foremost titles (Etadagga) upon the monks, He declared regarding Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīhanādikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolabhāradvājo = Monks, among my monk disciples who speak boldly like a lion's roar without fear, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja is the foremost."
202:
Thus He praised him and appointed him to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Sīhanādika"—those who speak boldly like a lion's roar.

This is the account of Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Thera.
