## (9) About Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta Thera
(The Elder's original name was Puṇṇa. He became known as Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta because he was the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī, the younger sister of the Great Elder Koṇḍañña).

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
This future Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta Thera was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in the city of Haṃsāvatī a hundred thousand eons ago, even before the appearance of the Buddha Padumuttara. On the day he was named, his parents and relatives named him Gotama.

When the Brahmin youth Gotama reached maturity, he studied the three Vedas and became proficient in all arts. While wandering about with an entourage of five hundred youths (disciples), he reflected upon the three Vedas and, seeing no path to liberation from Saṃsāra in them, he thought: "These three Vedas are like the trunk of a banana tree—smooth on the outside but without essence within. My wandering about cherishing these three Vedas is like pounding husks in the hope of getting rice. For me, with these three Vedas..."
203:
“What benefit is there? There is none.” Thinking thus, he further thought, “I shall become an ascetic, develop the Brahmavihāra jhānas, and without falling from them, be reborn in the Brahma realm.” He then went to the foot of a mountain with five hundred young disciples and lived as an ascetic.

The followers of that ascetic Gotama were eighteen thousand matted-hair ascetics. The teacher Gotama himself attained the five mundane superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight mundane meditative attainments (samāpatti). He then taught the eighteen thousand disciples the preliminary practice of kasiṇa. All eighteen thousand disciples, following the instruction of the teacher Gotama, also attained the five mundane superknowledges and the eight mundane meditative attainments.

After a long time had passed in this way and the teacher Gotama had grown old, Buddha Padumuttara attained Enlightenment. Having preached the first sermon of the Dhammacakka, the Buddha was staying at Haṃsāvatī, his birthplace, supported by the city, accompanied by one hundred thousand monks. One morning, Buddha Padumuttara surveyed the world of beings and saw the past merits of the eighteen thousand disciples of the ascetic Gotama that would lead to the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship. He also saw that if he went there, the teacher Gotama would make an aspiration: “In the dispensation of a future Buddha, may I be the most supreme and excellent among the monks who are skilled in preaching the Dhamma (Dhammakathika) and receive the title of Etadagga.” Thus, early in the morning, after performing his personal duties...
204:
...and taking his bowl and robes himself, the Buddha went in an inconspicuous manner while the disciples of Gotama the ascetic were away searching for roots and fruits. He stood at the entrance of Gotama's leaf-hut.

Although the teacher Gotama did not know beforehand that a Buddha had appeared, upon seeing Buddha Padumuttara from afar, he thought: “Judging by the perfection of this noble person's physical body, one endowed with such marks would become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) if he remained in the household life. If he renounces the world, he would surely be a Fully Enlightened Buddha who can break the roof of defilements. Therefore, this noble man who has arrived must be one who is liberated from the three worlds.” Recognizing him as a Buddha according to the treatise on the Marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), he immediately paid homage with great respect and invited him, saying, “Exalted Buddha, please come this way,” and prepared a seat. Buddha Padumuttara sat on the prepared seat and preached to Gotama the ascetic.

At that time, the matted-hair disciples returned, thinking, “We shall offer the best wild roots and fruits to our teacher and eat what remains.” Seeing the Buddha sitting on a high seat and their teacher on a low seat, they were surprised and said, “Look! we used to wander thinking, ‘There is no one more noble than our teacher in this world.’”
205:
“But now, we clearly see a great noble person sitting on a high seat while our teacher sits on a low seat. This noble person must indeed be very supreme and worthy of worship.” Thinking thus, they approached with their baskets of fruit.

The teacher Gotama, fearing that the disciples might pay homage to him in the presence of the Buddha, called out from afar, “Disciples, do not pay homage to me! The most supreme person in the world of beings, including devas and Brahmas, who is worthy of everyone's homage, is sitting here. Pay homage to that noble person.” The disciples, thinking, “The teacher would not say this without knowing,” all paid homage at the Buddha's feet.

The teacher said, “Disciples, we have no other food to offer the Buddha. Let us offer these wild roots and fruits.” They poured the best roots and fruits into the Buddha's bowl. Only after the Buddha had partaken of the wild roots and fruits did the teacher and his disciples eat.

After finishing the meal of fruit, the Buddha made a mental wish: “May the two chief disciples come to me, bringing one hundred thousand monks.” At that moment, the chief disciple, Venerable Mahādevala, wondered, “Where has the Buddha gone?”
206:
Realizing that the Buddha desired their presence, he took one hundred thousand monks, went to the Buddha, paid homage, and stood there.

The teacher Gotama said to his disciples, “Disciples, we have no other offerings for the Sangha. The monks are standing in hardship. Let us prepare flower seats for the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Quickly bring flowers from the water and the land.” The disciples immediately used their psychic powers to bring fragrant and beautiful flowers from the foot of the mountain and prepared flower seats as described in the story of Venerable Sāriputta. Then, the Buddha and the Sangha entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). The story of how the ascetics provided flower umbrellas and everything else should be understood as described in the story of Venerable Sāriputta.

On the seventh day, when the Buddha emerged from the attainment of cessation, he saw the ascetics standing around and said to the disciple who was foremost in preaching the Dhamma, “Dear son, this group of ascetics has performed a great act of honor. Preach a sermon of appreciation (anumodanā) regarding the flower seats to these ascetics.” That Arahant, who held the title of Etadagga, respectfully accepted the Buddha's command and, reflecting on the Tipitaka, preached the sermon of appreciation.
207:
When that monk finished the sermon, the Buddha himself, with a voice like Brahma's, continued to preach the Dhamma leading to the Path and Fruit. At the end of the discourse, all eighteen thousand matted-hair disciples, except for the teacher Gotama, attained Arahantship.

The teacher Gotama, unable to attain the special Dhamma (realization) in that existence, asked the Buddha, “Exalted Buddha, what is the name of the monk who preached first in Your Majesty's dispensation?” The Buddha replied, “Gotama, this monk who preached first is the most supreme and excellent among the preachers of Dhamma (Dhammakathika) in my dispensation, holding the title of Etadagga.” Then Gotama the ascetic made an aspiration, prostrating at the Buddha's feet: “Exalted Buddha, by the merit of this great deed performed over these seven days, may I also become the most supreme and excellent among the preachers of Dhamma (Dhammakathika), receiving the title of Etadagga in the dispensation of a future Buddha, just like this monk who preached first.”

Buddha Padumuttara, looking into the future and seeing that Gotama's wish would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy: “At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, Buddha Gotama will appear. At that time, you will become the most supreme and excellent among the preachers of Dhamma (Dhammakathika), receiving the title of Etadagga in the dispensation of that Buddha Gotama.”
208:
Having given the prophecy, the Buddha called the disciples who had attained Arahantship, saying, “Etha Bhikkhavo” (Come, monks). At that moment, the hair and beards of all the disciples disappeared (without shaving), and miraculously created bowls and robes appeared on their bodies. Their ascetic appearance vanished, and they became fully ordained monks, looking like senior elders of sixty or eighty years of age. Buddha Padumuttara then returned to the monastery with the assembly of monks.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

Gotama the ascetic served the Buddha for the rest of his life and performed as much merit as possible. He wandered only through the celestial and human realms for one hundred thousand aeons. During the time when our Buddha appeared, he was conceived in a wealthy brahmin family in the brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, near the city of Kapilavatthu. His parents and relatives named the boy “Puṇṇa”.

After the Buddha attained the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and preached the Dhammacakka sermon, he eventually arrived and stayed near the city of Rājagaha. At that time, Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña went to the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu in Kapilavatthu, ordained his nephew (his sister's son), the youth Puṇṇa, and taught him how to practice the Dhamma of a monk. The next day, he went to the Buddha, paid respectful homage, asked for permission, and departed for Lake Chaddanta to reside there permanently.
209:
209
Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, however, did not accompany his maternal uncle, Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, to the Buddha. He decided, "I will go to pay homage to the Blessed One only after I have reached the pinnacle of a monk's duty, which is Arahantship." Thus, he remained in Kapilavatthu. While he was diligently practicing the Dhamma, he soon attained Arahantship.
Five hundred noble sons were ordained under Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta. Because the Elder himself practiced and followed the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu)*, he also instructed those five hundred noble monks using those same ten subjects. Established in the advice and instructions of Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, all five hundred monks diligently practiced the Dhamma and attained Arahantship.
*The ten subjects of discourse are: (1) Appicchakathā = talk on fewness of wishes, (2) Santuṭṭhikathā = talk on contentment, (3) Pavivekakathā = talk on seclusion, (4) Asaṃsaggakathā = talk on non-association, (5) Vīriyārambhakathā = talk on arousing energy, (6) Sīlakathā = talk on virtue, (7) Samādhikathā = talk on concentration, (8) Paññākathā = talk on wisdom, (9) Vimuttikathā = talk on liberation (Arahantship), (10) Vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā = talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (Reviewing Knowledge). Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta himself followed these ten subjects of discourse and also instructed his disciples with them.
210:
210
Knowing that they had reached the pinnacle of their monk's duty (Arahantship), those five hundred monks approached their preceptor, Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, and said, "Venerable Sir, our monk's duty has reached its pinnacle. We have also easily mastered the ten noble subjects of discourse. It is now time for us to go and pay homage to the Blessed One."
Upon hearing the words of his five hundred disciples, the preceptor thought, "The Blessed One knows that I easily master the ten subjects of discourse. When I preach the Dhamma, I do so without letting go of these ten subjects. If I go together with these monks now, all five hundred will surround me. It is not appropriate for me to go and pay homage to the Blessed One surrounded by such a large group. Let these monks go first to pay homage to the Blessed One."
Having considered this, he said to them, "Friends, you go ahead and pay homage to the Blessed One. Also, pay homage to the feet of the Blessed One on my behalf with my message. I will follow later along the same path you take."
All of them were from Kapilavatthu, the birthplace of the Blessed One; all were Arahants whose taints were exhausted; and all were individuals who easily mastered the ten subjects of discourse. Without violating the advice and instruction of their preceptor, those five hundred monks gradually traveled on their journey and...
211:
211
...after traveling a distance of sixty yojanas, they arrived at the Veluvana Monastery in Rājagaha. They paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place.
Since it is the custom of the Buddhas to exchange pleasantries with visiting monks, the Blessed One spoke kindly to those five hundred monks, starting with, "Kacci bhikkhave khamanīyaṃ = Monks, is it bearable for you?" and then asked, "Monks, from where have you come?"
When the monks replied, "We have come from Kapilavatthu, the birthplace of the Exalted One," the Blessed One asked, giving priority to the monk who easily mastered the ten subjects of discourse, "Monks, among the monks from Kapilavatthu, my birthplace, which monk is praised by his fellow practitioners thus: 'This monk is himself one of few wishes and speaks to other monks on fewness of wishes (appicchakathā)'?"
Those five hundred monks unanimously replied to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is so praised by his fellow practitioners." Hearing this, Venerable Sāriputta greatly desired to meet Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.
Later, the Blessed One traveled from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. When Venerable Puṇṇa heard that the Blessed One had arrived in Sāvatthī...
212:
212
...thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Blessed One," he traveled alone to Sāvatthī and paid homage directly to the Blessed One at the Gandhakuṭī (without taking any other monk as a guide). The Blessed One preached to Venerable Puṇṇa the Dhamma related to the ten subjects of discourse. After hearing the Dhamma, Venerable Puṇṇa paid homage to the Blessed One and went to the Andhavana forest to spend the day in seclusion under a certain tree.
Venerable Sāriputta, hearing that Venerable Puṇṇa had gone to the Andhavana forest, followed him closely, keeping him in sight. Noting a suitable opportunity, he approached the foot of that tree in the evening. After exchanging pleasantries with Venerable Puṇṇa, he inquired about the sequence of the seven stages of purification (visuddhi). Venerable Puṇṇa answered every question asked by Venerable Sāriputta. Both great elders rejoiced in each other's words and expressed their appreciation (sādhu anumodanā). (The details of this account should be noted from the Rathavinīta Sutta, Opamma Vagga, Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi, Burmese translation, starting from page 204).
## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
Later, when the Blessed One was conferring the titles of Etadagga upon the monks, he declared regarding Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta:
"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ puṇṇo mantāṇiputto = Monks, among my
213:
213
disciple monks who are skilled in preaching the Dhamma, Puṇṇa, the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī, is the foremost."
Thus, the Buddha praised him and appointed him to the position of Etadagga in the category of "Dhammakathika = those skilled in preaching the Dhamma."
This is the account of Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.

## (10) The Account of Venerable Kaccāyana
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
The future Venerable Kaccāyana was born into a wealthy family during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching adulthood, he went to the monastery one day, like other future elders, and stood at the edge of the assembly. While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One appoint a certain monk to the position of Etadagga, declaring him "foremost among those who can explain in detail the meaning of what was taught in brief."
Seeing this, he thought, "This monk is truly great. The Blessed One praises him as the foremost among those who can explain in detail the meaning of what was taught in brief. I should also become such a monk who receives the Etadagga title in the dispensation of a future Buddha."
Having considered this, he invited the Blessed One and, following the method mentioned previously, offered a great alms-giving for seven days. Then he prayed, "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this great offering and honor performed over these seven days,
214:
214
I do not desire any other prosperity. Instead, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, I wish to attain the same Etadagga title and rank that was conferred seven days ago upon the monk whom You, Venerable Sir, appointed (as the foremost among those who can explain in detail the meaning of what was taught in brief)."
Having made this aspiration, he lay prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One. Padumuttara Buddha, looking into the future, saw that this noble son's wish would be fulfilled. He prophesied, "O noble son, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, Gotama Buddha will appear. In the dispensation of that Gotama Buddha, you will become the foremost among those who can explain in detail the meaning of what was taught in brief, receiving the Etadagga title."
After giving this prophecy and preaching the Dhamma of appreciation, the Buddha departed.
## Offering a Golden Brick
That noble son performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life. For one hundred thousand aeons, he did not fall into the lower realms but wandered through the celestial and human worlds. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born into a noble family in Bārāṇasī. When Kassapa Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he went to the site where the great golden stupa was being built. He made an offering of a golden brick worth one hundred thousand and prayed, "Glorious Blessed One, in whatever realm I am born..."
215:
“May my body be of golden hue,” he made this prayer and aspiration.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

Thereafter, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans for an entire incalculable interval between Buddhas (buddhantara), he was reborn as the son of the royal chaplain (purohita) in the city of Ujjenī during the time our Blessed One appeared in the world. On the day the boy was named, the father said, “My son has a body as bright as the color of gold; he has come bringing his own name,” and thus the parents and relatives named him “Prince Kañcana.” When Prince Kañcana grew up, he mastered the three Vedas, and upon the death of his father, the great chaplain, he succeeded to the position of royal chaplain. This Prince Kañcana, the brahmin chaplain, was also known as “Kaccāna” by virtue of his lineage.

King Caṇḍapajjota assembled his ministers and said, “O ministers, a Buddha has appeared in the world; let those ministers who are capable of inviting that Buddha go and invite Him.” The ministers replied, “O Great King, there is no one else capable of inviting the Buddha except the chaplain Kaccāna; only the teacher Kaccāna, the brahmin chaplain, is capable. Please send him.” When they had petitioned thus in unison, King Caṇḍapajjota summoned the chaplain Kaccāna and said, “Friend Kaccāna, go to the presence of the Buddha and invite Him.”
216:
The chaplain Kaccāna replied, “Great King, if I may receive permission to become a monk, I shall go.” King Caṇḍapajjota granted permission, saying, “Friend Kaccāna, you may do as you please in all matters, but please invite the Buddha to come.”

The teacher Kaccāna, the chaplain, reflected, “For one going to the presence of the Buddhas, there is no need for a large retinue,” and so, being the eighth person himself (meaning he took only seven companions), he went to the presence of the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the chaplain Kaccāna. At the conclusion of the discourse, the teacher Kaccāna, together with his seven companions, became Arahants attained to the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Then the Blessed One stretched out His right hand and called out, “Etha Bhikkhavo—Come, monks.” At that very moment, the hair and beards of all eight disappeared, and they were endowed with miraculously created bowls and robes, becoming monks like senior elders of sixty years of rains (vassa) or eighty years of age.

When the Venerable Kaccāyana had reached the pinnacle of a monk's duty (the fruit of Arahantship), he did not remain silent and indifferent, but like the Venerable Kāḷudāyī, he recited verses praising the journey for the Blessed One to travel to the city of Ujjenī. The Blessed One, hearing the words of the Venerable Kaccāyana, knew, “Kaccāna desires my journey to his birthplace, the city of Ujjenī.” Generally, Buddhas do not travel to places where it is not suitable to go based on a particular reason.
217:
Therefore, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Kaccāyana, “Dear son, you alone should go to the city of Ujjenī. If you go, King Caṇḍapajjota will gain faith.”

The Venerable Kaccāyana, reflecting that “there is no double-speech for the Buddhas,” paid respectful homage to the Blessed One and departed for the city of Ujjenī together with the seven monks who had accompanied him.

## The Story of the Two Daughters of Wealthy Merchants

While traveling to the city of Ujjenī, they wandered for alms in a market town named “Telapanāḷi.” In that town, there were two daughters of wealthy merchants. One of them was born into a merchant family that had lost its wealth; after her parents passed away, she lived depending on an old nurse. However, her physical form was exceedingly beautiful, graceful, and full. Her hair was longer, softer, and smoother than that of other women, with the dark, lustrous color of a bumblebee. In that same town, the other merchant's daughter had very little hair. Before the arrival of the Venerable Kaccāyana and his group, this wealthy daughter had sent someone to the poor merchant's daughter with beautiful hair, saying, “I will pay whatever price you ask, whether a hundred or a thousand, for that hair,” but she could not obtain it because the owner would not sell.

On the day the Venerable Kaccāyana entered for alms, the merchant's daughter with the beautiful hair saw the Venerable Kaccāyana surrounded by the seven monks,
218:
approaching with an empty bowl and no food. She thought, “This monk of the Brahma lineage, with a golden complexion, comes only with a washed bowl. I have no other wealth. That merchant's daughter has previously sent someone for my hair. Now, with the price obtained from my hair, I should be able to offer alms-food to the noble elder.” Having reflected thus, she sent her nurse to invite the elders and have them sit inside the house.

When the elders were seated, the merchant's daughter went into a room and had her nurse cut off her hair. She then said, “O mother, give this hair to that merchant's daughter and bring whatever price she gives. Let us offer alms-food to the noble ones.” The nurse wiped her tears with the back of one hand and, supporting her breast with the other, hid the hair from the sight of the elders and took it to the merchant's daughter (who had previously sent to buy it).

“It is the nature of things that even if a commodity is good and valuable, if the owner themselves delivers it to the buyer, the buyer tends to show no respect and lowers the price.”

Thus, the wealthy merchant's daughter (with thin hair) thought, “Previously, though I offered much wealth to buy it, I could not obtain this hair. Now, from the moment it is cut, that merchant's daughter will no longer be able to get the original value; she must accept whatever I say.” She then told the nurse, “O nurse, previously I offered much wealth to buy it from your mistress but could not obtain the hair. Now, these lifeless hairs that have fallen anywhere are worth only eight coins (kahāpaṇas),” and thus devaluing it, she gave only eight coins to the nurse.
219:
The nurse brought the eight coins and gave them to the (impoverished) merchant's daughter. The merchant's daughter prepared a meal worth one coin for each of the eight noble elders and offered it to them. When the Venerable Kaccāyana looked with foresight, he saw the powerful merit (upanissaya) of the merchant's daughter and asked, “Where is the merchant's daughter now?” When the nurse replied, “She is in the room, venerable sir,” the noble elder said, “Call that merchant's daughter who is the donor of this alms.”

Because of her great respect for the elders, the donor daughter came at the first call, paid homage to the elders, and repeatedly aroused great faith. (In this Dispensation, which is like a fertile field, the seed of alms-food sown with clear faith yields results even in the present life). Thus, at the very moment she paid homage to the elders,

the hair of the alms-donor merchant's daughter returned to its original state. The elders, having accepted the alms-food, flew up into the sky in the sight of the merchant's daughter and descended in King Caṇḍapajjota’s garden named “Kañcanavana.”

When the gardener saw the Venerable Kaccāyana, he went to the King and reported, “O Great King, my lord the chaplain Kaccāna has become a monk and has arrived at the royal garden.” King Caṇḍapajjota went to the garden, paid homage to the Venerable Kaccāyana—who had finished his meal—with the fivefold prostration, and sitting in a suitable place, asked, “Venerable Sir, where is the Blessed One?” The Venerable Kaccāyana replied, “Great King, the Blessed One has not yet come Himself but has sent me.” King Caṇḍapajjota then asked, “Venerable Sir, where did you receive today's alms-food?” The Venerable Kaccāyana, in accordance with the King's question, recounted the entire story of the difficult meritorious deed performed by the merchant's daughter who donated the alms.
220: King Caṇḍapajjota personally arranged the residence for the Venerable Kaccāyana and, after inviting the noble elder for the next day's alms, returned to the golden palace. He then summoned the merchant's daughter who donated the alms by royal decree and elevated her to the position of Chief Queen. This was the attainment of prosperity and happiness in the present life resulting from the first impulsive wholesome intention (pathamajavana kusala cetanā) of this alms-donor merchant's daughter.
221: (The meaning intended here is: Among the seven types of mahā-kusala javana-cetanā that arise when performing acts such as offering alms, the first javana-cetanā, if conditions are met, yields its result in the present life. Therefore, this first javana-cetanā is called diṭṭhadhamma-vedaniya kamma, meaning kamma that is experienced in the present life. The seventh javana-cetanā, if conditions are met, yields its result in the second life (the life immediately following). Therefore, this seventh javana-cetanā is called upapajja-vedaniya kamma, meaning kamma that is experienced upon rebirth. The cetanās of the middle five javanas, if conditions are met, yield their results from the third life onwards in successive existences. Therefore, these cetanās are called aparāpariya-vedaniya kamma, meaning kamma that is experienced in successive future lives. In the ripening of kamma, the results are of two kinds: bhava-vipāka (resultant existence) and bhava-sampatti (attainment of prosperity in existence). The resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) that arise at the moment of rebirth and during the course of life are called bhava-vipāka; these resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter are also called upapatti-bhava. The various types of wealth and enjoyments obtained and experienced in that life are called bhava-sampatti. Among the three types of kamma mentioned, upapajja-vedaniya kamma and aparāpariya-vedaniya kamma provide both types of results: bhava-vipāka and bhava-sampatti. However, the first javana-cetanā, which is diṭṭhadhamma-vedaniya kamma, when giving results in the present life, cannot provide bhava-vipāka (the mental aggregates and kamma-born matter) because that has already been provided by the janaka-kamma that caused the present rebirth. It can only provide bhava-sampatti, which consists of various types of wealth, possessions, and requisites to be enjoyed in this life. Therefore, the first javana-cetanā or diṭṭhadhamma-vedaniya kamma of this daughter of the merchant, who offered alms, provided only the bhava-sampatti in the form of the wealth and requisites of a Chief Queen to be enjoyed in this present life during the course of existence.) From that time onwards, King Caṇḍapajjota performed great offerings and honors to the Venerable Kaccāyana.
222:
Because they were inspired by the Dhamma discourse of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, many men of good family were ordained under him. From that time on, the entire city of Ujjenī was shimmering with the color of robes and was filled with the breeze caused by the movement of the monks. That queen also conceived and, after ten months, gave birth to a son. On the day of the prince's naming ceremony, he was named 'Prince Gopāla', taking the name of his grandfather, the wealthy merchant Gopāla. The queen became well-known as 'Queen Gopālamātā' in connection with her son's name. Queen Gopālamātā, having great faith in the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, asked the King for permission and built a large monastery for the Venerable Mahākaccāyana in the Kañcanavana garden. After establishing the people of Ujjenī in faith in the Sasana, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana returned to the presence of the Blessed One.

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

At a later time, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery and conferring Etadagga titles upon the monks, He took the (1) Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, (2) Kaccāyana Peyyāla, and (3) Pārāyana Sutta as the basis for the occasion and declared regarding the Venerable Mahākaccāyana:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhူnaṃ saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākaccāno = Monks, among my monk disciples who analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief, Mahākaccāna is the foremost.”
223:
“Among my monk disciples, the monk Mahākaccāna is the most distinguished and the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the Etadagga position. The teachings preached by this Venerable Mahākaccāna should be extracted and noted from the Apadāna Commentary, the Theragāthā Commentary, and so forth.

This is the account of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana.

## (11-12) About the Two Panthaka Brothers

## (a) The Previous Aspirations of the Elders

In the past, one hundred thousand eons ago, during the time when the Padumuttara Buddha appeared, two brothers who were householders in the city of Haṃsāvatī were filled with faith and devotion to the Triple Gem. They constantly went to the presence of the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma. One day, among those two brothers, the younger brother saw the Blessed One placing a monk who possessed two qualities in the Etadagga position, saying: “In my Sasana, among the monks who create mind-made bodies, and among the monks who are skilled in the field of Rūpāvacara Jhāna, this monk is the most distinguished and the foremost.” Seeing this, he thought, “This monk is truly great; being a single person, he fulfills two qualities and wanders about. I, too, in the future, should become a monk who fulfills these two qualities in the Sasana of a future Buddha.”

That younger householder, following the example of previous aspirants for the position of an Elder, invited the Blessed One and for seven days [offered a great donation].
224: ...offered a great donation and then made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, seven days ago from today, you placed a certain monk in the position of Etadagga for these two qualities: the quality of being able to create a mind-made body and the quality of being skilled and proficient in the field of Rūpāvacara jhāna, saying 'This monk is the most excellent and foremost in my Sāsana.' By the merit of this great wholesome kamma, may I also be one who can fulfill these two qualities just like that monk." The Blessed One, looking into the future and seeing that the householder's aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy: "At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, the Buddha Gotama will appear. That Blessed One will place you in these two positions of Etadagga." After delivering a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), the Buddha departed. (This was the aspiration of the younger brother). The elder brother, who was also a householder, one day saw the Blessed One placing a monk in the position of Etadagga for being "Saññā-vivaṭṭa-kusala" (skilled in the mastery of Arūpāvacara jhāna). Like his younger brother, he performed a great act of merit and aspired to attain that Etadagga position of "Saññā-vivaṭṭa-kusala." The Blessed One also gave a prophecy to the elder brother that his aspiration would be fulfilled. Both of those householder brothers performed wholesome deeds while the Buddha was still alive.
225: After the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, they made offerings of gold at the sacred Relic Stūpa (Sārīrika-cetiya). When they passed away from that life, they were reborn in the celestial realms. While those two brothers wandered through the celestial and human realms (without ever falling into the four woeful states), one hundred thousand aeons passed. (Among those two brothers, the meritorious deeds performed by the elder, Mahāpanthaka, during the intervening period are not specifically mentioned in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā). The younger brother, Cūḷapanthaka, became a monk during the Sāsana of the Buddha Kassapa and practiced the Odāta-kasiṇa meditation for twenty thousand years, after which he was reborn again in the celestial realm. Then, after our Blessed One became the Buddha and turned the Wheel of Dhamma, the time came when he was residing and dwelling in the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha. (At this point, I shall relate the intervening story of how the Panthaka brothers were born) — In the city of Rājagaha, the daughter of the wealthy merchant Dhanaseṭṭhī had a love affair with her own servant. Thinking, "Others will surely come to know of this deed of mine," she consulted with her husband, the servant: "We cannot continue to live in this place. If my parents should find out about this fault, they will surely cut me into pieces and kill me. Let us go and live in another place." Having agreed, they secretly took some gifts and wealth, went out through the first gate that opened, and consulted together, saying, "Let us go and live in a place where others will not know us," and they both departed. While those two were living in an obscure place, the merchant's daughter became pregnant as a result of their union.
226: When the time for the pregnancy to mature arrived, she spoke to her husband: "My lord, my pregnancy is now mature. To give birth to a child in a place far removed from relatives and friends is very difficult for both of us. Let us return to my parents' house." Her husband, saying "We shall go today, we shall go tomorrow," comforted her with words but let the days pass by. Then the merchant's daughter thought, "This fool, because his own crime is so great, does not dare to go. It is the nature of parents to certainly desire the welfare and happiness of their children. Whether this fool wants to follow or not, let him; I must go." Having thought thus, when the man went out of the house, the merchant's daughter packed and stored the household utensils, left word with the neighbors in the next house to tell him she was going to her parents' house, and set out on the journey alone. Later, when the man returned home and did not find the merchant's daughter, he asked the neighbors and, hearing the news that she had returned to her parents' house, he followed her quickly and caught up with her on the way. For that merchant's daughter, the labor of childbirth occurred right there at that spot where they met. When the husband asked, "Lady, what is this?", she replied, "My lord, a son has been born." When they consulted, "What shall we do now?", they agreed, "The purpose for which we were going to the parents' house was for the childbirth. Now, that matter of childbirth has already taken place on the way..."
227:
“It is finished. What shall we do by going to my parents' house? (It is of no use). Let us return.” Both agreed and returned from that very spot. The child was named “Panthaka” (Road-born) because he was born on the road.

Soon, the merchant's daughter became pregnant again. When that second pregnancy was mature, she gave birth on the way to her parents' house just like before. Therefore, the first-born elder son was named “Mahāpanthaka” (Great Road-born) and the younger son born later was named “Cūḷapanthaka” (Small Road-born).

Both husband and wife returned to their place, each carrying a son. While they were living there, the elder son Mahāpanthaka heard other children saying “uncle, elder uncle, grandfather, grandmother,” etc. He asked his mother, “O mother, other children say ‘grandfather, grandmother,’ etc. Do we not have any relatives?” The mother, the merchant's daughter, said, “Yes, dear son. You have no relatives in this place. In the city of Rājagaha, the great merchant Mahādhana is your grandfather. In that city of Rājagaha, your relatives are many.” Mahāpanthaka then asked, “O mother, why do you not go to that city of Rājagaha?”

The mother did not answer her son why she did not go to Rājagaha, but when the sons asked repeatedly...
228:
...she said to her husband, “O lord, these young sons are troubling me greatly. If my parents see us, they will not tear our flesh and eat it. Let us go and show the children their grandparents' house.” The husband said, “O lady, I do not dare to go before your parents. However, I will take you there.” The merchant's daughter said, “Very well, lord. It is proper to show the children their grandparents' house in some way.” Both husband and wife took the young sons and traveled, eventually reaching Rājagaha. They stayed at a rest house at one of the city gates. The mother of the children sent word to her parents that they had arrived.

When the parents heard the news, they said, “For those wandering in Saṃsāra, there is no one who has not been a son or a daughter. Those two have committed a very great offense against us. Both of them are unable and unworthy to stand before us. However, let them take this much wealth and go live happily wherever they wish. But let the two children be sent to our house.” They sent a messenger with this reply. The merchant's daughter took the wealth given by her parents and handed the two young sons to the messengers to be sent to the grandparents. The two brothers, Mahāpanthaka and Cūḷapanthaka, grew up happily in their grandparents' house.
229:
## (b) Ordaining in the Final Life

Among the two brothers, Cūḷapanthaka was still very young and tender. Mahāpanthaka always accompanied his grandfather, the merchant Dhanaseṭṭhi, to listen to the Buddha's Dhamma. Because Mahāpanthaka constantly heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, his mind inclined toward ordaining as a monk. Thus, Mahāpanthaka asked his grandfather, “Grandfather, if you permit, I would like to ordain as a monk.” The grandfather, Dhanaseṭṭhi, said, “What are you saying, dear grandson? For me, your ordination is better than the whole world ordaining. If you are able, do ordain, my grandson.” He spoke joyfully, accepted Mahāpanthaka's request, and took him to the Buddha. The Buddha asked, “Great merchant, how is it? Have you obtained the child?” Dhanaseṭṭhi replied, “Yes, Blessed One. This boy is my eldest grandson. He says he wishes to ordain in your presence, Bhante.”

The Buddha commanded a nearby alms-collecting monk, “Ordain this boy.” The Piṇḍacārika Elder explained the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. From the time he became a novice, Sāmaṇera Mahāpanthaka studied many of the Buddha's words, the Piṭakas, and when he reached the age of twenty...
230:
...he received full ordination as a bhikkhu. After becoming a monk, he strove in meditation and became proficient in attaining the four formless jhanas (arūpāvacara jhāna). Emerging from jhana, he practiced Vipassanā and reached the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). Thus, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka became the foremost and most excellent among the monks who were highly skilled in the field of formless jhanas.

## Ordaining the Younger Brother

Venerable Mahāpanthaka spent his time in the bliss of jhana and the bliss of fruition. One day, he thought, “Will I be able to give this bliss of jhana and fruition to my younger brother Cūḷapanthaka?” He went to the grandfather and asked, “Lay disciple, great merchant, if you agree, I wish to ordain Cūḷapanthaka.” The grandfather gave his permission, saying, “Ordain him as you wish, Bhante.” Then Venerable Mahāpanthaka ordained the boy Cūḷapanthaka and established him in the ten precepts.

Sāmaṇera Cūḷapanthaka, under the guidance of his elder brother Venerable Mahāpanthaka, [tried to learn]:

Padumaṃ yathā kokanadaṃ sugandhaṃ,
Pāto siyā phulla-mavītagandhaṃ.
Aṅgīrasaṃ passa virocamānaṃ,
Tapanta-mādicca-mivantalikkhe.

Kokanadaṃ = beautiful in color with rising petals, named Kokanada. Sugandhaṃ = possessing a fine, spreading fragrance.
231:
Padumaṃ = the Paduma lotus. Pāto = in the morning when the sun first rises. Phullaṃ = being in bloom. Avītagandhaṃ = not devoid of fine fragrance. Virocamānaṃ = beautiful and lovely to behold. Siyā yathā = just as it is. (Tathā = similarly). Sugandhaṃ = fragrant with the scent of physical beauty and virtue. Antalikkhe = in the expanse of the sky. Ādiccamiva = like the sun rising in the autumn (sarada). Tapantaṃ = shining brightly with the majesty of his power. Virocamānaṃ = beautiful and magnificent whenever seen. Aṅgīrasaṃ = the Buddha, from whose body rays constantly flash and emit. Passa = passāhi = behold with faith appearing clearly in the mind—

He learned this verse. Every time he learned a new section, as he tried to learn the subsequent sections, the previous ones would completely disappear. For Sāmaṇera Cūḷapanthaka, four months passed while he strove to learn this verse (meaning even after four months, he could not memorize it).

(In the time of Kassapa Buddha, Cūḷapanthaka had been a monk and a learned person. He had mocked another slow-witted monk who was learning Pali. That slow-witted monk, out of great shame from the mockery, did not dare to learn Pali or recite anymore. Due to that unwholesome kamma, now in his life as Cūḷapanthaka, even after becoming a novice, his wisdom was terrifyingly dull and sluggish. Therefore, every time he learned a section, as he learned the subsequent ones...
232:
...they would completely disappear and be forgotten. — From the Aṅguttara Commentary).

Then, the elder brother Venerable Mahāpanthaka said to Sāmaṇera Cūḷapanthaka, “Cūḷapanthaka, you are an unfit person (abhabba puggala) who cannot attain the Path and Fruit in this Dispensation. You cannot even learn one verse in four months. How can you, who cannot learn a single verse in four months, reach the summit of a monk's duty (Arahatship)? You will not be able to reach it. Therefore, leave this monastery.” He drove him out. Being driven out by his elder brother, Sāmaṇera Cūḷapanthaka did not dare stay in the monastery and stood weeping at the edge of the monastery (where his brother could not see him).

At that time, the Buddha was residing in the Mango Grove monastery donated and built by the physician Jīvaka, depending on Rājagaha as his alms-resort. Then, Jīvaka sent a man, saying, “Go and invite the Buddha to come for a meal tomorrow along with five hundred monks.” At that time, Venerable Mahāpanthaka was the one who had received the authorization as the meal-assigner (bhattuddesaka). Thus, when the lay disciple who came to invite them for the meal said, “Bhante, please accept the meal for five hundred monks,” Venerable Mahāpanthaka replied, “I accept the meal for the remaining monks, excluding Cūḷapanthaka” (speaking words of rejection toward Cūḷapanthaka).
233:
## The Buddha Giving the Meditation Subject
Upon hearing those words, Cūḷapanthaka became exceedingly distressed. The Buddha, seeing Cūḷapanthaka’s exhaustion and reflecting, "When I depart, Cūḷapanthaka will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation," approached him. Manifesting himself clearly at a short distance, he asked, "Dear Panthaka, why are you weeping?" Cūḷapanthaka replied, "Venerable Sir, my elder brother, the Elder, has expelled me from the monastery." The Buddha then spoke words of encouragement: "Dear Panthaka, your elder brother does not possess the Knowledge of Inclinations and Latent Tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) of beings. You are a person to be guided by the Buddha (buddha-veneyya)." He then gave him a piece of clean, coarse cloth created by his psychic power and instructed, "Dear Panthaka, hold this cloth in your hand and meditate by repeatedly reciting: 'Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ' (Removal of dust, removal of dust)."

(In this regard: In a previous life, Cūḷapanthaka was a king. While touring the city in a clockwise direction, his forehead perspired, and he wiped it with a clean piece of cloth. The cloth became soiled. That king (the future Cūḷapanthaka) then perceived the notion of impermanence (anicca-saññā), thinking, "Due to this impure body, such a clean piece of cloth has lost its original nature and become soiled. Indeed, conditioned things are impermanent!" Therefore, for Cūḷapanthaka, this 'Rajoharaṇa-kammaṭṭhāna' (the meditation on the cloth that removes dust) became
234:
a powerful supporting condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship. Thus, the Buddha, seeing Cūḷapanthaka’s past merit as mentioned, and wishing to urge him toward a meditation subject suitable for that merit, gave him the piece of clean, coarse cloth).

## The Attainment of Arahantship by Venerable Cūḷapanthaka
Cūḷapanthaka sat rubbing the piece of cloth given by the Buddha with his hand, repeatedly reciting, "Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ" (Removal of dust, removal of dust). As he continued to rub it, the threads of that coarse cloth became soiled. Rubbing it further, it became even more soiled, like a cleaning rag. As Cūḷapanthaka’s wisdom matured, he visualized the nature of decay and passing away (khaya-vaya) in that coarse cloth and reflected: "This piece of coarse cloth was originally pure and clean. However, because of this physical body (upādinnaka), it has become soiled. This mind is also of a similar nature; though this mind is originally pure and clean in its state as life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta), it becomes soiled due to its association with unwholesome states such as greed, hatred, and delusion (rāga, dosa, moha)." Reflecting and meditating thus within his own body, he practiced concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) and attained the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna). Using those jhānas as a basis, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) and reached the Fruit of Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa); he became an Arahant who had attained the analytical insights. Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, having masterfully attained the mind-made fine-material sphere jhānas,
235:
became a possessor of psychic power (iddhividha) who could manifest as many from one, and as one from many. Furthermore, for this venerable one, through the Path of Arahantship itself, the three Pitakas were mastered and the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) were attained. (This type of attainment is called scriptural knowledge accomplished through the Path (magga-siddha-pariyatti) and supernormal knowledge accomplished through the Path (magga-siddha-abhiññā). It means that upon reaching the Path of Arahantship, one has already mastered the Pitakas and attained the supernormal knowledges without having specifically studied the scriptures or specifically strived for the supernormal knowledges; they are called scriptural and supernormal knowledges completed by the power of the Path).

On the following day, the Buddha, together with 499 monks, went to the house of the physician Jīvaka and sat down to receive a meal. Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, however, did not follow because his elder brother, the Elder Mahāpanthaka, had not accepted a meal for him. The physician Jīvaka first prepared to offer rice gruel (yāgu). The Buddha did not accept the gruel but covered his bowl with his hand. When Jīvaka asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you not accept the gruel?", the Buddha replied, "Lay disciple Jīvaka, there is still one monk remaining at the monastery."

Then, Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Friend, go and invite the venerable one who remains at the monastery and bring him here." Before that man arrived, Venerable Cūḷapanthaka had already used his psychic power to create a thousand monks, making each monk's appearance and activities, such as the arranging of robes,
236:
different from the others.

The man sent by Jīvaka saw a great number of monks at the monastery and (since Jīvaka had sent him to invite only one monk, he did not dare to invite them) returned and said to Jīvaka, "O master Jīvaka, there are more monks at the monastery than there are here at your house. Therefore, I am unable to identify or decide which noble one should be invited."

Jīvaka asked the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of the monk who remains at the monastery?" The Buddha replied, "Lay disciple Jīvaka, the monk who remains at the monastery is named Cūḷapanthaka." Jīvaka then sent the man again, instructing him, "Friend, go once more and ask, 'Which venerable one is named Cūḷapanthaka?' and then invite him."

The man went to the monastery and asked, "Which venerable one is named Cūḷapanthaka?" All one thousand monks replied, "I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!" The man returned again and told Jīvaka, "Master, all one thousand monks said, 'I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!' I was unable to identify or decide which monk I should invite."
237:
Because Jīvaka was a noble lay disciple (ariya-dāyaka) who had realized the Four Noble Truths, he understood through this means that the monk remaining at the monastery was a possessor of psychic powers. He sent the man back, saying, "Friend, go. Tell the very first monk who speaks, 'The Buddha calls for you,' and then take hold of the hem of that monk's robe and invite him." When the man went back to the monastery and did as Jīvaka had instructed, the one thousand monks vanished at that very moment. Only then did the man invite and bring Venerable Cūḷapanthaka. Only at that moment did the Buddha accept and partake of the rice gruel.

After the Buddha had finished his meal and returned to the monastery, a discussion arose among the monks in the Dhamma Hall: "How truly great are the Buddhas! They can make a monk, who could not even memorize a single verse (gāthā) in four months, become one so greatly possessed of psychic power." The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of those monks, went to the Dhamma Hall, sat on the prepared Buddha-seat, and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" The monks replied, "Venerable Sir, we are not discussing anything else; we are only speaking of your virtues, saying, 'Cūḷapanthaka has received a great gain from the Blessed One.'" The Buddha then said, "Monks, it is not surprising that he has now received the supramundane inheritance (lokuttara-dāyajja) by following my advice.
238:
In the distant past, even while his wisdom was not yet mature, this Cūḷapanthaka received a mundane inheritance by following my instruction." When the monks requested, "When was that, Venerable Sir?", the Buddha related the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka of the past as follows:

## Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a wise and learned treasurer named Cūḷaseṭṭhi who was skilled in all omens. One day, while going to serve the king, the treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi saw a dead mouse on the road. Looking at the stars in the sky and reflecting, he made a prediction: "A young man of good family with the eye of wisdom could take this dead mouse and be able to support a wife and children, or start a business."

A certain obscure poor man heard the prediction of the wise treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi and thought, "This wise treasurer would not speak without knowing." He picked up the dead mouse, went to a market, and sold it as cat food, receiving one small coin (kākaṇika). With that coin, he bought molasses. Then, carrying a pot of drinking water, he met some flower-gatherers returning from the forest. He gave them small pieces of molasses and provided them with clean drinking water using a ladle.
239:
offered them water to quench their thirst. The flower sellers, out of gratitude, each gave the poor man a handful of flowers.

(From this point on, because this poor young man of good birth was wise and was a disciple who followed the methods of the wise Treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi, he shall be referred to as the "Wise Young Disciple"). On the following day, using the proceeds from the flowers given by the flower sellers, the Wise Young Disciple took as much molasses and clean pots of drinking water as he could carry and went back to the flower garden. On that day, the flower sellers gave the Wise Young Disciple half of all the flowers they had picked before returning. In this manner, the Wise Young Disciple soon collected and saved eight pieces of silver (kahāpaṇas).

Later, on a day of heavy wind and rain, the Wise Young Disciple went to a neglected old garden. While he was gathering the firewood that had been blown down by the wind into piles, he received sixteen pieces of silver from a potter who served the king. When the Wise Young Disciple had a total of twenty-four pieces of silver—eight from the flowers and sixteen from the dry firewood—he thought to himself, "I have a good means and stratagem to acquire wealth; if I act as a donor of cool water to the grass-cutters, it will be a good means to gain wealth." He then placed a large water jar not far from the city gate and served drinking water to five hundred grass-cutters who came from the outskirts of the city, acting as their water donor. The grass-cutters said, "Friend, you have been very helpful to us. What service can we do for you?"
240:
When they asked, "What can we do to help you?", the Wise Young Disciple replied, "When a matter arises where I need your assistance, please help me then." After accepting their offer, he traveled here and there and established friendships and intimacy with the superintendent of land-routes and the superintendent of sea-routes.

One day, the superintendent of land-routes gave him a piece of good news, saying, "Tomorrow, a horse trader will come to this city of Vārāṇasī bringing five hundred horses." Upon hearing the words of the land-route superintendent, the Wise Young Disciple informed the grass-cutters and had each of them bring one more bundle of grass than on previous days. Then, at the time when the horses were being brought into the city, the Wise Young Disciple sat at the inner city gate, having piled up the one thousand bundles of grass where the horse trader could see them. Although the horse trader searched throughout the city, he could not find any fodder for the horses. Therefore, he gave the Wise Young Disciple one thousand silver coins and took those one thousand bundles of grass.

A few days later, his friend, the sea-route superintendent, sent word saying, "A large merchant ship has arrived at the ocean port." The Wise Young Disciple thought, "Another good means and stratagem to acquire wealth has arisen." He rented a carriage fully equipped with all its trappings for eight silver coins for a short time and went to the ocean port.
241:
Upon arrival, he gave a ring to the chief merchant of the ship as a deposit. He then had a pavilion-like enclosure with curtains neatly set up not far from the port. While sitting inside that pavilion, he gave orders to his (hired) attendants, saying, "If external merchants come, inform me through a three-tiered reporting system (meaning, having three levels of reporting stations)."

Having heard the news that a large merchant ship had arrived, about one hundred great merchants from Vārāṇasī came to the port, thinking, "We shall buy the merchandise." The Wise Young Disciple's men, who were already at the port, met them and said, "You will not get the merchandise. A great merchant residing in such-and-such a place has already given a deposit for all the goods." When the hundred Vārāṇasī merchants heard this, they went to the Wise Young Disciple (the one referred to as the great merchant).

As previously instructed, the Wise Young Disciple's attendants respectfully announced the arrival of the great merchants through the three-tiered reporting system, making it as grand as possible. The hundred merchants each gave the Wise Young Disciple a gift of one thousand coins to become shareholders in the ship's cargo. Then, they each gave him another one thousand coins as profit to buy him out of his share, thereby making the ship's merchandise their own property.
242:
The Wise Young Disciple thus acquired two hundred thousand silver coins in a single sitting. He returned to the city of Vārāṇasī and, reflecting, "It is proper that I should be a person who knows gratitude (kataññū)," he took one hundred thousand coins and went to the wise Treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi.

Then, the wise Treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi asked the Wise Young Disciple, "Dear son, how did you acquire these silver coins and wealth?" The Wise Young Disciple recounted all the events, saying, "My lord, by following the excellent stratagem you mentioned while looking at the dead mouse, I have acquired two hundred thousand and twenty-four silver coins within four months." When the wise Treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi heard the young man's words, he reflected, "It is not proper to let such a wise young man become the wealth of others; I should make him my own." He then gave his grown daughter in marriage to the wise young man and elevated him to be the master and head of the household. When the wise Treasurer Cūḷaseṭṭhi passed away, that wise man of good birth received the position of Treasurer in the city of Vārāṇasī and, after living out his life span, passed away according to his kamma.

After the Buddha had related these two stories—the story of the present and the story of the past—He connected the two and, now that He had attained Buddhahood, He spoke this verse:

"Appakena pi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo.
Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhamaṃ."
243:
Bhikkhave = O monks, my dear sons. Puriso = A wise man. Aṇuṃ = A small, negligible. Aggiṃ = Fire. Sandhamaṃ = Sandhamanto = By striving without rest, adding fuel and blowing with the breath from the mouth. Mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ = A great mass of fire. Samuṭṭhāpeti iva = Just as one causes to arise. Evaṃ = In the same way. Vicakkhaṇo = One who is skilled and shrewd in trade. Medhāvī = A wise person who considers the future and the past. Appakena pi = With even a small, negligible. Pābhatena = Capital. Mahādhanayasaṃ = Great wealth and glory. Samuṭṭhāpetvā = Having caused to arise. Tattha = In that great wealth and glory. Attānaṃ = Himself. Samuṭṭhāpeti = He can elevate himself to the status of a millionaire.

Thus, the Buddha preached this verse and this account of the origin of the matter to the monks assembled in the Dhamma hall.

## (C) Attaining the Foremost Titles (Etadagga)

At another time, while the Buddha was seated on the Dhamma throne surrounded by the community of Noble Saṅgha, during the ceremony of conferring the foremost titles (Etadagga) upon many venerable monks, He declared concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ manomayaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimminantānaṃ yadidaṃ cūḷapanthako (1),
244:
Cetovivaṭṭakusalānaṃ yadidaṃ cūḷapanthako, (2) = Monks, among my disciple monks who can create a physical body made by the mind (produced by the mind of higher knowledge), Cūḷapanthaka is the foremost (1). Among my disciple monks who are skilled in mental transformation (in the field of Rūpāvacara Jhāna), Cūḷapanthaka is the foremost (2)."

With these words of praise, the Buddha conferred these two foremost titles upon him.

Regarding his elder brother, the Elder Mahāpanthaka, the Buddha declared:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saññāvivaṭṭakusalānaṃ yadidaṃ mahāpanthako = Monks, among my disciple monks who are skilled in the transformation of perception (in the field of Arūpāvacara Jhāna), Mahāpanthaka is the foremost."

With these words of praise, He conferred the foremost title in the field of Saññāvivaṭṭakusala upon him.

(In this regard: When other monks create a mind-made body through the higher knowledge of psychic power, they create only a few, such as three or four; they do not create many. In such creation, they create created-forms (nimmitas) that look like themselves, the possessor of psychic power, and perform only one single type of action. The Elder Cūḷapanthaka, however, created a thousand created-monks with just a single moment of advertence (one cognitive process). In that creation, he made the created-forms appear different from one another in appearance and in action—one having one appearance and another having another, one performing one task and another performing another.
245:
He created them in this way. Therefore, he received the foremost title in creating mind-made bodies. Although the meanings of Cetovivaṭṭakusala and Saññāvivaṭṭakusala are explained in various ways in the Commentaries, they are not mentioned here to avoid confusing the reader's intellect. The teachings related to these two brothers, the Panthaka Elders, should be noted in detail from the Apadāna Commentary, Theragāthā Commentary, Dhammapada Commentary, Udāna Commentary, and so forth.)

This is the story of the two Panthaka brothers.
**********
## (13) The Story of Elder Subhūti
## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This noble man, the future Elder Subhūti, was born into a wealthy Brahmin family one hundred thousand aeons ago, before the appearance of the Buddha Padumuttara, and was known by the name of Nanda the youth.

When Nanda the youth reached maturity, he studied and mastered the three Vedas. Finding no essence of truth in those Vedic texts, he became an ascetic at the foot of Mount Nisabha together with his retinue of forty-four thousand youths. He developed the five mundane higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. He also guided his forty-four thousand disciple ascetics to become possessors of jhāna and higher knowledge.

At that time, the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world and resided near the royal city of Haṃsāvatī as his resort village. One day, at dawn, when he surveyed the world of beings, he saw the disciples of the ascetic Nanda...
246: Seeing that the forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics would attain Arahantship and that Nanda ascetic would aspire for the rank of a Great Disciple endowed with two qualities, the Buddha performed his morning ablutions early. Taking his bowl and robes, he proceeded to Nanda ascetic's leaf-hut in the same manner as described in the story of the Elder Sāriputta. It should be understood that the offering of various fruits, the preparation of the flower-seat, and the Buddha's entry into the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) occurred as previously described in the story of the Elder Sāriputta. Specifically, when the Buddha emerged from the attainment of cessation, he commanded a certain Elder disciple who possessed two qualities—(1) the quality of living peacefully free from defilements, and (2) the quality of being worthy of the highest offerings—saying, 'Dear son, preach a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the flower-seat offering to the group of ascetics.' The Elder, established in his own domain, reflected upon the Three Pitakas and preached the discourse of appreciation. At the conclusion of that Elder's discourse, the Padumuttara Buddha himself preached the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, all forty-four thousand disciple ascetics attained Arahantship. Their teacher, Nanda ascetic, however, was focused on the mental image of the monk preaching the appreciation discourse and was unable to direct his wisdom to follow the Buddha's Dhamma. (This means that because he was so absorbed in the monk preaching the appreciation discourse, his wisdom could not penetrate the Buddha's teaching.)
247: The Buddha stretched out his golden hand and called the remaining forty-four thousand disciples with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, monk) ordination, saying, 'Etha Bhikkhavo' (Come, monks). At that moment, their hair and beards disappeared, and they were instantly provided with miraculously created requisites. They became majestic monks, appearing like senior elders of sixty rains (vassa) or eighty years of age. Nanda ascetic paid homage to the Buddha and, standing before him, asked, 'Venerable Sir, what is the name of the monk who preached the discourse of appreciation for the flower-seat offering in Your Majesty's dispensation?' The Buddha replied, 'That monk is the one who has attained the foremost rank (Etadagga) in my dispensation for these two qualities: the quality of living peacefully free from defilements and the quality of being worthy of the highest offerings.' Then Nanda ascetic made an aspiration, saying, 'Venerable Sir, by the merit of this great deed performed over these seven days, I do not desire any other worldly or heavenly bliss. Instead, in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I become a person who receives the foremost rank, endowed with these two qualities, just like this Elder who preached the discourse of appreciation.' Seeing that Nanda ascetic's aspiration would be fulfilled without hindrance, the Buddha gave him the prophecy (byādika) and departed. Nanda ascetic also listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha regularly and, having attained unwavering meditative absorptions (jhāna), was reborn in the Brahma realm immediately after death. (This is the past merit and aspiration of the Elder Subhūti. The Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā) does not mention his meritorious deeds during the intervening period within this one hundred thousand aeons.)
248: ## (b) Ordination in the Final Life. After one hundred thousand aeons had passed and this dispensation era arrived, the future Elder Subhūti was born in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of the wealthy merchant Sumana (the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika) and was named Subhūti. Later, when our Buddha appeared and was residing near the city of Rājagaha, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika brought trade goods from Sāvatthī to the house of his friend (and brother-in-law), the merchant of Rājagaha. Hearing that the Buddha had appeared, he visited the Buddha who was staying in the Sītavana grove. Upon his first meeting, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He then invited the Buddha to visit Sāvatthī. Along the forty-five yojana journey between Sāvatthī and Rājagaha, he spent one hundred thousand coins at every yojana to build rest houses. In Sāvatthī, he purchased Prince Jeta's grove, which was eight karīsas in area, by covering the ground with gold coins edge to edge. He then built the great Jetavana monastery for the Buddha and donated it. (For the detailed account of this, one should refer to the story of Anāthapiṇḍika in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 20, from page 180 to page 222.)
249:
(From page 180, starting from the account of the wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍika up to page 222, one should look and take note).

On the day of the dedication ceremony of the great Jetavana Monastery, this young man Subhūti (the son of a wealthy merchant) went together with his elder brother, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. Upon hearing the Dhamma, great faith arose in him, and he entered the monkhood. After becoming a monk, Venerable Subhūti well-studied and mastered the two Mātikās. Having been taught the meditation subjects, he resided in a forest monastery and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse with great diligence. By taking Mettā-jhāna (loving-kindness absorption) as the basis and developing Vipassanā (insight), he attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

## (c) Receiving Two Etadagga Titles

When the Venerable Subhūti preached the Dhamma, he did not use the Puggalādhiṭṭhāna method (referring to or pointing out specific individuals) at all, but preached only the pure Dhamma according to the method taught by the Blessed One using the Dhammādhiṭṭhāna method. (This is the reason for receiving the Etadagga title in the category of “Araṇavihārī = one who dwells in peace, free from defilements”).

When the Elder went for alms, at every house, he would reflect, “By doing this, it will be of great benefit to the donors,” and he would enter Mettā-jhāna. After emerging from that Mettā-jhāna, he would accept the alms. (This is the reason for the Elder receiving the Etadagga title in the category of “Dakkhiṇeyya = one worthy of noble offerings”).
250: Therefore, later, when the Buddha held a ceremony to confer the foremost titles (Etadagga) upon the monks, he praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying: 'Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ araṇavihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ subhūti (1), dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ yadidaṃ subhūti (2). Monks, among my disciple monks who live peacefully free from defilements, Subhūti is the foremost (1). Among my disciple monks who are worthy of the highest offerings, Subhūti is the foremost (2).' Thus, he conferred these two foremost titles upon him. (In this context: (1) Regarding the Araṇavihārī title, defilements such as lust are called 'raṇa' because they cause weeping and lamentation. The noble Arahants who live peacefully and are free from these causes of lamentation—defilements like lust—are called Araṇavihārī individuals. Although other Arahant Elders also live peacefully free from defilements, when they preach the Dhamma, they may use the method of personal reference (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) to mention specific individuals, highlighting their virtues or faults. However, the Venerable Subhūti, as mentioned before, preached only the pure Dhamma in a strictly impersonal way (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), just as the Buddha had taught. Therefore, he received the foremost title among those who live peacefully free from defilements.)
251: In this regard, according to the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi: (1) Following the Middle Way without indulging in the two extremes; (2) When speaking or preaching, if one uses personal reference (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) and says 'this person is praiseworthy,' it is called 'exalting,' and if one says 'this person is blameworthy,' it is called 'disparaging.' Without such exalting or disparaging, one should point out only the nature of the Dhamma through the impersonal method (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), saying 'this quality is praiseworthy' or 'this quality is blameworthy'; (3) Distinguishing between the two types of happiness—internal happiness (ajjhatta-sukha) gained through tranquility and insight meditation, and external happiness (bahiddha-sukha) gained through the five external sense objects—and then cultivating only internal happiness; (4) Speaking about a person's affairs, whether in their presence or absence, only if it is true and beneficial; (5) Speaking or preaching without haste and in a smooth, clear manner; (6) When going to another region, not conflicting with or rebelling against the local dialects used there (even if they differ from one's own). (a) Not indulging in the two extremes, following the Middle Way. (b) Neither exalting nor disparaging, preaching the Dhamma. (c) Distinguishing the two types of happiness, cultivating the internal. (d) Knowing what to say, both in presence and absence. (e) Speaking without haste, smoothly and gently. (f) Not conflicting with local speech; these are the six Araṇa qualities. According to this mnemonic verse, one should understand the 'Araṇavihāra Dhamma'—the six qualities for living peacefully free from defilements. (2) Regarding the Dakkhiṇeyya title, although other Arahant Elders are also worthy of the highest offerings, the Venerable Subhūti, when going for alms, at every house...
252:
Reflecting, "This will be of particularly great benefit [to the donor]," he would enter the absorption of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna) and, after emerging from that absorption, accept the alms-food. For this reason, he was awarded the foremost title (Etadagga) among the disciples who are "Dakkhiṇeyya = worthy of noble offerings."

In this regard, "The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, purifies the object. (To 'purify the object' means that by entering the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), he purifies himself as the recipient of noble offerings to ensure great benefit). Venerable Subhūti purifies the gift. (To 'purify the gift' means that through his meditation on loving-kindness, he causes the donors to give with a gentle heart and great devotion; thus, because of the donor, he causes the gift to be pure, flourishing, and of great benefit). To elaborate—when Venerable Sāriputta went for alms, he would stand at the door of a house and enter nirodha-samāpatti for a set duration until the alms-food was brought; only when the donor approached would he emerge from nirodha-samāpatti and accept the offerings. Venerable Subhūti, likewise, would enter mettā-jhāna and only when the donor approached would he emerge from mettā-jhāna and accept the offerings." (This passage from the commentary on the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta, page 193 of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Aṭṭhakathā, should be specially noted).

The teachings concerning Venerable Subhūti should be understood from the Apadāna Pali Commentary and other sources.

This concludes the account of Venerable Subhūti.
**********
## (14) The Account of Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata
## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration
(The original name of this Elder was Revata. He was the youngest brother of Venerable Sāriputta. Because he resided in a forest monastery in an acacia (khadira) forest, which was uneven, rugged, and full of gravel,
253:
he became known as 'Khadiravaniya Revata = Venerable Revata who dwells in the acacia forest.' In writing the account of the Elder, for the sake of brevity, I shall refer to him simply as Venerable Revata).

One hundred thousand eons ago, during the time when the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world, this Bodhisatta (the future Venerable Revata) was a citizen of Haṃsāvatī. At that time, he lived as a ferryman at the Payāga landing-place on the great Ganges River. Then, the Buddha Padumuttara, while traveling on a journey together with a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, arrived at the Payāga landing-place (to cross to the other side).

When the noble youth, the future Revata, saw the Buddha, he thought, "It is not possible for me to see the Buddha constantly. This time, when the Buddha has arrived, is a great opportunity for me to perform meritorious deeds." Having so considered, he constructed a large raft by joining boats together. Above that raft, he fixed a white canopy and decorated it with hanging garlands of fragrant flowers. On the floor below, he spread exquisite mats woven from fine flaxen thread and transported the Buddha, along with the one hundred thousand monks, to the other side.

At that time, the Buddha appointed a certain forest-dwelling monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of 'Āraññaka = forest-dwelling.' The noble youth, the ferryman, seeing this event, thought, "I too
254:
should become a person who receives the foremost title (Etadagga) as the best among forest-dwelling monks in the dispensation of a future Buddha, just like this monk." Having thus resolved, he invited the Buddha and performed a great almsgiving (mahādāna) for seven days. Afterward, prostrating at the feet of the Buddha, he made the aspiration: "O Blessed One, just like that Venerable monk whom You have praised and appointed to the foremost position, may I also, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become the most excellent and foremost person among forest-dwelling monks."

The Buddha, seeing that the aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you will become the most excellent and foremost person among forest-dwelling monks, receiving the Etadagga title." Having given this prophecy, He departed. (The Mahā-aṭṭhakathā does not mention any other meritorious deeds of the Elder during the intervening period).

## (b) Ordination in His Final Life
That noble youth, the ferryman, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, without falling into the four woeful states, wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time when our Buddha appeared, he was conceived in the womb of the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī in the Brahmin village of Nālaka, within the territory of Magadha. He was the youngest brother of three elder brothers—Upatissa, Cunda, and Upasena—and three elder sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā. He was named Revata.
255:
Thereafter, Revata's parents consulted each other, saying, "As our children grow up, the monks who are sons of the Buddha take them away and ordain them. Let us bind our son Revata with the fetters of household life while he is still young (before the monks can ordain him as a novice)."

(In this context: Venerable Sāriputta, after his own ordination, had ordained his three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—and his two brothers—Cunda and Upasena. Only the boy Revata remained at home. Therefore, the parents consulted in this manner).

Having agreed upon this, the parents brought a young girl from a family of equal caste, lineage, and wealth. They had her pay respects to Revata's aged grandmother and said as a blessing, "O daughter, may you live to be older than your grandmother here."

(The parents spoke this blessing because they wished for the young girl to have a long life. At that time, the grandmother was one hundred and twenty years old; her hair was white, her teeth had fallen out, her skin was wrinkled, her body was covered in dark spots, and she was extremely bent at the waist like the rafters of an old house).

## Revata’s Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega)
When Revata heard his parents' blessing, he thought, "This girl is young and in her first stage of life. It is said that this girl's youthful and beautiful
256:
appearance will become shriveled, decayed, and aged just like my grandmother's. I will ask my parents to understand their intention." He then asked, "O mother and father, with what purpose did you say this?" The parents replied, "Dear son, we spoke this blessing so that your bride, this girl, may reach old age like your grandmother." Then Revata, truly not understanding, asked, "O mother and father, will this girl's very youthful appearance really become aged like the grandmother's?" At that, the parents explained, "Dear son, what are you saying? Only those with great merit live to be as old as your grandmother."

Revata reflected, "It is said that this girl's beautiful and youthful appearance will have white hair, lost teeth, and wrinkled skin just like this grandmother's. Why should I be attached to a form that is subject to such shriveling, decay, and old age? It is of no benefit. I shall follow the path taken by my elder brothers."
