Having so reflected, he pretended to want to play like a child and said to his peers, "Friends, come, let's play a running game."

Although his parents forbade him, saying, "Dear son, do not go outside the house on your wedding day," Revata pretended to want to play with the boys. When it was his turn to run, he ran only a short distance and delayed time by pretending to clean his limbs before
257:
returning. When his second turn to run came, he ran as if faster than before and returned. When his third turn came, he realized, "This is the right time for me to escape." He ran with all his might in whatever direction he was facing. When he reached a forest monastery where monks who practiced the dhutaṅga of wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūla) resided, he paid respects to the Elders and requested them to ordain him as a novice.

The Elders declined, saying, "O young man, we do not know whose son you are. Moreover, you have come wearing full ornaments. Who would dare to ordain you? We certainly do not dare."

Then Revata raised both his arms and cried out, "I am being robbed! I am being robbed!"

Monks gathered from here and there and asked, "O young man, there is no one here who would rob you of your clothes or ornaments. Yet you cry out 'I am being robbed.' To what are you referring?" Then the boy Revata said:

"Venerable sirs, I am not referring to being robbed of clothes or ornaments. In truth, for me (because I am not being ordained), I am being robbed of the three types of happiness—human, divine, and Nibbāna. (In this context, the three types of happiness—human, divine, and Nibbāna—
258:
are mentioned in terms of their sequential stages). It is in reference to being robbed of these three types of happiness that I speak. Even if you, Venerable sirs, do not ordain me, do you at least know my eldest brother?"

They asked, "What is your eldest brother's name?" The boy Revata replied, "When my eldest brother was a layman, his name was Upatissa. Now that he is a monk, everyone says his name is Sāriputta, Venerable sirs."

Then the monks said, "Friends, if that is so, this noble youth is our youngest brother. Our elder, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, previously instructed us, 'My relatives are all of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). If anyone comes saying they are my relative, ordain them by whatever means possible.' This boy is the biological younger brother of our elder, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. Therefore, let us ordain him." They all agreed, explained the meditation on the fivefold skin-parts (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), and ordained the boy Revata as a novice. Later, when he reached the age of twenty, they gave him full ordination and encouraged him to strive in the practice of meditation.
259:
After receiving the meditation subject, Venerable Revata entered an acacia forest (khadiravana) that was not too far from his teachers and preceptors, yet was uneven, rugged, and full of gravel and stones. There, he exerted himself in the practice of a monk. He made a firm resolution: "I shall not go to see the Blessed One or my elder brother, the Great Elder, until I have attained Arahantship." While he was thus practicing meditation with great perseverance, three months passed. For a well-born youth who was delicate and refined, having to consume very coarse food caused his mind to shrink as if it were shriveled skin (according to the Sri Lankan version, it means his mind could not become soft and refined). The work of meditation did not immediately lead to liberation. However, Venerable Revata did not slacken his mental resolve. After the three months had passed and the Pavāraṇā ceremony was held at the end of the Vassa, he did not move to another place but continued to strive in the same acacia forest. As he practiced with such predominant energy (vīriyādhipati) and determination, his mind became increasingly steady and concentrated. Continuing his practice of Vipassanā, he eventually attained Arahantship.

## The Buddha's Arrival with Many Monks
From the time Venerable Sāriputta heard that his younger brother Revata had ordained, he had been requesting the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, my younger brother Revata has ordained. He may be delighted in this Dispensation, or he may not be. I would like to go and see how he is doing."
260:
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that Venerable Revata was still intensely engaged in the work of Vipassanā, forbade him twice. However, when the request was made for the third time, the Blessed One, perceiving that Venerable Revata had already attained Arahantship, said: "Dear Sāriputta, I too shall go with you. Inform the monks."

Venerable Sāriputta gathered the Sangha and announced: "Friends, the Blessed One wishes to go on a journey. Let those monks who wish to follow come along." When the Blessed One set out on the journey, very few monks remained at the monastery. Most monks wished to follow, thinking: "We shall constantly behold the golden physical body (rūpakāya) of the Blessed One and listen to his sweet Dhamma discourses." Thus, the Blessed One, surrounded by a large assembly of monks, departed from the monastery to visit Revata.

## The Supernatural Power of Venerable Sīvali
While they were traveling, Venerable Ānanda reached a fork in the road and asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, there are two paths here. By which path does the Blessed One wish the Sangha to go?"
261:
The Blessed One asked: "Dear Ānanda, of these two paths, which one is straight?" Venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Sir, the straight path (the shortcut) is thirty leagues (yojanas) long, but it is ruled by yakkhas (ogres); food is scarce and it is full of dangers. The winding path (the usual route) is sixty leagues long, but it is safe and food is abundant." Then the Blessed One asked: "Dear Ānanda, is the monk Sīvali following along with us?" When Venerable Ānanda replied, "He is following, Venerable Sir," the Blessed One said: "Dear Ānanda, if that is so—if the monk Sīvali is with us—then let the Sangha take the straight path which is full of danger and scarce in food. We shall test the power of Sīvali's merit."

After saying this, the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, set out on the forest path that was dangerous and scarce in food to personally witness the power of Venerable Sīvali's past merit. From the moment they entered that path, the devas created a large city at every league and prepared monasteries for the Sangha headed by the Buddha to reside in. At every monastery where the Buddha and the Sangha arrived, the devas appeared like workers sent by the king of that city.
262:
(They appeared in the form of royal servants) and brought gruel, snacks, and alms-food, asking: "Where is Venerable Sīvali? Where is Venerable Sīvali?" Venerable Sīvali would accept all those offerings and go to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, together with the Sangha, partook of the alms-food, snacks, meals, and gruel that were respectfully offered by the devas to Venerable Sīvali.

In this manner, receiving such offerings and honors, the Blessed One traveled one league each day. The difficult journey of thirty leagues was completed in one month. They then arrived at the acacia forest monastery, which had been prepared and leveled by Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata. Knowing in advance that the Blessed One would be coming, Venerable Revata had used his psychic powers to create enough dwellings for the Sangha headed by the Buddha, a Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) for the Blessed One, and places for night and day retreat. He then went out to welcome the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the monastery via the beautifully decorated path. After the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭī, the other monks entered their respective dwellings according to their seniority. The devas, knowing that it was not the time for a meal, brought and offered the eight kinds of drinks (syrups made from: rose-apple, mango, grape, edible lily, honey-tree fruit, two kinds of banana, and water lily roots). In this way, while the Blessed One
263:
was receiving and enjoying these offerings and honors, half a month (fifteen days) passed.

## The Misconception of the Restless Monks
At that time, some restless and distracted monks sat together and criticized: "The Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and men, saying 'He is the younger brother of my Chief Disciple,' has come to visit a monk who spends his time only in construction work (navakamma) like this. What is the use of Jetavana or Veḷuvana monasteries when compared to this monastery of Venerable Revata? This monk Revata is merely one who performs such construction work. How can a monk who is so busy with construction work practice the Dhamma of a recluse? He will not be able to do so."

Then the Blessed One thought: "If I stay here for a long time, this place will become crowded with the four classes of disciples. Forest-dwelling monks desire solitude. If I stay long, it will be uncomfortable for Revata." Having considered this, he went to Venerable Revata's place of day-retreat. Venerable Revata was sitting alone on a stone slab, leaning against a backrest at the end of his walk-way. Seeing the Blessed One from afar, he went to welcome him and paid his respects with great reverence.

The Blessed One asked Venerable Revata: "Dear Revata, this place is the habitat of lions, leopards, tigers, and wild beasts. When you hear the sounds of wild elephants, horses, and such,
264:
what do you do, my son?" Venerable Revata replied: "Venerable Sir, when I hear the sounds of those wild elephants and horses, delight in the forest (araññarati) arises in me repeatedly." The Blessed One, in that place of day-retreat, delivered a Dhamma discourse to Venerable Revata consisting of five hundred verses on the benefits of forest-dwelling. The next day, after wandering for alms in a nearby area, the Blessed One sent Venerable Revata back (without returning to the acacia forest monastery). He then used his psychic power to cause the restless and distracted monks, who had spoken ill of Venerable Revata, to forget their walking sticks, sandals, oil tubes, and umbrellas.

When those restless monks returned to Venerable Revata's monastery to retrieve their belongings, although they traveled by the same path they had come, they could not recognize the place. Indeed, on the previous days, they had traveled on a beautifully decorated path (created by psychic power), but on the day of their return, they had to travel on the uneven (natural) path, resting here and there out of exhaustion. In some places, they had to crawl on their knees. Having painfully struggled through small trees, bushes, and thorns, they reached a place that looked like where they had stayed. Only then did they see their umbrellas, sandals, oil tubes, and walking sticks hanging or leaning against the acacia stumps. It was then that those restless monks [realized...]
265:
265
Knowing that "this Venerable Revata is a monk of psychic power," the monks took their requisites and, marveling, "Oh, how wonderful is the offering prepared for the Blessed One!", they proceeded to Sāvatthī.

Visākhā, the great lay-supporter, invited the monks who had arrived ahead in Sāvatthī for a meal at her house. While they were seated, she asked, "Venerable sirs, is the monastery where Venerable Revata resides pleasant?" Then, those monks who had arrived first replied, "Lay-supporter, the monastery where Venerable Revata resides is very pleasant and delightful; that monastery is exactly like the Nandavana and Cittalata celestial gardens."

Afterward, the lay-supporter asked the distracted (uddhacca) monks who arrived after all the other monks, "Noble sirs, is the monastery where Venerable Revata resides pleasant?" Then, the distracted monks replied, "Do not ask, lay-supporter. That place where Venerable Revata resides is not even fit to be mentioned in conversation. That place where Venerable Revata resides is a barren wasteland, and moreover, it is a great acacia forest (khadiravana) with very uneven ground full of gravel, stone slabs, and boulders. In that place, Venerable Revata lives miserably." They answered according to what they had last seen.
266:
266
Upon hearing the different and contrasting answers from the monks who arrived first and those who arrived later, Visākhā, the great lay-supporter, wondered, "Which monks' words are true?" To know clearly, she took perfumes and flowers in the afternoon and went to visit the Blessed One. After paying homage and sitting in a suitable place, she asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, some elders praise the dwelling place of Venerable Revata, while other elders disparage it. Why is there this twofold difference in their answers, Venerable Sir?"

Then the Blessed One said to Visākhā, "Visākhā, whether it be a place called delightful by the world or a place not delightful, the place where the minds of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) find delight, that place alone is truly delightful."

He then spoke this verse:

"Gāme vā yadi vāraññe,
Ninne vā yadi vā thale.
Yattha arahanto viharanti,
Taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ.

Visākhe = O Visākhā, mother of Migāra, lay-supporter of Pubbārāma monastery. Gāme vā = whether in a village crowded with the five cords of sensual pleasure. Yadi = or else. Araññe vā = in a forest far removed from the five cords of sensual pleasure. Ninne vā = in a valley lush with trees and flowing streams. Yadi = or else. Thale vā = in a parched upland area, devoid of trees and filled with dust. Yattha = in whatever place.
267:
267
Arahanto = the Worthy Ones, whose taints are exhausted. Viharanti = dwell with balanced and joyful postures. Taṃ ṭhānaṃ = that place where the Worthy Ones dwell. Bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ = is truly a delightful place on earth."

He preached this verse. (This collection of words is from the Aṅguttara Commentary).

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At a later time, when the Blessed One was holding a ceremony to confer the titles of Etadagga (foremost) upon the monks, he spoke in praise of this Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āraññakānaṃ yadidaṃ revato khadiravaniyo = Monks, among my disciple monks who dwell in the forest, Revata of the acacia forest is the foremost."

Thus, he placed him in the position of Etadagga in the category of "forest-dwellers" (āraññaka).

(In this regard: While other elders, when dwelling in the forest, would choose and note forests that were suitable (sappāya), water that was suitable, and alms-villages that were suitable before dwelling there, this Venerable Revata did not prioritize or care for those suitable things. He dwelt in an acacia forest that was a barren wasteland, abundant with gravel, stone slabs, and boulders, and where the ground was uneven. Therefore, it should be specially noted that this noble elder alone was placed in the position of Etadagga in the category of "forest-dwellers.")
268:
268
The teachings related to this Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata should be extracted and noted from the Apadāna Pāḷi Commentary, Dhammapada Commentary, and so on.

This is the account of Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata.

**********

## (15) The Account of Venerable Kaṅkhārevata

## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration

One hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this Kaṅkhārevata, like other noble future elders, went to the monastery with a group of people. While standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One appoint a monk to the position of Etadagga—the foremost among those who "practice Jhana" (jhāyī). He reflected, "It would be well if I too could become like this monk in the future."

When the Dhamma assembly ended, he invited the Blessed One and, like other noble future elders, performed a great offering for seven days. Then he addressed the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, because of this meritorious deed of service (adhikāra), I do not long for other riches. Indeed, just as the monk whom the Blessed One placed in the position of Etadagga—the foremost among those who practice Jhana—seven days ago, may I also in the future become one who receives the title of Etadagga, being the foremost among the monks who practice Jhana in the Dispensation of a future Buddha."

Thus, he made his aspiration.
269:
269
When Padumuttara Buddha looked into the future and saw that the aspiration of this young man of good family would be fulfilled, he gave the prophecy: "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, the Blessed Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. In the Dispensation of that Buddha, you will become the foremost among the monks who practice Jhana, receiving the title of Etadagga." Having said this, he departed.

## (B) Ordination in the Final Life

That young man of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the celestial and human realms for one hundred thousand aeons (without falling into the four lower realms). During the time when our Blessed One appeared, he was born into a wealthy merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī and was named Revata. One day, in the afternoon, the merchant's son Revata went to the Jetavana monastery along with a group of people who were going to listen to the Dhamma. While standing at the edge of the assembly and hearing the Blessed One's Dhamma discourse, faith arose in him. He entered the Dispensation as a monk and, after receiving meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One, he practiced the preliminary meditative work (parikamma) for concentration (samādhi).

He became a monk who attained mundane Jhana. Using that Jhana as a basis (pādaka), he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā kammaṭṭhāna) and attained the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala); he became an Arahant.

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

That Venerable Kaṅkhārevata, setting aside only a few of the attainments (samāpatti) that the Blessed One entered, entered many other attainments.
270:
270
He was proficient and masterful in the Jhana attainments day and night. Later, when the Blessed One was holding a ceremony to confer the titles of Etadagga upon the monks, he spoke in praise of this Venerable Kaṅkhārevata:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhူnaṃ jhāyīnaṃ yadidaṃ kaṅkhārevato = Monks, among my disciple monks who practice Jhana, Kaṅkhārevata is the foremost."

Thus, he placed him in the position of Etadagga in the category of "those who practice Jhana."

## The Reason for the Name Kaṅkhārevata

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was traveling from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha, Venerable Kaṅkhārevata entered a shed where molasses was being cooked (a hut where palm sugar molasses was being made). He saw that flour and bran were being added to the molasses (to make the molasses or palm sugar hard, people were adding a little flour and bran into the boiling molasses). Because of this, he had doubts and scrupulousness (kukkucca), thinking, "Molasses containing unallowable food (āmisa) is not allowable; because it contains flour and bran, which are āmisa, it is not allowable to consume this molasses in the afternoon."

Consequently, he and his followers did not consume the molasses in the afternoon. Other monks who trusted and followed the elder's words also did not consume the molasses. When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
271:
271
The Blessed One asked the monks, "Monks, why do people add flour and bran to molasses?" When the monks replied, "They add it to make it hard, Venerable Sir," the Blessed One said, "Monks, if people add flour and bran to molasses to make it hard, that added flour and bran are reckoned simply as molasses. Monks, I allow you to consume molasses as you wish." Thus, he laid down the permissive rule (anujñāta sikkhāpada).

Venerable Kaṅkhārevata also saw mung beans sprouting in dung along the way and said, "Mung beans are not allowable; even cooked mung beans sprout." Having such doubts and scrupulousness, he and his followers did not consume mung beans. Other monks who trusted and followed the elder's words also did not consume mung beans. When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One said, "Monks, even if cooked mung beans sprout, I allow you to consume them as you wish." Thus, he laid down the permissive rule. (These accounts appear in the Vinaya Mahāvagga, 6. Bhesajjakkhandhaka, Burmese translation pages 303, 304).

In this way, because this Venerable Revata had great scrupulousness regarding the Vinaya (vinaya-kukkucca), doubting even allowable things as unallowable, he became known as Venerable Kaṅkhārevata—meaning Venerable Revata who has great doubts.
272:
Furthermore, the accounts concerning this Elder Kankhārevata should be extracted and noted from the Apadāna Pāḷi Commentary, the Theragāthā Commentary, and so forth.

This is the account of the Venerable Kankhārevata Thera.

**********

## (16) The Account of the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa Thera

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This noble person, the future Soṇa Koḷivisa Thera, was born into a wealthy merchant family during the time of Padumuttara Buddha in the distant past and was named "Sirivaḍḍha, the merchant's son." When Sirivaḍḍha reached the age of maturity, he went to the monastery like the future elders of old. While standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the position of foremost (Etadagga) among those who are "Āraddhavīriya = those who exert strenuous effort." He then thought, "It would be well if I too were to become like this monk in the future." After the Dhamma talk concluded, he invited the Buddha and offered a great donation (Mahādāna) for seven days, making an aspiration just as the future elders of old had done. The Buddha, seeing that the merchant son's aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy as in the previous cases and returned to the monastery.

## Life as a Noble Son in Bārāṇasī

Sirivaḍḍha, the merchant's son, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. After one hundred thousand aeons had passed, in this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon),
273:
after the Parinibbāna of Kassapa Buddha and before the appearance of our Buddha, he was born into a noble family in the city of Bārāṇasī. One day, that noble youth was playing in the water of the Ganges River together with his friends.

At that time, a Paccekabuddha whose robes were worn out reflected, "I shall make Bārāṇasī my resort village, build a leaf-hut on the banks of the Ganges, and observe the Rains Retreat (Vassa)." He was collecting and gathering pieces of wood and rattan vines that were floating down with the current. Then, the noble youth went there with his friends, paid respects to the Paccekabuddha with great reverence, and asked, "Venerable Sir, what work are you doing?" The Paccekabuddha replied, "Young man, as the Rains Retreat is approaching, it would be proper for monks to have a dwelling place."

Then the noble youth said, "Venerable Sir, I would like you to wait for just this one day by whatever means possible; I will build and offer a monastery to you tomorrow, Bhante." The Paccekabuddha, having come with the intention of favoring that noble youth, accepted his invitation. Knowing that the Paccekabuddha had accepted, the noble youth returned home. The next day, after preparing various offerings, he stood waiting for the arrival of the Paccekabuddha.
274:
The Paccekabuddha also reflected, "Where shall I receive alms today?" and knowing the situation, he proceeded to the door of the noble youth's house.

Seeing the Paccekabuddha arrive, the noble youth was filled with great affection and joy. He took the bowl, offered alms-food, and requested, "Venerable Sir, please come only to my door for the entire three months of this Rains Retreat." Having received the commitment, and after the Paccekabuddha had finished his meal and departed, the youth went with his friends and had a leaf-hut, a cloister (caṅkama), and places for night and day rest constructed within a single day, and offered them to the Paccekabuddha.

Furthermore, when the Paccekabuddha was about to enter the leaf-hut, the youth spread his own red woolen rug (kambala) worth one hundred thousand—which he used to wrap around himself—on the ground smeared with fresh cow dung, with the intention: "May the feet of the Paccekabuddha not be soiled by mud." Seeing the color of the red rug and the radiance of the Paccekabuddha's body matching perfectly, he was filled with extreme faith and devotion and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, just as the color of this rug is exceedingly beautiful from the moment you step on it, so too, in whatever life I am born in Saṃsāra, may the color of my hands and feet be as beautiful as the deep red of the Hibiscus (Bandhujīvaka) flower. May the touch of my body be as soft as
275:
the touch of a layer of cotton teased a hundred times."

The noble youth attended to the Paccekabuddha for the entire three months of the Rains Retreat. When the retreat ended and the Pavāraṇā ceremony was completed, he offered a set of three robes (ticīvara). The Paccekabuddha, being fully provided with bowl and robes, departed for Mount Gandhamādana.

## Ordination in the Final Life

That noble youth, without ever falling into the four lower realms, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of our Buddha, he took rebirth in the house of the merchant Usabha in the city of Caṃpā. From the time he was conceived, thousands of gifts and presents arrived at the merchant's house. On the day he was born, the entire city of Caṃpā was covered with offerings and honors. On the day of his naming, his parents said, "Our son has come bringing his own name; the color of our son's skin is like that of molten red gold." Thus, they named him "Soṇa, the merchant's son." (Thus, the name given by his parents was Soṇa; because he belonged to the Koḷivisa clan, he became famous by combining his name and clan as "Soṇa Koḷivisa, the merchant's son"). Subsequently, sixty nurses were appointed for him, and he was raised in comfort like a son of the devas.
276:
## How the food was prepared for the merchant's son

The manner in which food was prepared for him was as follows:

First, after plowing and planting a field sixty royal measures (pe) in extent, the Sāli rice plants were nurtured and grown using three types of water: (1) milk, (2) scented water, and (3) ordinary water.

Into the channels that would carry water into the field, many large jars of milk and scented water had to be poured.

When the Sāli ears began to fill with milky grain, in order to protect them from the danger of being eaten by birds and insects, and to make the grain tender, poles were erected around the field and at intervals within it. Rafters and crossbeams were placed, covered with mats, and surrounded by screens and curtains, while guards stayed at the outer edges.

When the grain was ripe, the granaries were smeared and smoothed with four kinds of perfumes (saffron/kunkuma, cloves, tagara, and kakkū powder), and the interior was made fragrant with most excellent scents. Then, many workers entered the field, respectfully cut the Sāli ears from the stalks, made them into bundles, tied them with ropes, and dried them.

After that, a layer of perfume was spread at the bottom of the granary, and the dried bundles of grain were spread over it. In this way, alternating layers of perfume and grain were laid until the granary was full, then the door was closed and it was kept for three years.
277:
Only after three years was the granary opened. When it was opened, the scent of the perfume covered the entire city of Caṃpā.

When that Sāli rice was milled, drunkards would scramble to buy the coarse and fine bran. The broken rice and fragments were taken by the servants and attendants. The whole, prime Sāli grains were selected for the merchant's son.

The method of cooking the rice was as follows: The prime Sāli grains were placed in a rice-washing basket woven with gold thread and rinsed one hundred times. Then, they were dipped only once into boiling water (not kept for long) and removed. At that moment, every part that emerged from the boiling water was already cooked, becoming a meal of rice resembling jasmine flowers.

That rice was placed in a gold bowl, and that gold bowl was placed on top of a silver bowl filled with boiling, waterless, thick sweet milk-rice (to keep it from cooling) and brought to be set before the merchant's son.

Soṇa Koḷivisa, the merchant's son, would eat only as much of that Sāli rice as was sufficient for him, and then rinse his mouth and wash his hands and feet with scented water. After he had washed his hands and feet, various kinds of betel and other items were offered to him to make his breath fragrant.

Wherever the merchant's son went, excellent and wonderful carpets were spread for him. The merchant's son's
278:
palms and soles were as red as the Hibiscus flower. The touch of the merchant's son was as soft as a layer of cotton teased a hundred times. On the surface of his soles, there grew fine hairs the color of lotus filaments, which stood curling to the right like a ruby earring. If the merchant's son became angry with someone, he would say threateningly, "Be careful and take note; I shall step on the ground right now!"

When the merchant's son reached maturity, (as in the section on Yasa, the merchant's son below), three palaces suitable for the three seasons were built, and his parents had female dancers and attendants wait upon him. The merchant's son lived in great luxury and comfort, like a son of the devas.

Later, after our Buddha had attained Enlightenment and preached the Dhammacakka Sutta, while He was residing near the city of Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra of Magadha summoned Soṇa, the merchant's son. He was sent to the Buddha along with eighty thousand village headmen. After hearing the Dhamma, Soṇa was filled with great faith and requested the Buddha to ordain him as a monk.

At that time, the Buddha asked Soṇa, "Have your parents given permission for you to ordain?" Upon learning that permission had not yet been granted, the Buddha declined, saying, "Dear Soṇa, the Buddhas do not ordain a son whose parents have not given permission." The merchant's son replied, "Very well, Bhante."
279:
Having placed the Buddha's instruction upon his head, he returned to his parents to obtain their permission. Upon returning to the Buddha's presence, he was ordained as a monk under a certain elder according to the Buddha's command. (This is a brief account; the detailed story of how the merchant's son Soṇa became a monk can be found in the Myanmar translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga, 5-Cammakkhandhaka, starting from page 263).

After Ven. Soṇa had attained monkhood and while residing in the city of Rājagaha, many of his relatives and friends offered him great honor and hospitality. They spoke many words of praise regarding the Elder's beautiful appearance and virtuous qualities. Ven. Soṇa thought, “Many people are coming to me. If they continue to come like this, how will I be able to practice the work of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation? I will not be able to practice. It would be good if, after hearing the meditation instructions from the Buddha, I go to the Sītavana forest cemetery to strive and develop the Dhamma of a recluse. Indeed, people will not come there as they find the 'cemetery' repulsive. If they do not come, my work as a monk will reach its peak, the fruit of Arahatship.” Having reflected thus, after hearing the meditation instructions from the Buddha, he went to the Sītavana forest and renewed his efforts to develop the Dhamma of a recluse.

## Intense Exertion

Ven. Soṇa reflected, “My body is very delicate; certainly, I am not able to reach the bliss of the Path and Fruit easily. Therefore, it is only proper that I develop and practice the Dhamma of a recluse by making my body weary.”
280:
Having reflected thus, he gave up lying down and sitting altogether, and undertook only the two postures of standing and walking (cankama), exerting himself intensely in his primary task. For the Venerable Soṇa, blisters and swellings appeared on the very delicate and tender soles and edges of his feet, and they broke open, leaving the entire walkway stained red with blood. When the Elder could no longer walk with his feet, he practiced the Dhamma of a recluse by crawling on all fours using his elbows and knees. His elbows and knees also broke open in the same way, and the entire walkway was stained red with blood. Even though he exerted his energy so intensely, he was unable to produce the signs or light of meditation.

He then thought: “If anyone else besides me were to exert energy intensely, they would only be like me or exert as much as I have; they could not exert more than this. Yet, even though I exert myself in this way, I am unable to produce the Path and Fruit. Therefore, I must certainly not be a person capable of attaining the Path and Fruit, such as an Ugghaṭitaññū, Vipañcitaññū, or Neyya. I must be only a Padaparama person. Therefore, what benefit is there for me in being a monk? There will be none. I shall return to the lay life, enjoy worldly pleasures, and (while enjoying worldly pleasures) also perform meritorious deeds.”

Thus he thought.
281:
## Vīṇovāda = The Teaching on the Lute Strings (Neither too loose nor too tight)

## Delivering the Instruction

At 그 때, the Buddha, knowing the Elder's thoughts, went to that place in the evening surrounded by a group of monks. Seeing the walkway stained red with blood, he asked the monks (though he already knew, with the intention of preaching), “Monks, whose walkway is this, stained red with blood like a slaughterhouse?” The monks replied, “Venerable Sir, the soles of the feet of the Venerable Soṇa, who practiced the Dhamma while walking with intensely exerted energy, have broken. This walkway, which is now seen stained red with blood like a slaughterhouse, is the walkway of that monk Soṇa.” Then the Buddha went to Ven. Soṇa's meditation dwelling and sat on the prepared seat.

Ven. Soṇa also came to the Buddha, paid his respects, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Buddha asked Ven. Soṇa directly, as mentioned before, whether such a thought had occurred in his mind. Ven. Soṇa admitted that it was true. Then the Buddha taught Ven. Soṇa the “Vīṇovāda = The Teaching on the Lute Strings (Neither too loose nor too tight)” as follows:

(The Buddha)
“Dear Soṇa, what do you think of the words I am about to ask? You may answer as you see fit. Were you not skilled in playing the lute when you were a layman?”
282:
(Soṇa)
“Yes, Venerable Sir.”

(In this regard: When Ven. Soṇa was young, his parents thought, “If our son learns other arts, he will be weary. This art of playing the lute is one that can be learned while sitting comfortably.” Thus they had him learn the lute, and the Elder became proficient and skilled in the art of playing the lute.

The Buddha also knew, “For this monk Soṇa, other meditation subjects will not be beneficial. This monk was proficient and skilled in the art of the lute when he was a layman. If I preach the Dhamma based on his knowledge of the lute, he will understand quickly.” Therefore, he questioned and preached as mentioned above.)

(The Buddha)
“Dear Soṇa, what do you think of the words I am about to ask? When your lute strings are too tight, does your lute have a melodious sound or is it fit to be played for a long time? Is the sound pleasant? Is it durable for playing?”

(Soṇa)
“Venerable Sir, that is not possible. The sound is not pleasant, nor is it durable for playing.”

(The Buddha)
“Dear Soṇa, what do you think of the words I am about to ask? When your lute strings are too loose, does your lute have a melodious sound or is it fit to be played for a long time? Is the sound pleasant? Is it durable for playing?”
283:
(Soṇa)
“Venerable Sir, that is not possible. The sound is not pleasant, nor is it durable for playing.”

(The Buddha)
“Dear Soṇa, what do you think of the words I am about to ask? When your lute strings are neither too tight nor too loose, but are tuned to an even quality, does your lute then have a melodious sound or is it fit to be played for a long time? Is the sound pleasant? Is it durable for playing?”

(Soṇa)
“It is so, Venerable Sir. The sound is pleasant and it is durable for playing, Venerable Sir.”

(The Buddha)
“Dear Soṇa, in the same way, energy that is too intensely exerted leads to restlessness (uddhacca). Energy that is too slack leads to laziness (kosajja). Therefore, dear Soṇa, you should maintain the balance of energy and concentration. Know the equality of the faculties such as faith (saddhā), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). When they are thus balanced, produce the sign of Samatha and so on.”

(Soṇa)
“Very well, Venerable Sir.”

After the Buddha had instructed Ven. Soṇa with the aforementioned Vīṇovāda—the teaching on the lute strings being neither too loose nor too tight—and had taught the meditation on how to practice balancing energy and concentration,
284:
He returned to the monastery on Gijjhakūṭa Hill.

Ven. Soṇa, having received the personal advice and instruction from the Buddha, practiced the Dhamma of a monk neither too loosely nor too tightly, and before long, he was established in the fruit of Arahatship; he became an Arahant.

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

If one reviews and reflects on the way Ven. Soṇa Koḷivisa practiced the Dhamma, this point becomes clear: “For other monks, energy is something to be increased and developed (as it is often slack). For this noble one, energy was something to be relaxed (as it was too tight).” Therefore, at a later time, when the Buddha held a ceremony to confer Etadagga titles upon the monks, he declared regarding Ven. Soṇa Koḷivisa:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āraddhavīriyānaṃ yadidaṃ soṇo koḷiviso = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess fervent energy, Soṇa of the Koḷivisa clan is the foremost.”

Thus, he was placed in the Etadagga position for “Āraddhavīriya = possessing fervent energy.”

This is the account of Ven. Soṇa Koḷivisa.
285:
## (17) The Story of Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa

(This Elder was named Soṇa by his parents. Because he used to wear an ear ornament worth one crore (kuṭi) when he was a layman, the two names were combined, and he became known as “Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.”)

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, a virtuous man, also went to the monastery along with a group of people during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the Etadagga position as the foremost among those who speak with sweet and pleasant speech. He reflected, “It would be good if I too, in the future, under the dispensation of a Buddha, become a person who receives the Etadagga title as the foremost among those who speak with sweet and pleasant speech.” Having thought thus, he invited the Buddha and offered a great Mahādāna for seven days. Then he made a wish: “Venerable Sir, seven days ago from today, you placed a certain monk in the Etadagga position as the foremost among those who are Kalyāṇavākkaraṇa = speakers of sweet and pleasant speech. May I also, by the merit of this great deed, in the future under the dispensation of a Buddha, become a person who receives the Etadagga title in that same position of Kalyāṇavākkaraṇa = speaking sweet and pleasant speech.”
286:
"May I become such a person," he made this prayer and aspiration. The Buddha, seeing that this noble son's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you will be the foremost (etadagga) among the monks who are speakers of pleasant Dhamma (kalyāṇavākkaraṇa)," and then the Buddha departed.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That noble son also performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, for a hundred thousand aeons (without falling into the four woeful states), wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Before our Buddha appeared, he took rebirth in the womb of the female lay disciple named Kāḷī, the wife of a merchant in the city of Kuraraghara in the Avanti country. When her pregnancy was mature, that merchant's wife returned to her parents' home in the city of Rājagaha.

At that time, our Buddha had already attained Omniscience and was preaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in the Isipatana Deer Park (on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era). Devas and Brahmas from ten thousand world systems gathered in harmony at the Isipatana Deer Park where the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta was being preached. In that assembly, the Yakkha general Sātāgira, who was one of the twenty-eight Yakkha generals, heard the Buddha's Dhamma discourse.

(In this regard, the detailed account of the two great Yakkha generals should be reviewed and noted from the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume II, Chapter 10, starting from page 430.)
287:
In particular, the passages from the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume II, Chapter 10, page 430 onwards, are written based on the commentary to the Hemavata Sutta of the Suttanipāta. According to that commentary on the Hemavata Sutta, while the deity Sātāgira was listening to the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, his mind wandered as he remembered his friend, the deity Hemavata. Therefore, he did not yet attain the Path and Fruit. It is stated that only after he went to fetch his friend and returned did both Yakkha generals become Stream-enterers (sotāpanna).

However, the explanation in the commentary to the Ekanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, starting from page 186, is that the deity Sātāgira became a Stream-enterer after listening to the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Then, while going to fetch his friend Hemavata, they met in the sky above the house of the merchant's daughter Kāḷī (from the city of Kuraraghara) in Rājagaha. Hemavata questioned Sātāgira about the Buddha's bodily conduct (kāya-samācāra), livelihood (ājīva), and mental conduct (mano-samācāra). Sātāgira answered each question. Thus, through the power of the questions and answers regarding the Buddha's physical and spiritual virtues, at the conclusion of the Hemavata Sutta, the deity Hemavata directed his wisdom according to the sequence of his friend Sātāgira's discourse and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). (Such differences in accounts should be understood as variations according to the traditions of the Reciters [bhāṇakas]).

When the Yakkha general Sātāgira noticed that his friend Hemavata had not arrived at the assembly of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he went to fetch him. The two great Yakkha generals met in the sky above the house of the merchant's wife Kāḷī (from Kuraraghara) in Rājagaha. Right there in the sky, Hemavata questioned Sātāgira about the Buddha's bodily conduct and so forth, and Sātāgira answered every question.

At that time, this merchant's wife Kāḷī, while the Dhamma was being preached to another, without even seeing the Buddha, through overhearing from a distance—
288:
—developed faith (saddhā) and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), like one who eats food gathered for another. That merchant's wife became the very first female noble disciple (ariyasāvikā) who was a Stream-enterer among all women, thus becoming the elder sister of all noble ones.

As for the merchant's wife Kāḷī, immediately after becoming a Stream-enterer, she gave birth that very night. On the day of naming the child, he was named "Soṇa." After staying at her parents' house as long as she wished, Kāḷī returned to the city of Kuraraghara. The merchant's son Soṇa wore an ear ornament worth ten million (one crore), and thus he became known as the merchant's son "Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa."

## The Merchant's Son Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa Gaining Spiritual Urgency
## and Entering the Monkhood

At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was residing on the mountain named Papata (alternatively Pavatta or Upavatta), depending on the city of Kuraraghara for his alms-resort. The female lay disciple Kāḷī, the merchant's wife, attended to and supported the Venerable Mahākaccāna. The Elder went regularly to the house of the lay disciple Kāḷī. The youth Soṇa also frequented the presence of the Elder and became intimately acquainted and friendly with him.

Whenever he had the opportunity, the merchant's son Soṇa went to pay respects to the Elder. The Elder also constantly preached the Dhamma to Soṇa. Consequently, Soṇa became one who possessed much spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and—
289:
—lived with an intense effort to practice the Dhamma. On one occasion, while the merchant's son Soṇa was traveling to the city of Ujjeni with a caravan of traders to conduct business, the caravan made camp to rest in a forest along the way. During the night, fearing the crowded and cramped conditions of staying with many people, he moved away to sleep in a suitable secluded spot. At dawn, the caravan rose and departed. No one noticed or woke the merchant's son Soṇa; everyone forgot him and left.

When Soṇa woke up in the morning and saw no one, he followed the path taken by the caravan quickly. He reached a banyan tree. At that banyan tree, he saw a male peta (hungry ghost) of considerable size, hideous to behold, who was himself picking up and eating the pieces of flesh that were falling off his own bones. Soṇa asked, "Who are you?"

When the peta replied, "Sir, I am a peta," Soṇa asked again, "Friend, why are you doing this?" The peta replied, "I am doing this because of my past deeds (kamma)." Soṇa then asked, "What kind of past deed was it that you committed?"

Then the peta replied, "Sir, in the past, I was a dishonest merchant in the city of Bharukaccha. I lived by cheating and deceiving others of their property. Not only that, when the members of the Saṅgha—
290:
—came for alms, I spoke abusive words to them, saying, 'Why don't you just eat your own flesh?' Because of that unwholesome deed, I am now experiencing the suffering and misery that you, noble son, are witnessing." Upon hearing this account, the merchant's son Soṇa was greatly moved by spiritual dread (saṃvega).

Continuing his journey from there, he encountered two young petas with dark blood constantly oozing from their mouths. He questioned them in the same manner as before. Those young petas also told Soṇa about the unwholesome deeds they had committed in the past. The story they told was: when they were young in their previous lives as humans in the city of Bharukaccha, they made a living by trading in perfumes. When their mother invited Arahants and offered them alms-food, they would return home and abuse and curse them, saying, "O mother, why do you give our property to these monks? May dark blood gush from the mouths of the monks who eat the food given by our mother!"

Because of that unwholesome deed, those youths had suffered in hell, and as a remaining result (vipāka) of that deed, they were born in the peta realm. Thus, when they met Soṇa, they were experiencing such misery. Hearing this, Soṇa's spiritual dread increased twofold. (These stories of the causes of spiritual urgency appear in the Udāna Commentary, page 279, and the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Volume III, pages 296-297.)
291:
When the merchant's son Soṇa reached the city of Ujjeni and completed his business affairs, he returned to Kuraraghara and visited the Venerable Mahākaccāna to report these matters. The Elder then preached a Dhamma discourse to Soṇa, clearly illustrating the faults and dangers of wandering in saṃsāra (becoming) and the benefits and advantages of escaping from saṃsāra (cessation). Soṇa paid obeisance to the Elder and returned home. After eating his evening meal, he went to bed but slept only a little. Upon waking, he sat on his bed and began to contemplate the Dhamma he had heard from the Venerable Mahākaccāna.

As he contemplated the Dhamma and recalled the state of those petas, the suffering of saṃsāra appeared extremely terrifying to Soṇa's wisdom. His mind became strongly inclined toward becoming a monk.

At dawn, after performing his morning ablutions, Soṇa went to visit the Venerable Mahākaccāna and expressed his thoughts: "Venerable Sir, when I contemplate the Dhamma preached by you in various ways, I see that it is truly not easy for one living in the household life to practice this holy life (the three trainings) in its complete and utter purity, like a polished conch shell." He then expressed his desire to ordain: "Venerable Sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into the homeless life of a monk." He then requested: "Therefore, Venerable—
292:
—Mahākaccāna, I would like you to ordain me."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, considering whether the wisdom of the merchant's son Soṇa was mature or not, perceived that "Soṇa's wisdom has not yet reached maturity." Wishing to wait for the time when his wisdom would be mature, he said to Soṇa: "Soṇa, it is very difficult to practice the holy life, which involves sleeping alone and eating alone, for as long as life lasts. Therefore, Soṇa, I encourage you to remain as a layperson in that household life and first practice the holy life—the teaching of the Buddha which involves sleeping alone and eating alone—according to the appropriate times (such as Uposatha days)."

At that time, because Soṇa's faculties (indriya) were not yet mature and his wisdom of spiritual urgency was not yet very sharp, his effort to ordain subsided. Although it subsided, he did not live carelessly but remained well-established in the practice instructed by the Elder, visiting the Elder regularly and listening to the Dhamma. After some time had passed, the inclination to ordain arose for a second time in Soṇa's mind as mentioned before, and he again requested the Elder. On that occasion too, the Elder spoke in the same manner as before.

When he requested for the third time, because the merchant's son Soṇa's wisdom had reached maturity—
293: The Venerable Mahākaccāna, reflecting that it was now time to ordain Soṇa, gave him the novice ordination. Although he intended to give him the higher ordination (upasampadā) immediately after, at that time most monks resided only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), and in that city of Kuraraghara, only two or three monks were staying. These monks lived separately, one in one village, two in another market town, and so on. The preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna, invited two or three monks from various villages and market towns for the higher ordination of his resident pupil, the novice Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa. However, while he was searching for and inviting other monks, the monks he had previously invited would depart for other places due to some business. When he again waited for a while and went to search for and invite those who had left, the monks who were already present would again depart for other places due to some business. In this way, because he had to invite them repeatedly, it was only after three years had passed that a group of ten monks could be gathered. At that time, the higher ordination ceremony (upasampadā kamma) could only be performed when a group of ten monks was assembled. The Venerable Mahākaccāna himself was living alone (ekacārī) at that time. Thus, with great exhaustion and after more than three years, a group of ten monks finally assembled, and the preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna, with great difficulty and hardship, gave the higher ordination to his resident pupil, the novice Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.
294: (These details are extracted and presented from Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Vol. 3, pp. 298-299). After receiving the higher ordination, Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa learned meditation subjects from his preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna. While striving and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained the fruit of Arahantship within that very rainy season. Having become an Arahant, he learned and mastered the Sutta Nipāta in the presence of the Great Elder. When the rainy season ended and the Pavāraṇā ceremony was completed, Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, greatly desiring to pay respects to the Blessed One, asked permission from his preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna. (For the detailed account of this request, one should refer to the Myanmar translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, pages 284-285). Then, his preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna, said: "Soṇa, when you arrive, the Blessed One will have you stay in the same Gandhakuṭī building and will urge you to recite the Dhamma. According to that urging, you shall recite the Dhamma. The Blessed One will be greatly pleased with your Dhamma talk and will grant you a boon. When you accept the boon, take such and such boons (these boons will be clear later). Pay homage to the Blessed One's feet on my behalf with the message I have given you." Having said this, he gave his kind permission. After being permitted by his preceptor, Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa went to the house of his mother, the lay devotee Kālī, the merchant's wife, and informed her of the matter. His mother, the lay devotee Kālī, the merchant's wife, also said:
295: "Very well, dear son. If you are going to visit the Blessed One, take this woolen rug and offer it as a floor covering in the Gandhakuṭī where the Blessed One resides." Having said this and given the instructions, she handed over the woolen rug. Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa took the woolen rug given by his mother, packed his bedding and belongings, and set out on his journey. In due course, he arrived at the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī. While the Blessed One was seated on the Buddha-throne of Dhamma, Soṇa approached, paid humble respects, and stood at a respectful distance. After the Blessed One had exchanged friendly greetings (paṭisandhāra) with Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, He specifically instructed Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, prepare a lodging for this monk." (In this regard: If the Blessed One wishes to stay in the same Gandhakuṭī building with a visiting monk, He gives a special instruction to prepare a place for that monk. For a visiting monk with whom He does not wish to stay in the same Gandhakuṭī, He does not give such a special instruction. For such a monk, the elders in charge, such as Venerable Ānanda, would prepare a place in a suitable building.) Venerable Ānanda, sensing the Blessed One's intention, prepared a place for Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa within the Gandhakuṭī building itself. Then, the Blessed One spent much of the night sitting and entering into meditative attainments (samāpatti).
296: After spending the time, He entered the Gandhakuṭī monastery. Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa also spent much of the night sitting and entering into meditative attainments, and then entered the Gandhakuṭī monastery. Because the Blessed One wished to show hospitality to Venerable Soṇa by entering into meditative attainments, He spent much of the night sitting in the open air, entering into all the attainments common to disciples in both forward and reverse order. Then, having washed His feet, He entered the monastery. Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, knowing the Blessed One's intention, also spent much of the night sitting in the open air, entering into all those attainments as was appropriate for the occasion. Then, having washed his feet, he entered the monastery. After entering, with the Blessed One's permission, he arranged a robe as a curtain and spent the time sitting at the Blessed One's feet. The Blessed One, in the last watch of the night, took the lion's posture (sīhasayya)—lying on His right side with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Rising before dawn, He sat down and, perceiving that Soṇa's physical exhaustion must have subsided by this time, He urged Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa: "Dear monk, let the Dhamma to be recited appear in your mind." With a very sweet and pleasant voice, without missing or distorting even a single syllable, Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa recited the sixteen suttas known as the Aṭṭhakavagga from the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi,
297: beginning with the Kāma Sutta. When the suttas were finished, the Blessed One gave the 'Sādhu' (well done) to Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa and said: "Dear monk, you have learned all the sixteen suttas of the Aṭṭhakavagga well. You have memorized them well. You are endowed with a beautiful voice (perfect in articulation and phonetics). You are endowed with speech that is clear, faultless, fluent, and capable of conveying the meaning. Dear monk, how many rainy seasons (vassa) have you?" When asked, Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa replied: "Blessed One, I have only one rainy season." Then the Blessed One asked: "Dear monk, why did you wait so long to ordain?" Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa replied: "Blessed One, I have seen the danger in sensual pleasures for a long time. However, the life of those living in the household is very narrow, with many duties and many things to be done." Then, the Blessed One, knowing this reason—that the mind of one who sees the danger in sensual pleasures as it really is, even after a long time, does not enter into the household life but recoils and slides away like a drop of water on a lotus leaf—uttered this Verse of Exultation (Udāna): "Having seen the danger in the world, and having known the Dhamma which is free from acquisitions, the Noble One does not delight in evil; the pure one does not delight in evil."
298:
“Loke = In the entire world of formations. Ādīnavam = Because of seeing clearly with the eye of Vipassanā-knowledge the faults of impermanence, suffering, and changeability. Nirūpadhiṃ = Because of knowing with the fourfold Path-knowledge the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the true state of being free from the four Upadhis (attachments). Ariyo = The Noble One who is far from defilements. Pāpe = In the collection of evil deeds and misconduct. Na ramati = Does not delight, does not take pleasure, and does not enjoy. (Kasmā = Why is that?). Suci = A person who has pure bodily actions and so forth, like a king of swans. Pāpe = In the collection of unwholesome states which are thick with filth and comparable to a dirty place. Na ramati = Has no custom of delighting or taking pleasure. (Tasmā = Therefore).”

He uttered this Udāna verse.

At that time, the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa thought, “The Blessed One has spoken words of welcome to me; it is now time to report the message sent by my preceptor.” He rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe over his left shoulder, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable Sir, my preceptor, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, pays homage to the feet of the Blessed One with his head. He also submits this message:

‘Venerable Sir, the southern region of Avanti has few monks. I, after more than three years had passed...’
299:
with great hardship and exhaustion, that I was able to gather a group of ten monks from various places to grant ordination. I do not know if the Blessed One will allow (or perhaps he might allow) the higher ordination (upasampadā) in the Southern region of Avanti with a group of fewer than ten monks. (1)
Blessed One, in the Southern region of Avanti, the ground marked by cattle hooves is rough and thorny. I do not know if the Blessed One will allow (or perhaps he might allow) multi-layered sandals in the Southern region of Avanti. (At that time, only single-layered sandals were permitted, which is why this request was made). (2)
Blessed One, in the Southern region of Avanti, people place great importance on bathing; they believe in purification through water. I do not know if the Blessed One will allow (or perhaps he might allow) frequent bathing in the Southern region of Avanti. (At that time, monks were permitted to bathe only once every fifteen days, which is why this request was made). (3)
Blessed One, in the Southern region of Avanti, people use skins such as sheepskins, goatskins, and deerskins as mats. Blessed One, just as in the districts of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) they use mats made of Biriṇa grass, Muñja grass, Babbaja grass, and cloth-like grass, even so, in the Southern region of Avanti..."
300: They spread skins of sheep, goats, and deer. I do not know if the Blessed One will allow the use of skins such as sheepskin, goatskin, and deerskin in Southern Avanti; perhaps He might allow it. (This was asked because at that time, monks were not yet permitted to use skins). (4) Lord, nowadays, when people see monks going to the boundary (sīmā), they say, 'We offer this robe to such-and-such a monk,' and thus they offer robes. The fellow monks who hear this go to the monks who are to receive the robes and say, 'Friends, such-and-such people offer robes to you.' Then, those monks who are to receive the robes, thinking, 'Let there not be an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya) for us,' feel remorse and do not accept them. I do not know if the Blessed One will preach a method (pariyāya) that is allowable regarding robes; perhaps He might preach it. (5)' Thus he sent the message." So he reported. Then, the Blessed One, on account of this matter reported by the Venerable Sona Kuṭikaṇṇa, gave a Dhamma discourse and addressed the monks as follows: "Monks, in Southern Avanti, there are few monks. Monks, in all border regions...
301: ...I allow ordination (upasampadā) by a group (gaṇa-saṅgha) of five monks, with a Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) as the fifth. In this context, the border regions are: In the East, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond it is a large Sal tree; beyond that Sal tree are the border regions, and inside is the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). In the South-East, there is a river named Salalavatī; beyond the Salalavatī river are the border regions, and inside is the Middle Country. In the South, there is a market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that market town are the border regions, and inside is the Middle Country. In the West, there is a brahmin village named Thūna; beyond that village are the border regions, and inside is the Middle Country. In the North, there is a mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that mountain are the border regions, and inside is the Middle Country. Monks, in such border regions, I allow ordination by a group of five monks, with a Vinaya expert as the fifth. (1) Monks, in Southern Avanti, the ground is rough, hardened by the trampling of cattle hooves. Monks, in all border regions, I allow the wearing of multi-layered sandals. (2)
302: Monks, in Southern Avanti, people value bathing and believe in purification by water. Monks, in all border regions, I allow constant bathing. (3) Monks, in Southern Avanti, people spread skins of sheep, goats, and deer. Monks, just as in the districts of the Middle Country, people spread mats of Birana grass, mats of Muñja grass, mats of Babba grass, and mats of Khīra-paṇṇī; even so, monks, in Southern Avanti, people spread skins of sheep, goats, and deer. Monks, in all border regions, I allow the use of skins of sheep, goats, and deer as mats. (4) Monks, if people, seeing monks going to the vicinity of a boundary (upacāra-sīmā), say, 'We offer this robe to such-and-such a monk,' and thus offer robes; monks, as long as the robe has not reached the hand, it does not count towards the number of days for determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Monks, I allow you to accept such robes. (5)"—thus He said. Then, Venerable Sona Kuṭikaṇṇa, having paid homage to the Blessed One with the words sent by his mother, the lay devotee, said, "Lord, this woolen garment is offered by the lay devotee Kālī Upāsikā to be used as a floor covering in the Gandhakuti where the Blessed One resides." Having offered the woolen garment to the Blessed One, he rose from his seat, paid respects to the Blessed One, and returned to his own place...
303: ...at the Papatta mountain monastery in the city of Kuraraghara in Southern Avanti. When Venerable Sona Kuṭikaṇṇa arrived in the presence of his preceptor (upajjhāya), he reported the entire matter. The next day, he went to the door of his mother, the lay devotee Kālī the wealthy lady, and stood for alms. The mother, hearing the news that "My son is standing at the door," came quickly, paid homage, took the bowl from the Elder's hand, prepared a seat inside the house, and offered alms-food. Then, after he had finished his meal, the mother and the Elder conversed as follows: (Mother) "Dear son, did you see the Blessed One?" (Elder) "Yes, lay devotee, I saw Him." (Mother) "Did you pay homage to the Blessed One on my behalf with the words I sent?" (Elder) "Yes, lay devotee, I paid homage. That woolen garment you offered, I myself spread it as a floor covering in the Gandhakuti where the Blessed One resides, just as you requested." (Mother) "Dear son, is it true that you recited the Dhamma to the Blessed One...
304:
“...it is said that you recited and submitted [the Dhamma], and it is said that the Blessed One gave you a Sadhu-applause.”

(The Elder)
“Mother, how do you know these things?”

(The Mother)
“Dear son, the deity who guards and oversees my house told me, ‘On the day the Buddha gave a Sadhu-applause to your son, the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world systems also gave Sadhu-applause.’ Dear son, I desire and hope that you will preach to me the same Dhamma discourse that you recited and preached to the Blessed One, in the same manner, dear son.”

The Elder accepted his mother's request by remaining silent. Knowing that the Elder had accepted, the mother had a large pavilion built at the entrance of her house and had him preach the Dhamma in the same manner as he had recited and submitted it to the Blessed One. Thus, a great Dhamma assembly was held.

## (c) Receiving the Etadagga Title

Later, while the Blessed One was sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, He declared regarding the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kalyāṇavākkaraṇānaṃ yadidaṃ soṇo kuṭikaṇṇော =”
305:
“Monks, among my monk disciples who preach the Dhamma with a sweet and pleasant voice, the monk Kuṭikaṇṇa Soṇa is the most distinguished and the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the Etadagga position in the category of “Kalyāṇavākkaraṇa = preaching with a pleasant and sweet voice.”

This is the account of the Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.

**********

## (18) About the Venerable Sīvali

## (a) The Previous Aspiration of the Elder

This aspirant for the position of Venerable Sīvali, a man of good family, also went to the monastery during the time of the Padumuttara Buddha, just like previous aspirants. While standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One placing a monk in the Etadagga position—the most distinguished and foremost among those who receive abundant offerings. He reflected, “I, too, in the future, should become a person who receives the Etadagga title as the most distinguished and foremost among those who receive abundant offerings, just like this monk.” He then invited the Blessed One to his house and, after giving a great donation (Mahādāna) for seven days in the same manner as previous aspirants, he made an aspiration:

“Venerable Sir, because of this meritorious deed of merit, I do not desire any other prosperity; indeed, in the future, in the Sasana of a future Buddha, may I also become a monk who is the most distinguished and foremost among those who receive abundant offerings, just like the monk whom Your Reverence placed in the Etadagga position seven days ago.”
306:
The Blessed One, seeing that the aspiration of this man of good family would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy: “This aspiration of yours, donor, will be fulfilled in the future in the Sasana of Gotama Buddha,” and then returned to the monastery.

## Life as a Villager

That man of good family, the future Sīvali, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and (without falling into the four woeful states) wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time of the Vipassī Buddha (who appeared ninety-one eons ago from this eon), he was born as a man of good family in a village not far from the royal city of Bandhumatī.

At that time, the citizens of Bandhumatī were consulting and discussing among themselves in a competitive spirit to outdo King Bandhuma in giving, and they offered a great donation to the Vipassī Buddha. One day, when all the citizens gathered to give the donation, they looked around to see what items were missing from their offering. Realizing that honey and curd were missing, they agreed, “We must get that honey and curd from wherever they can be found by some means,” and they stationed a man at the road entering the city from the countryside.

At that time, this future Venerable Sīvali, the villager, brought a pot of curd from his village.
307:
Thinking, "I will exchange this for some household items," he went towards the city. He thought, "I will enter the city only after washing my face and cleaning my hands and feet." While looking around for a suitable place with water, he found a large honeycomb, about the size of a plow-head, which was untouched by bees. Thinking, "This untouched honeycomb has appeared due to my merit," he took it and entered the city.

A man stationed as a guard by the city folk saw this noble son from the forest village and asked, "Friend, for whom are you carrying this honey and curd?" The villager replied, "Sir, I am not carrying this honey and curd for anyone in particular; indeed, I have brought it to sell." The guard then said, "Friend, if that is so, take this one kahāpaṇa from my hand and give me your honey and curd."

Then, the noble son from the forest village, the future Sīvali, thought, "This honey and curd I have brought is not worth much. Yet, this man offers a high price at the very first instance. I should investigate further." He then told the city man, "O Sir, I cannot give it, I cannot sell it for one kahāpaṇa." The city man raised the price, saying, "If you cannot sell it for one kahāpaṇa, take two kahāpaṇas and give the honey and curd to me." The villager bargained, saying, "I cannot give it for two kahāpaṇas either." In this manner...
308:
...the price was raised higher and higher until it reached one thousand kahāpaṇas.

The villager thought, "It is not appropriate to hold out for too long. Let it be; I shall ask about this man's purpose." He then asked the city man, "This honey and curd are not worth such a high price. Yet, you offer an excessively large amount. For what purpose do you wish to take this honey and curd at such an exorbitant price?" Then the city man replied, "Friend, in this royal city of Bandhumatī, the citizens are competing with the King to offer alms to Vipassī Buddha. They have not found these two items, honey and curd, for their offering and are searching for them by any means. If they do not obtain these two, the citizens will lose the competition. Therefore, I wish to take them by giving one thousand kahāpaṇas."

When the whole matter was explained, the villager asked again, "O Sir, is it only the city folk who should perform this meritorious deed of almsgiving? Can other forest villagers not give as well?"

Then the city man said, "Friend, no one's offering is forbidden. (Anyone, whether city dweller or villager, can give.)" The villager then asked, "O Sir, among the citizens giving alms now, is there anyone who gives one thousand kahāpaṇas in a single day?" The city man replied, "There is no one, friend." The villager then asked firmly once more, "O Sir, do you not know that this honey and curd I have brought are worth one thousand kahāpaṇas?"
309:
The city man replied, "Yes, I know, friend." Then the villager said, "O Sir, if that is so, please go. Tell the many citizens, 'A man from a forest village will not give these two items, honey and curd, for money. He wishes to offer them with his own hands. You citizens may remain without worry regarding the acquisition of these two items.' As for you, sir, I wish for you to be a witness in person that I am the greatest, most abundant, and most valuable donor in this offering ceremony."

## Offering Honey and Curd Mixed

After saying this, the villager bought five kinds of spices with a small coin (one pè) he had brought from home for his provisions. He ground them into powder, squeezed the whey from the curd, and then squeezed the honeycomb into that whey. Mixing it with the five kinds of spices, he placed it on a Paduma lotus leaf, prepared it well, and sat waiting for his turn to offer it at a place not far from the Buddha.

While waiting for his turn among the various offerings brought by the citizens, he realized his turn had come. He approached the Buddha and requested, "Exalted Buddha, this offering is a poor man's gift. My..."
310:
...accept this poor man's gift, this object of offering, out of compassion." Out of compassion for the forest villager, the Buddha accepted the offering in a stone bowl presented by the Four Great Kings. He then made a resolution so that the offering would not be exhausted even after being distributed to six million eight hundred thousand (6,800,000) monks.

After the Buddha had finished the meal, the noble son from the forest village paid respects to the Buddha and, standing in a suitable place, made an aspiration: "Exalted Buddha, today all the citizens of the royal city of Bandhumatī have witnessed my offering to You. By the result of this meritorious deed, in whatever life I am born in Saṃsāra, may I be one who reaches the pinnacle of gains, and the pinnacle of retinue and fame." Vipassī Buddha said, "Evaṃ hotu kulaputta—May it be as you have aspired, noble son." After delivering a discourse of appreciation to the noble son and the citizens, the Buddha returned to the monastery.

## (b) Ordaining in the Final Life

That noble son, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time when our Buddha appeared, he was conceived in the womb...
311:
...of the Koliyan princess named Suppavāsā, of the Koliyan Sakyan clan.

## Miracles During Pregnancy

From the time the noble son was conceived, hundreds of gifts arrived continuously, day and night, to the mother, Princess Suppavāsā. Princess Suppavāsā became more prosperous than before. (According to the Sihala version, Princess Suppavāsā received five hundred gifts in the morning and five hundred in the evening.)

Later, one day, to test the power of her merit, the great relatives had the princess touch baskets filled with seeds. When those seeds were sown, hundreds and thousands of sprouts grew from each single seed. From a single field the size of a royal pè, fifty or sixty cartloads of grain were produced.

When filling the granaries with grain, the great relatives also had the princess touch the granary doors. Due to the princess's merit, whenever grain was taken out, the place from which it was taken became full again. Furthermore, when they served rice from a full pot, saying, "This is the merit of the princess," and gave it to all the people who came, the rice was not exhausted for as long as they wished to give.
312:
While the boy remained in his mother's womb, seven years passed. When the seven years were complete and the fetus was mature, the princess suffered great labor pains for seven days. Princess Suppavāsā endured that great suffering with these thoughts:

"Truly, the Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering. Indeed, that Blessed One is endowed with the Omniscient Knowledge that clearly perceives all truths. (1)

Truly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well, practicing to abandon such suffering. Indeed, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples practices the training well. (2)

Truly, that Nibbāna is very blissful, where such suffering and painful feelings do not exist at all. Indeed, that noble Nibbāna is exceedingly blissful. (3)"

With these three kinds of thoughts—(1) a good thought related to the virtues of the Buddha, (2) a good thought related to the...
313:
...virtue of the Saṅgha being 'suppaṭipanna' (practicing well), and (3) a good thought related to the 'santi-sukha' (peaceful bliss) of Nibbāna—she endured the pain. (That is, she endured the great labor pains without complaining, repeatedly reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and Nibbāna as described.)

When the seventh day arrived, the Koliyan princess Suppavāsā called her husband, the Koliyan prince, and said, "I wish to give alms while I am still alive. O Prince, please go, report my condition to the Buddha, and invite Him. Carefully note what the Buddha says and tell me upon your return." The Koliyan prince went and reported the news of Princess Suppavāsā to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "May the Koliyan princess Suppavāsā be well and happy, free from disease. May she give birth to a healthy son, being well and happy herself."

As soon as the Buddha spoke these words, the Koliyan princess Suppavāsā became well and happy, free from disease, and gave birth to a healthy son. All the people surrounding her, moving from a time of weeping to a time of joy, went to report the news of the son to the Koliyan prince. As for the Koliyan prince, after listening to what the Buddha said and paying respects to Him, he returned towards the village.
314:
When the Koliya prince saw the joyful manner in which those men came running to meet him, he reflected, "It seems the words spoken by the Blessed One have reached a successful completion." The Koliya prince then went to Princess Suppavāsā and relayed the message spoken by the Blessed One. The princess said, "The 'living alms' (the child) invited by my lord will indeed be an auspicious alms-meal. Please go back again and invite the Blessed One to accept alms for seven days." The Koliya prince did exactly as the princess said. For seven days, the prince and princess provided a great offering of alms to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha.

The child was born pure, bringing peace to the anxious minds of all his relatives; therefore, they named the child "Prince Sīvali." Because Prince Sīvali had remained in his mother's womb for seven years, from the moment of his birth, he was capable of performing all the tasks that a seven-year-old youth could do. For this reason, while the great alms-giving was being offered for seven days, from the day he was born, Prince Sīvali took the dhamakaraka (water filter) and served filtered water to the Sangha.

On the seventh day, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, engaged in conversation with Prince Sīvali. During their conversation, the Elder asked, "Sīvali, after having experienced such a mass of suffering, is it not appropriate for you to become a monk?"
315:
When asked, Prince Sīvali replied, "Venerable Sir, if I receive permission from my parents to become a monk, I would very much like to do so." Princess Suppavāsā, seeing her son Sīvali talking with the Elder, thought joyfully, "What is this? My son is talking with the Elder, the General of the Dhamma!" She approached the Elder and asked, "Venerable Sir, what words is my son speaking with you?"
