The Venerable Sāriputta replied, "He is speaking of the suffering he experienced while dwelling in the mother's womb, and says that if you, his parents, give permission, he will become a monk." Princess Suppavāsā then gave her permission, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir, please ordain Prince Sīvali."

Then the Elder took Prince Sīvali to the monastery, gave him the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), and ordained him, saying, "Sīvali, there is no need for any other instruction for you. (Meaning, no other advice is necessary). Just contemplate the very pain and suffering you experienced for seven years." Prince Sīvali replied, "Venerable Sir, your responsibility is only to ordain me. I myself will contemplate and develop the practice of mental reflection to the best of my ability."

At the very moment the first lock of hair was shaved, the novice Sīvali was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). When the second lock of hair...
316:
...was shaved, he was established in the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala). When the third lock of hair was shaved, he was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). Immediately upon the completion of shaving all his hair, he was established in the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). (The completion of the shaving and the realization of the Fruit of Arahantship occurred almost simultaneously).

From the day the novice Sīvali was ordained, the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine—appeared in abundance for the Sangha of monks as desired. Thus, the story of Venerable Sīvali took place in the city of Kuṇḍikā.

(Note: The present-day story of Venerable Sīvali should be extracted and noted from the Udāna Pali, Myanmar Translation [Khuddaka Nikāya 1, starting from page 86]. The detailed account of the past unwholesome kamma that caused the mother and son to suffer for seven years and seven days in the womb [gabbhavāsa-dukkha] and the suffering of obstructed birth [gabbhamūḷha-dukkha] should be extracted and noted from the Udāna Commentary.

In brief: In a past life, the Elder and his mother were the Chief Queen and the Prince of Bārāṇasī. At one time, the King of Kosala attacked and killed the King of Bārāṇasī with a large army, took the Chief Queen, and installed her as his own Chief Queen.

When the Prince of Bārāṇasī's father was defeated and passed away, the Prince escaped secretly through a water pipe, gathered a large force, and came to Bārāṇasī. He sent an ultimatum to either return the throne or fight. His mother, the Chief Queen inside the city, advised him that if they fought, many people would suffer, so he should instead blockade and surround the city. Following his mother's advice, the Prince blockaded the four main gates so that no one could enter or exit, and besieged the city for seven years.
317:
Although the city was blockaded, the citizens went out through small gates to bring in grass, firewood, and other supplies, so there was no significant change. When the mother queen heard this news, she again advised him to blockade the small gates as well.

Following that advice, the small gates were also blockaded. After seven days, the citizens, being in a difficult position, cut off the head of the King of Kosala and presented it to the Prince. The Prince entered the city and took over the kingship.

Due to this aforementioned unwholesome kamma, the Elder and his mother suffered the pain of carrying the pregnancy for seven years, the pain of dwelling in the womb, and the mother suffered the pain of obstructed birth for seven days.)

## The Elder Testing His Own Merit

At another time, when the Blessed One arrived at Sāvatthī, Venerable Sīvali respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One and requested, "Blessed One, I wish to practically test my merit. Please allow five hundred monks to accompany me as companions." The Blessed One permitted him, saying, "Dear Sīvali, take them and go."

Venerable Sīvali took the five hundred companion monks and set out toward the Himavanta (Himalayas), traveling along the forest path. (1) At that time, at the first stopping place, they encountered a large Banyan tree. The deity residing in the Banyan tree provided alms for seven days to the Elder. In this manner, Venerable Sīvali:

(1) First encountered the large Banyan tree (as mentioned).
318:
(2) For the second time, at Paṇḍava Mountain,
(3) For the third time, at the Aciravatī River,
(4) For the fourth time, at the ocean named Varāsāgara,
(5) For the fifth time, at the Himavanta Mountain,
(6) For the sixth time, at Chaddanta Lake,
(7) For the seventh time, at Gandhamādana Mountain,
(8) And then for the eighth time, at the place of Venerable Revata—

He arrived and visited these places. At every single location, deities offered great alms to Venerable Sīvali for seven days each.

In particular, when they reached Gandhamādana Mountain, a deity named Nāgadatta offered alms for seven days, alternating between milk-alms one day and ghee-alms the next. At that time, the Sangha of monks asked, "Friends, we do not see this deity milking any cows, nor do we see him churning curds to make ghee. Lay devotee deity, by what merit are these milk and ghee offerings so abundantly produced for you?" The deity Nāgadatta replied, "Venerable sirs, the fact that I can offer milk and ghee without having cows or churning curds is the result of the merit of offering 'ticket-milk-alms' (salāka-khīradāna) during the time of Kassapa Buddha."

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At another time, when the Blessed One went to visit Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata (as mentioned previously in the story of Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata), on the journey through a dangerous wilderness far from people, the deities provided alms daily, specifically intending them for Venerable Sīvali. Based on this occurrence, the Blessed One praised Venerable Sīvali, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lābhīnaṃ yadidaṃ sīvali = Monks, among my disciples who are monks and are pre-eminent in receiving offerings, Sīvali is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha placed him in the rank of Etadagga as "Lābhī" (the foremost among those who receive offerings).

(These Dhamma accounts concerning Venerable Sīvali should be extracted and noted from the Apadāna Commentary, Dhammapada Commentary, etc. Similarly, Dhamma accounts concerning subsequent Elders should also be noted. In this Great Chronicle of Buddhas, the focus will be on these three points: (a) The Elder's past aspiration, (b) Ordination in the final birth, and (c) Receiving the title of Etadagga).

This is the account of Venerable Sīvali.

## (19) The Account of Venerable Vakkali

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This noble Elder also, in the distant past during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, went to the monastery as previously described. While standing at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One placing a certain monk in the rank of Etadagga as the foremost among those with great and supreme faith. He thought, "It would be well if I too, in the future, could become one who receives the title of Etadagga as the foremost among those with supreme faith (saddhādhimutta), just like this monk." Following the established method, he invited the Blessed One and provided a great alms-giving for seven days. Then, paying homage to the Blessed One, he made the aspiration: "Blessed One, by the power of this meritorious deed of service, may I too, in the future, under the dispensation of a Buddha, become the foremost among those with supreme faith, just like the monk whom the Blessed One has placed in the rank of Etadagga."

The Blessed One, seeing that the noble youth's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy (byādika) and then returned to the monastery.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Birth

That noble youth performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered only through the celestial and human realms. During the time of our Blessed One, he was conceived and born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī.
321:
321
His parents and relatives named the boy "Vakkali."

When the youth Vakkali reached adulthood, he mastered the three Vedas. On one occasion, he saw the Buddha entering the city of Sāvatthī surrounded by a company of monks. Upon beholding the splendor of the Buddha’s physical body (rūpakāya), he could not get enough of gazing at that glorious form. Consequently, he followed the Buddha wherever He went. When the Buddha returned to the monastery, he followed Him there as well, remaining standing just to gaze upon the splendor of the Buddha’s physical body. When the Buddha preached in the assembly of Dhamma, he would stand directly in front of the Buddha and listen to the discourse.

Because the youth Vakkali was filled with overwhelming faith (saddhā), he reflected: "If I live as a householder in the lay life, I will not have the opportunity to constantly behold the Buddha; (only by becoming a monk will I have that chance)." Having considered this, he requested ordination and became a monk in the presence of the Buddha.

From the time of his ordination, Venerable Vakkali spent all his time, except for the time of taking meals, standing in a place where he could behold the Buddha. He completely neglected and abandoned the duties of studying the scriptures and practicing meditation, and spent his time only gazing at the Buddha. The Buddha, waiting for the time when Venerable Vakkali’s wisdom (paññā) would mature, allowed him to spend a long time gazing at His physical splendor.
322:
322
While Venerable Vakkali continued to wander about merely gazing at the Buddha’s physical form, the Buddha remained without saying anything. When the time was right, the Buddha knew, "Now the wisdom of this monk Vakkali has reached maturity; it is now possible to make him realize the truth."

He then said:
"Vakkali, what is the use of you looking at this foul body? It is of no use. Vakkali, truly, he who sees the Dhamma sees Me; he who sees Me sees the Dhamma. Vakkali, only one who beholds the Dhamma is one who beholds the Buddha; one who beholds the Buddha must be one who beholds the Dhamma."

In this way, the Buddha spoke of His own physical body as a mere corpse in order to encourage Venerable Vakkali to practice meditation.

Even though the Buddha admonished him in this way, Venerable Vakkali was unable to leave the place where he could see the Buddha and go elsewhere by any means. Then the Buddha, realizing, "If this monk does not gain a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he will not realize the Four Noble Truths," waited until the time for the rains retreat (vassa) approached. He then traveled to Rājagaha and, on the day of entering the retreat, directly dismissed Venerable Vakkali, saying, "Vakkali, go away from My presence."

Buddhas are such that their words must be followed by others; others—
323:
323
—cannot defy the words of the Buddhas. Therefore, Venerable Vakkali, unable to remain in opposition to the Buddha’s command and not daring to come into the Buddha's presence for the entire three months of the rains retreat, became despondent and thought: "What can I do now? There is nothing I can do. The Buddha has dismissed me. I will never have the chance to see the Buddha face-to-face again. What is the use of my life? It is of no use anymore." In despair, he climbed Gijjhakūṭa Hill to a place where there were many precipices.

The Buddha, knowing that Venerable Vakkali’s mind was extremely exhausted and discouraged, reflected: "If this monk Vakkali does not find relief from Me, he might destroy his past wholesome merits which are the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits." He then emitted the Buddha-rays (Buddha-rasmi) to the place where Vakkali was to manifest Himself. (One should visualize the Buddha’s form from the edge of that light like a searchlight). When the Buddha-rays were emitted and he saw the Buddha clearly with his own eyes, the great arrow of sorrow (soka) that had been so heavy in Venerable Vakkali’s heart was instantly removed.

Just as one might pour a great stream of water into a dried-up reservoir, the Buddha, in order to arouse strong rapture (pīti) and happiness (somanassa) in Venerable Vakkali’s mind, spoke this verse found in the Dhammapada:

"Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane.
Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukhaṃ."
324:
324
"Vakkali = Dear Vakkali. Pāmojjabahulo = The monk who has abundant joy (pāmojja) through focusing on the glorious Buddha. Bhikkhu = The monk who contemplates the dangers of saṃsāra and the nature of the aggregates (khandha). Buddhasāsane = Being devoted with clear faith in the Buddha’s Dispensation of the threefold training. Adhigacche = Can reach the state of Arahattaphala, realizing for himself. Santaṃ = The peaceful state of Nibbāna. Saṅkhārūpasamaṃ = Which is the cessation of all conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Sukhaṃ = The true and certain bliss of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)."

He preached this verse. Not only that (according to the Aṅguttara Commentary), the Buddha called out to Venerable Vakkali, stretching out His golden hand and saying, "Ehi Vakkali = Come, dear Vakkali."

(According to the Dhammapada Commentary), after preaching the verse beginning with "Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu," the Buddha stretched out His golden hand to Venerable Vakkali and said:

"Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi, paṅke sannaṃva kuñjaraṃ.

Vakkali = Dear Vakkali. Ehi = Come now into the presence of the Buddha. Mā bhāyi = Do not be afraid or hold back. Olokehi = Behold with a joyful heart. Tathāgataṃ = The Buddha who has come in the same way as previous Buddhas."
325:
325
(This is the meaning of the first half of the verse).

Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds of beings. Paṅke sannaṃ kuñjaraṃ iva = Like a great elephant sunk in deep, thick mud. Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi = I shall lift you, who are sunk in the deep mud of saṃsāra throughout the beginningless cycle of births (anamatagga saṃsāra), and bring you to the safe shore of Nibbāna.

Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi, rāhugggahaṃva sūriyaṃ.

(The first half of the verse is to be understood as before). The meaning of the second half is: Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds of beings. Rāhuggahaṃ sūriyaṃ iva = Like the sun-disk, radiant with crystal light, when it is caught in the hands of Rāhu. Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi = I shall now liberate you, the sun-chariot, who are caught in the hands of Rāhu, which is the defilements (kilesa).

Ehi Vakkali mā bhāyi, olokehi tathāgataṃ.
Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi, rāhuggahaṃva candimaṃ.

(The first half of the verse is to be understood as before). The meaning of the second half is: Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds of beings. Rāhuggahaṃ candimaṃ iva = Like the moon-orb, the delightful celestial chariot, when it is caught in the hands of Rāhu. Ahaṃ taṃ mocayissāmi = I shall now liberate you, the moon-chariot, who are caught in the hands of Rāhu, which is the defilements (kilesa).
326:
326
"—I shall liberate you now."

The Buddha preached these verses. At that moment, Venerable Vakkali thought, "Oh, I have seen the Buddha, and I have even been called 'Dear son, come'!" Filled with intense rapture (pīti), he could not even see the path he should take. He leaped into the open sky towards the Buddha. While suspended in the air, even as he was about to land on the first mountain peak, he contemplated the verses preached by the Buddha. While still in the sky, he suppressed his rapture and practiced insight meditation (vipassanā). He became an Arahant attained to analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-patta) and, while still paying homage to the Buddha, descended to the ground and stood in the Buddha's presence.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

Later, while the Buddha was seated in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and was praising and conferring the various titles of Etadagga (foremost) upon the monks, He declared regarding Venerable Vakkali:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saddhādhimuttānaṃ yadidaṃ vakkali = Monks, among my disciple monks who are liberated through faith (saddhādhimutta) [those who have overwhelming faith], Vakkali is the foremost."
327:
...praising him thus, the Buddha placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) as "the best and most excellent among those released through faith (saddhādhimutta)."

(In this regard, it should be specially noted: The faith of other monks, being naturally weak, had to be increased — it had to be deliberately preached and cultivated to grow. However, because the Venerable Vakkali's faith was naturally very strong, it had to be diminished — even to the point of being sent away by a certain means to reduce it. Therefore, the Great Elder received the Etadagga title in the category of those released through faith.)

This is the account of the Venerable Vakkali.

## (20-21) The Accounts of Venerable Rāhula and Venerable Raṭṭhapāla
## (a) The Past Aspirations of the Two Elders

The future versions of these two Great Elders were born respectively into wealthy merchant families with great riches in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī, during the early part of the era of the Buddha Padumuttara, a hundred thousand aeons ago. (The names and lineages of these two during their youth are not mentioned in the ancient commentaries.)

When these two sons of merchants reached the age of maturity, they established households (meaning they got married). Upon the death of their respective fathers, both summoned their treasurers who managed their granaries and treasuries. While inspecting their wealth and property, they saw such vast amounts of treasure that it was beyond counting or comparison, and thought, "Oh, this much..."
328:
328

"My ancestors, such as my grandfathers and great-grandfathers, collected countless hoards of wealth but were unable to take it with them. Now, we should find a way to take this wealth to the next world." Thinking thus, both friends began to practice great charity at four locations (according to the Sinhalese version, at the four city gates) for the destitute, travelers, and others.

Among the two, one wealthy man, whenever he arrived at his alms-hall, would ask the recipients what they desired and then provide whatever they needed, such as gruel or food. Therefore, he became known as 'Āgatapāka' (one who gives after asking those who have come). The other wealthy friend, without asking, would simply fill every bowl brought by the recipients to the brim. Therefore, he became known as 'Anaggapāka' (one who gives without measure).

One day, both wealthy friends went outside the village early in the morning to wash their faces. At that time, two powerful ascetics from the Himalayas arrived through the air to collect alms. They descended to the ground not far from the two friends and, thinking "Let those wealthy men not see us," they stood still, suppressing their radiance by the side of the road.

The two wealthy friends, however, saw the two ascetics as they were preparing their utensils, such as gourds and bowls,
329:
329

and heading towards the village for alms. They approached the ascetics and paid their respects respectfully. Then the ascetics asked the two wealthy men, "Great meritorious lay devotees, when did you arrive?" The two men replied, "We have just arrived, Venerable Sirs." They took the gourds and bowls from the ascetics' hands, and each invited one ascetic to his own home. After the ascetics had finished their meal, the men obtained a promise from them to always come to their homes for alms.

Among the two ascetics, one (the one invited by the wealthy man who would become the future Venerable Rāhula) was of a bilious and irritable temperament, and thus his body felt hot. Using his psychic powers, he split the waters of the Great Ocean and went to the mansion of the Naga King named Pathavindhara to spend the day. After enjoying the suitable climate and returning to the human world, when he preached the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) at the home of his supporter (the future Rāhula), he would say, "May it be like the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara." Later, one day, the supporter asked the ascetic, "Venerable Sir, when you perform the appreciation, you say, 'May it be like the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara.' We do not know the meaning of these words. What is the meaning intended by this statement?" When asked, the alms-collecting ascetic replied, "Indeed, householder, I say this wishing that your wealth and happiness
330:
330

may be like the wealth and happiness of the Naga King Pathavindhara." He then explained the greatness of the Naga King's wealth. From that time on, the wealthy man constantly directed his mind toward the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara.

The other ascetic (the one invited by the wealthy man who would become the future Venerable Raṭṭhapāla) went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and spent the day in a very quiet mansion named 'Serīsaka,' where a large celestial Sirīsa tree grew at the entrance. On his way to and fro, he saw the wealth of Sakka, the king of gods, every day. When he preached the discourse of appreciation to his supporter (the future Raṭṭhapāla), he would say, "May it be like the mansion of Sakka." Then, the wealthy man asked the meaning (just as his friend had asked his ascetic), and the ascetic replied, "Indeed, householder, I say this wishing that your wealth and happiness may be like the wealth and happiness of Sakka." He then explained the greatness of Sakka's wealth. Upon hearing the ascetic's words, the wealthy man constantly directed his mind toward the mansion of Sakka from that time on.

When both wealthy friends passed away from that life, they were reborn according to their aspirations: one became the Naga King Pathavindhara in the Naga realm, and the other became Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

The moment the Naga King Pathavindhara was reborn in that realm, he looked at his own physical form and thought, "The venerable ascetic who used to come to my house for alms
331:
331

told me of the virtues of a place that is not pleasing. This Naga realm is a place where one must move about by crawling on one's breast. It seems that teacher ascetic knew of no other realm besides this Naga realm." Thinking thus, he became dissatisfied. At that moment, Naga dancers, fully adorned with various ornaments, began to play celestial musical instruments and dance to entertain him in all directions. At that very moment, the Naga King discarded his Naga form and took on the appearance of a celestial youth.

In particular, once every half-month, the four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika realm go to pay their respects to Sakka. Thus, one day, the Naga King Pathavindhara also went with the Naga King Virūpakkha to pay respects to Sakka. Sakka saw the Naga King Pathavindhara coming from afar and recognized him. Then Sakka greeted the Naga King Pathavindhara, who had come near to pay respects, saying, "Friend, in which realm have you been reborn?" The Naga King Pathavindhara replied sadly, "Do not ask, Lord Sakka. I have been reborn in the Naga realm where one must travel by crawling on one's breast. You, Lord Sakka, have indeed found a good friend." Sakka then said, "Friend, do not be troubled by various thoughts like 'I have been reborn in an unsuitable realm.' The Buddha Padumuttara has appeared in the world. After performing great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) in the presence of that Blessed One, you should aspire for this very realm of Sakka,
332:
332

and we two shall live happily together." Thus Sakka gave words of encouragement and advice. The Naga King Pathavindhara agreed, saying, "Very well, Lord Sakka, I will follow your advice." He then went to the Blessed One Padumuttara, invited the Buddha (to visit his mansion the next day to receive offerings), and together with his Naga retinue, spent the three watches of the night preparing various offerings in his Naga realm.

At dawn the next day, the Blessed One said to his attendant, the Venerable Sumana Thera, "Dear Sumana, today the Buddha will go to a distant place for alms. Do not let worldling (puthujjana) monks follow. Let only Arahants who are masters of the Tipitaka, possess the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and the six higher powers (chaḷabhiñña) accompany me." After hearing the Buddha's command, the Thera informed all the monks of the matter.

Then, the Blessed One, accompanied by one hundred thousand Arahants who were masters of the Tipitaka, possessors of analytical knowledges, and the six higher powers, flew into the sky and proceeded to the mansion of the Naga King Pathavindhara. When the Naga King Pathavindhara came with his Naga retinue to welcome the Buddha, he saw the community of monks surrounding the Buddha, walking upon the emerald-colored waves of the ocean surface. He was filled with joy and looked first at the Buddha and then at the most junior of the Saṅgha (saṅghanava), the young novice named Uparevata, the son of the Buddha, who was at the very end, and thought:
333:
333

"The psychic power of the other disciple monks is not yet worthy of snapping one's fingers in admiration. Only the psychic power of this very young and tender novice is truly worthy of snapping one's fingers in admiration!" Thinking thus, he was exceedingly delighted.

After the Blessed One had sat down in the Naga King's mansion, and the remaining monks had also sat down in their respective places according to their seniority starting from the end, the seat of the young novice Uparevata happened to be directly in front of the Blessed One. The young novice Uparevata sat in that place. Then, while the Naga King Pathavindhara was offering gruel and food, he looked repeatedly, first at the Buddha and then at the Venerable Uparevata.

On the body of the Venerable Uparevata, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) were clearly visible, just as they were on the body of the Blessed One. Therefore, the Naga King looked at the Blessed One and the Venerable Uparevata alternately. Then the Naga King thought, "This novice is very similar in appearance to the Buddha. How might they be related?" He then asked a monk sitting nearby, "Venerable Sir, how is this young novice related to the Blessed One?" The monk who was asked replied, "Naga King, this young novice is the son of the Blessed One." Upon hearing this, the Naga King Pathavindhara thought, "This monk is indeed very great; he has attained the status of being the son of the Blessed One, who has reached the pinnacle of such beauty. The body of this young novice also..."
334:
334
"In some respects, he greatly resembles the physical form of the Buddhas. It would be well if I, too, were to become like this young novice in the future." Having reflected thus, he gave a great offering (Mahādāna) for seven days and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the power of this meritorious deed of service, may I become the son of a future Buddha, just like this young novice Uparevata." The Buddha, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: "In the future, you will indeed be the son of the Buddha Gotama." (This is the receiving of the prophecy by the future Venerable Rāhula).

When the next half-month arrived, the Naga King Pathavindhara again went to pay respects to Sakka, the King of Devas, together with the Naga King Virūpakkha. At that time, Sakka asked the Naga King Pathavindhara, who was standing near him, "Friend, have you made an aspiration for this world of the Tāvatiṃsa devas?" When the Naga King Pathavindhara replied, "I have not made such an aspiration, O Sakka," Sakka asked again, "Seeing what fault do you not desire it?" Then the Naga King Pathavindhara said, "There is no fault, O Sakka. However, I have seen the wonderful young novice Uparevata, the son of the Buddha. From the moment I saw that young novice, my mind no longer inclines toward any other aspirations. I have made the aspiration: 'In the future, may I indeed become the son of a future Buddha, just like this young novice Uparevata.' O Sakka, you also...
335:
335
...should make an aspiration. May you and I not be separated in whatever realm or existence we may arise throughout Saṃsāra," he urged.

Sakka accepted the words of the Naga King Pathavindhara. Having seen a monk of great power, he reflected, "From what family did this noble son renounce the world to become a monk?" He then came to know: "This noble son is the distinguished son of a noble family capable of reconciling divided kingdoms. After fasting for fourteen meals (seven days), he requested and obtained permission from his parents to become a monk." Having known this well, he pretended not to know and questioned the Buddha Padumuttara. After performing a great offering for seven days, he made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, as a result of this merit, may I become the foremost (Etadagga) among those who go forth out of faith (Saddhā-pabbajita) in the Dispensation of a future Buddha, just like this noble monk in Your Dispensation." The Buddha, seeing that Sakka's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: "O Sakka, King of Devas, in the future, in the Dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you will become the foremost among those who go forth out of faith, receiving the title of Etadagga." After giving this prophecy, the Buddha departed.

Sakka, the King of Devas, having received the prophecy from the Buddha Padumuttara, returned to his own celestial realm.
336:
