(This is the receiving of the prophecy by the future Venerable Raṭṭhapāla).

## The Life of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla as a Manager of Services

Both of them, after passing away from their lives as Sakka and the Naga King Pathavindhara, wandered through the realms of devas and humans for many thousands of aeons. Specifically, ninety-two aeons ago from this present aeon, the Buddha Phussa appeared in the world of the three types of beings. The father of the Buddha Phussa was King Mahinda. The Buddha Phussa had three half-brothers. Every day, King Mahinda, being intensely possessive, thought, "The Buddha is my Buddha alone; the Dhamma is my Dhamma alone; the Saṅgha is my Saṅgha alone." He continuously offered alms-food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha without allowing others the opportunity to serve.

Then one day, the frontier (paccantarit) of King Mahinda was on the verge of being destroyed by a rebellion. The King said to his three sons, "Dear sons, a rebellion has broken out at the frontier. Either you or I must go. If I must go, you must serve the Buddha in this manner." Then all three princes replied simultaneously, "Father King, it is not a matter for you to go. We ourselves will go and quell the danger of the rebels." Having thus spoken in unison,
337:
337
they paid respects to their father, the King, went to the frontier, suppressed the rebellion, and after winning the battle, returned to the capital.

On the way, the three princes consulted with their trusted personal attendants, saying, "Friends, as soon as we reach the capital, our father, the King, will grant us a boon. What boon should we take?" The trusted attendants advised, "O Princes, for you, there is nothing difficult to obtain when the King passes away. However, you should only take the boon of having the opportunity to serve your elder brother, the Buddha Phussa." The princes accepted the advice, saying, "Friends, you have given good advice." All being in agreement, they returned to the capital and went to meet their father, the King.

At that time, the King was very pleased with his sons and granted them a boon. When the princes requested, "We wish to serve the Buddha for three months," the King said, "I cannot grant this boon. Choose another boon instead." The princes firmly requested, "Father King, we have no need for any other boon. If you wish to grant us a boon, please give us only this boon (the opportunity to serve the Buddha for three months)." As the princes requested repeatedly,
338:
338
the King, having already promised to give whatever boon they desired, thought, "I cannot avoid giving it." He then said to his sons, "Dear sons, I will grant the boon you desire as I promised. However, I wish to tell you this: Buddhas travel alone and are very difficult to approach, like maned lion kings. Therefore, when you serve the Buddha, do so without negligence."

The three brothers consulted and agreed, "If we are to serve the Buddha, we should do so in a manner worthy of the Buddha's physical presence." They undertook the ten precepts and, being entirely free from the "stench of unwholesomeness" (nirāmagandhā), they appointed three leading men to strive and carry out the work in the donation hall where offerings were to be made to the Buddha.

* Nirāmagandhā (Commentary) = The Ṭīkā explains this as being entirely free from the stench of unwholesomeness and the stench of defilements. Indeed, in this context, the constant arising of defilements is called a "stench" or "āmagandha." This is because if those defilements are constantly arising, they are unpleasant, mixed with the impurities of defilements, loathed by the virtuous, and tend to carry an extremely foul and putrid odor. To provide evidence or an indicator of how unwholesome defilements carry a foul odor: those who are thick with defilements are extremely putrid and foul-smelling. For this reason, the corpse of a person free from defilements does not become foul-smelling. This is specifically extracted from the Ṭīkā.
339:
339
Among those three men, one took the lead in producing wealth and grain. Another took the lead in measuring and distributing the wealth and grain to cover the daily expenses. The third took the lead in managing the affairs of the donation to ensure its completion. Among those three, in this present final existence during the time of our Buddha, the first man who led the production of wealth became King Bimbisāra. The second man who led the measuring and distributing of wealth became the merchant Visākha. The third man, the manager of the donation services (veyyāvaccamhu), became the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.

## Venerable Rāhula's Life as Prince Pathavindhara

During the time of the Buddha Kassapa, the Venerable Rāhula became the eldest son of King Kikī, the ruler of the Kāsī kingdom. His parents named him Prince Pathavindhara. That prince had sisters who were:
(1) The future Theri Khemā = Princess Samaṇī,
(2) The future Theri Uppalavaṇṇā = Princess Samaṇaguttā,
(3) The future Theri Paṭācārā = Princess Bhikkhunī,
(4) The future Theri Kuṇḍalakesī = Princess Bhikkhudāyikā,
(5) The future Theri Kisāgotamī = Princess Dhammā,
(6) The future Theri Dhammadinnā = Princess Sudhammā,
340:
(7) The future Visākhā Upāsikā = Princess Saṅghadāyikā—

Thus, there were seven sisters. When the seven royal sisters had each built and offered seven precincts for the Buddha Kassapa, Prince Pathavindhara attained the position of Heir Apparent. Upon attaining this rank, the prince spoke to his seven sisters, saying, "Sisters, please share one of the seven precincts you have built with me." The princesses replied, "Brother, you are established in the position of Heir Apparent; it is you who should give to us, your younger sisters. We wish for you to build another new precinct of your own."

After hearing the words of his sisters, Prince Pathavindhara, in a manner befitting his status as Heir Apparent, built and offered five hundred large monasteries. (Some say five hundred precincts). Prince Pathavindhara performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, upon passing away from that existence, was reborn in the celestial realm.

## (B) Renunciation in the Final Life

When the era of our Buddha's dispensation arrived, Prince Pathavindhara took conception in the womb of Queen Yasodharā, the chief consort of our Bodhisatta (Prince Siddhattha), and became famous as Prince Rāhula.
341:
The friend of that Rāhula was born as the son of a wealthy merchant named Raṭṭhapāla in the merchant's house of Raṭṭhapāla in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the Kuru kingdom.

(The detailed account of how Prince Rāhula was ordained as a novice should be looked up in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, page 132. The preaching of the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta and many other Dhamma teachings concerning Venerable Rāhula should be looked up in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 4, starting from page 173.)

## Concerning Venerable Rāhula's Desire for the Three Trainings

(As previously stated in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, page 132), after the Buddha had him ordained as a novice, He constantly admonished the novice Rāhula by preaching the Rāhulovāda Sutta found in the Sutta Nipāta Pali. (See the Burmese translation of Khuddakapāṭha, etc., pages 310-311.) The essence of this "Abhiṇha-rāhulovāda Sutta" should be understood according to this mnemonic verse:

(Associate with good friends, dwell in the forest, be moderate in three things.
Do not cling to the four requisites, act to extinguish craving.
Ensure the purity of virtue in the Pātimokkha restraint.
Guard the six doors of the senses, keeping them calm and closed.
Keep mindfulness firm on the body, contemplate the weariness of the aggregates.
Avoid and stay away from signs of beauty, contemplate to master the mind in Jhana.
Contemplate the signless (animitta) to remove conceit.
By practicing in this way, the three rounds of suffering will surely be extinguished.
Our Buddha preached this daily to Rāhula.)
342: Novice Rāhula would also rise early from bed, take a handful of sand, and say, "May I receive today as much instruction and advice from the Blessed One and my preceptors as there are grains of sand here." Consequently, his reputation spread among the community of monks: "Novice Rāhula is indeed one who accepts instruction easily; he is truly a noble and worthy son to his father, the Blessed One." The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the monks, reflected, "If I go there, a Dhamma discourse will arise, and the virtues of Rāhula will become more prominent." He went to the Dhamma hall, sat on the Buddha's seat on the Dhamma throne, and asked the monks, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit gathered here now?" When the monks replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing the virtues of Novice Rāhula regarding his ease in accepting instruction," the Buddha preached the Tipallatthamiga Jātaka (Ekanipāta, 2-Sīlavagga, 6th Jātaka) concerning that matter. (The detailed account of that Jātaka should be noted from the Ekanipāta of the 550 Jātaka stories.) Even when Ven. Rāhula was a young novice of seven years, the Buddha, intending that "Since Rāhula is young, he might tell a lie; let him not tell a lie even for the sake of fun," preached the Ambalaṭṭhika-rāhulovāda Sutta (found in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa of the Majjhima Nikāya).
343:
The Buddha preached it. (That account has been written in detail in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, starting from page 167.)

At the age of eighteen, while still a novice, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta was preached to him. (This was described in detail in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 4, starting from page 173.)

To enable Venerable Rāhula to strive in Vipassanā practice, the Buddha preached the Rāhula Saṃyutta (a collection of 22 suttas) and the Rāhula Sutta from the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta (page 483).

Thereafter, the Buddha, knowing that Venerable Rāhula's wisdom had matured, preached the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta (from Majjhima Nikāya 3, 324) shortly after Rāhula became a monk and before he had spent his first Vassa. (That account was described in detail in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 4, page 207.)

## (C) Attaining the Foremost Title (Etadagga)

At a later time, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and conferring Etadagga titles upon the monks, the Buddha praised Venerable Rāhula, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhākāmānaṃ yadidaṃ rāhulo = Monks, among my disciple monks who are desirous of the three trainings (Sikkhā), Rāhula is the foremost."

Thus, He praised him and placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Sikkhākāma" (those who desire the three trainings).
344: ## The Ordination of Ven. Raṭṭhapāla. The Buddha, while wandering in the Kuru country, arrived at the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika (a town where granaries were always full of grain in every house). The merchant's son Raṭṭhapāla, having heard the Buddha's teaching, developed great faith. After obtaining permission from his parents with great difficulty (similar to the case of the merchant's son Sudinna), he approached the Buddha and, according to the Buddha's direction, was ordained as a novice and a monk under a certain monk. From the day Raṭṭhapāla was ordained, whenever the wealthy father saw monks coming to his house door, he would utter insults and complaints: "What business do you have at this house? We had only one son. You have already taken that only son away; what more will you do now?" The Buddha stayed in Thullakoṭṭhika for only fifteen days (half a month) and then returned to Sāvatthī. In Sāvatthī, Ven. Raṭṭhapāla practiced Vipassanā with great effort and attained Arahantship. After asking permission from the Buddha, Ven. Raṭṭhapāla went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his parents. While wandering for alms from house to house, he received stale barley bread from his father's house (just like in the section on Ven. Sudinna). He ate that stale barley bread with relish as if it were the food of the gods (amṛta).
345:
The Elder partook of the meal. When his father, the wealthy merchant, met him and spoke words of reproach, he invited the Elder to the house for a meal. However, (as the meal for that day was already finished), the Elder only accepted for the following day. The next day, after having the meal at his father's house, the Elder induced the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) regarding the group of women who were fully adorned. While still standing, he preached the Dhamma and then, like an arrow shot from a bow, he flew into the sky and arrived at King Koravya's Migacīra garden, where he sat upon the auspicious stone slab.

After he was seated, the garden keeper informed King Koravya, who came to pay his respects. The Elder preached in detail the discourse concerning the four Dhamma summaries (Dhammuddesa) adorned with the four types of loss (pārijuñña). Gradually continuing his journey, he eventually returned to the presence of the Buddha. Thus, the story of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla unfolded. (The detailed current life story of this Elder should be looked up in the Majjhima Nikāya, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, page 244, and the Burmese translation, Volume 2, starting from page 255.)

## Venerable Raṭṭhapāla Attaining the Foremost Title (Etadagga)

At a later time, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and conferring Etadagga titles upon the monks, the Buddha praised Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saddhāpabbajitānaṃ yadidaṃ raṭṭhapālo = Monks, among my disciple monks who have gone forth out of faith...
346:
...among my disciple monks who have gone forth out of faith, Raṭṭhapāla is the foremost."

Thus, He praised him and placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Saddhāpabbajita" (those who have gone forth out of faith).

(In this regard, it should be specially noted: From the day he became a novice, Venerable Rāhula would wake up early every morning, take a handful of sand, and make a wish: "May I receive as many instructions and admonitions from the Buddha and my preceptors today as there are grains of sand in my hand." Therefore, he became the recipient of the Etadagga title in the category of "Sikkhākāma" (those who are extremely desirous of practicing the three trainings).

Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, developed extraordinary faith and fasted for fourteen meals (seven days), undergoing great hardship to get his parents' permission to ordain. Therefore, he became the recipient of the Etadagga title in the category of "Saddhāpabbajita" (those who ordain with great faith). This distinction should be noted.)

This is the account of the two Elders, Venerable Rāhula and Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.

**********

## (22) The Account of Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna

## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration

The future version of this Elder Kuṇḍadhāna was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. As mentioned previously, while he was at the monastery listening to the Dhamma...
347:
Upon seeing Padumuttara Buddha appointing a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) of being 'the first among those who receive the voting tickets (salāka)', he performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) for the Buddhas and made an aspiration for that very position. Padumuttara Buddha, seeing that this noble son's aspiration would be fulfilled without any obstacles, gave him the prophecy (byādika) as in previous instances and then departed for the monastery.

## The Elder's Past Bad Deed Following Him

After receiving the prophecy from Padumuttara Buddha, that noble son, the future Kuṇḍa-Dhāna Thera, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity (bhummadeva).

Notably, during the eras of long-lived Buddhas, the Uposatha was not observed every fifteen days (half-month) as it is in the time of our current Buddha. Indeed, during the time of Vipassī Buddha, the Uposatha and the recitation of the Pātimokkha were performed once every six years. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, the Pātimokkha was recited and Uposatha was observed once every six months.

On one occasion, when the six-month period was complete and it was time for the recitation of the Ovāda Pātimokkha and the Uposatha of Kassapa Buddha, two very close friends who were Elders living in a distant region set out for the place where Kassapa Buddha resided, saying, 'We shall observe the Uposatha.' At that time, the aforementioned terrestrial deity thought, 'The loving-kindness and affection between these two Elders is
348:
exceedingly firm. I wonder, if someone were to cause a rift, would the loving-kindness of these two Elders break and perish, or would it not?' Thus, he followed closely behind the Elders, watching for an opportunity to cause a division between them.

## Causing a Rift

Subsequently, one Elder entrusted his bowl and robes to the other and went to a secluded place near water to attend to his personal needs and bodily hygiene. After finishing his business and washing his hands and feet, he emerged from near a thicket.

The terrestrial deity followed closely behind the Elder who had been cleaning himself, having transformed into the form of an extremely beautiful woman. He acted as if he were shaking out and arranging his hair into a bun, and as if he were adjusting and wearing his sarong (htamein). Following right in the footsteps of the Elder, he emerged from the thicket along with him.

## The Rift and Misunderstanding

The companion Elder, who was standing and waiting in a suitable place, saw this occurrence and became distressed. He thought, 'Now, the loving-kindness that has existed between me and this monk for a long time has perished. If I had known this monk was so immoral, I would not have maintained such a long and intimate friendship with him.' Thinking thus,
349:
as soon as the Elder who had been cleaning himself reached him, he spoke words of severance: 'Friend, here, take your bowl and robes. I will by no means travel the same path with a friend as immoral as you.'

(From here on, for ease of reference, the monk who accuses will be called the 'Codaka' (Accuser) Elder, and the monk who is accused will be called the 'Cuditaka' (Accused) Elder.)

Upon hearing these words of severance, the heart of the Cuditaka Elder, who was truly a conscientious and virtuous person, felt as if it had been pierced with great force by a very sharp spear. He then asked the Codaka Elder, 'Friend, what kind of words are you speaking? For all this time, I have not been aware of committing even a minor offense (dukkaṭa). (Meaning: I have not committed even a minor offense). Yet today, you call me a "pāpa" (evil person). What did you see?' The Codaka Elder replied, 'Friend, what else is there to see? Did you not just emerge from the thicket together from the same spot with a woman (mātugāma) who was fully adorned and decorated in such a manner?' When he accused him according to what he had seen, the Cuditaka Elder spoke honestly, 'Friend, no such thing happened to me. I did not see or encounter any such woman as you describe.' Although the Cuditaka Elder spoke honestly in this way three times, the Codaka Elder could not believe his words at all, holding only to what he had seen
350:
as the truth. He no longer traveled the same path with the Cuditaka Elder and went to Kassapa Buddha by another route. The Cuditaka Elder also went to Kassapa Buddha by a different path.

## The Deity's Remorse

Later, when the community of monks entered the Uposatha hall (sīmā), the Codaka Elder saw the Cuditaka Elder inside and said, 'There is such an immoral monk present in this Uposatha hall. I cannot possibly perform the Uposatha together with that immoral monk.' Having said this, he left the Uposatha hall and stood outside.

The terrestrial deity thought, 'Oh, I have committed a grave deed,' and feeling remorse, he approached the Codaka Elder in the guise of an old layman (upāsaka) and asked, 'Venerable sir, why are you standing here outside the Uposatha hall?' The Elder replied, 'Layman, an immoral monk has already entered this Uposatha hall. I said I cannot possibly perform the Uposatha with that immoral monk and have come out to stand here.' The terrestrial deity then explained, 'Venerable sir, please do not think so. That (Cuditaka) monk is indeed one of pure virtue. The woman your reverence saw was actually me. I did this to you both, wondering "Is the loving-kindness of these two Elders firm or not?"
351:
and wishing to see and know who was a conscientious monk and who was a shameless one. Therefore, I assumed the form of a woman and followed behind the Cuditaka Elder.'

When the Elder asked, 'O good man, who are you?', the terrestrial deity replied, 'Venerable sir, I am a terrestrial deity (bhummadeva).' While speaking, he stood revealed in his divine power, prostrated at the Elder's feet, and pleaded, 'Venerable sirs, please forgive me. The (Cuditaka) Elder knows nothing of this fault. Please perform the Uposatha with peace of mind.' Thus he apologized to the Elder and led him into the Uposatha hall. Although that Elder performed the Uposatha in the same place, he never again lived in the same place in close friendship with the (Cuditaka) Elder. (The Great Commentary does not specifically mention the meditation practice of this Codaka Elder). As for the Cuditaka Elder, he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) in stages and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

Due to the consequences of that bad kamma, the terrestrial deity could not escape from the woeful states (apāya) for an entire interval between two Buddhas (buddhantara), an incalculable period of time between Kassapa Buddha and our Buddha. Even when he was occasionally reborn as a human, whatever faults others committed would fall upon him alone.
352:
## (b) Ordaining in the Final Life

During the time of our Buddha, he was reborn into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī. His parents named him 'Young Dhāna'. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas. In his old age, he heard the Dhamma of the Buddha, developed great faith, and entered the monkhood as a servant of the Sāsana.

## The Retribution Follows

From the day Venerable Dhāna ordained, a woman fully adorned and decorated—not a real woman, but a resultant image of his past kamma—would follow him into the village whenever he entered. When the Elder came out, she came out with him; when the Elder stood, she stood; when the Elder walked, she walked. In this way, it appeared as if she were always following closely behind the Elder. Venerable Dhāna himself could not see this female figure, but due to the consequences of that past bad kamma, others could see her. (How fearsome indeed are unwholesome kammas!)

Women and noblewomen who offered gruel and alms-food in the town and village would mock him, saying, 'Venerable sir, this ladle of gruel is for you; this ladle of gruel is for our friend, this woman who follows behind you.' This caused great mental distress for Venerable Dhāna. Even when he returned to the monastery, novices and young monks would surround Venerable Dhāna and mock him, saying, 'Dhāno Koṇḍā Jāto =
353:
Venerable Dhāna has become a womanizer.' Because of this, from that time on, Venerable Dhāna became known by the name 'Kuṇḍa-Dhāna Thera'.

As Venerable Kuṇḍa-Dhāna could no longer endure the mockery and ridicule of the novices and young monks who repeatedly gathered and spoke to him, he retaliated, saying, 'Only you are womanizers! Only your preceptors (upajjhāya) are womanizers! Only your teachers (ācariya) are womanizers!' Then, the other monks reported the matter of Venerable Kuṇḍa-Dhāna to the Buddha, saying, 'Exalted Buddha, the monk Kuṇḍa-Dhāna speaks such harsh and coarse words to the young monks and novices.' The Buddha had Venerable Kuṇḍa-Dhāna summoned and asked, 'Monk, is it true?' When Venerable Kuṇḍa-Dhāna admitted, 'It is true, Exalted Buddha,' the Buddha asked again, 'Why do you speak such harsh and coarse words?'

Venerable Kuṇḍa-Dhāna explained the reason, saying, 'Exalted Buddha, I spoke thus because I could not endure being constantly tormented and distressed.' The Buddha then said, 'My son, even until today, you have not been able to exhaust (extinguish) the bad kamma you committed in the past. My son, do not speak such harsh words again,' and he spoke as follows:
354:
“Do not speak harshly to anyone; those spoken to might answer you back. Indeed, contentious speech is painful; retaliatory blows may touch you.”

(O dear son named Dhāna), do not speak harsh words, which are like the teeth of a saw, to anyone. If you speak harsh words, others might speak harsh words back to you. Indeed, contentious speech, where one tries to outdo another, is very painful. Retaliatory physical or verbal punishments will surely reach you, just like dust thrown against the wind reaches the thrower, for behaving and speaking harshly towards your fellow monks.

“If you keep yourself as still as a broken gong, you have already reached Nibbāna; no contention is found in you.”

(O dear son named Dhāna), if you can strive to keep yourself as still and silent as a broken bronze gong that does not produce a sound even when struck, then you are one who has personally reached the supreme Nibbāna, the end of the cycle of suffering.
355:
“You have become (such a person). (If it be so), there will not be even a slight amount of contentious speech or action in your mind, thinking ‘I can defeat him, I am superior.’”

The Buddha preached these two verses of Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. (Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 37.)

## King Kosala’s Personal Investigation
The monks reported this matter (regarding Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna wandering together with a woman) to King Pasenadi of Kosala. King Kosala sent his men, saying, “Friends, go and investigate.” He himself, along with a small retinue, went to the dwelling of Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna, observed carefully, and stood in a suitable place.

At that time, Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna was sitting and sewing a robe. That woman (the phantom form of his past kamma) appeared to be standing near the Elder. King Kosala, thinking, “There is certainly something unusual about this,” went to the spot where the woman (the phantom form) was standing. When the King approached, the woman (the phantom form) appeared to enter the monk’s cell where the Elder resided. The King also entered the cell along with that woman (the phantom form).
356:
Although the King searched everywhere inside the cell, he did not see that woman (the phantom form). He reflected and realized, “This woman is not a real female. She is merely the result (vipāka) of a certain kamma of the Elder.” Although he had initially followed her into the cell near the Elder, he did not pay respects to the Elder until he had personally seen the unreality of the matter. After realizing it, he approached the Elder, paid respects, and sat in a suitable place, asking, “Venerable Sir, are you comfortable with your alms-food?” The Elder replied, “It is sufficient, Great King.”

King Kosala then said, “Venerable Sir, I understand your words. What I wish to say further is: who will have faith in you while you wander and live with such a source of defilement (the female form)? No one will have faith. From this time onwards, there is no need for you to go elsewhere for any purpose. I will support you with the four requisites. Venerable Sir, please do not be negligent in your meditation practice.” Thus, he provided alms-food daily.

Having received the support of King Kosala and having a steady mind due to suitable food, Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna practiced Insight Meditation (Vipassanā) with great effort and attained the Fruit of Arahantship; he became an Arahant. From the moment the Elder attained Arahantship, that woman (the phantom form of his past kamma) disappeared completely.
357:
## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
One day, Mahāsubhaddā, the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍika, while living with her husband’s family who held wrong views in the city of Ugga, reflected, “May the Blessed One protect me.” She observed the Uposatha precepts, and being free from the foul scent of defilements, she stood on the upper floor of the palace and made an Act of Truth: “May these jasmine flowers not fall elsewhere, but stay as a canopy above the Blessed One. By this sign, may the Blessed One accept my alms-food tomorrow together with five hundred monks.” She then threw eight handfuls of jasmine flowers into the sky. The flowers traveled through the air and remained as a canopy above the Blessed One while he was preaching.

The Blessed One, seeing the canopy of jasmine flowers, mentally accepted Subhaddā’s invitation. At dawn the next day, he addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, today we shall go to a distant place for alms. Do not give the voting tickets (salāka) to the worldling (puthujjana) monks; give them only to the noble (ariya) monks.” Venerable Ānanda told the monks, “Friends, the Blessed One will go to a distant place for alms today. Let the worldling monks not take the voting tickets; let only the noble monks take them.”

Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna said, “Friend, bring the voting ticket,” and was the very first to stretch out his hand (to take the ticket).
358:
Venerable Ānanda thought, “The Blessed One did not intend for worldling monks like Kuṇḍadhāna to be given the voting ticket; he intended it only for noble monks.” He went to the Blessed One and reported the matter. The Blessed One said, “Ānanda, if the monk Kuṇḍadhāna wishes to carry—to take—the voting ticket, give it to him.”

Then Venerable Ānanda reflected, “If it were not proper to give the voting ticket to Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna, the Blessed One would have forbidden it. (Since he did not), there must be a reason.” He decided, “I will give the voting ticket to Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna as he requested,” and prepared to go and give it. Before Venerable Ānanda arrived, Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā), and standing in the air by psychic power, he spoke boldly: “Friend Ānanda, bring the bowl of voting tickets. The Blessed One knows me. The Blessed One does not forbid a monk like me from taking the voting ticket first.” He then stretched out his hand and took the voting ticket. (This was one of the originating incidents).

Furthermore, on the day when Cūḷasubhaddā (the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍika) invited him and the Blessed One traveled to the city of Sāketa, among the five hundred monks, it was this Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna who was the first to take the voting ticket.
359:
Furthermore, when the Blessed One traveled through the air to the Sunāparanta region, it was also Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna who was the first to take the voting ticket.

Therefore, at a later time, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and conferring the titles of Etadagga (foremost), the Blessed One praised Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ yadidaṃ kuṇḍadhāno.”
“Monks, among my disciple monks who are the first to receive the voting ticket, Kuṇḍadhāna is the foremost.”

Thus, he was placed in the foremost position (Etadagga) as the “Paṭhama-salākagāhaka” (the first to receive the voting ticket).

This is the story of Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna.
**********
## (23) The Story of Venerable Vaṅgīsa
## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration
The future Venerable Vaṅgīsa was born into a wealthy family (mahābhoga) in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Like the future elders of old, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. He saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those with “inspired wit” (paṭibhāna).
360:
He performed great meritorious deeds for the Blessed One and made an aspiration: “May I also in the future become the foremost among monks who possess inspired wit (paṭibhāna).” Padumuttara Buddha, seeing that the young man’s aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy as in previous cases and then returned to the monastery.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That young man performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of our Blessed One, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī. His parents named the youth “Vaṅgīsa.” When Vaṅgīsa reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas. He pleased his teacher with his services and learned the “Chavasīsa-mantra” (the skull-mantra), a mantra by which one can know the destination of a deceased person by chanting it and tapping the skull of the dead with one’s fingernail. By doing so, he could know, “This dead person is reborn in such and such a place.”

The Brahmins realized, “This skill of Vaṅgīsa’s Chavasīsa-mantra will be a means of livelihood for us.” They had Vaṅgīsa sit in a covered carriage and traveled through villages, market towns, and royal cities. They would camp at city gates or the gates of villages and market towns. When a crowd gathered, they would say, “Whoever sees the youth Vaṅgīsa will gain wealth, attendants, and fame...”
361:
...they spread the word, saying, 'One can attain and even reach the celestial realms.' Hearing the propaganda of these Brahmins, many people gave bribes and gifts, wishing to see Vaṅgīsa.

Kings and great ministers went to those propagandizing Brahmins and asked, 'Teachers, what is the special knowledge of your teacher Vaṅgīsa?' The Brahmins replied, 'You do not know the reason. In the entire island of Jambudīpa, there is no other wise person equal to our teacher Vaṅgīsa. If teacher Vaṅgīsa taps the skull of someone who died more than three years ago with his fingernail and looks at it, he can know: "This deceased person was of such a clan and is now born in such a life."' To dispel the doubts of the multitude, Vaṅgīsa would use the power of mantras to invoke those various deceased persons and have them speak of their own destinations (gati). Based on this, he received a hundred or a thousand coins from the hands of the people.

## Vaṅgīsa's Time for Liberation Arrives

The Brahmins took the youth Vaṅgīsa and traveled through whatever villages, market towns, and royal cities they desired, and then they brought him back to the city of Sāvatthī. Vaṅgīsa stood near the Jetavana monastery and reflected, 'People say that the ascetic Gotama is a wise man. As for me, it is not proper to spend all my time merely following the words of these Brahmins and wandering around the island of Jambudīpa. I should also go and approach the wise.' Having considered this, he said to the Brahmins, 'You go ahead; I will go with the people...'
362: "O Vangīsa, do not take pleasure in seeing the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama is one who deceives those who come to see him with a trick called the alluring magic (āvaṭṭanī māyā)," the Brahmins said, trying to prevent him. Without heeding the words of those Brahmins, the young Vangīsa went to the presence of the Blessed One, exchanged pleasant and polite greetings, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One began the conversation by asking, "Vangīsa, do you know any particular art?" The young Vangīsa replied, "O Venerable Gotama, yes, I know a certain mantra called the Chavasīsa-manta (the skull-tapping mantra)." Again, the Blessed One asked, "Vangīsa, what can that Chavasīsa-manta which you know do? What kind of power does it have?" The young Vangīsa replied, "O Venerable Gotama, by reciting that mantra and tapping the skull of someone who died up to three years ago with my fingernail, I can see the realm where they have been reborn." By his psychic power, the Blessed One brought and displayed four skulls in order: (1) the skull of one reborn in hell, (2) the skull of one reborn in the human world, (3) the skull of one reborn in the deva world, and (4) the skull of an Arahant who had attained Parinibbāna. Vangīsa tapped the first skull and said, "O Venerable Gotama, the owner of this skull has gone to hell."
363: "Sādhu, sādhu, Vangīsa! You have seen correctly and well," the Blessed One praised him. Then, showing the second skull, He asked, "To what destination (gati) has this being gone?" Vangīsa replied, "O Venerable Gotama, this being has reached the human world." Again, showing the third bone, He asked, "To what destination has this being gone?" and Vangīsa replied, "O Venerable Gotama, this being has reached the deva world." In this way, Vangīsa was able to correctly answer the destinations of the three beings. When the Blessed One showed the fourth skull, which belonged to an Arahant, and asked him, Vangīsa recited his mantra and tapped the skull with his fingernail repeatedly, but despite his contemplation, he could see neither the beginning nor the end. Then the Blessed One asked Vangīsa, "Vangīsa, are you no longer able to see?" Vangīsa replied, "O Venerable Gotama, wait; I will examine it further," and he repeatedly recited the mantra and tapped the skull. How could he know the destination of an Arahant through a worldly (bāhiraka) mantra? He simply could not know. At that moment, sweat began to pour from Vangīsa's forehead. Feeling very ashamed, Vangīsa remained silent (tuṇhībhāva). Then the Blessed One asked, "Are you tired, dear Vangīsa?" Vangīsa replied, "Yes, Venerable Gotama, I am very tired. I cannot know the destination of this being. If you, Venerable Sir, know it, please tell me," he said, surrendering and pleading. The Blessed One then said, "Dear Vangīsa, I know this being, and I know even beyond that," and He preached these two verses found in the Dhammapada:
364: "He who knows in every way the passing away and the rebirth of beings, who is unattached, well-gone (sugata), and awakened (buddha)—him I call a Brahmin." Vangīsa = Dear Vangīsa. Yo = That Arahant. Sabbaso = In every way and in all aspects. Sattānaṃ = Of beings. Cutiñca = The passing away and death. Upapattiñca = And the reaching of a new existence through rebirth. Vedi = Has clearly understood and seen. Asattaṃ = Who is not attached to the five sense objects. Sugataṃ = Who has traveled straight to the city of Nibbāna through the noble practice of right conduct (sammā-paṭipatti). Buddhaṃ = Who clearly understands the Four Noble Truths. Taṃ = That noble Arahant. Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds. Brāhmaṇaṃ = Call a 'Brahmin' because he has discarded evil (bāhita-pāpa). Brūmi = I declare this so that it is known to gods and men. "Whose destination neither gods, gandhabbas, nor humans know, whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), an Arahant—him I call a Brahmin." Vangīsa = Dear Vangīsa. Yassa = Of which Arahant. Gatiṃ = The destination. Devā = The gods of the celestial realms. Gandhabba-mānusā = The celestial musicians called gandhabbas and human beings. Na jānanti = Do not clearly know.
365: (The reason the Blessed One preached these two verses to the monks in the Dhammapada was to let them know that Ven. Vangīsa had become an Arahant. The reason for preaching them to the young Vangīsa now was to let him know that the owner of the fourth skull shown was an Arahant, whose destination cannot be found in the five realms because he has attained Parinibbāna.) Then the young Vangīsa said to the Blessed One, "O Venerable Gotama, there is no loss for one who exchanges a mantra for a mantra. Therefore, I will give you the 'Chavasīsa' mantra which I know; please give me this 'Buddha' mantra which you have just spoken." The Blessed One then said, "Vangīsa, we do not exchange mantra for mantra. We give it freely out of compassion to those who desire it." The young Vangīsa said, "Very well, Venerable Gotama, please give me the mantra," and showing clear respect, he sat down with his hands folded in the shape of a lotus bud, in a posture of requesting. The Blessed One asked the young Vangīsa, "Vangīsa, in your Brahmin tradition, is there no practice of preliminary duties (vatta) for those who request and receive a valuable mantra or anything else?"
366: "There is, O Venerable Gotama," Vangīsa replied. Then the Blessed One asked, "Vangīsa, do you think our mantra has no practice of preliminary duties—no living in probation (parivāsa)?" It is the nature of Brahmins never to be satisfied with mantras. Therefore, the young Vangīsa spoke with total surrender, saying, "O Venerable Gotama, I will follow and practice according to the methods and rules you prescribe." The Blessed One said to him, "Vangīsa, if we are to give this Buddha-manta, we give it only to one who has the same appearance as us." The young Vangīsa thought, "I should do everything the Venerable Gotama commands, learn the mantra, and then leave." He then told his fellow Brahmins, "Do not be troubled if I become a monk. Once I have learned this Buddha-manta, I will become the greatest teacher in the entire Jambudīpa. When this happens, it will be good for you as well." After giving this encouraging message, he ordained as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One in order to learn the Buddha-manta. (In this account, the teacher who ordained the young Vangīsa was the Arahant Elder Nigrodhakappa. To clarify further: at the time Vangīsa was about to ordain, the Arahant Elder Nigrodhakappa was near the Blessed One. The Blessed One said to him, "Dear Nigrodhakappa, since this young Vangīsa wishes to receive ordination, you, my son, should ordain this young Vangīsa.")
367:
“Ordain him as a monk,” the Buddha commanded. Following the Buddha's instruction, the Elder taught the meditation on the five skin-parts (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained the youth Vangīsa. (From the Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, Vol. II, p. 75).

The Buddha said, “Dear Vangīsa, practice the mantra-observance for a while,” and taught him the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), also known as mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). Being a man of sharp wisdom, while reciting and contemplating the thirty-two parts of the body, Vangīsa clearly perceived the nature of rise and fall (impermanence) within those thirty-two parts. By developing and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

When the Elder Vangīsa attained Arahantship, the Brahmins consulted one another, saying, “What has happened to Vangīsa? How is he doing? Let us go and see him.” They went to the Elder Vangīsa and asked, “O Vangīsa, how is it? Have you finished learning the mantra from the ascetic Gotama?” When the Elder Vangīsa replied, “Yes, I have finished learning it,” the Brahmins invited him, saying, “If so, come, let us go.” The Elder Vangīsa spoke decisively, “You may go. For me, the business of going together with you is finished.” The Brahmins then quarreled with him, saying, “We told you from the beginning that the ascetic Gotama is one who deceives those who come to him with a magic called the 'enticing art' (āvaṭṭanī māyā). It is true—now you have fallen under the influence of the ascetic Gotama.”
368:
“What business do we have with you anymore? There is nothing left to do,” they said, and departed by the same way they had come.

(This Elder was a very famous Arahant in the Dispensation, known for his Pali verses. This can be known by looking at the Vangīsa Saṃyutta in the Sagāthāvagga).

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

Whenever this Elder Vangīsa approached the Buddha, from the moment he saw the Buddha, he would praise the Buddha’s virtues with hundreds and thousands of verses, using metaphors such as the moon, the sun, the sky, the great ocean, a noble elephant, and a maned lion king. Therefore, at a later time, in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, the Buddha praised the Elder Vangīsa, saying:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭibhānavantānaṃ yadidaṃ vangīso = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess brilliant wit (paṭibhāna), Vangīsa is the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha appointed him to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) as the foremost among those who possess brilliant wit (paṭibhānavanta).

This is the account of the Elder Vangīsa.
369:
## (24) The Story of Venerable Upasena Vangantaputta

(The original name of this Elder was Upasena. He was the younger brother of Venerable Sāriputta. Because he was the son of the Brahmin Vanganta, he was called Upasena Vangantaputta, meaning Upasena, the son of Vanganta).

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This noble being, the future Elder, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. When he came of age, like other future Elders, he went to the Buddha to listen to the Dhamma. He saw Buddha Padumuttara appoint a monk to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) as the foremost among those who are inspiring in all aspects (samantapāsādika). After performing great meritorious deeds for the Buddha, he made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha, seeing that the aspiration of this young man of good family would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy as in previous cases and then departed to the monastery.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That young man of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time when our Buddha appeared, he was born as the son of the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī in Nālaka village, within the region of Magadha, and was named Upasena. When the youth Upasena came of age, he mastered the three Vedas.
370:
After hearing the Dhamma from the Buddha, he developed great faith and was ordained as a monk in the Dispensation.

When Venerable Upasena himself had attained only one year of seniority (vassa), with the intention of “expanding the great residence of the Noble Saṅgha,” he ordained a young man of good family as a novice and then as a monk. After completing the rains retreat that year and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, when his resident pupil (saddhivihārika) had one year of seniority and he himself had two years, he thought, “The Buddha will be pleased when he sees me.” He then took his resident pupil and went to visit the Buddha.

After Venerable Upasena had paid homage to the Buddha and sat in a suitable place, the Buddha asked, “Monk, how many years of seniority (vassa) do you have?” When Venerable Upasena replied, “Venerable Sir, I have two years,” the Buddha asked further, “Monk, how many years of seniority does this monk who is with you have?” Venerable Upasena replied, “He has one year, Venerable Sir.” The Buddha asked again, “Monk, how is this monk who has one year related to you?” When Venerable Upasena replied, “He is my resident pupil (saddhivihārika), Venerable Sir,” the Buddha rebuked him, saying, “Hollow man (mogha purisa), who has not attained the Path or Fruition and has not finished his task, you wander about for the sake of quickly gaining an abundance of the four requisites.” After rebuking him in many ways,
371:
the Buddha censured him. Regarding this incident where Venerable Upasena, before completing ten years of seniority, acted as a preceptor (upajjhāya) and ordained a resident pupil, the Buddha laid down these two training rules:

“Monks, a monk with less than ten years of seniority should not ordain another. If he does so, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Monks, I allow a monk who has completed ten years or more to ordain another.”

(The detailed account of this story can be found in the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Mahāvagga, starting from page 77).

After receiving only censure instead of the praise he had initially expected from the Buddha, Venerable Upasena paid homage to the Buddha and thought, “One day, because of my followers, I will make the Buddha give me his blessing with that very mouth which is as glorious as the full moon.” With this thought, he went to a certain place that very day and practiced insight meditation (vipassanā kammaṭṭhāna). Before long, he attained the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

## Training and Nurturing Disciples

Later, Venerable Upasena was not only one who had renounced a great family to become a monk, but he also became a very famous and excellent preacher of the Dhamma (dhammakathika) on earth.
372:
Consequently, many young men of good family, out of devotion to his Dhamma talks and having left their relatives and friends, were ordained as novices under the Arahant Elder Upasena. In ordaining them, Venerable Upasena would say, “Young men, I am a forest-dweller (āraññaka) and a practitioner of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). If you also can be forest-dwellers and practitioners of the ascetic practices, then become novices.” He would then explain the thirteen ascetic practices. Only those who said, “We are able to do so,” were ordained as novices. Those young novices practiced the various ascetic duties according to their ability. When Venerable Upasena himself reached ten years of seniority and had mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka, he acted as the preceptor and ordained all those novices as monks. In this way, the retinue of monks who received ordination under Venerable Upasena reached about five hundred.

At that time, while the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, he informed the Saṅgha, “Monks, I wish to stay in solitary retreat for half a month (15 days).” The Saṅgha then made a pact: “Whichever monk approaches to see the Buddha, that monk shall be made to confess a Pācittiya offense.”
373:
Then, Venerable Upasena thought, “I will go and see the Buddha.” He went to the Jetavana Monastery together with his followers, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place. To initiate a conversation, the Buddha asked one of the Elder's young resident pupils, “Dear monk, do you delight in rag-robes (paṃsukūla)?” The young monk then prefaced his words by saying, “Venerable Sir, I do not delight in rag-robes,” and then explained to the Buddha that he practiced the rag-robe ascetic practice out of respect for his preceptor. In this context, the Buddha gave a great blessing to Venerable Upasena, saying, “Sādhu, Sādhu, Upasena...” and spoke words of praise for his virtues in many ways. (This is a summary; the detailed story should be noted from the Burmese translation of the Vinaya Piṭaka, Pārājika Pāḷi, page 355, 2-Kosiya Vagga, 5-Nisīdanasanthata Sikkhāpada. Note: In the Vinaya Pāḷi, it says, “Icchāmahaṃ bhikkhave temāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ = Monks, I wish to stay in solitary retreat for three months.” In the Aṅguttara Commentary, it says “half a month (15 days).” One should follow the Pāḷi text and record it as “three months”).

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At another time, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, the Buddha, regarding Venerable Upasena in this Dispensation—
374:
“Monks, among my disciple monks who are inspiring in all aspects (including their retinue), Upasena, the son of Vaṅkanta, is the foremost.”

Having uttered this praise, the Buddha appointed him to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being “foremost among those who are inspiring in all aspects” (Samantapāsādika).

## The Parinibbāna of Ven. Upasena

At one time, Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Upasena were staying in the Sappasoṇḍika Cave (a cave shaped like a cobra's hood) in the Indasāla Wood near Rājagaha. At that time, a venomous snake fell onto Ven. Upasena’s body.

(In this regard: After finishing his meal, Ven. Upasena took his outer robe and sat in the shade of the cave, enjoying the gentle breeze blowing through the window while sewing his double-layered under-robe. At that moment, two small venomous snakes were playing on the roof of the cave, and one of them fell onto the Elder’s shoulder. This was no ordinary snake, but a deadly one known as 'Phuṭṭhavisa,' whose venom takes effect upon mere contact. Therefore, from the point of contact, the venom spread through the Elder’s body, destroying it rapidly, just as a flame consumes the oil in a lamp.

The Elder, perceiving the intense spread of the venom, knew that by its natural power, his body would normally burst into flames and disintegrate instantly. However, through his own spiritual power...)
375: 375 (...made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna), saying, "May this body not disintegrate inside the cave," and thus held it together. Then, Venerable Upasena called the monks and said, "Friends, come. Before this body scatters like a handful of chaff in this very place, place this body of mine on a small couch and carry it outside." Then, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upasena: "We do not see any alteration in Venerable Upasena's physical movements, nor any alteration in his faculties such as the eyes. Yet, Venerable Upasena says, 'Friends, come. Before this body scatters like a handful of chaff in this very place, place this body of mine on a small couch and carry it outside.'" (In this regard: Ordinary people near death experience physical trembling and the distortion of their eyes and face, but since Venerable Upasena had none of these signs, Venerable Sāriputta spoke thus.) Then, Venerable Upasena addressed Venerable Sāriputta:)
376: 376 "Friend Sāriputta, it is only in a person who has the misconception of 'I' through wrong view (diṭṭhi) and the misconception of 'mine' through craving (taṇhā), thinking 'I am the eye, the eye is mine; I am the ear, the ear is mine; I am the nose, the nose is mine; I am the tongue, the tongue is mine; I am the body, the body is mine; I am the mind, the mind is mine'—it is only in such a person that there would be an alteration of physical movements or an alteration of faculties like the eyes at the time of death. Friend Sāriputta, for me, there is absolutely no misconception through wrong view or craving such as 'I am the eye, the eye is mine... (p) ...I am the mind, the mind is mine.' In me, who is without such things, how could there be any alteration of physical movements or faculties like the eyes now that death is near? There is simply none." Thus he replied. Then, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upasena: "It is indeed fitting that there is no alteration of physical movements or faculties in Venerable Upasena at this time of death. For Venerable Upasena has long ago completely uprooted the three things: the view of 'I' (diṭṭhi), the craving of 'mine' (taṇhā), and the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya). That is why in Venerable Upasena, misconceptions through wrong view or craving such as 'I am the eye, the eye is mine... (p) ...I am the mind, the mind is mine' can no longer occur."
377:
“...there is no longer any possibility of wrong views through craving or conceit, such as ‘this is mine’ or ‘this is I’.” Thus, he spoke words of praise.

Afterward, the monks placed Ven. Upasena’s body on a small couch and carried it outside. At that moment, right there (on the couch where he was placed after being carried out), Ven. Upasena’s body disintegrated and scattered like a handful of chaff, and he entered Parinibbāna, ending the cycle of existence.

(These events are recorded in the Upasena Āsီvisa Sutta of the Saḷāyatana Vagga Saṃyutta and its commentary.)

This is the account of Ven. Upasena Vaṅkantaputta.

## (25) The Account of Ven. Dabba

## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration

This noble being, the future Ven. Dabba, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, like the future elders before him, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. He witnessed Padumuttara Buddha appointing a monk to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being “foremost among those who assign lodgings to the Saṅgha.” After performing great meritorious deeds, he made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha, seeing that the noble youth’s aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy as in previous cases...
378:
...and after delivering the prophecy, the Buddha returned to the monastery.

## Practicing Dhamma on the Mountain Top

That noble youth performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time when the dispensation (Sāsana) of Kassapa Buddha was declining, he was born into a good family and ordained as a monk. He and six other monks, making a group of seven virtuous monks, shared the same intention. Seeing others acting disrespectfully toward the Sāsana, they consulted one another: “What Sāsana work can we accomplish by living in these towns and villages? We will surely achieve nothing. Let us go to a secluded place and strive in the monk’s practice to end the suffering of Saṃsāra.” Having agreed, they went to a very high mountain, climbed to the top using a ladder, and said: “Let those who know the power of their own minds push down the ladder. Let those who still cling to life descend now, so they do not feel remorse later.” All seven monks, agreeing to sacrifice their lives for the practice, pushed the ladder away. They exhorted one another: “Friends, do not be negligent in your practice.” Each stayed in a place of his choosing and strove diligently in the Dhamma, risking their lives.

Among those seven monks, the eldest Thera attained Arahatship on the fifth day...
379: 379 He reflected, "My task as a monk is finished. What more is there for me to do on this mountain peak? There is nothing more to do." Using his psychic power, he brought almsfood from the northern continent of Uttarakuru and said to the remaining six companions, "Friends, please partake of this food. Let the task of collecting alms be my responsibility. You friends should only strive in your meditation." Then the remaining six monks asked, "Friend, when we pushed the ladder off the mountain, did we make any agreement such as, 'The one who first realizes the supramundane Dhamma must collect alms and feed the others, and the remaining monks will eat that food and continue their practice'?" When the Elder replied, "No, friends, there was no such agreement," the six monks said, "Venerable sir, you have attained Arahantship through your past merits. We too, if we are able, will bring an end to the suffering of Saṃsāra. Please go wherever you wish, venerable sir." The Elder, unable to convince the six monks despite various attempts, eventually ate his meal in a pleasant place and departed as he wished. The second elder (Anutthera) attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) on the seventh day. Like the first elder, he brought food from Uttarakuru and invited them, but when they refused as before, he ate his meal in a pleasant place...
380:
...and after traveling to wherever he desired, he passed away from that life and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

The remaining five monks, not having attained any special stages of the Path or Fruit in that life, passed away and wandered through the realms of devas and humans for an entire incalculable interval between Buddhas (Buddhandara). During the time of our Buddha’s appearance, they were born into various families: (1) One was born as King Pukkusāti in the palace of Taxila in the Gandhāra Kingdom. (2) Another was born as the wanderer Sabhiya, conceived in the womb of a female wanderer in the Pabbateyya (or Majjhantika) region. (3) Another was born into a wealthy family in the Bāhiya region as Bāhiya. (4) Another was born into a wealthy family in Rājagaha as the youth Kumāra Kassapa. (5) The other (the future Ven. Dabba) was conceived in the palace of a Malla prince in the city of Anupiya in the Malla Kingdom.

When the child’s mother was about to give birth, she passed away. Her physical remains were taken to the cemetery, placed on a funeral pyre, and cremated. Due to the intense heat of the fire, her abdominal wall burst open. By the power of his own merit, the child flew into the air and landed on a pile of dabba grass. People picked him up and handed him to his grandmother. When the grandmother named the child, because he had fallen onto a pile of dabba grass...
381:
381
Because he survived, the boy was given the name "Dabba."
(Note: In the Aṅguttara Commentary, Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, and Theragāthā Commentary, it is explained as "dabbatthambe nipati," which could be translated as "he fell near a woodpile (or a wooden post)." However, in the Apadāna Pāli, Volume II, page 124, verse 143 of the Dabba-mallaputta Thera Apadāna, it states "patito dabbapuñjamhi, tato dabboti vissutā," which means "he fell upon a heap of Dabba grass (Kusha grass)." Therefore, it is translated here as "falling on a heap of Dabba grass." If he had fallen on a woodpile or a wooden post, he likely would not have survived. The word "Dabba" also refers to Dabba grass; "dabbapuñjamhi" means on a heap of Dabba grass. Only by translating "patito" as "he fell" [on the grass] does the meaning become clear and his survival plausible.)

When the boy Dabba was seven years old, the Blessed One, while wandering through the Malla country accompanied by a company of monks, arrived at the town of Anupiya and stayed in the Anupiya Mango Grove. Having seen the Blessed One, the boy Dabba was filled with great faith and devotion. Desiring to ordain as a monk, he asked his grandmother for permission, saying, "O Grandmother, please allow me to ordain as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One."

His grandmother replied, "Very well, dear grandson," and taking the boy Dabba to the Blessed One, she said, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy Dabba, my grandson."

The Blessed One gave a sign to a monk who was near him, saying, "Monk, ordain this boy." After hearing the Blessed One's words, that Elder, while ordaining the boy Dabba, gave him the meditation on the five parts ending in the skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna).
382:
382
(Shaving the hair is the beginning of the ordination process. It is customary for the preceptor to explain the taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna to the candidate just before shaving the hair. Therefore, the boy Dabba meditated and reflected on the taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna explained by the Elder while his hair was being shaved.)

Because the boy Dabba was one who possessed the requisite merits for the paths and fruits, and had received a prophecy for the rank of a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka) in the presence of Padumuttara Buddha a hundred thousand aeons ago, he attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) as soon as the first lock of hair was shaved. When the second lock was shaved, he attained the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala). When the third lock was shaved, he attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). Simultaneously with the completion of the shaving of all his hair, he realized the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). Thus, at the very end of the razor's work, he became an Arahant.

The Blessed One stayed in the Malla country as long as there were beings to be converted, and then proceeded to the city of Rājagaha, where he resided comfortably at the Veluvana Monastery. The Arahant Elder Dabba also followed along with the Blessed One. In Rājagaha, the Arahant Dabba, while in seclusion, reflected on the completion of his own task as a monk. Wishing to devote himself to the service of the Saṅgha (saṅghaveyyāvacca), he thought: "It would be good if I were to assign lodgings and appoint meals for the Saṅgha."

The Arahant Elder Dabba went to the Blessed One and informed him of his intention. The Blessed One expressed his approval (sādhu) and granted him two formal appointments (sammuti): (1) Appointment by the Saṅgha as the one who assigns lodgings for the Saṅgha =
383:
383
Recognition as the Assigner of Lodgings (senāsanapaññāpaka-sammuti); and (2) Appointment by the Saṅgha as the one who appoints meals for the Saṅgha = Recognition as the Appointer of Meals (bhattuddesaka-sammuti).

Thereafter, the Blessed One, being pleased and satisfied that "this Dabba, though only seven years old, has attained a great state (the state of an Arahant endowed with the analytical insights, the six direct knowledges, and the three true knowledges)," allowed him to receive the full ordination (upasampadā) even though he was only seven years old. (Based on this, it should be understood that other young novices who became Arahants, such as Paṇḍita Sāmaṇera, Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera, Sopāka Sāmaṇera, and Venerable Sāriputta’s youngest brother Khadiravaniya Revata Sāmaṇera, were also granted full ordination despite not being twenty years old, in consideration of their attainment of Arahatship. Although these noble ones were young in age, because their attainment of Arahatship was so great, or because they were endowed with firm and stable virtue, they are referred to and described in the scriptures as "Thera" or Elder.)

From the time he became a monk, the Elder Dabba assigned sleeping places and lodgings for all the monks residing in Rājagaha. He also took responsibility for accepting the meals offered by donors for the Saṅgha and directed them according to the seniority of the monks without error.

The reputation of the Elder Dabba’s good intentions in assigning lodgings for the Saṅgha spread throughout all directions: "Friends, the Elder Dabba, the son of the Mallas, assigns lodgings in a single area for monks of similar temperament. Even for visiting monks from afar,
384:
384
he assigns lodgings exactly as they request. He even escorts those monks who are unable to go by using his psychic powers." 

At that time, visiting monks would approach the Elder Dabba both at the proper time and at improper times, saying, "Friend, please assign us lodgings in the Jīvaka Mango Grove monastery," or "Friend, please assign us lodgings in the Maddakucchi Deer Park monastery," and so on. They would follow him just to see the psychic power of Venerable Dabba. The Elder Dabba would then use his psychic power to create mind-made emanations (manomaya-nimmita), providing one emanation of himself for each Elder. Then, with his finger glowing like a torch, he would walk ahead of the visiting monks and say, "This is the couch, Venerable Sir; this is the bench, Venerable Sir." After thus fully explaining and assigning the lodgings, he would return to his own residence. (This is a summary; the detailed story is found in the Vinaya Pārājika Pāli, Duṭṭhadosa Sikkhāpada, page 243 of Volume I.)

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

The Blessed One, taking the Elder's good intentions and skill in assigning lodgings for the Saṅgha as the occasion, later sat in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and declared of the Elder Dabba:
385:
385
"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ yadidaṃ dabbo mallaputto = Monks, among my disciple monks who assign lodgings for the Saṅgha, Dabba the son of the Mallas is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the rank of Etadagga as the "Senāsanapaññāpaka"—the one who assigns lodgings for the Saṅgha without any deficiency.

(In this regard: From the time the Elder Dabba received the senāsanapaññāpaka-sammuti, when he assigned lodgings for the Saṅgha, there was no compound in the eighteen great monasteries around Rājagaha that was unswept, no lodging that was uncleaned or unprepared, no couch or bench that was unwashed or uncleaned, and no drinking water or utility water that was not set out. Therefore, he became the recipient of the Etadagga title as the foremost among those who assign lodgings for the Saṅgha.)

## The Elder Being Accused

Even though he was a true virtuous person, a group of wicked monks led by the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka falsely accused the Elder of misconduct with a nun named Mettiyā. (The details of this matter should be sought in the Vinaya Pārājika Pāli, Saṅghādisesa Duṭṭhadosa Sikkhāpada, and the Vinaya Cullavagga Pāli, Samathakkhandhaka, Sativinaya, starting from page 185.) This accusation was the result of an unwholesome kamma from ninety-one aeons ago, when he had falsely accused a pure Arahant disciple of Vipassī Buddha, knowing him to be innocent.
386:
386
## The Parinibbāna of the Elder

One day, when he was to attain Parinibbāna, the Elder Dabba entered the city of Rājagaha for alms. After finishing his meal and returning to the Veluvana Monastery, he performed his duties toward the Blessed One and went to his place of day-rest. He took water from a jar, washed his feet, cooled his body, spread out his leather mat (cammakhaṇḍa), sat down, and entered into a meditative attainment for a determined period.

Emerging from the attainment at the determined time, the Elder reflected on his own life-force (āyusaṅkhāra—the continuity of physical and mental life). Seeing that only about two or three moments (muhutta) of life remained, he thought: "It would not be proper for me to attain Parinibbāna while sitting here at my place of day-rest without informing the Blessed One or the Saṅgha of my fellow monks. It would be better if I approach the Blessed One, inform him of my impending Parinibbāna, pay homage to him, and then, to clearly demonstrate the power of the Dispensation to lead one out of the round of rebirths, I shall sit in the air, display my psychic powers, enter the fire-kasiṇa (tejokasiṇa) jhāna, and then attain Parinibbāna. If I attain Parinibbāna after displaying such powers, faith and devotion will arise in the hearts of those who lack faith in me (due to the false accusations of the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka). Such faith will lead to their long-term welfare and happiness."
387:
Having approached the Blessed One and paid homage, he sat in a suitable place and addressed the Blessed One: "Parinibbānakālo me dāni sugata—O Blessed One, who speaks well, it is now the time for my Parinibbāna."

The Blessed One, having reflected upon and seen that the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) of Venerable Dabba was indeed exhausted, said: "Dear Dabba, you now know the time for your Parinibbāna."

Then, Venerable Dabba Mallaputta paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times clockwise, and standing in a suitable place, said:

"O Blessed One, for a hundred thousand aeons, I have met and lived with you in various existences and performed meritorious deeds, doing so with the aspiration for this present benefit of becoming an Arahat. That benefit has now reached its pinnacle (Arahatta-phala) and is fulfilled. This present seeing of the Blessed One is my final seeing."

Thus he spoke these sorrowful words. Among the monks present there, some who were worldlings (puthujjana), Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and Once-returners (sakadāgāmī) felt great compassion. Some monks wept.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts and intentions of Venerable Dabba, said: "Dear Dabba, if that is so,
388:
you, dear son, should perform miracles (pāṭihāriya) for me and for the Saṅgha (before entering Parinibbāna)." At that very moment, the entire assembly of monks gathered together. Then, Venerable Dabba Mallaputta performed all the miracles pertaining to disciples, such as "being one and becoming many, being many and becoming one, appearing and disappearing," and so forth. Having done so, he again paid homage to the Blessed One.

After paying homage, the Elder flew up into the sky, created earth in the sky, and sitting upon that earth, entered the fire-kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa) jhāna. Emerging from that jhāna, he reflected upon his body and resolved that the fire element should blaze up from this body and consume it. After making this resolution, he again entered the fire-kasiṇa jhāna which serves as the basis for supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). (The previous jhāna was the basis for the resolution; this jhāna is the basis for the supernormal knowledge). Emerging from that jhāna, the process of supernormal knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-vīthi-citta) arose. As soon as that supernormal impulsion (abhiññā-javana) occurred once, his entire body blazed with fire. Within a moment, like the fire that destroys the world, that fire, by the power of his resolution, consumed everything without leaving even a trace of ash or the smallest particle of the conditioned body (saṅkhāra), and then it was extinguished. The Elder, emerging from the supernormal consciousness (iddhi-citta), entered Parinibbāna and brought the cycle of suffering to an end with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) that performs the function of death (cuti-kicca) following the supernormal impulsion.
389:
(This account of the Elder's Parinibbāna is extracted from the Udāna Commentary, starting from page 387).

This is the story of Venerable Dabba.
