## (26) The Story of Venerable Pilindavaccha
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
This noble being, the future Pilindavaccha Thera, was born into a wealthy family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Like other future Elders, while listening to the Dhamma of the Blessed One, he saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost (etadagga) position of being "most beloved by the devas." Having performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra), he made an aspiration for that same position. The Blessed One, seeing that the noble son's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy as in previous cases.

## Honoring the Stupa and the Saṅgha
That noble son performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered between the worlds of devas and humans. During the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born again in the human world. When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, he made great offerings to the Buddha's stupa (cetiya) and gave great donations to the Saṅgha.
390:
## Life as a Universal Monarch
When that noble son passed away from that life, he continued to wander only in the worlds of devas and humans. In one life before a Buddha had appeared, he became a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). He established the masses in the five precepts and led them to reach the happy celestial realms.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
Before our Blessed One appeared, that noble son was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī. His personal name was "Pilinda" and his clan name was "Vaccha"; thus, he became famously known by the combined name "Pilindavaccha." Being one who felt much weariness with the cycle of birth (saṃsāra), he became a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). He mastered the mantra art known as Cūḷagandhāra. By means of that art, he became a Vidyādhara who could fly through the sky and know the thoughts of others. He lived in the city of Rājagaha, reaching the pinnacle of gain and following.

At that time, our Blessed One appeared in the world and, while traveling on his journey, arrived at the city of Rājagaha. From the time the Buddha arrived in Rājagaha, the Cūḷagandhāra art of the wandering ascetic Pilindavaccha became imperfect and could no longer accomplish its tasks. (Even when he recited the mantras, he could no longer fly in the sky or know the thoughts of others as before). Then, the wandering ascetic Pilindavaccha thought: "I have heard from teachers and teachers' teachers that
391:
the Cūḷagandhāra art cannot be perfected in a place where the Mahāgandhāra art is present. Since the Noble Ascetic Gotama arrived in this city of Rājagaha, my Cūḷagandhāra art has become imperfect. Without a doubt, the Noble Ascetic Gotama is one who knows the Mahāgandhāra art. It would be good if I were to approach the Noble Ascetic Gotama and learn that Mahāgandhāra art from him." Having considered this, he approached the Buddha and requested: "Noble Ascetic, I wish to learn a certain art from you. Please grant me permission."

The Blessed One said, "If you wish to learn that art, you must become a monk." The wandering ascetic Pilindavaccha, thinking that "becoming a monk is the preliminary work (parikamma) for the art," was ordained. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to Venerable Pilindavaccha and gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament. Since Venerable Pilindavaccha was endowed with the past merit (upanissaya) for attaining the fruit of Arahatship, he soon developed insight (vipassanā) and reached the fruit of Arahatship; he became an Arahat. (From Udāna Commentary, 63).

## The Habit of Harsh-sounding Speech
When the Arahat Elder Pilindavaccha spoke with either laypeople or monks, he was in the habit of using the address "Vasala-samudācāra" (calling others 'outcaste' or 'wretch') in every sentence, such as: "Ehi vasala—Come, wretch; Gaccha vasala—Go, wretch; Āhara vasala—Bring it, wretch; Gaṇha vasala—Take it, wretch."
392:
Taking note of those words, the monks asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, do those who are Noble Ones (Ariyas) speak harsh and rude words?" The Blessed One replied: "Monks, in the hearts of Noble Ones, there is no harsh or rude speech intended to disparage others (out of the anger of disparagement). However, rude-sounding speech may occur by the power of habitual tendencies (vāsanā), which are the lingering traces of defilements practiced and cultivated over many past lives." Then the monks asked: "Venerable Sir, Venerable Pilindavaccha repeatedly says 'Vasala, vasala' when speaking with laypeople or monks. Venerable Sir, what is the reason for this? Why does he speak in this way?"

Then the Blessed One said to the monks: "Monks, this habit of my son Pilindavaccha speaking rudely is not a practice that started only now. Indeed, in the past, for five hundred consecutive births, this Pilindavaccha was born into a Brahmin family that was accustomed to calling others 'Vasala' (wretch). Thus, my son Pilindavaccha speaks such rude-sounding words only because of the habitual tendency (vāsanā) from past lives. He does not speak with the unwholesome intention of harsh speech (pharusa-vācā). It is true—the speech of Noble Ones, though it may sound rude, is pure because the intention (cetanā) is not rude. In such rude-sounding speech of Noble Ones,
393:
not even the slightest bit of evil is found." Having said this, he spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:

Akakkasaṃ viññāpaniṃ,
Giraṃ saccamudīraye.
Yāya nābhisaje kañci,
Tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

Bhikkhave = O monks, my dear sons. Yāya girāya = by which speech. Kañci = any other person. Nābhisaje = one does not offend or strike, as if with a thorn. (Khīṇāsavo nāma = one who is called an Arahat, whose taints are exhausted). Akakkasaṃ = not harsh in sound. Viññāpaniṃ = easy to understand in meaning. Saccaṃ = true and unerring. Tādisaṃ giraṃ = such excellent speech. Udīraye = one should utter. Taṃ = that person who is not harsh in speech and is an Arahat. Ahaṃ = I, the Teacher of the three worlds. Brāhmaṇaṃ = call a true Brahmin, a noble person, because of the literal meaning of having warded off evil (bāhitapāpa). Brūmi = I declare so to make it known to devas and humans.

The Buddha preached this verse. At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. (In this regard, it should be noted that although the word 'Vasala' used by the Arahat Elder Pilindavaccha sounds rude, it is not called 'pharusa-vācā' (harsh speech) because the intention is not rude; it is not the misconduct of harsh speech.)
394: ## Long Pepper Fruits Turning into Mouse Droppings One day, while the Venerable Pilindavaccha was entering the city of Rājagaha for alms, he saw a man entering the city carrying a bowl full of long pepper fruits. The Elder asked, "Wretch, what is in your bowl?" The man thought, "This monk has spoken harsh and rude words to me so early in the morning, calling me a 'wretch,' which is an ill omen and inauspicious. It is only fitting that I reply with harsh and rude words that match his." With such a malicious thought in his mind, he replied rudely, "Venerable sir, there are mouse droppings in my bowl." (In this instance, although the Elder's words were harsh in their utterance by calling him 'wretch,' his intention was not harsh; it was very gentle. He spoke that way only due to his habitual tendency (vāsanā). The man's reply, "There are mouse droppings," was spoken with anger and malice, thus it became the unwholesome kamma of harsh speech (pharusavācā), committed against an Arahant. Therefore, his unwholesome kamma of harsh speech bore its ill result immediately.) Then the Great Elder said, "Evaṃ bhavissati vasala = Wretch, it shall be as you say; they will indeed become mouse droppings." As soon as the man had moved out of the Elder's sight, all the long pepper fruits in his bowl turned into mouse droppings. The man thought, "These long pepper fruits appear exactly like mouse droppings. Are they truly mouse droppings or not?" and thinking thus,
395: he pressed and crushed them with his hand to investigate. When he realized they had truly become mouse droppings, a powerful wave of mental distress (balavadomanassa) arose within him. The man worried greatly, thinking, "Have only the long pepper fruits in this bowl turned into mouse droppings, or have those on the cart also become mouse droppings?" He went to check his cart where the long pepper fruits were loaded and saw that all the fruits on the cart had also become mouse droppings. Feeling extreme anguish, he beat his breast and thought, "This is not the work of anyone else. This is only the work of the monk I saw earlier. Surely there must be a way to resolve this. (According to the Sihala version) Surely that monk must be one who knows a kind of magic. I will follow him to where he went, investigate, and find out about this matter." After considering this, he inquired about the path the Great Elder had taken and followed him. At that time, another man saw the owner of the long pepper fruits (now the owner of mouse droppings) walking along in great agitation and asked, "O man, you are walking with such great agitation. Why are you going like this?" The owner of the long pepper fruits then told him the whole story. Upon hearing the man's words, the other said, "O friend, do not be so troubled. That must be my master, the Venerable Pilindavaccha.
396:
“Young man, take this very bowl, fill it with the existing rat droppings, and go stand before the Elder. At that time, the Elder will ask, ‘You wretch, what are those things in your bowl?’ When he asks, you must reply, ‘They are long peppers, venerable sir.’ Then the Elder will say, ‘Evaṃ bhavissati vasala = You wretch, let them be long peppers as you say.’ At that moment, both the rat droppings in the bowl and all the rat droppings in the cart will return to their original form and become nothing but long peppers.” Thus, he gave the advice. The man who owned the long peppers followed the advice exactly as told. All the long peppers returned to their original state as long peppers.

## (c) Receiving the Pre-eminent Title

In a past life before the appearance of the Buddha, Ven. Pilindavaccha was a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) who established the people in the five precepts and led them to the heavenly realms. Most of the devas in the six kama-sphere heavens had followed the teachings of this future Ven. Pilindavaccha when he was a Cakkavatti. Looking at their divine bliss in their respective heavenly realms, they reflected: “By relying on whom did we obtain this divine bliss?” They saw Ven. Pilindavaccha and, realizing “We have obtained this divine bliss by relying on the Elder,” they visited him out of gratitude and joy, morning and night, to pay homage. Therefore, the Buddha...
397:
...at a later time, while sitting in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, the Buddha spoke in praise of Ven. Pilindavaccha:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ devatānaṃ piyamanaāpānaṃ yadidaṃ pilindavaccho = Monks, among my disciple monks who are beloved and pleasing to the devas, the monk Pilindavaccha is the foremost.”

Thus, he appointed him to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being “foremost among those who are beloved and pleasing to the devas” (Devatānaṃ piyamanaāpa).

This is the account of Ven. Pilindavaccha.

## (27) The Account of Ven. Bāhiya Dārucīriya

(The original name of this Elder was “Bāhiya” because he was born in the Bāhiya region. Later, as will be described in the story, he wore bark or wood shavings as clothing; therefore, he was also known as “Dārucīriya = one who wears wood-shavings.” Combining the two names, he is called “Ven. Bāhiya Dārucīriya.”)

## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration

This noble being, the future Ven. Bāhiya Dārucīriya, was also born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Like the future elders before him, while listening to the Buddha’s Dhamma teaching, he saw Padumuttara Buddha appointing a monk to the pre-eminent position (Etadagga) of being “foremost among those who attain swift realization (Khippābhiññā).”
398:
Having witnessed this, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha, seeing that the noble youth’s aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy as in previous cases.

## Practicing Dhamma on the Mountain Top

That noble youth performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time when the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining, as mentioned in the story of Ven. Dabba above, he climbed a mountain top with his fellow monks (see the story of Ven. Dabba on page 378) and practiced the Dhamma. Being one with pure and perfect virtue, he was reborn in the heavenly realm at the end of his life.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That noble deva remained in the heavenly realm for an entire incalculable interval between Buddhas (Buddhandara). During the time of our Buddha’s appearance, he was born into a good family in the Bāhiya region. Upon reaching maturity, while living as a householder, he thought one day, “I shall engage in trade.” He boarded a ship bound for Suvaṇṇabhūmi. The ship they were on did not reach its destination but was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. All the people on the ship became food for fish and turtles.

However, because this noble Bāhiya was in his final existence (Pacchimabhavika), he did not die but survived by clinging to a piece of wood.
399: Relying on that, he reached the shore at the port of Suppāraka on the seventh day. When he reached the inhabited area, he reflected, "It is not appropriate to approach people in my current state without clothes." He took a mass of moss from a nearby reservoir, wrapped it around his body, picked up a discarded broken bowl, and entered the village for alms. When the people saw Bāhiya, they thought, "If there are Arahants in the world, they must be like this venerable one. Why is it so? Is it because he practices the most excellent austerity that he does not accept clothes? Or would he accept them if they were offered?" Wanting to test him, they brought clothes from various places and offered them. Bāhiya thought, "If I had not come in this current state (i.e., if I had come well-dressed), these people would not have faith in me. I must do something to deceive these people and find a way to survive." Thinking thus, he pretended to be one of few desires and did not accept the clothes offered by the people. The people's faith increased exceedingly, and they performed great acts of honor and offerings. After Bāhiya had finished his meal, he went to a shrine located not far from the village. The people followed Bāhiya and cleared and cleaned the shrine for him. Then Bāhiya thought, "These people perform such acts of honor and offerings to me just because I wear moss.
400:
...performing such acts of honor and offerings. Thinking, "It would be appropriate for me to become like one who has the highest (ukkhaṭṭha) practice among these people," he searched for and took light wooden slats, sliced them thinly, strung them together with fiber, made a wooden garment, wore it, and lived by that livelihood. (From this time on, his name became Bāhiya Dārucīriya — Bāhiya who wears wooden clothing).

## The Great Brahmā Coming to Give a Warning

Subsequently, among the seven monks who had climbed the mountain peak together to practice the Dhamma when the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa was declining, the second elder reached the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahmā realm. Immediately after being born in the Suddhāvāsa realm, that Brahmā looked at the Brahma-bliss he had attained and reflected on where he had come from. After seeing the place where the seven monk friends had climbed the mountain peak to cultivate the Dhamma, he continued to reflect on the destination and rebirth of his remaining six monk friends. He clearly saw that one had attained Parinibbāna and the other five were reborn in the celestial realms of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and he used to reflect on those five friends constantly.

At this time, thinking, "Where are my friends now?" he reflected and saw Bāhiya Dārucīriya living by a livelihood of making wonders and relying on the seaport of Suppāraka. He thought, "This foolish man is surely ruined! Because he was one of extremely high (ukkhaṭṭha) practice while cultivating the Dhamma during the era of the Buddha Kassapa..."
401:
Even though he did not consume the food brought by the Arahant, now, for the sake of his livelihood, he is wandering about deceiving the world by claiming to be an Arahant when he is not. He does not yet know that the Buddha has appeared in the world. I shall go right now; after going, I shall cause my friend to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and inform him that the Buddha has appeared in the world.” Having reflected thus, at that very moment, he descended from the Brahma realm and appeared clearly before Bāhiya Dārucīriya at the port of Suppāraka during the night, with a radiant aura.

Bāhiya Dārucīriya, seeing the light at his place, went outside and stood there. Looking at the Great Brahma and raising his hands in prayer, he asked, “Who are you, venerable sirs?” Then the Great Brahma said, “I am your old friend. When the dispensation of the Kassapa Buddha was declining, I climbed the mountain peak with you to practice the Dhamma. By practicing, I reached the fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmiphala) and was reborn in the Brahma realm. Among the seven of us, the eldest Thera reached the fruit of Arahatship and attained Parinibbāna. You five were reborn in the celestial realms of the sense sphere. I have come to admonish you because I see you making a living here by performing wonders.” Having explained the cause and effect, he said:

“O Bāhiya, (1) you are not an Arahant whose taints are exhausted, (2) nor are you one who has reached the Path of Arahatship, (3) [let alone reaching that state],
402:
you do not yet possess even an atom’s worth of the right practice to reach the Path and Fruit of Arahatship.”

Thus he spoke plainly. After that, the Great Brahma informed Bāhiya Dārucīriya that the Buddha had appeared in the world and was currently residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. He urged Bāhiya Dārucīriya, saying, “Go to the presence of the Buddha,” and then returned to the Brahma realm.

## Bāhiya Dārucīriya Becoming an Arahant

When Bāhiya Dārucīriya heard the words of the Great Brahma, he was greatly moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Thinking, “I shall seek the true path to Nibbāna,” he traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty (120) yojanas in a single night and arrived at Sāvatthī. It was morning when Bāhiya Dārucīriya reached Sāvatthī.

The Buddha, knowing that Bāhiya Dārucīriya was coming to him, reflected and knew: “Bāhiya’s spiritual faculties (indriya), such as faith, have not yet reached maturity; they will reach maturity in a short while.” Waiting for the time when Bāhiya’s faculties would mature, the Buddha, surrounded by a large company of monks, entered Sāvatthī for alms at that moment.
403:
After the Buddha had gone for alms, Bāhiya entered the Jetavana Monastery and saw many monks walking back and forth on the ambulatory in the open air to dispel physical heaviness after finishing their morning meal. He asked, “Venerable sirs, where is the Buddha residing now?” The monks replied, “The Buddha has just entered Sāvatthī for alms.” They then asked, “Where have you come from?” When Bāhiya replied, “I have come from the port of Suppāraka,” the monks said to him patiently, “You have come from a long distance. Sit down for a while, wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest for a bit. You will see the Buddha when he returns from the alms round.”

Then Bāhiya said, “Venerable sirs, I do not know the danger to my life. I have traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night without stopping or sitting for long anywhere. I will rest only after seeing the Buddha.” Having spoken thus, he entered Sāvatthī in haste and came face to face with the Buddha, who was beautiful with incomparable Buddha-glory. When Bāhiya saw the Buddha walking along the road, he thought, “I have seen the Buddha after a very long time.” His body was suffused with the five kinds of rapture (pīti), and due to the force of rapture, his eyes were wide and unblinking. Bowing his body from where he saw him, he entered into the radiance of the Buddha’s body and went near the Buddha.
404:
Approaching the Buddha, he prostrated with the fivefold touching and, massaging and kissing the Buddha’s feet, he made this request:

“Exalted One, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma. May the Well-Spoken One teach me the Dhamma. Such Dhamma taught by the Buddha will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time.”

Then the Buddha said to Bāhiya Dārucīriya:

“Dear Bāhiya, it is not yet the time to teach the Dhamma. We have entered the city for alms.”

(In this matter, one might ask: Is there still a time when the Buddha should not practice for the benefit of the world of beings? The answer is: Here, 'time' refers to the maturity of the one to be tamed (veneyya). At that time, it was very difficult to know whether Bāhiya’s spiritual faculties (indriya), such as faith, were mature or not. (In fact, at that time, Bāhiya’s faculties were not yet mature. If the Buddha had answered, 'It is not yet time to teach because your faculties are not mature,' Bāhiya would not have understood.) Therefore, the Buddha did not mention that reason (the immaturity of Bāhiya’s faculties) but instead pointed to his own alms round in the city, which Bāhiya could understand, as the reason for not teaching the Dhamma. (The point is): Although it is said that the Buddha teaches the Dhamma to serve the interests of those to be tamed, he teaches only after knowing the maturity of the faculties of the person to be tamed, like a true knower of the right time (kālaññū).
405:
He does not teach the Dhamma when the faculties of the person to be tamed are not yet mature. At that time, Bāhiya’s faculties were not yet mature. (Therefore, even if he taught the Dhamma at that time when the faculties were not mature, Bāhiya would not have attained the Path and Fruit.) If he had said, “Bāhiya, because your faculties such as faith are not yet mature, it is not yet the proper time to teach you,” Bāhiya, being a person from outside the Dispensation, would not have understood. Therefore, it should be specially noted that the Buddha mentioned only the “entering the city for alms,” which Bāhiya could understand, as the reason.)

When the Buddha spoke thus, Bāhiya Dārucīriya requested for the second time:

“Exalted One, it is indeed difficult to know for certain whether there will be danger to the life of the Blessed One, or whether there will be danger to my own life. Therefore, Exalted One, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma. May the Well-Spoken One teach me the Dhamma. Such Dhamma taught by the Buddha will be for my benefit and happiness for a long time.”

At that time too, the Buddha spoke in the same manner as before: “Dear Bāhiya, it is not yet the time to teach the Dhamma. We have entered the city for alms.” (It should be specially noted that he spoke this refusal because the faculties were not yet mature.)
406:
(In this matter: Bāhiya Dārucīriya, being one in his final birth (pacchimabhavika), made this request focusing on the danger to life because he was urged by his own cause (for Arahatship), his past merit. Indeed, for those in their final birth, it is impossible to die without reaching the Fruit of Arahatship.

One might ask: “Why did the Buddha refuse twice even though he wished to teach Bāhiya?” The answer is: At that time, the thought occurred to the Buddha, “From the moment he saw me, this Bāhiya’s entire body has been suffused and covered with joy (pīti). The force of rapture is still too strong. Even if he hears the Dhamma, he will not yet be able to penetrate the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. It is better to wait until equanimity (majjhattūpekkhā) arises. Furthermore, because he traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in haste (overnight), Bāhiya’s body is still greatly exhausted. It is better to wait until that exhaustion subsides.” Therefore, he refused twice. This is the answer.)

Bāhiya Dārucīriya requested the Buddha for the third time in the same way as the second time. When he requested for the third time, the Buddha saw that in Bāhiya’s body:
(1) Equanimity (majjhattūpekkhā) had arisen,
(2) The exhaustion from the journey had subsided,
(3) Bāhiya’s faculties such as faith had matured,
407:
(4) The danger to Bāhiya’s life was drawing near—
Knowing this, the Buddha reflected, “Now it is the time to teach Bāhiya,” and he taught this brief Dhamma discourse as follows:

“(1) Dear Bāhiya, if that is so, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen, let there be just the seen (of various forms); in the heard, let there be just the heard (of various sounds); in the sensed (smells, tastes, touches), let there be just the sensed; in the cognized (mental objects), let there be just the cognized.’ Thus, dear Bāhiya, you should train yourself.

(2) Dear Bāhiya, when (or because) you can strive and practice so that in the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized objects, there is just the seen, just the heard, just the sensed, and just the cognized; then, dear Bāhiya, you will not be one who is lustful, hateful, or deluded (i.e., one who is associated with greed, hatred, and delusion) in relation to those seen, heard, sensed, and cognized objects.

(3) Dear Bāhiya, when (or because) you are not one who is associated with—not lustful, not hateful—in relation to those seen, heard, sensed, and cognized objects,”
408:
If you are indeed one who is not deluded, dear Bāhiya, then at that time (or for that reason), you will not be one who is dependent on what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized through craving, conceit, or views (meaning: one who does not cling to these four objects as 'mine' through craving, as 'I' through conceit, or as 'my soul' through views).

(4) Dear Bāhiya, when you are indeed one who is not dependent on what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized through craving, conceit, or views, then, dear Bāhiya, at that time (precisely because you are not dependent through craving, conceit, or views), you will not be in this present life, which is the human realm (manussagati); nor will you be in the life beyond, which consists of the remaining four destinations (the realms of devas, hell, animals, and hungry ghosts); leaving aside these two—this present life of the human realm and the life beyond of the other four destinations—there is no other destination to go to. This very absence of the recurrence of new mind and matter in this present life and the life beyond is the end of the suffering of defilements and the suffering of the round of rebirths."

Thus, the Buddha preached, concluding with the attainment of Parinibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).

(In this context: Bāhiya-Dārucīriya was a person of quick understanding (saṅkhittaruci), one who delights in concise teachings. Therefore,
409:
when the Blessed One preached the meditation on the six sense objects to Bāhiya-Dārucīriya, He did not preach them in six groups. Instead, He grouped the objects of smell, taste, and touch under the single term 'muta' (the sensed), and preached them in four categories: diṭṭha (the seen), suta (the heard), muta (the sensed), and viññāta (the cognized).

(1) Among the four sections of the Dhamma teaching mentioned above, the first section states: "In the group of conditioned phenomena consisting of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, you must practice so that there is only the seen in the seen, only the heard in the heard, only the sensed in the sensed, and only the cognized in the cognized." This means: when eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) arises seeing a form, when ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) arises hearing a sound, when nose-consciousness (ghānaviññāṇa) arises smelling an odor, when tongue-consciousness (jivhāviññāṇa) arises tasting a flavor, when body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa) arises feeling a touch, or when the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) arises knowing various mental and physical phenomena—at the moments these consciousnesses arise, there should be only the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, with no trace of lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), or delusion (moha). (If possible, the reader is encouraged to contemplate the process of the five-door and mind-door cognitive series).

(Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—these five types of consciousness are called the fivefold consciousness or pañcaviññāṇa). Just as during the moments of the fivefold consciousness and the mind-door adverting consciousness in the cognitive series, there is only the nature of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or knowing without any lust, hatred, or delusion, so too, when the impulsion (javana) series follows—which occurs with force and fully experiences the taste of the object—
410:
at the time that impulsion arises, you must strive and practice so that lust, hatred, and delusion are entirely absent (meaning: so that impulsions of greed, hatred, or delusion do not occur). This is the intended meaning of the Buddha's teaching.

Furthermore, the Blessed One's intention in teaching "You must practice so that impulsions of greed, hatred, and delusion do not occur regarding the four groups of seen, heard, sensed, and cognized objects" is this: "Dear Bāhiya, if you wrongly perceive those four groups of conditioned phenomena as permanent, pleasant, beautiful, or substantial, then impulsions of greed, hatred, and delusion can occur. Only if you perceive them as impermanent, suffering, not beautiful, and non-substantial will impulsions of great wholesome insight (vipassanā mahākusala javana) occur instead of greed, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, you must practice to arouse only the impulsions of great wholesome insight that correctly perceive the four groups of conditioned phenomena as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta), rather than wrongly perceiving them as permanent (nicca), pleasant (sukha), beautiful (subha), or self (atta)."

Therefore, it should be understood that by this first section of the teaching, the Buddha pointed out the contemplation of the four groups of conditioned phenomena as anicca, dukkha, asubha, and anatta, thereby concisely teaching the lower six purifications (visuddhi) and the ten insight knowledges.

(2) In the second section of the teaching, the intended meaning is: "Dear Bāhiya, if you successfully practice the ten insight knowledges regarding the four groups of conditioned phenomena—the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—you will reach the Path Knowledge (maggañāṇa). You will then have eradicated greed, hatred, and delusion through the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna), and you will truly not be one who lusts, hates, or is deluded." Thus, it should be understood that this second section refers to the four Paths.
411:
(3) For the Noble Ones, when they reach the Noble Fruition, there is absolutely no attachment of craving, conceit, or views as 'I', 'mine', or 'my soul' regarding the four groups of conditioned phenomena. Thus, it should be understood that the third section of the teaching refers to the Noble Fruition (ariyaphala).

(4) By this fourth section of the teaching, it should be understood that for an Arahant, after the decease-consciousness of Parinibbāna, there is the cessation where no new mind and matter arise in this present life (the human realm) or in the life beyond (called huraṃ), which refers to the remaining four destinations. (This very cessation is called Parinibbāna without clinging or anupādā-parinibbāna).

While listening to the Buddha's teaching, Bāhiya-Dārucīriya purified the four types of virtue and, relying on the mental concentration he attained, practiced insight meditation right there in that single sitting. Because he was a person of quick realization (khippābhiñña), he exhausted the four taints (āsava) at that very moment and attained the Fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). He thus became an Arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges.

After Bāhiya-Dārucīriya reached the Fruition of Arahantship and mastered the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa), prompted by the Dhamma, he requested the Blessed One to ordain him as a monk. The Blessed One asked, "Are your bowl and robes complete?" When Bāhiya replied, "They are not yet complete, Bhante," the Buddha said, "If so, seek a bowl and robes first," and continued His alms round into the city of Sāvatthī.

(During the time of Kassapa Buddha, while practicing the Dhamma as a monk for twenty thousand years, Bāhiya had thought,
412:
"If a monk receives the four requisites himself, he should use them himself by practicing generosity as appropriate." He did not, however, offer or support any other fellow monk with a bowl or robes. Therefore, in Bāhiya's continuity of existence, there was no supportive merit (upanissaya) sufficient for the Buddha to call him with the "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, Monk) ordination. Thus, the Blessed One did not use the "Ehi Bhikkhu" formula. Some teachers, however, say: "In a Buddha-empty world-cycle, Bāhiya was a thief. While carrying a bow and quiver and committing robbery in the forest, he encountered a Paccekabuddha. Out of greed for the bowl and robes, he shot and killed that Noble Paccekabuddha with an arrow and stole the bowl and robes. Therefore, even if the Blessed One were to call him 'Ehi Bhikkhu', the miraculous bowl and robes would not have appeared for him. Knowing this, the Blessed One did not call him 'Ehi Bhikkhu'." (From Udāna Commentary, page 85). The unwholesome kamma mentioned by these teachers correlates very well with the fact that Bāhiya had to wear a bark-cloth instead of good cotton robes.)

## Bāhiya's Death by a Cow's Goring

After parting from the Blessed One, Bāhiya wandered within the city of Sāvatthī seeking a bowl and robes. While he was thus wandering, a cow with a young calf ran after him and gored him, causing his death.

(In the past, four sons of a wealthy man took a prostitute to a park and enjoyed themselves all day. At sunset, one of the wealthy sons suggested to the other three friends, "Friends, this prostitute has a thousand pieces of silver, much gold, and
413:
valuable ornaments with her. There is no one else in this park, and it is now night. Come, let us kill this prostitute and take all her wealth." All four friends agreed and attempted to kill her. While they were punching, kicking, and beating her to death, the prostitute thought, "These men are shameless and heartless. After enjoying themselves with me according to their lust, they are killing me, an innocent person, purely out of greed for wealth. Let them kill me this once (while I am weak), but may I become a female ogre (yakkhinī) and be able to kill these four men many times over!" With this prayer, she died.

Among those four men, one became the noble son Pukkusāti. One became (the present) Bāhiya-Dārucīriya. Another became Tambadāṭhika the executioner, and the other became Suppabuddha the leper. In this way, the prostitute, having become a cow (or a yakkhinī in the form of a cow), had killed these four men in many hundreds of existences. All four of them, due to the consequences of that unwholesome kamma, met their death prematurely in their respective lives. Thus, it should be noted that Bāhiya's sudden death occurred because of the aforementioned unwholesome kamma. From Udāna Commentary, page 262.)
414:
After the Buddha had gone for alms in Sāvatthī and finished his meal, he departed from the city accompanied by a group of monks. Seeing the physical remains (utujarūpa) of Bāhiya lying on a rubbish heap, he addressed the monks: "Monks, go and stand at a house door, obtain a small couch, carry this physical body of Bāhiya out of the city, cremate it, and build a stupa for his relics." The monks did exactly as the Buddha had instructed.

After completing this task, the monks returned to the monastery, approached the Buddha, and reported what they had done. They then asked: "Venerable Sir, what is the destination (gati) of Bāhiya? What is his future state in the next life? (Alternatively) Venerable Sir, what was Bāhiya's status—was he an Ariya (Noble One) or a Puthujjana (worldling)? What is his future state—is it rebirth in the cycle of Saṃsāra, or is it the cessation of existence?"

Then the Buddha addressed the monks: "Monks, Bāhiya was wise. He practiced the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. He did not trouble me because of the Dhamma. Monks, Bāhiya has attained Parinibbāna and reached the end of the cycle of rebirth."

(Note: By ordering the construction of a stupa for the relics of Venerable Bāhiya-Dārucīriya, the fact of his Parinibbāna was already clear in meaning. However, the monks who did not realize or understand this asked the question for clarity. Alternatively, it should be noted that they asked to make the matter especially well-known.)
415:
## Preaching the Dhammapada Verse

When the Buddha declared that Venerable Bāhiya-Dārucīriya had attained Parinibbāna, the monks asked: "Venerable Sir, you have said that Bāhiya-Dārucīriya reached the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). When did Bāhiya-Dārucīriya reach the Fruit of Arahatship?" The Buddha replied: "He reached the Fruit of Arahatship immediately after hearing my Dhamma."

The monks then asked the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, when did you preach the Dhamma to Bāhiya-Dārucīriya?" The Buddha replied: "Today, while I was walking for alms, I stood on the road and preached the Dhamma to him." The monks then remarked: "Venerable Sir, the Dhamma you preached while standing on the road was very brief. How could Bāhiya-Dārucīriya attain the extraordinary Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala) with such a small amount of Dhamma?"

Then the Buddha addressed the monks: "Monks, why do you speak of my Dhamma in terms of 'little' or 'much'? Even if there are thousands of verses, if they are not connected with benefit, they are not worthy of praise and are not noble. If a word is connected with benefit, even a single verse is worthy of praise and is truly noble." Having said this, he preached the following verse from the Dhammapada:
416:
Sahassamapi ce gāthā, anatthapadasañhitā.
Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammati.

Bhikkhave = O monks, my dear sons. Sahassamapi ce gāthā = Even if there are a thousand verses. Anatthapadasañhitā = If they are connected with useless words such as descriptions of clouds or mountains. Na seyyo = They are in no way worthy of praise and are not noble. Yaṃ = That single verse, such as "Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ" (Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless). Sutvā = When heard with the ear of faith. Upasammati = All the heat of defilements is completely extinguished. Taṃ ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ = That single excellent verse of Dhamma that causes the cessation of defilements. Seyyo = Is especially worthy of praise and is truly noble.

At the end of this Dhamma teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and so forth.

## (C) Praising with the Etadagga Title

At another time, while the Buddha was seated in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, he praised the late Arahant Bāhiya-Dārucīriya:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ yadidaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo = Monks, among my disciple monks who possess quick intuition (khippābhiññā) in attaining the Path and Fruit, Bāhiya who wore the bark-cloth is the foremost and the most excellent."
417:
Thus, the Buddha placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) as the one who is most excellent in "Khippābhiñña = attaining the knowledge of the Path and Fruit quickly."

This is the story of Venerable Bāhiya-Dārucīriya Thera.

## (28) The Story of Venerable Kumārakassapa Thera

## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Elder was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Like other future Elders, while listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, he saw Padumuttara Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who preach eloquent Dhamma. He performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that same rank (ṭhānantara). The Buddha, seeing that the young man's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy as in previous cases.

## Practicing Dhamma on a Mountain Top

That young man performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. When the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining, as mentioned in the story of Venerable Dabba Thera (see page 378 of the story of Venerable Dabba), he climbed a mountain top with fellow monks to practice the Dhamma. Because he possessed pure and perfect virtue, he was reborn in the deva realm at the end of his life.
418:
## (B) Ordination in the Final Life

That young deva did not fall into the lower realms for an entire incalculable aeon (buddhantara), enjoying the bliss of humans and devas. During the time when our Buddha appeared, he was conceived in the womb of a merchant's daughter in the city of Rājagaha. This merchant's daughter had asked her parents for permission to ordain as a nun even before she was married, but she did not receive it. When she reached maturity, she had to go to the house of a husband and became pregnant.

Without knowing she was pregnant, the young woman pleaded with her husband until he consented, and she ordained as a nun under the bhikkhunīs who were followers of Devadatta. When the signs of her pregnancy became apparent, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta. Devadatta said, "She is no longer a nun," and expelled her from his group.

The young nun sought refuge with the bhikkhunīs who were disciples of the Buddha. Those bhikkhunīs reported the matter to the Buddha, who then assigned Venerable Upāli Thera the responsibility of deciding the case.

Venerable Upāli Thera summoned the noblewomen of Sāvatthī along with the great lay-supporter Visākhā. He entrusted the noblewomen with the task of investigating whether the pregnancy had occurred while she was a layperson or after she became a bhikkhunī. Upon investigation, it was clearly proven that the pregnancy occurred while she was a layperson. Based on the evidence, it was stated: "The child was conceived while she was still a layperson."
419:
Therefore, he decisively ruled, "The status of this young nun as a renunciant is blameless." The Buddha praised Venerable Upāli Thera, saying "Sādhu" (Well done), for resolving the legal case so well.

When the time came, the young nun gave birth to a son who looked like a golden statue. King Pasenadi of Kosala took the child to the palace and raised him in comfort, just like a prince. The boy was named "Kassapa." Later (when the boy Kassapa was about seven years old), the King had him beautifully adorned and brought him to the Buddha to be ordained as a novice.

(The detailed account of this story should be noted from the Nigrodhamiga Jātaka in the Ekaka Nipāta of the 550 Jātaka stories.)

## Being Named Kumārakassapa

Because he was ordained as a novice at a very young age, the Buddha would say, "Call Kassapa here," or "Give this fruit or this food to Kassapa." When the monks asked, "To which Kassapa should we give it, Venerable Sir?", the Buddha replied, "Give it to Kumāra-Kassapa." Because he was addressed and named in this way, even when he grew older, he was still called "Venerable Kumārakassapa."

(Alternatively) In the Pali language, a prince is called "Kumāra." Since this Elder was also a prince raised by King Kosala, he was recognized as "Kumāra + Kassapa = Prince + Kassapa."
420:
## The Origin of the Vammika Sutta Teaching

From the time he became a novice, Venerable Kumārakassapa practiced Vipassanā meditation. He also studied the Piṭaka, the words of the Buddha. Thus, he exerted effort in both study (pariyatti) and practice (paṭipatti). One day, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, Venerable Kumārakassapa was staying in the Andhavana forest near the Jetavana Monastery, diligently practicing the Dhamma of a monk.

At that time, a Mahābrahmā, who had previously climbed the mountain top to practice Dhamma with him during the end of Kassapa Buddha's dispensation and had attained the stage of Anāgāmī (Non-returner) to be reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm, looked back and saw Venerable Kumārakassapa. He thought, "Oh, my friend is struggling with his Vipassanā work. I shall go and provide him with the essence of Vipassanā methods and create a skillful means for him to reach the Path and Fruit."

While still in the Brahma realm, he prepared fifteen questions. At midnight, he appeared clearly with a radiant light at the place where Venerable Kumārakassapa was staying in the Andhavana forest.

Seeing the radiance, the Elder asked, "Who is it that has appeared here?" The Brahmā replied, "I am the Brahmā who, in the past (during the time of Kassapa Buddha), practiced the Dhamma together with you, attained the stage of Anāgāmī, and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm." Venerable Kumārakassapa Thera then asked directly, "For what purpose have you come now?" Then, the Brahmā, in order to clearly reveal the reason for his visit—

The wise disciple took the weapon and dug repeatedly, and seeing 14-a piece of meat, he said: "Venerable sir, it is a piece of meat." The teacher brahmin said: "Wise disciple, throw away the piece of meat; take the sword and dig repeatedly." The wise disciple took the sword and dug repeatedly, and seeing 15-a cobra (nāga), he said: "Venerable sir, it is a cobra." The teacher brahmin said: "Let the cobra remain; do not disturb the cobra; pay homage to the cobra." Monk, you should approach the Blessed One and ask him about these matters; remember the meaning as the Blessed One explains it to you. Monk, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.'
423: 423 Having said this, the Great Brahmā vanished right there. Then, when the night had passed, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and reported in full the conversation he had with the Great Brahmā the previous night, and then asked: "1. Venerable Sir, what is the anthill? 2. What is fuming by night? 3. What is blazing by day? 4. Who is the teacher brahmin? 5. Who is the wise disciple? 6. What is the sword? 7. What is digging repeatedly? 8. What is the door-bolt? 9. What is the swelling frog? 10. What is the fork in the road? 11. What is the strainer? 12. What is the tortoise? 13. What is the cleaver and the chopping block? 14. What is the piece of meat? 15. What is the cobra?" Thus he asked these fifteen questions. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa:
424: 424 "1. Monk, 'anthill' is a name for this body. 2. Monk, what one thinks and ponders at night about the work to be done during the day—this is 'fuming by night.' 3. Monk, what one performs by way of body, speech, and mind during the day according to what was thought and pondered at night—this is 'blazing by day.' 4. Monk, 'teacher brahmin' is a name for the Tathāgata. 5. Monk, 'wise disciple' is a name for a monk who is a trainee (sekha) still practicing the three trainings. 6. Monk, 'sword' is a name for mundane and supramundane wisdom. 7. Monk, 'digging repeatedly' is a name for the exertion of energy (viriya). 8. Monk, 'door-bolt' is a name for ignorance (avijjā-moha). 'Throw away the door-bolt' means abandon ignorance. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 9. Monk, 'swelling frog' (uddhumāyika) is a name for intense anger (kodha). 'Throw away the swelling frog' means
425: 425 abandon intense anger. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 10. Monk, 'fork in the road' is a name for doubt (vicikicchā). 'Throw away the fork in the road' means abandon doubt. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 11. Monk, 'strainer' is a name for the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that obstruct and block the attainment of jhāna, path, and fruit: (1) sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), (2) ill will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa), (3) sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa), (4) restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa), (5) doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa). 'Throw away the strainer' means abandon the five hindrances that obstruct jhāna, path, and fruit. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 12. Monk, 'tortoise' is a name for the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), which are the objects of clinging: (1) the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha), which is subject to change and disturbance, (2) the aggregate of feeling (vedanakkhandha), which experiences,
426: 426 (3) the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), which marks and recognizes, (4) the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), which constructs, (5) the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), which cognizes—these are the five aggregates of clinging. 'Throw away the tortoise' means abandon the five aggregates of clinging. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 13. Monk, 'cleaver and chopping block' is a name for the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguna), which are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and captivating: forms cognizable by the eye... sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... touches cognizable by the body—these are the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Throw away the cleaver and chopping block' means abandon the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question. 14. Monk, 'piece of meat' is a name for delight and lust (nandī-rāga) and craving (taṇhā). 'Throw away the piece of meat' means abandon delight and lust. 'Wise disciple, take the sword of wisdom and dig repeatedly' means exert effort repeatedly—this is the meaning of this question.
427: 427 15. Monk, 'cobra' (nāga) is a name for a monk who is an Arahant. 'Let the cobra remain; do not disturb the cobra; pay homage to the cobra'—this is the meaning of this question." Thus the Buddha explained in detail. (Here, I shall explain the meaning briefly: 1. This body is called the anthill. 2. Planning and pondering at night is the fuming smoke. 3. Exerting effort in various tasks of body and speech by day is the blazing fire. 4. The Supreme Buddha is the teacher brahmin. 5. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is the wise disciple. 6. Insight and path-wisdom is the sharp sword. 7. Strenuous effort (viriya) is called digging. 8. Ignorance is the door-bolt that blocks the way. 9. Intense anger (kodha) is the swelling frog. 10. Doubt (vicikicchā) is the fork in the road. 11. The five hindrances are shown as the strainer. 12. The five aggregates of clinging are compared to the tortoise. 13. The five cords of sensual pleasure are the cleaver and chopping block. 14. Delight and lust (nandī-rāga) is the piece of meat; it must be abandoned. 15. The Arahant, free from taints, is compared to the cobra. These are the fifteen riddles.) This summary verse of the Vammika Sutta should be memorized if possible. Among these fifteen riddles:
428: 428 1. Just as a natural anthill emits various creatures like snakes, mongooses, mice, lizards, and termites, so too this body emits repulsive impurities such as eye-wax from the eyes and ear-wax from the ears; therefore, this body is called an 'anthill.' (There are three other reasons why the body is like an anthill; see Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 2, pp. 34-35.) 2. One must plan and consider various tasks at night for the work to be done during the day. This various planning at night is called 'fuming by night.' 3. When day comes, implementing and speaking about the tasks as planned at night through body and speech is called 'blazing by day.' 4, 5, 6, 7. The metaphors and their meanings are easy to understand. 8. Just as people's movement in and out of a city is cut off when the city gate is closed and the door-bolt is dropped, so too when the bolt of ignorance (avijjā-moha) falls upon the door of one's wisdom, the path of wisdom that leads to Nibbāna is completely cut off. Therefore, ignorance is called a 'door-bolt.' 9. The swelling frog (uddhumāyika) is not naturally large, being only about the size of a fingernail. it usually lives among old leaves, bushes, or vines. If touched by the tip of a stick, a vine, or a bit of dust, it becomes angry and gradually its body stretches and rounds out like an egg, growing to the size of a ripe wood-apple. With its four legs pointing to the sky, it loses its ability to move and is carried away to the land of enemies like crows. Similarly, the mental factor of anger (kodha) at its onset only slightly disturbs the mind; if suppressed at that moment with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), it is easily handled.
429:
it can be extinguished. If not suppressed at that moment, it grows and causes the face to contort and grimace. If not suppressed at that moment, it grows and causes the jaw to quiver in preparation for uttering harsh and abusive words. If not suppressed at that moment, it leads to the actual speaking of harsh and abusive words. If not suppressed at that moment, it causes one to look around in all directions to see if there is any help or threat for the other person. If not suppressed at that moment, it leads to the state of pulling and dragging to strike the other person. If not suppressed at that moment, it leads to the handling and grasping of stones, sticks, clubs, and swords with the hands. If not suppressed at that moment, it leads to the commission of a crime, such as striking with a stick or cutting with a sword. If suppressed at that moment, it is well; if not suppressed, it leads to the ultimate path of killing others or killing oneself.

In this metaphor, when the four legs of the *uddhumāyika* toad (a bloated toad) are pointing towards the sky, its movement is cut off. That toad, falling under the power of its enemies, becomes food for crows and other creatures. In the same way, a person who is overwhelmed and oppressed by anger (*kodha*) can no longer develop meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*). The movement of wisdom is cut off. Falling under the power of the enemy known as defilements (*kilesa*), they reach a state where they must bow down and endure whatever oppression Māra desires. Therefore, anger (*kodha*) is preached as the *uddhumāyika* toad.

10. A man carrying much gold and silver wealth, traveling through a rugged wilderness, reaches a fork in the road and thinks, "Should I go by this path, or should I go by that other path?" Being filled with doubt and unable to decide, he stands still in that very place. Then, bandits and villains arise, overwhelm, and oppress that man, leading him to ruin and destruction. In the same way, a monk who sits down taking up his primary meditation subject, when doubt (*vicikicchā*) arises regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and so on, can no longer develop his meditation. Right there at that fork of doubt,
430:
he stands contemplating. Then, all kinds of enemies such as the Māra of defilements (*kilesamāra*) cause that monk to reach ruin and destruction. Thus, because the mental state of doubt is like a fork in the road, the Blessed One has preached doubt (*vicikicchā*) as a fork in the road.

11. When laundrymen pour water into a filter called an ash-filter, whether it is one pot, two pots, ten pots, twenty pots, or a hundred pots, all that is poured flows out and drains away rapidly. Not even a handful of water remains. In the same way, in the mental continuum of a person filled with the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the water of merit (*kusala*) does not remain; it does not stay. Therefore, the five hindrances are preached as the laundryman's ash-filter.

12. Just as a tortoise has five limbs—four legs and a head—in the same way, if all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*) are grasped with wisdom, they are merely the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). Therefore, the five aggregates of clinging are preached as the tortoise.

13. In the world, meat is placed on a chopping block and minced with a cleaver. In the same way, these beings who seek and struggle through defilement-sensuality (*kilesa-kāma*) to obtain objective-sensuality (*vatthu-kāma*) are, in terms of reality, said to be placed upon the chopping block of objective-sensuality and minced with the cleaver of defilement-sensuality. Therefore, the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are objective-sensuality, are preached as the cleaver and the chopping block.

14. In the world, what is called a piece of meat is desired and craved by people such as kings, and by animals such as crows and birds. Because of the desire for this piece of meat, suffering increases stage by stage. Similarly, because these beings are intoxicated by ignorance (*avijjā*), they cannot realize that the craving of delight and lust (*nandī-rāga-taṇhā*) is the cause of suffering.
431:
They merely follow closely after that delight and lust (*nandī-rāga*), like following a piece of meat, and thereby increase the suffering of the round of rebirths (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*). Alternatively, just as a piece of meat sticks to wherever it is placed, so too these beings, being bound by the craving of delight and lust, cling to the phenomena of the round of rebirths. Even though they encounter misery and suffering, they do not become weary of it. Thus, because the craving of delight and lust is like a piece of meat, the Blessed One has preached the craving of delight and lust (*nandī-rāga-taṇhā*) as a piece of meat.

15. The reason why Arahants are called 'Nāga' is because (according to the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary 1, 157: *chandādīhi na gacchantīti nāgā*) they do not go to the wrong paths (*agati*) through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion; and because (*tena tena maggena pahīne kilese na āgacchantīti nāgā*) the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not return to them; and because (*nānappakārakaṃ āguṃ na karontīti nāgā*) they do not commit various kinds of evil. For these reasons, the noble Arahants are called 'Nāga'.

According to the commentary explaining the veneration of the *Khīṇāsava-Buddha-Nāga* (the Buddha-Nāga whose taints are exhausted) based on the phrase in the riddle, "*Namo karohi nāgassa* = Pay homage to the Nāga," one should pay homage in the following manner:

*Buddho bodhāya deseti, danto yo damathāya ca.*
*Samathāya santo dhammaṃ, tiṇṇova taraṇāya ca.*
*Nibbuto nibbānatthāya, taṃ lokasaraṇaṃ name.*

(The Buddha, the refuge of the world, who is the Buddha-Nāga, the incomparable supreme one; having personally realized the four noble truths, he teaches the Dhamma for the awakening of those who are ready to be liberated. Having personally become tamed in the six sense faculties, he teaches for the taming of those who are ready to be liberated. Having personally become)
432:
peaceful and free from the heat of defilements, he teaches for the peace of those who are ready to be liberated. Having personally crossed over the rough currents of the abyss of Saṃsāra and reached the other shore, he teaches so that those who are ready to be liberated may also cross over. Having personally attained the cessation of defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*) through four victories and become extinguished and free from all dangers, he teaches for the extinguishment of those who are ready to be liberated. For forty-five years, with compassion as his guide, he has preached the radiant wheel of Dhamma to devas and humans. To that Buddha-Nāga, the incomparable supreme one, the refuge of the three worlds, I pay homage and bow down with body, speech, and mind, humbling my pride and joining my palms in reverence.

## Ven. Kumāra Kassapa Becoming an Arahant
According to the commentary on the *Vammika Sutta* (*iti idaṃ suttaṃ therassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi*), this *Vammika Sutta* became the meditation subject for the Elder Kumāra Kassapa's Vipassanā practice. Thus, after the Elder Kumāra Kassapa learned and listened to this *Vammika Sutta* as answered and preached by the Blessed One, he went to the Andhavana forest, practiced Vipassanā meditation, and soon attained the fruit of Arahantship, becoming an Arahant.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
From the time the noble Elder Kumāra Kassapa became an Arahant, whenever he preached the Dhamma to the four assemblies—monks, nuns,
433:
laymen, and laywomen—he preached the Dhamma in a marvelous way, adorned with many illustrative metaphors.

Later, the Blessed One, referring to the *Pāyāsi Sutta* (the 10th sutta of the *Mahāvagga, Dīgha Nikāya*) which was preached by the Elder Kumāra Kassapa to King Pāyāsi, adorned with fifteen riddles, praised him saying:

"*Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cittakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ kumārakassapo* — Monks, among my disciple monks who are eloquent speakers (*cittakathika*), Kumāra Kassapa is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha appointed him to the position of *Etadagga*, the foremost in the category of "*cittakathika* = those who preach the Dhamma in a marvelous and eloquent way."

This is the account of the Elder Kumāra Kassapa.

**********

## (29) About the Elder Koṭṭhita
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
This future noble Elder was born into a wealthy family (*mahābhoga*) with abundant riches and possessions in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Dhamma of Buddha Padumuttara, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the position of *Etadagga* among those who had attained the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā-patta*).
434:
the foremost and most excellent. Seeing this, like the future elders of old, he performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position of *Etadagga* among those who have attained the analytical insights. The Blessed One also gave him the prophecy and then departed.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That future noble Elder Koṭṭhita performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the period when our Blessed One appeared, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī. His parents and relatives named him "Young Koṭṭhita." When Young Koṭṭhita reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas. One day, upon hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One, great faith arose in him, and he entered the monkhood in the Dispensation. From the time he became a monk, the Elder Koṭṭhita practiced Vipassanā meditation and attained the fruit of Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), thus becoming a *paṭisambhidā-patta* Arahant.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
After becoming an Arahant, the Elder was always proficient and skilled in the four analytical insights. Whenever he was asked a question, he usually asked questions related only to the analytical insights. Therefore, the Blessed One later, referring to the *Mahāvedalla Sutta* (found in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya*), [appointed] the Elder Koṭṭhita—
435:
“Monks, among my disciple monks who have attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), Mahākoṭṭhita is the foremost (etadagga).”

Having praised him thus, the Buddha placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) in the category of “those who have attained the four analytical insights.”

This is the account of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita.

**********
## (30) The Account of the Venerable Elder Ānanda
## (a) The Elder’s Aspiration in the Past

Counting back from this aeon (kappa), one hundred thousand aeons ago, the Buddha Padumuttara appeared in the world. The royal capital where the Buddha Padumuttara was born was the city of Haṃsāvatī. His father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā. His two chief disciples were the Elder Devala and the Elder Sujāta. His two chief female disciples were the Elder Nun Amitā and the Elder Nun Asamā. His personal attendant (upaṭṭhāka) was the Elder Sumana. At that time, the Buddha Padumuttara, while honouring his royal father, resided in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī as his resort village, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks.

During the time when the Buddha Padumuttara was still a layman, he had a younger half-brother named Prince Sumana (the future Elder Ānanda). King Ānanda had appointed his son, Prince Sumana, as the governor of a region located one hundred and twenty yojanas away from the royal city of Haṃsāvatī.
436:
The governor, Prince Sumana, would occasionally come to the royal city of Haṃsāvatī to pay respects to his royal father and his elder brother, the Buddha Padumuttara.

One day, the border regions (paccantarit) were in a state of ruin due to the uprising and disturbances caused by rebels and bandits. When Prince Sumana sent a messenger to inform his royal father of this matter, King Ānanda sent back a reply, saying, “Why have I placed you in that region? Was it not to suppress the danger of rebels?” Upon receiving his father’s reply, the governor, Prince Sumana, attacked and defeated the rebels and bandits, bringing peace to the country. He then sent a message to his father, saying, “Noble Father, the province (janapada) is now peaceful and prosperous.” The royal father was greatly pleased and issued a command, summoning him: “Let my son come to me quickly.”

The governor, Prince Sumana, had one thousand ministers. As the Prince was travelling to his father together with those ministers, he consulted with them along the way, saying, “If my royal father is so pleased that he grants me a boon, what boon should I take?” Then, some ministers advised the Prince in various ways, saying, “Please take elephants,” “Please take horses,” “Please take a province,” or “Please take the seven kinds of jewels.” However, other wise and far-sighted ministers said:
437:
“Prince, you are the son of the lord of the land. For you, worldly possessions such as gold and silver are not difficult to obtain; they are very easy to acquire. Even if you obtain them, you must eventually leave all those worldly treasures behind. One must go to the afterlife carrying only one’s meritorious deeds. Therefore, if the great King, your father, grants you a boon, please take only the boon of serving your elder brother, the Buddha Padumuttara, for the entire three months of the rainy season (vassa).”

Prince Sumana said, “You are indeed my good friends. I did not have such a thought, but you have made it occur to me. Very well, I shall follow your advice.” Upon arriving at the royal city, he paid respects to his royal father. The King embraced his son’s neck, kissed him on the head, and said, “Dear son, I grant you whatever boon you desire.” When he said this, the Prince replied, “Noble Great King, my father, I, your son, wish to serve my elder brother, the Buddha, with the four requisites for the entire three months of the rainy season, so that the life I have obtained in this present existence may not be barren. Royal Father, please grant me this boon of serving the Buddha for the three months of the rainy season.” The King replied, “Dear son, I cannot grant this boon. Choose and take some other boon.” Prince Sumana then said, “Royal Father, it is not the custom for kings who own the land to speak with two tongues.
438:
Please grant me, your son, that very boon I have requested. I do not desire any other boon.” He spoke thus with firm determination.

King Ānanda said, “Dear son, the will of the Buddhas is very difficult to know. If the Buddha does not wish to go to the place where you invite him, even if I, your father, grant the boon, how could it be possible?” He spoke these words to deflect the request. Prince Sumana replied, “Very well, Royal Father. I myself will approach my elder brother, the Buddha, and act so as to know the Buddha’s will.” Having said this, he went to the monastery where the Buddha was residing.

At that time, the Buddha had finished his meal and had entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī). Prince Sumana went to the monks who were assembled in the Dhamma Hall (dhamma-sālā). Then, the monks asked Prince Sumana, “Prince, why have you come?” The Prince replied, “I have come to see the Buddha. Venerable sirs, please show me the Buddha.” The monks then replied, “Prince, we ourselves do not get the opportunity to see the Buddha at every moment we desire.” The Prince asked again, “Venerable sirs, which venerable one gets the opportunity to see the Buddha at every moment he desires?” The monks replied, “Prince, the Elder named Sumana gets the opportunity to see the Buddha at every moment he desires.” The Prince then asked, “Venerable sirs, where is that Elder Sumana now?”
439:
Having asked for the Elder’s location, he went there, paid respects, and requested, “Venerable sir, I wish to see the Buddha. Please show me the Buddha.”

While Prince Sumana was watching, the Venerable Elder Sumana entered the water-kasiṇa absorption (āpo-kasiṇa-jhāna) and resolved, “Let the great earth become water.” He then dived into the ground that appeared as water and emerged clearly in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) where the Buddha was residing. Then, the Buddha asked the Elder Sumana, “Dear Sumana, why have you come?” The Elder replied, “Venerable Buddha, your younger brother, Prince Sumana, is here to pay respects to you.” The Buddha then said, “Dear monk, if that is so, prepare the seat.” Then, while Prince Sumana was still watching, the Venerable Elder Sumana took the Buddha’s seat, dived into the Fragrant Chamber, and appeared clearly outside the precinct, where he arranged the Buddha’s seat. Seeing these two wonders, Prince Sumana reflected, “This monk is indeed great in psychic power and status.”

The Buddha Padumuttara came out from the Fragrant Chamber and sat upon the prepared seat. Prince Sumana paid respects to the Buddha and spoke words of greeting. When the Buddha asked, “Prince, at what time did you arrive?” the Prince replied, “Venerable Buddha, I arrived while you were inside the Fragrant Chamber. The monks told me, ‘We do not get the opportunity to see the Buddha at every moment we desire,’
440:
and they sent me to the Venerable Elder Sumana. The Elder, with just a single word, showed me the Buddha; he acted so that I could have the opportunity to see you. Venerable Buddha, I think the Venerable Elder Sumana is one who is intimate with your Sāsana.”

The Buddha said, “Yes, it is so, Prince. This monk Sumana is indeed one who is intimate with my Sāsana.” When he said this, the Prince asked, “Venerable Buddha, by performing what kind of merit can one become intimate with the Sāsana of the Buddhas?” The Buddha replied, “Prince, by giving alms (dāna), by undertaking the precepts (sīla), and by practicing the Uposatha, one can become intimate with the Sāsana of the Buddhas.” Then, Prince Sumana (having found the right opportunity) requested, “Venerable Buddha, I wish to become one who is intimate with the Buddha’s Sāsana like the Venerable Elder Sumana. Please accept my alms-food tomorrow.” The Buddha accepted the Prince’s invitation by remaining silent. The Prince returned to his temporary palace, and after preparing great offerings throughout the night, he grandly gave what is called “temporary palace alms-food” for seven days.

On the seventh day, Prince Sumana paid respects to the Buddha and said, “Venerable Buddha, I have already obtained the boon from my royal father to serve you for the three months of the rainy season.
441:
Please accept and be pleased to reside in my monastery for the three months of the rainy season (vassa).” The Buddha considered, “Will there be benefit if I go to the place where this Prince invites me?” and seeing that there would be benefit, he said, “Prince, the Buddhas delight in secluded places.”

Prince Sumana said, “I understand, Blessed One. I understand, O Buddha of Good Speech. Venerable Buddha, I shall go ahead first and build a monastery. When the monastery is completed and I send an invitation, please come together with one hundred thousand monks.” Having obtained the Buddha’s consent (after the Buddha spoke words of agreement to come), he went to his royal father and said, “Royal Father, my elder brother, the Buddha, has given me his promise to come to the place where I invite him. Only when I send an invitation, please escort the Buddha to my residence.” Having given these instructions, he paid respectful homage to his father and departed from the royal city. Along the way, he had a monastery built at every yojana, and thus travelled the distance of one hundred and twenty (120) yojanas. Upon reaching his own fief city, while searching for a site to build the great monastery, he found the garden of a householder named Sobhaṇa.
442:
After purchasing the garden for one hundred thousand coins, he spent another hundred thousand on labor costs to have the great monastery constructed.

In that garden of the merchant Sobhaṇa, he had a Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber) built for the Buddha, and for the other monks, he had cells, caves, and pavilions constructed for their use during the night and day. After completing the surrounding walls and gateways, he sent a messenger to his father, the King, saying, "Your Majesty, all the necessary works on my part have been completed. Please escort my elder brother, the Buddha, to our region."

His father, King Ānanda, after offering alms-food to his son, the Padumuttara Buddha, and the one hundred thousand disciple monks, addressed Him: "Exalted Son, all the necessary works on the part of your younger brother, Prince Sumana, have been completed. He is waiting with great longing for Your arrival, Bhante." The Buddha, surrounded by one hundred thousand disciple monks, traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas without any hardship, resting and staying overnight comfortably in the monasteries that had been prepared at every yojana along the way.

Upon hearing that the Buddha was arriving, Prince Sumana went out for a distance of one yojana to welcome Him. After honoring Him with scents, flowers, and other offerings, he respectfully escorted the Buddha into the monastery compound.

"Satasahassena me kītaṃ, satasahassena māpitaṃ.
Sobhaṇaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ, paṭiggaṇha mahāmuni."
443:
"Mahāmuni = O Buddha, the Supreme Sage who is the head of all classes of sages, such as householder-sages and others. Me = I, your disciple known as Sumana. Sobhaṇaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ = This garden, established by the merchant Sobhaṇa and known by the name Sobhaṇa. Satasahassena = With one hundred thousand coins. Kītaṃ = Has been purchased at its valued price. Satasahassena = With one hundred thousand coins. Māpitaṃ = This great monastery has been created and constructed. Paṭiggaṇha = Please accept this out of compassion, Bhante."

With this verse, he addressed the Buddha and offered the monastery to Him.

After giving alms on the day of entering the Rains Retreat (Vassa), Prince Sumana called his wife, children, and ministers and said, "The Buddha has traveled from a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas to come to us. Buddhas truly value only the Dhamma; they do not value or look toward material requisites (āmisa). Therefore, throughout these three months of the Rains, I shall wear only two garments, observe the ten precepts, and reside right here in this monastery where the Buddha dwells. You all should continue to offer alms in this manner to the one hundred thousand Arahants, headed by the Buddha, throughout the three months of the Rains."

After giving these instructions, he observed the ten precepts, wore only two garments, and remained in the monastery.
444:
While residing in a place near the dwelling of Elder Sumana, the Buddha's attendant, Prince Sumana saw the Elder performing all the major and minor duties for the Buddha. He reflected, "This Elder is truly proficient in this position of Upaṭṭhāka (attendant). I should make an aspiration for this very position of the Elder." As the day of Pavāraṇā (the end of the Rains Retreat) approached, around the 8th day of the waxing moon of Thadingyut, he entered the city and gave great alms for seven days. On the seventh day, he placed sets of triple robes (ticīvara) at the feet of the one hundred thousand monks. Then, bowing respectfully to the Buddha, he made his aspiration: "Glorious Buddha, all the meritorious deeds I have performed, starting from the alms-food at the temporary pavilion in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī, were not done out of a desire for the bliss of Sakka, the King of Devas. Nor were they done out of a desire for the bliss of Māra or Brahmā. Indeed, they were performed only out of a desire for the position of an attendant (upaṭṭhāka) monk to a Buddha. Therefore, Bhante, in the future, may I become an attendant to a Buddha, just like the Venerable Elder Sumana."

Padumuttara Buddha, seeing that Prince Sumana's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, granted him the prophecy (byākata) and then departed. Upon hearing the Buddha's prophecy, Prince Sumana reflected, "Buddhas do not speak words that are double-edged; their words are certain and unchanging." From the second day after receiving the prophecy,
445:
he became one whose heart was filled with rapture, like one who would follow closely in the footsteps of the Inconceivable Supreme Lord of the Three Worlds, Gotama Buddha, carrying His bowl and robes.

## Meritorious Deeds in the Intermediate Period

Prince Sumana performed meritorious deeds of dāna for one hundred thousand years during the era of Padumuttara Buddha's Dispensation. After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. Later, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was a virtuous person who offered his own upper robe to be placed under the alms-bowl of a certain Elder who was on his alms-round.

After passing away from that life, he was again reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī in this human world. One day, while on the upper terrace of his palace, he saw eight Paccekabuddhas arriving through the air from Mount Gandhamādana. He invited them to the golden palace and offered alms-food. He then built eight hermitages for those eight Paccekabuddhas in his royal garden. Furthermore, he prepared eight large jeweled seats (in-pyin) for them to sit on when they came to the palace, and ruby bowl-stands for their alms-bowls.
