He served those eight Paccekabuddhas for ten thousand years. These are his prominent deeds; besides these, he performed many other meritorious acts during this period of one hundred thousand aeons.
446:
## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

While sowing the seeds of dāna for one hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. After passing away from that life, he became the son of Amitodana the Sakyan in the royal city of Kapilavatthu. He was named "Prince Ānanda" because his birth brought joy and delight to all his relatives. After the Buddha had renounced the world and attained Enlightenment, He returned to Kapilavatthu for the first time. When the Buddha departed from the city again, many Sakyan princes were ordained to become His followers. At that time, Prince Ānanda, along with Prince Bhaddiya and others, renounced the world and was ordained in the presence of the Buddha at the mango grove named Anupiya, near the town of Anupiya. (Refer back to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, page 145).

## Venerable Ānanda's Attainment of Stream-entry

Not long after his ordination, Venerable Ānanda heard a Dhamma discourse from Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). This can be known by referring to the Ānanda Sutta in the Theravagga (9), Khandhavagga Saṃyutta (Samyutta Nikāya), (Saṃ-Myan 2, page 81). The essence of that sutta is as follows:

While the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, one day Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks, "Friends..." and when the monks responded, "Friend," he spoke these words:
447:
"Friends, Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was of great help to us when we were junior monks. He instructed us with this teaching. His way of instruction was: 'Friend Ānanda, it is only by depending (on something) that the three types of papañca (proliferation) such as "I am" arise; they do not arise without depending. By depending on what do the three types of papañca such as "I am" arise, and by not depending do they not arise? By depending on form (rūpa), the three types of papañca such as "I am" arise; they do not arise without depending. By depending on feeling (vedanā)... perception (saññā)... mental formations (saṅkhāra)... consciousness (viññāṇa), the three types of papañca such as "I am" arise; they do not arise without depending.

Friend Ānanda, for example, suppose a young woman or man, fond of ornaments, were to look at the reflection of their own face in a clean, bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water. They would see it only by depending (on the mirror or water); they would not see it without depending. Friend Ānanda, in the same way, it is only by depending on form that the three types of papañca such as "I am" arise; they do not arise without depending. By depending on feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness, the three types of papañca such as "I am" arise; they do not arise without depending.

Friend Ānanda, what do you think about this—is form permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, friend. (The discourse continues according to the three rounds of the teaching as in the Anattalakkhana Sutta) ... He knows: there is no further task for this path.' Thus he instructed me."
448:
"Friends... the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is of great service to us who are junior monks. That Venerable admonishes us with this aforementioned advice. Because of hearing this Dhamma teaching from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, I have come to know the Four Noble Truths — I have become a Noble One who is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)."

This is the intended meaning. Based on this sutta, it should be understood that the Venerable Ānanda reached the fruit of Stream-entry through the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta's teaching on the simile of the mirror (ādāsa).

## Accepting the Position of Attendant (Upaṭṭhāka)

During the first twenty years of the Buddha's ministry, known as the Pathama-bodhi, there was no permanent attendant. Occasionally, the Venerable Nāgasamāla would carry the Buddha's bowl and robes and follow him. Occasionally, the Venerable Nāgita, occasionally the Venerable Upavāna, occasionally the Licchavī prince Sunakkhatta (as a monk), occasionally the Venerable Cunda (the younger brother of Venerable Sāriputta), occasionally the Venerable Sāgata, occasionally the Venerable Rādha, and occasionally the Venerable Meghiya would carry the Buddha's bowl and robes and follow him.

Among those elders, on one occasion, while the Buddha was traveling on a long journey together with the Venerable Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road. The Venerable Nāgasamāla stepped off the path and said, "Venerable Sir, I will go by this path." The Buddha said, "Come, dear monk, let us go by this path."
449:
When the Blessed One told him to go by another way, the Elder Nagasamāla said, "Well then, Blessed One, please take Your own bowl and robes; I shall go by this path," and speaking defiantly, he made as if to place the Buddha's bowl and robes on the ground. Then the Blessed One said, "Monk, bring them," and taking His own bowl and robes, He proceeded on His way. The Elder Nagasamāla also went by the other path he had mentioned, parting from the Blessed One. After going a short distance, robbers plundered the Elder's bowl and robes, and his head was broken from their beating. Thinking, "Now only the Buddha is my refuge; there is no other refuge," he came to the Blessed One, his whole body covered in blood. When the Blessed One asked, "Son, what is this? How did this happen?", the Elder reported the matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One consoled him, saying, "Son, do not be disheartened by many thoughts; it was for this very reason that I forbade you." (This was one such occasion).
Furthermore, on another occasion (when He spent His 13th vassa on Mount Cālika), the Elder Meghiya was the Buddha's temporary attendant. While walking along the bank of the river named Kimikālā after wandering for alms in Jantu village, he saw a mango grove and said, "Blessed One, please take Your bowl and robes..."
450:
...I shall practice the Dhamma of a recluse in that mango grove." Although the Blessed One forbade him three times, he did not listen and went to that mango grove. As soon as he sat on a stone slab, he was oppressed by the three types of unwholesome thoughts (akusala vitakka). He returned to the Blessed One and reported the matter. The Blessed One also consoled him, saying, "Son, it was because I foresaw this that I forbade you." (The detailed account of Elder Meghiya should be noted from page 193 of the fourth volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas below). (This was also another occasion).
Because of these reasons, later, while the Blessed One was seated on the Buddha-throne (dhammapallaṅka) prepared within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī in the Jetavana Monastery of the noble city of Sāvatthī, surrounded by the assembly of monks, He addressed the monks:
"Monks, I am now advanced in years (at that time, the Buddha's age was over fifty-five). Some monks, even when I say, 'Let us go by this path,' leave Me and go by another path (referring to Elder Meghiya). Some monks go so far as to almost place My bowl and robes on the ground (referring to Elder Nagasamāla). You should consider a monk who will serve Me as a permanent attendant."
451:
When they heard these words, a great sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose within the monks.
Then the Elder Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and pleaded, "Blessed One, I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for an asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons, aspiring only for You. Is it not fitting that a person of great wisdom like myself should be the attendant (upaṭṭhāka) for the Buddhas? Please let me serve the Buddhas." The Blessed One praised him but declined his request, saying, "It is not suitable, son Sāriputta. Indeed, the place where you reside is never void of the Dhamma. Truly, your instruction and advice are equal to the instruction and advice of the Buddhas. Therefore, there is no need for you to serve Me." In this manner, starting from the Elder Mahā-Moggallāna, the eighty Great Disciples rose one by one and pleaded with the Blessed One for the opportunity to serve Him. The Blessed One declined all of those Great Disciples.
## The Elder Ānanda Receiving the Eight Boons
The Venerable Elder Ānanda, however, sat in silence without asking for the opportunity to serve. Then the monks urged the Elder, "Friend Ānanda, the Saṅgha is currently requesting the position of attendant (upaṭṭhāka)..."
452:
...you should also request that position of attendant." The Venerable Elder Ānanda replied, "Friends, what kind of position is it that must be obtained by asking? Does the Blessed One not see me? He certainly does. If the Blessed One desires, He will say, 'Let Ānanda serve Me.'"
Then the Blessed One said to the monks, "Monks, Ānanda is not one who will serve Me only when urged by others. He will serve Me of his own accord, knowing [my needs]." Then the monks urged him again, "Friend Ānanda, arise! Friend Ānanda, arise! Request the boon to serve the Blessed One." Only then did the Elder Ānanda rise from his seat and request the eight boons, consisting of four refusals and four acceptances.
The four refusals were: "Blessed One, if the Lord does not give me the fine robes He receives (1); if He does not give me the fine alms-food He receives (2); if He does not allow me to stay in the same Gandhakuṭī with the Lord (3); if He does not take me along when invited by lay devotees (4)—if the Lord grants these four boons I request, I shall serve the Lord, Bhante."
453:
The Blessed One asked, "Son Ānanda, what fault do you see in these four matters you have requested?" Ānanda replied, "Blessed One, if I were to receive these four things, people would say, 'Elder Ānanda enjoys the fine alms-food received by the Buddha (1); he wears the fine robes (2); he stays in the same Gandhakuṭī with the Buddha (3); and he accompanies the Buddha to invitations (4). He serves the Buddha because he receives these four great gains. What burden could there be for Elder Ānanda who serves while receiving such great gains?' Critics would clearly emerge. I see this fault, Bhante," he said, requesting the four boons of refusal.
The four acceptances were: "Blessed One, if the Lord will go to the place of invitation to which I have invited Him (1); if I shall have the opportunity to let the people who come from other countries and regions to see the Buddha do so at the very moment they arrive (2); if I shall have the opportunity to approach and question the Lord at the very moment doubt concerning the Dhamma arises within me (3); and furthermore, if the Blessed One will compassionately preach to me..."
454:
...the Dhamma He has preached in my absence when He returns (4)—if the Lord grants these four boons I request, I shall serve the Lord, Bhante."
The Blessed One asked, "Son Ānanda, what benefit do you see in these four matters you have requested?" Ānanda replied, "Blessed One, in this Dispensation of eight wonders, when sons of good family with great faith do not get the chance to invite the Buddha themselves, they will say to me, 'Venerable Ānanda, please accept alms at our house tomorrow together with the Blessed One.' If the Blessed One does not go to the place thus invited (1); if I do not get the opportunity to let the people who come from other countries and regions to see the Buddha do so at the very moment they desire (2); if I do not get the opportunity to approach and question the Lord at the very moment doubt arises (3); then critics will clearly emerge, saying, 'Why is Elder Ānanda serving the Buddha? The Buddha does not even show him this much favor.' Therefore, I desire the first three boons to prevent such criticisms from arising. Furthermore, in the Lord's absence, people will ask me, 'Friend Ānanda, where did the Blessed One preach this verse, this sutta, or this Jātaka?' If I..."
455:
...cannot answer that question fully, critics will clearly emerge, saying, 'Friend, you do not even know this much. Why have you been following and serving the Buddha for so long like a shadow?' Therefore, I desire that the Lord repeat the Dhamma preached in my absence (the 4th boon). If the four boons I request are granted, the aforementioned criticisms and blame will not arise at all. I see this benefit in these four matters, Bhante." he said, requesting the four boons of acceptance. The Blessed One then granted these eight boons—the four refusals and the four acceptances—requested by the Venerable Elder Ānanda.
## Serving the Buddha Unrivalled
Thus, the Venerable Elder Ānanda took these eight boons—the four refusals and the four acceptances—and became the permanent attendant. He reached the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramīs) he had practiced for a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of this position.
From the day he received the position of attendant (upaṭṭhāka), he performed duties such as offering hot and cold water to the Blessed One, offering the three types of tooth-sticks (large, medium, and small), massaging the Buddha's hands and feet, scrubbing His back when He bathed, and sweeping the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī.
456:
He attended to the Buddha with various duties, both large and small, reflecting and planning, "At such a time, such an object would be suitable for the Blessed One; such a task should be performed." Thus, he spent the entire day moving about in the vicinity of the Buddha. 

When the day passed and night arrived, he would hold a torch and circumambulate the Gandha-kuṭī precinct nine times every single night. Indeed, this thought occurred in the Elder's mind: "If sloth and torpor (thina-middha) were to overcome me, I would not be able to respond if the Blessed One should have a need and call for me." Therefore, he never let go of the torch throughout the night, always holding it. This was the background for his receiving the pre-eminent (etadagga) titles.

## (c) Attaining the Five Pre-eminent Titles

At another time, while the Blessed One was residing in the Jetavana monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, He praised the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, through various means and declared:

"Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning (bahussuta), Ānanda is the foremost (1).
Monks, among my monk disciples who are mindful (satimanta), Ānanda is the foremost (2).
Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great retentive power (gatimanta), Ānanda is the foremost (3)."
457:
"Monks, among my monk disciples who are resolute (dhitimanta), Ānanda is the foremost (4).
Monks, among my monk disciples who are attendants (upaṭṭhāka), Ānanda is the foremost (5).
That is to say, Ānanda."

—Monks, among my monk disciples who possess great learning, Ānanda is the most excellent and foremost (1).
(Among my monk disciples) who are mindful (possessing the memory to retain the Buddha's teachings for a long time), Ānanda is the most excellent and foremost (2).
(Among my monk disciples) who possess the wisdom to understand (the meanings of the words as taught by me), Ānanda is the most excellent and foremost (3).
(Among my monk disciples) who possess energy and effort (in learning, retaining, and reciting the Buddha's teachings, as well as in attending to Him), Ānanda is the most excellent and foremost (4).
(Among my monk disciples) who attend to me, Ānanda is the most excellent and foremost (5).

Thus, the Buddha praised and appointed the Elder to the pre-eminent (etadagga) positions in these five categories: bahussuta, satimanta, gatimanta, dhitimanta, and upaṭṭhāka.
458:
## Venerable Ānanda's Attainment of Arahatship

Since the account of Venerable Ānanda's attainment of Arahatship is connected with the First Great Council, I shall describe it based on the account of the First Great Council (Paṭhama-mahāsaṅgīti-kathā) starting from page 3 of the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā.

From the preaching of the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, until the guidance and liberation of the wanderer Subhadda, the Buddha performed all the various Buddha-duties. Then, in the Sal-tree grove of the Malla kings in the city of Kusināra, between a pair of young Sal-trees, on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha) in the Great Era 148, in the morning watch, the Blessed One entered the Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna). After that, (1) for the first seven days, the Malla kings honored the Buddha's physical remains with perfumes, flowers, and so on, and held a grand festival of worship (sādhukīḷana). These seven days are called "Sādhukīḷana-sattāha."

Thereafter, the physical remains were placed upon a pyre of scented wood for cremation. They had to wait until the arrival of Venerable Mahākassapa, and only upon his arrival on the seventh day did the fire element consume the remains. (2) These seven days are called "Citaka-sattāha."

Then, for another seven days, while surrounded by layers of spear-guards, the Malla kings performed the highest worship of the bodily relics (sārīrika-dhātu) in the royal pavilion. (3) These seven days are called "Dhātupūjā-sattāha."
459:
After these three periods of seven days had passed, on the 5th day of the waxing moon of Nayon, the great distribution of relics was held. On that day of relic distribution, seven hundred thousand (700,000) monks gathered. At that assembly, the Elder Mahākassapa, who was the Sangha-elder, recalled the rude and harsh words spoken by the old monk Subhadda (who had gone forth in his old age) on the seventh day after the Buddha's Parinibbāna (while traveling on the road from Pāvā to Kusināra): "Enough, friends! Do not sorrow, do not lament, do not weep. Now we are well rid of that Great Ascetic. That Great Ascetic used to bother us by saying, 'This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you.' But now we shall do what we want, and we shall not do what we do not want."

Recalling these words, and also reflecting on the rarity of such a great assembly of the Sangha occurring again, he thought:

"If wicked monks, thinking 'The Teacher's word is now a thing of the past since the Master has passed away,' gain a following, it will soon lead to the disappearance of the three types of True Dhamma and the three types of Sāsana. It would be well if I were to lead the performance of a Council (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If such a Council is held, this Sāsana of the three True Dhammas will endure for a long time.

Furthermore, the Blessed One honored me by exchanging robes with me for use, and by placing me on an equal footing with Himself in terms of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), such as the nine successive meditative attainments (anupubbavihāra-samāpatti) and the six higher powers (abhiññā), saying: 'Monks, just as I can enter and dwell in the first jhāna as long as I wish, so too can Kassapa enter and dwell in the first jhāna as long as he wishes,' and so on.
460:
In the same way, the Blessed One praised me uniquely, like waving His hand in the sky, for having a mind unattached to the four classes of people and for my practice being like the moon (candūpama). For such honors and praises, there is no other way to repay the debt than by holding a Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

Just as a Great King, wishing to ensure the continuity of his royal lineage, honors his legitimate eldest son (orasa) by conferring upon him his own royal insignia and all his authority, so too the Blessed One, seeing that 'This Kassapa will be the legitimate eldest son who can ensure the continuity of my Dhamma-lineage,' honored me with this honor that is not shared with others; He indeed praised me with this extensive and noble praise."

Reflecting deeply in this manner, for the purpose of holding the Dhamma and Vinaya Council, he addressed the Venerable monks present in that assembly (revealing the harsh and rude words of the old monk Subhadda mentioned above):
461:
"Come now, friends, let us perform a Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya before what is not Dhamma (adhamma) shines forth and Dhamma is withheld; before what is not Vinaya (avinaya) shines forth and Vinaya is withheld; before those who speak what is not Dhamma become powerful and those who speak Dhamma become weak; before those who speak what is not Vinaya become powerful and those who speak Vinaya become weak."

Thus he spoke words of encouragement and coordination for the sake of the Sāsana.

Then the Venerable monks in the assembly said, "Venerable Mahākassapa, if that is the case, may the Elder select the monks for the purpose of holding the Dhamma and Vinaya Council." Following the request and urging of the Sangha, Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine (499) Arahats who were bearers of the five Nikāyas and the three Piṭakas, and who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), the three knowledges (tevijja), and the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā), most of whom had been praised and appointed to pre-eminent (etadagga) positions by the Buddha Himself.

(In this regard, one might ask: Why did the Elder select four hundred and ninety-nine (499) monks? The answer is: He left one spot vacant to allow for the Venerable Ānanda.)
462:
To elaborate: At that time, Venerable Ānanda was not yet an Arahat; he was still only a trainee (sekha-ariya). Therefore, the Council could not yet be held with him. However, regarding the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine factors (aṅga), and the eighty-four thousand groups of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) taught by the Buddha, there was nothing that Venerable Ānanda had not personally realized; he had mastered and retained them all by heart. Therefore, the Council could not be held without Venerable Ānanda either.

One might ask again: "If that is so, since he was of great service to the Dhamma Council even as a sekha-ariya, why did Venerable Mahākassapa not select Venerable Ānanda as a Council-performing (saṅgītikāraka) monk from the start?" The answer is: He did not select him because he wished to avoid the danger of being reproached by others (parūpavāda).

To elaborate: The Elder was very close and intimate with Venerable Ānanda. For that reason, even though white hairs were growing on Venerable Ānanda's head (even though he had reached the age of eighty), the Elder would admonish him by calling him a "boy" (kumāraka), saying, "Navāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsi — This boy does not know his measure." (For the full details of this account, one should look at the Nidānavagga, 5-Kassapa Saṃyutta, 11-Cīvara Sutta of the Piṭaka Burmese Translation). Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda was a Sakyan prince and also a cousin (son of the paternal uncle) of the Buddha. If he had selected Venerable Ānanda as a Council-performing person in that assembly, some monks might have thought he was following the path of favoritism (chandāgati) and might have accused him, saying, "Venerable Mahākassapa did not select many Arahats who have attained the analytical knowledges, but instead showed favoritism by selecting Venerable Ānanda, who is a sekha-ariya." To remain free from such danger of reproach from others—
463:
463
(Wishing to avoid this, he thought, "The Council of the Dhamma cannot be held in any way without the Venerable Ānanda; therefore, I will select the Venerable Ānanda as a member of the council only with the consent and agreement of the Saṅgha of monks," and thus he left him unselected at first.)

Then the Saṅgha of monks themselves, wishing to elect the Venerable Ānanda as a member of the council, addressed the Venerable Mahākassapa: "Venerable Mahākassapa, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a trainee (sekha), he is one who is incapable of falling into the four types of bias (agati). Not only that, but this Venerable Ānanda has learned much of the Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One. Venerable Mahākassapa, if that is so, we request that the Venerable also elect the Venerable Ānanda as a member of the council." Thus, they made a unanimous request. Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa elected the Venerable Ānanda as a member of the council.

In this way, including the Venerable Ānanda who was elected according to the unanimous wish of the Saṅgha, there were five hundred (500) elder monks selected as members of the council.

Then, the elder monks in the assembly consulted and discussed, "Where shall we hold the Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya?" They agreed, "The city of Rājagaha has an extensive area for alms-resort (gocaragāma) and many large monasteries. It would be well if we spend the rains retreat (vassa) in Rājagaha and hold the Council of the Dhamma and Vinaya there, while other monks do not spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha."
464:
464
They deliberated and reached a decision. (The reason they deliberated and decided thus was because they considered: "The performance of the Dhamma Council is a task we must carry out daily and constantly. If we do not prohibit other monks from spending the rains retreat in Rājagaha by a formal act (ñatti-kammavācā), some disagreeable person who speaks against the Dhamma (adhamma-vādī) might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and cause disturbance or obstruction.")

Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa, by means of a formal act with one motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma), announced:

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is suitable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize these five hundred monks to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha for the purpose of chanting the Dhamma and Vinaya, and let no other monks spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha. This is the motion."

Reciting the kammavācā in this manner, he designated (1) that only the five hundred council-performing monks should spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha to hold the Dhamma and Vinaya Council, and (2) that other monks should not spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha.

This kammavācā is the one that arose on the twenty-first (21st) day after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. After reciting this kammavācā, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the venerable monks:

"Friends, forty days are now allowed for you. After that, you will not be allowed to say, 'I still have such and such an impediment (palibodha).' Therefore, within these forty days, those monks who have impediments regarding illness,
465:
465
monks who have impediments regarding teachers or preceptors, monks who have impediments regarding mother or father, and monks who have tasks such as firing bowls or sewing robes—all should complete and cut off their respective impediments and must perform the work of the Dhamma and Vinaya Council without fail."

Having spoken thus, the Venerable Mahākassapa, surrounded by his retinue of five hundred monks, set out for the city of Rājagaha. Other great elders who had received the designation as council members also took their respective retinues of student monks and departed for various directions, wishing to comfort the people who were deeply pierced by the thorn of sorrow. The Venerable Puṇṇa, however, remained in the city of Kusinārā with his retinue of seven hundred monks, intending to comfort all the people who arrived at the place of the Buddha's Parinibbāna by offering them the deathless medicine of the cool Dhamma water.

The Venerable Ānanda, just as he had done before the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, personally took the Blessed One's bowl and robes and traveled toward the city of Sāvatthī together with five hundred student monks. As he traveled, the retinue of monks following the elder increased more and more. Wherever the Venerable Ānanda arrived, there was intense weeping.
466:
466
In due course, when the Venerable Ānanda arrived at Sāvatthī, the people of Sāvatthī, hearing the news that "Venerable Ānanda has arrived," came out to meet him with perfumes, flowers, and the like. They wept and lamented, saying, "Venerable Ānanda, in former times you used to come together with the Blessed One; but now (this time), where have you left the Blessed One that you come alone?" There was intense weeping, just as on the day the Blessed One entered Parinibbāna.

While the people were thus weeping and lamenting, the Venerable Ānanda brought them to right understanding and right vision through Dhamma discourse connected with impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). He then entered the Jetavana monastery, respectfully paid homage to the Gandhakuṭī (Perfumed Chamber) where the Blessed One used to reside, opened the door, took out the couches and stools, dusted them, swept and cleaned the Gandhakuṭī, and discarded the withered flowers and rubbish. Then, he brought the couches and stools back in, placed them in their original positions, and performed all the duties exactly as he had done when the Blessed One was alive.

While performing all these duties, when the Venerable Ānanda was sweeping the bathroom or setting out the water for use and drinking, he would pay homage to the Gandhakuṭī and, while weeping, say: "Blessed One, is this not the time for Your bath?
467:
467
Is this not the time for preaching the Dhamma? Is this not the time for giving exhortation to the monks? Is this not the time for resting and reclining on the right side like a lion king? Is this not the time for using the water to wash Your face?" Thus he performed his duties while weeping. He performed his duties while weeping because he well knew the deathless essence of the Blessed One's virtues, because his faith-based love (saddhā-pema) and metta-based love (mettā-pema) were very strong, because he himself was not yet an Arahant whose taints were exhausted, and because his heart was extremely tender due to the special gratitude for the mutual help they had rendered each other over hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.

## The Admonition by the Forest Deity

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spent much of his time not only in great lamentation for the Blessed One himself but also in preaching the Dhamma to the people who were burning with the fires of sorrow and lamentation due to the Buddha's Parinibbāna, giving them right understanding and right vision. Then one day, the Venerable Ānanda was staying in a forest grove in the Kosala country. A forest deity, out of compassion and a desire for the Venerable Ānanda's welfare, approached him and addressed him with this verse:

"Having entered the thicket at the foot of a tree,
Having placed Nibbāna in your heart,
Meditate, Gotama, do not be negligent!
What will this babbling do for you?"
468:
468
"O Gotama, Venerable Ānanda born of the Gotama clan! You, having entered the thicket at the foot of a tree seeking seclusion (viveka), and having placed Nibbāna—the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)—in your heart in two ways, namely by task and by object*, should enter into and dwell in the two types of jhāna, namely meditation on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Do not be negligent or lose mindfulness. What benefit will this babbling—speaking words to quench the heat of the people who come to you—do for your attainment of the higher paths and fruits? It will certainly not benefit the attainment of the higher paths and fruits."

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having gained a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) from the forest deity's address, and because his body was heavy with the element of discomfort (dosa-mala) due to much sitting and standing since the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, took a milk purgative on the second day to relieve himself and remained in the monastery.

On that very day, the young man Subha, the son of the (deceased) wealthy brahmin Todeyya, sent a messenger to invite him. 

* One who strives with energy, thinking "I shall reach Nibbāna," is said to have placed Nibbāna in the heart by way of task (work). One who dwells having entered the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object is said to have placed Nibbāna in the heart by way of object. (From the Commentary).
469:
469
The Venerable Ānanda told the young messenger, "Young man, today is not the time. Today I have taken a milk purgative. Perhaps I may be able to come tomorrow." On the following day, the Venerable Ānanda, together with his attendant monk, the Venerable Cetaka, went to the house of the young man Subha and, being questioned by him, preached the Subha Sutta, which is the tenth sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga of the Dīgha Nikāya. (That sutta should be noted from the Myanmar translation of the Piṭaka.)

Thereafter, the Venerable Ānanda had the broken, worn, and damaged parts of the great Jetavana monastery repaired. As the time for the rains retreat (vassa) drew near, he left his retinue of monks and departed for the city of Rājagaha. Similarly, the other elder monks who were designated as council members and compilers of the Dhamma also arrived at Rājagaha as the rains retreat approached. Those elder monks who were designated as council members performed the Uposatha together on the full moon day of Āsāḷha and entered the rains retreat in Rājagaha on the first day of the waning moon of Āsāḷha.

At that time, there were eighteen (18) great monasteries surrounding the city of Rājagaha. All those monasteries had been abandoned by the monks, and in some places they were broken and damaged, in some places they were covered with thick dust, and in some places they were moldy. Indeed, when the Blessed One entered Parinibbāna, all the monks had taken their bowls and robes, abandoned the monasteries and precincts, and gone to Kusinārā.
470:
470
They departed. Consequently, the monasteries became dilapidated and in disrepair, covered in thick dust and mold.

At that time, the Great Elders assembled and deliberated: "Friends, the Blessed One praised the restoration and repair of dilapidated structures. Come, friends, let us spend the first month repairing what is broken and ruined. When the middle month arrives, let us assemble in unity to hold the Dhamma and Vinaya Recitation (Saṅgāyana)." Their deliberation was based on two reasons: (1) the desire to honor the Blessed One's teachings in the Senāsana-khandhaka of the Vinaya (concerning the duties regarding lodgings), and (2) to avoid the danger of being accused by heretics (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation, who might say, "The disciples of the Ascetic Gotama cleaned the monasteries only while their teacher, the Ascetic Gotama, was alive. Now that their teacher has attained Parinibbāna, they have abandoned them. The vast wealth donated by the four classes of lay devotees is perishing needlessly when it should not."

After the Great Elders had deliberated and reached this decision, they went and stood at the gate of King Ajātasattu's palace the following day. King Ajātasattu came out, paid homage, and asked about the duty he should perform: "Venerable sirs, for what reason have you come?" The Great Elders replied that they had come because they required manual labor (hatthakamma) to repair the eighteen major monasteries.
471:
471
The King provided the laborers for the manual work to the Great Elders. The Elders had all the monasteries repaired during the first month. After the repairs were completed, they informed King Ajātasattu: "Great King, the work of repairing the monasteries is finished. Now we shall hold the Dhamma and Vinaya Recitation." King Ajātasattu replied: "Very well, venerable sirs. May you perform the Recitation with complete freedom. Let my secular authority be the power behind your spiritual authority (Dhamma-cakka). Please command me, venerable sirs; what task should I perform?" When he asked this, the Elders replied: "Great King, we wish for a place to be prepared where the monks performing the Recitation may assemble."

When King Ajātasattu asked again, "In which place should it be built, venerable sirs?", the Elders replied: "Great King, it is suitable to build it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, where the Carali tree grows, on the side of Mount Vebhāra."

## King Ajātasattu Building the Great Council Pavilion

Then King Ajātasattu, consenting with the words "Very well, venerable sirs," had a great Council Pavilion constructed, which resembled one created by the divine architect Vissakamma. (1) This great pavilion was arranged with its respective rooms, kept clean, and fitted with walls, pillars, and staircases. Furthermore, it was adorned with exquisite paintings of floral designs and creeping vines. (2) This great pavilion—
472:
472
—was exceedingly beautiful, as if surpassing the glory of the King's golden palace, and was so magnificent that it seemed to mock the splendor of celestial mansions. (3) It was as delightful as a hall of auspiciousness, like a pleasant haven where the birds—the eyes of gods and men—gather in unison, and as if all the delightful things in the world had been brought together in one place.

Above that great Council Pavilion, a magnificent jeweled ceiling was hung with various floral garlands suspended from it. On the floor below, various kinds of flower carpets were spread, appearing like a vast slab of ruby intricately fashioned with diverse gems. The ground was made beautiful and level, decorated as grandly and neatly as the abode of the Great Brahmā. Inside the pavilion, five hundred priceless seats (kappiya-akhing) were prepared for the five hundred Arahants who were the performers of the Recitation. Furthermore, inside the pavilion, a Thera-āsana (Elder's seat) or Dhamma-pallaṅka was prepared for the Questioner (Puccaka) to reside in, positioned against the southern side and facing north. In the center of the pavilion, a Dhamma-āsana was prepared for the Answerer (Vissajjaka) to sit, facing east, a seat worthy of the Blessed One himself. An ivory fan was placed upon that seat. Then, the King sent a messenger to inform the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, all the tasks to be undertaken by me have been fully and completely accomplished."

That day was the 4th day of the waning moon of Sāvaṇa (Wagaung). At the assembly of the Saṅgha on that day, some monks—
473:
Referring to Venerable Ānanda, they spoke words of reproach, hinting: "In this assembly of monks, a certain monk wanders about spreading the scent of raw flesh (alternatively, the scent of defilements)." When Venerable Ānanda heard these words, he reflected, "In this assembly of monks, there is no monk other than myself who wanders about spreading the scent of raw flesh (alternatively, the scent of defilements). Surely, these monks are speaking words of reproach by hinting at me." Upon this reflection, he attained great spiritual urgency (Dhamma-saṃvega). Some monks, however, spoke words of encouragement, saying, "Friend Ānanda, tomorrow the Great Council (Saṅgāyana) assembly (Sannipāta) will take place. You, friend, are still only a Noble Trainee (Sekha-ariya) with tasks remaining for the higher paths. Because you are still a Sekha-ariya (and not yet an Arahant), it is not appropriate for you to attend the Great Council assembly. Therefore, we wish for you to be one who is not negligent in the practice and exertion of the Dhamma in time for the Great Council."

## Venerable Ānanda Attaining Arahantship Free from the Four Postures

Then, Venerable Ānanda reflected, "Tomorrow the Great Council assembly will take place. It is not appropriate for me to go to the assembly while remaining only a Sekha-ariya (a Sotāpanna Ariya)." Having so reflected, he spent many hours of the night in the practice of Mindfulness of the Body (Kāyagatāsati). At the time of dawn, he descended from the walking path, entered the monastery, and thinking, "I shall lie down for a moment," he slowly reclined his body while maintaining constant mindfulness.
474:
474
In the interval when his two feet had left the ground but his head had not yet touched the pillow, the Great Elder became an Arahant, having exhausted all taints (āsavas).

To clarify further: The Great Elder had spent the time outside the meditation cell walking on the walkway, practicing the Dhamma of a monk throughout the night. When he was unable to realize the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit, he thought: "Did not the Blessed One say to me when he was about to attain Parinibbāna, 'Dear Ānanda, you have performed much merit; exert yourself in meditation, and you will soon become an Arahant'? There is no fault in the words spoken by the Buddhas. However, I have exerted my energy (vīriya) too intensely (meaning his energy was excessive). Therefore, my mind is prone to restlessness (meaning because energy was excessive, uddhacca occurred, and he remained without attaining the Path and Fruit). Come, I shall now strive to make energy and concentration (samādhi) equal." Having so reflected, he stood at the place for washing feet, washed his feet, entered the meditation cell, and sat on the small couch. Thinking "I shall rest a little," he slowly laid himself down on the small couch with unremitting mindfulness. In the interval when his two feet had left the ground but his head had not yet touched the pillow, the Great Elder reached the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala) and became an Arahant, having exhausted all taints.

Therefore, if it is asked, "In this Dispensation, which monk reached the Fruit of Arahantship while being free from the four postures (not lying, not sitting, not standing, and not walking)?"
475:
475
It is proper to answer: "It is Venerable Ānanda."

## Venerable Mahā Kassapa Giving the Cry of Approval (Sādhu)

Then, on the following day, the 5th day of the waning moon of Sāvaṇa (after Venerable Ānanda had become an Arahant), the Great Elders who were the performers of the Recitation, having finished their meal, put away their alms-bowls and robes and assembled in unity at the "Dhamma Recitation Pavilion." (In this context, according to the usage of the Middle Country, the period from the full moon of Āsāḷha to the full moon of Sāvaṇa is called one month. During that month, the Elders supervised the repair of the dilapidated monasteries. From the 1st day of the waning moon of Sāvaṇa, King Ajātasattu had the great Council Pavilion built, which took three days to complete. On the 4th day of the waning moon, Venerable Ānanda became an Arahant. On the 5th day of the waning moon, the great assembly for the Recitation began). At that time, Venerable Ānanda went to the assembly as an Arahant.

Regarding the manner of his arrival: When the monks of the assembly were complete and it was the appropriate time to enter the assembly, Venerable Ānanda, with a joyful and delighted mind, adjusted his robe over one shoulder. Like a ripe palm fruit falling from its stalk, like a ruby placed upon a pure white woolen cloth, like the full moon rising in a cloudless sky, and appearing radiant and magnificent upon meeting the light of the rising sun—
476:
He proceeded as if announcing his attainment of Arahattaphala, with a countenance of great majesty, radiant and shimmering, exceedingly pure and stainless like a newly blossomed lotus.

(Here, a question may arise: "For what purpose did the Venerable Ānanda proceed as if clearly announcing his attainment of Arahattaphala?" The answer is: He reflected, "The Blessed One praised the act of making one's attainment of Arahattaphala known to others through some sign or manner, without directly declaring in words, 'I have reached Arahattaphala.'" He did so, firstly, to cause joy (somanassa-vedanā) in the hearts of the elder monks who were waiting and thinking, "Though he is a Sekkha-ariya and thus not yet suitable to be selected for the Council of Dhamma and Vinaya, we shall select him as a reciter (saṅgītikāraka) because of his great learning (bāhusacca)." Secondly, he wished to demonstrate the efficacy of the instruction given by the Blessed One: "Be not heedless." Thus, he approached as if clearly announcing his attainment of Arahattaphala. This is the answer.)

At that time, upon seeing the Venerable Ānanda, the thought arose in the mind of the Venerable Mahākassapa: "Oh, how beautiful is the Venerable Ānanda who has arrived having reached Arahattaphala! If the Blessed One were still alive today, He would surely grant the Venerable Ānanda a 'Sādhu' (Well done). Come now, I shall grant the 'Sādhu' on behalf of the Buddha, which the Blessed One would have given to the Venerable Ānanda." Having thus reflected, the Elder Mahākassapa said, "Friend Ānanda, your attainment and realization of Arahattaphala is indeed beautiful."
477:
Saying such words, he shouted the 'Sādhu' three times. 

## The Commencement of the Council

When the Venerable Elder Ānanda had arrived and the monks selected as reciters (saṅgītikāraka) were all present, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Friends, between the Dhamma and the Vinaya, which shall we recite first? Shall we recite the Dhamma (Sutta and Abhidhamma) first, or shall we recite the Vinaya first?" The monks replied:

"Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the lifeblood of the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana). For when the Vinaya endures, the Sāsana endures. Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya first."

When they had replied in unison, the Venerable Mahākassapa asked again: "Whom shall we place at the head to recite the Vinaya?" The monks replied: "Let us place the Venerable Upāli at the head to recite the Vinaya." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked: "Is it because the Venerable Ānanda is unable?" The monks replied: "It is not that the Venerable Ānanda is unable; he is indeed capable. However, while the Blessed One was still alive, on account of his mastery in learning the Vinaya,
478:
the Blessed One placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position (Etadagga), saying: 'Monks, among my disciples who learn the Vinaya, the monk Upāli is the foremost.' Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya by questioning the Venerable Upāli." Thus they replied in unison, stating the reason.

In this First Council, the Venerable Mahākassapa acted as the Sanghamahānāyaka (Great Leader of the Sangha). Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa appointed himself as the questioner of the Vinaya (Vinaya-pucchaka), and the Venerable Upāli appointed himself as the answerer of the Vinaya (Vinaya-vissajjaka). They sat in their respective places on the Dhamma-seats (Dhammāsana). Regarding each training rule (sikkhāpada) of the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa asked all necessary details such as the occasion (vatthu), the origin (nidāna), the person (puggala), the primary rule (mūlapaññatti), the secondary rule (anupaññatti), what constitutes an offense, and what does not. To every question, the Venerable Upāli gave a complete answer. After that, the 500 monks of the Council recited together in unison, following the order of the questions and answers (incorporating connecting phrases such as 'Tena samayena...' [At that time...], 'Tena kho pana samayena...' [Now at that time...], 'Atha kho...' [Then...], 'Evaṃ vutte...' [When this was said...], starting with 'Tena samayena Buddho Bhagavā Verañjāyaṃ viharati'). (This collective chanting is called Saṅgāyana).

When the recitation of the first Pārājika was completed, this great earth shook violently as far as the water's edge, as if giving a 'Sādhu' praise.
479:
In this same manner, they recited the remaining three Pārājika rules and all the two hundred and twenty-seven (227) training rules, one by one, through questioning and answering. They designated this Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, titled Pārājika-kaṇḍa Pāḷi, as the 'Mahāvibhaṅga' and established it as the Vācanāmagga (the tradition of oral recitation). When the collective recitation of the Mahāvibhaṅga was finished, the great earth shook violently as before.

Then, they recited the three hundred and four (304) training rules found in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, one by one, through questioning and answering. They designated it as the 'Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga.' These two parts, the Mahāvibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, were designated as the 'Ubhatovibhaṅga,' consisting of 64 Bhāṇavāras, and established as the Vācanāmagga. When the collective recitation of the Ubhatovibhaṅga was finished, the great earth shook violently as before.

In this very manner, they recited the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga of the Khandhaka Pāḷi, consisting of eighty Bhāṇavāras, and the Parivāra Pāḷi, measuring twenty-five Bhāṇavāras. They designated this as the 'Vinaya Piṭaka.' When the collective recitation (Saṅgāyana) of the Vinaya Piṭaka was finished, the great earth shook violently as before.

## Entrusting the Vinaya Piṭaka to the Venerable Upāli

After thus reciting the Vinaya Piṭaka, the 500 elder monks of the Council entrusted it to the Venerable Upāli, saying: "Friend, please teach and pass on this Vinaya Piṭaka to the disciples who take dependence (nissaya) under you."
480:
When the recitation of the Vinaya Piṭaka was completed, the Venerable Upāli placed the ivory fan on the seat, descended from the Dhamma-seat, paid homage to the senior elders, and sat in the place designated for him.

After the Vinaya was recited, desiring to recite the Dhamma (Sutta and Abhidhamma), the Venerable Mahākassapa inquired of the Sangha's will: "Friends, for the recitation of the Dhamma, which elder shall we place at the head?" All the monks of the Council replied in unison: "Let us place the Venerable Ānanda at the head to recite the Dhamma."

Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa appointed himself as the questioner of the Dhamma (Dhamma-pucchaka), and the Venerable Ānanda appointed himself as the answerer of the Dhamma (Dhamma-vissajjaka). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the senior elders, and sat on the Dhamma-seat holding the ivory fan. Once he was seated, the Venerable Mahākassapa and the monks of the Council discussed the recitation of the Dhamma as follows:

(Mahākassapa)
"Friends, since the Dhamma consists of two parts, the Suttanta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which Piṭaka shall we recite first?"
481:
(The Elders)
"Venerable Sir, let us recite the Suttanta Piṭaka first." (It should be specially noted that the three Piṭakas were recited in the order of the three trainings: the Vinaya Piṭaka primarily teaches the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the Suttanta Piṭaka primarily teaches the training in higher mentality (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka primarily teaches the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).)

(Mahākassapa)
"Friends, in the Suttanta Piṭaka, there are four great Nikāyas (collections of discourses) to be recited. Which Nikāya shall we recite first?"

(The Elders)
"Venerable Sir, let us recite the Dīgha Nikāya first."

(Mahākassapa)
"Friends, in the Dīgha Nikāya, there are 34 suttas and 3 vaggas (divisions). Which vagga shall we recite first?"

(The Elders)
"Venerable Sir, let us recite the Sīlakkhandhavagga first."

(Mahākassapa)
"Friends, in the Sīlakkhandhavagga, there are 13 suttas. Which sutta shall we recite first?"

(The Elders)
"Venerable Sir, the Brahmajāla Sutta is a discourse adorned with the three types of virtue: the minor, the middle, and the major (cūḷa, majjhima, mahā). It is a discourse capable of dispelling and destroying practices unsuitable for the Sāsana, such as various forms of wrong livelihood, hypocrisy (kuhana), and flattery (lapana).
482:
It is also where the sixty-two (62) types of wrong views are explained and resolved. It is a discourse that caused the ten thousand world systems to shake sixty-two times. Therefore, let us recite that Brahmajāla Sutta first."

After discussing thus, the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda all necessary details regarding the Brahmajāla Sutta, such as the origin (nidāna), the person (puggala), and the occasion (vatthu). The Venerable Ānanda gave a complete answer to every question. When the questioning was finished, the 500 Arahant monks of the Council recited the Brahmajāla Sutta together in unison. At the conclusion of the recitation of the Brahmajāla Sutta, the great earth shook violently as before.

After reciting the Brahmajāla Sutta, they recited the remaining twelve suttas, such as the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, in full through questioning and answering. They designated these thirteen suttas, including the Brahmajāla Sutta, as the 'Sīlakkhandhavagga' and established it as the Vācanāmagga.

Following the Sīlakkhandhavagga, they recited the ten suttas of the Mahāvagga, and following the Mahāvagga, they recited the eleven suttas of the Pāthikavagga in full through questioning and answering. These three vaggas, containing 34 suttas and measuring 64 Bhāṇavāras, were thus compiled.
483:
After collectively reciting the words of the Buddha, they designated it as "Dīgha Nikāya" (the Collection of Long Discourses). All the Elders who participated in the Council then entrusted this noble Dhamma of the Dīgha Nikāya to the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Friend, please teach this Dīgha Nikāya to the disciples who reside under your guidance (nissaya)."

Then the Elders of the Council recited the words of the Buddha in the Majjhima Nikāya, which consists of eighty bhāṇavāras, through a process of questioning and answering. They then entrusted it to the disciples of the Venerable Sāriputta, saying, "Friends, please preserve this Majjhima Nikāya so that it does not disappear."

Then the Elders of the Council recited the words of the Buddha in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which consists of one hundred bhāṇavāras, through a process of questioning and answering. They then entrusted it to the Venerable Mahākassapa, saying, "Venerable Sir, please teach this Saṃyutta Nikāya to the disciples who reside under your guidance."

Then the Elders of the Council recited the words of the Buddha in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which consists of one hundred and twenty bhāṇavāras, through a process of questioning and answering. They then entrusted it to the Venerable Anuruddha, saying, "Please teach this Aṅguttara Nikāya to the disciples who reside under your guidance."
484:
Then the Elders of the Council recited the seven books of the Abhidhamma: Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna. As before, the great earth shook violently.

Then the Elders of the Council recited the Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Suttanipāta, Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, and Therīgāthā, and designated them as the "Khuddaka Nikāya." Regarding this Khuddaka Nikāya, the Elders who were bearers of the Dīgha Nikāya stated, "It has been recited and included within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka." However, the Elders who were bearers of the Majjhima Nikāya stated, "These thirteen texts, along with the Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka—all fifteen texts—are named the Khuddaka Nikāya and are included within the Sutta Piṭaka."

(The above is the explanation from the Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā, pages 3 to 16. In this context, the term "bhāṇavāra" is a council terminology referring to the amount of text recited at one time. One bhāṇavāra takes approximately half an hour to recite. The formal act (ñatti) by which Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Upāli, and Venerable Ānanda appointed themselves for the Council is found in the Pañcasatika-khandhaka of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga.)

In this way, during the First Council, the Venerable Ānanda took responsibility for the Sutta Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka, known as the Dhamma, and answered questions with great courage and brilliance.

This is the significance of Venerable Ānanda in the First Council.
485:
## The Parinibbāna of Venerable Ānanda

Since Venerable Ānanda was born on the same day as the Buddha, he was eighty years old in the year 148 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), the year the Buddha attained Parinibbāna and the First Council was held. Forty years after the Buddha's Parinibbāna and the First Council, when the Elder was one hundred and twenty years old, he one day reflected upon his own life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), known as the continuity of life (jīvita-santati). Realizing it was exhausted, he informed his lay and monastic disciples, "Seven days from today, I shall enter Parinibbāna."

Upon hearing this news, among those living on both sides of the Rohiṇī River (the river that was the subject of the water dispute between the Sākiya and Koliya princes), the people on this side said, "We have been greatly benefited by the Elder. Therefore, the Elder will attain Parinibbāna in our presence." The people on the other side said the same.

The Elder, hearing the words of the people on both sides, thought: "The people on both sides have been greatly beneficial to me. It cannot be said that 'such and such people did not help.' If I attain Parinibbāna on this side, the people on the other side will quarrel with the people on this side to obtain my bodily relics (sārīrika-dhātu). If I attain Parinibbāna on the other side, the people on this side will likewise quarrel."
486:
"If that quarrel arises, it will be because of me; if it is to be peaceful, it must be because of me. If I do not manage this, conflict will break out; if I manage it well, conflict will be averted." Having reflected thus, he said:

"O lay devotees, the people on this side have been very kind to me, and the people on the other side have also been very kind to me. There is no one who has not been kind. Let the people on this side assemble only on this side, and let the people on the other side assemble only on the other side."

On the seventh day, the Elder sat cross-legged in the air (at a height of about seven palm trees) over the middle of the Rohiṇī River and first preached the Dhamma to the multitude.

After preaching, he made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): "Let my body split in half from the middle; let one half fall on this side, and let the other half fall on that side." After making this resolution, he entered the Tejo-kasiṇa jhāna (fire-kasina meditation), which is the basis for supernormal powers (abhiññā). Emerging from that jhāna, when the process of supernormal power (abhiññā-vīthi) arose, flames burst forth from his body simultaneously with the supernormal power. Immediately following that process, the Elder's final consciousness (pacchima-cuti-citta) ceased, and he entered Parinibbāna, ending the cycle of existence.
487:
According to his resolution, his body split in half from the middle; one half fell on this side, and the other half fell on the other side. At that time, the people on both sides wept bitterly. The sound of their weeping was like the sound of the earth collapsing. It was even more heart-rending than the weeping when the Buddha attained Parinibbāna. The people wept for four months, wandering about and lamenting, "While the Elder who carried the Buddha's bowl and robes was present, it was as if the Buddha himself were still with us. Only now has our teacher, the Buddha, truly attained Parinibbāna."

## Verse of Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega-gāthā)

Hā saṃyogā viyogantā,
Hā aniccāva saṅkhatā.
Hā uppannā ca bhaṅgantā,
Hā hā saṅkhāradhammatā.

Saṃyogā = All unions, such as meeting and living with teachers, donors, friends, relatives, children, and spouses, Viyogantā = must inevitably end in separation, either by departing to a distant land or by the separation of death across different lives; these two forms of separation are unavoidable. Hā... = Alas, what a sea of various sufferings like sorrow and lamentation; how terrifying indeed! Saṅkhatā = All conditioned things, brought together and formed by the four causes—kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment.
488:
Aniccāva = are truly impermanent, not lasting, and do not endure for long. Hā... = Alas, what a sea of various sufferings like sorrow and lamentation; how terrifying indeed! Uppannā ca = All conditioned things that have arisen and are visible, Bhaṅgantā = must inevitably end in breaking, destruction, and cessation. Hā... = Alas, what a sea of various sufferings like sorrow and lamentation; how terrifying indeed! Saṅkhāradhammatā = The natural way of conditioned things (saṅkhāra), characterized by impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). Hā... Hā... = Since this is the true fundamental cause that sinks one into the whirlpool of the ocean of suffering, how truly trembling and terrifying it is!

This is the account of the Venerable Ānanda.

## (31) The Story of Venerable Uruvela Kassapa
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Elder, a virtuous man, was conceived in a noble family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma of the Buddha Padumuttara, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the pre-eminent position (etadagga) of "having a great following." He reflected, "It would be well if I too, in the future, could attain such a pre-eminent title of having a great following like this monk." He then performed a great deed of merit (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
489:
On the seventh day, after offering a set of the triple robes (ticīvara) to each member of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he respectfully prostrated before the Buddha and made an aspiration to become a person who attains the pre-eminent title (etadagga) of having a great following.

The Buddha Padumuttara, seeing that the noble youth's aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you will become the most eminent among monks who have a large following." After saying this, the Buddha departed.

## Life as the Younger Brother of the Buddha Phussa

That noble youth, after performing meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence where he received the prophecy, wandered through the celestial and human realms. Counting back ninety-two aeons (kappas) from this present Bhadda-kappa, he became the elder half-brother (same father, different mother) of the Buddha Phussa. That prince had two other younger brothers. (The detailed account of how these three princes served the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha Phussa with the four requisites during the three months of the rainy season can be found in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 2, starting from page 607, and in this Volume 6, starting from page 336.)

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

When those three royal brothers completed the rainy season retreat, having offered excellent requisites to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha...
490:
490
After making offerings and performing meritorious deeds throughout their lives, they did not fall into the four woeful states. Long before our Buddha appeared in this Bhadda-kappa, they were born into a Brahmin family. By their lineage, all three brothers were named Kassapa. When the three Kassapa brothers reached maturity, they studied and mastered the three Vedas. Among the three brothers, the eldest had a retinue of five hundred young disciples, the middle brother had three hundred, and the youngest had two hundred.

When all three brothers examined the essence of their Vedic texts, they saw only mundane benefits and did not see any benefits for the hereafter. Thereafter, the eldest brother, the great teacher Kassapa, went to the Uruvela forest together with his retinue of five hundred disciples, became an ascetic, and (based on his location) became known as the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa. The middle brother likewise became an ascetic at a bend in the Ganges River with his retinue of three hundred disciples and became known as the teacher Nadī Kassapa. The youngest brother likewise became an ascetic at Gayāsīsa with his retinue of two hundred disciples and became known as the teacher Gayā Kassapa.

While these three brothers were living as great teachers in their respective locations such as the Uruvela forest after becoming ascetics, many days and months passed. Then, our Buddha appeared and spent the first rains retreat (vassa) in the Isipatana Migadāya forest.
491:
491
While observing the rains retreat, the Buddha preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and liberated the five monks of the group of five (Pañcavaggī). He also disciplined and liberated fifty-five young men led by the merchant's son Yasa. Thus, sixty human Arahants emerged in the world. At the end of that year's rains retreat, he sent the sixty Arahants on missions to spread the Sasana. The Buddha himself then set out for the Uruvela forest. On the way, in the Kappāsika forest, he disciplined and liberated the thirty Bhaddavaggī princes, establishing them in the stage of Sekkha Ariyas (Noble Learners) and ordaining them all as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Considering the past merits which served as the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruition of the great ascetic Uruvela Kassapa, the Buddha realized, "If I go to them, all three brothers, along with their retinues, will attain the Fruition of Arahantship."

Knowing this, the Buddha traveled alone to the Uruvela forest. As described below, he disciplined the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa along with his five hundred disciples through three thousand five hundred miracles, beginning with the subduing of the Naga king, and ordained them all as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Upon learning that their eldest brother had become a monk, the two younger brothers also became monks along with their respective retinues. All of them became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. (The detailed accounts of this section should be noted by referring back to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 2, pages 543–579).

The Buddha took those one thousand monks and went to Gayāsīsa. While sitting on the stone plateau of Gayāsīsa, he considered, "What kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable (sappāya) for these monks?"
492:
492
Upon reflection, the Buddha realized, "These people, before becoming monks in the Sasana, lived wandering about while serving the fire. It is only appropriate to teach these monks by using the metaphor of a house burning with a bright, fierce fire to represent the three realms of existence. It is fitting to preach the 'Fire Sermon' to these fire-worshippers." Knowing this, he preached the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, all of them attained the Fruition of Arahantship.

Accompanied by those one thousand Arahants, the Buddha proceeded to the Palm Grove (Laṭṭhivana) in the city of Rājagaha, as he had previously given a promise to King Bimbisāra ("I shall visit Rājagaha after attaining Buddhahood"). King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Buddha had arrived, went to the Buddha together with one hundred and twenty thousand (120,000) Brahmin householders. After paying homage, he sat at a respectful distance. The Buddha looked at the entire assembly and saw that the people were highly impressed by and respectful toward Uruvela Kassapa alone. He thought, "These people do not clearly know who is superior between me and Uruvela Kassapa. Those whose minds are divided by various thoughts are unable to receive the Dhamma discourse." He then addressed the Elder Uruvela Kassapa, saying, "Dear Kassapa, you yourself must cut off the wrong thoughts and doubts of your supporters," giving the Elder a sign to perform a display of psychic power.
493:
493
The Elder respectfully accepted the Buddha's word, rose from his seat, and paid homage to the Buddha with the five-point prostration. He then flew into the air to the height of a palm tree and performed various forms of psychic powers. He declared, "Exalted Buddha, the Glorious Buddha is my teacher; I am the disciple. Exalted Buddha, the Glorious Buddha is my teacher; I am the disciple." Having said this, he descended and prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet. In this manner, when he reached the seventh time, he flew into the air to the height of seven palm trees, descended again, paid homage to the Buddha's feet as before, and sat at a respectful distance.

Only then did the multitude of people clear their doubts about the Buddha, thinking, "The Great Buddha is indeed the most supreme monk in the world." Then, the Buddha preached the Dhamma to the multitude. At the conclusion of the discourse, King Bimbisāra, along with one hundred and ten thousand (110,000) Brahmin householders, was established in the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Ten thousand Brahmin householders declared themselves as lay followers (Upāsakas) who take refuge in the Triple Gem; this means they became Upāsakas established in the Three Refuges.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

Those one thousand monks who were the retinue of the Elder Uruvela Kassapa also thought according to their habit:
494:
494
"In our case, the task of a monk has reached its pinnacle. Why should we wander about outside? There is no more work to be done by wandering outside." Thinking thus, they continued to live and travel only by surrounding the Elder Uruvela Kassapa.

At a later time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, in the midst of the Noble Sangha, he praised the Elder Uruvela Kassapa, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ mahāparisānaṃ yadidaṃ uruvelakassapo = Monks, among my disciple monks who have a large retinue, Uruvela Kassapa is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha placed him in the position of Etadagga, the foremost in having a large retinue (Mahāparisa).

(In this regard: Other Elders sometimes had many followers and sometimes few. For the Elder Uruvela Kassapa, however, the one thousand monks, including his two younger brothers (Elder Nadī Kassapa and Elder Gayā Kassapa), were always his retinue. If each of those one thousand monks ordained one disciple, there would be two thousand disciples. If each ordained two disciples, there would be three thousand disciples. Therefore, the Elder Uruvela Kassapa was the most supreme among the monks who have large retinues. From Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, page 231).

This is the account of the Elder Uruvela Kassapa.
495:

## (32) About the Elder Kāḷudāyī

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Elder, a virtuous man, was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Dhamma of Padumuttara Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the position of Etadagga, the foremost in making relatives have faith and devotion even before they had seen the Buddha. He performed great meritorious deeds (adhikāra) and made an aspiration to attain that position. Padumuttara Buddha also gave him a prophecy.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That young man of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. When he passed away from that life, he did not fall into the four woeful states but wandered through the celestial and human realms. On the very day our Bodhisatta was conceived in his mother's womb, he was conceived in the house of a minister in the city of Kapilavatthu. Since he was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, his parents sent him to King Suddhodana on that very day, laying him in white swaddling clothes, to serve and attend to the Noble Bodhisatta.

## The Naming of Kāḷudāyī

Later, on the day he was named, because he was born on a day when the whole city was excited and joyful due to the birth of the Bodhisatta,
496:
496
he was named Udāyī. Because his complexion was slightly dark, the word 'Kāḷa' (meaning black/dark) was added, and he became well-known as the youth 'Kāḷudāyī'. That youth Kāḷudāyī grew up playing the joyful games of young princes together with the Bodhisatta in the golden palace of Kapilavatthu.

Later, the Bodhisatta went forth into the forest, practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, and became the Buddha. After preaching the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and benefiting the world of beings, he was residing in the city of Rājagaha, using it as his alms-resort. (That time was the winter season, after the full moon of Phussa in the year 103 of the Great Era, following his enlightenment). At that time, the Buddha's father, King Suddhodana, heard the good news that his son, the Buddha, was residing at the Veluvana Monastery in Rājagaha. He said, "I must bring my son, the Buddha, to this royal city of Kapilavatthu," and sent a minister along with a retinue of one thousand men. That minister traveled the distance of sixty yojanas and arrived at the Veluvana Monastery while the Buddha was preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly. The minister thought, "Let the message my King sent me wait for a moment (I shall listen to the Dhamma first)." Standing at the edge of the assembly, he listened to the Buddha's Dhamma and, while still standing, attained the Fruition of Arahantship along with his one thousand followers. Then, the Buddha addressed them:
497: "Etha bhikkhavo—Come, monks," the Buddha uttered, stretching forth his right hand. At that very moment, the appearance of all those men as royal attendants vanished, and they were transformed into senior elders of sixty years' standing (eighty years of age), possessing great composure and wearing supernatural requisites. Since it is the nature of Noble Ones to be indifferent to all worldly affairs from the moment they reach the Fruit of Arahantship, those thousand monks did not convey the message sent by King Suddhodana to the Buddha, but remained only in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). King Suddhodana, feeling restless because the minister who went did not return and no news was heard, addressed another minister, saying, "Come, dear son, you go as well," and sent him a second time with a thousand attendants in the same manner as before. That minister also went to the presence of the Buddha, and just like the first minister, he listened to the Dhamma and reached the Fruit of Arahantship along with his retinue of a thousand attendants, and remained silent. In this way, although he sent nine ministers and nine thousand attendants one after another, all of them completed their tasks as monks (all became Arahants) and remained silent without sending back any news.
498:
## Sending the Minister Kāludāyī
Then King Suddhodana reflected: "These nine ministers and nine thousand attendants have no affection or love for me at all, and thus they have not made any request to the Buddha to visit our city of Kapilavatthu. Even if other ministers go, they will not be able to invite the Buddha. My son Udāyī, however, was born on the same day as the Buddha and is of the same age; not only was he a childhood playmate, but he is also one who is affectionately devoted and intimate with me." Having considered this, he summoned the minister Kāludāyī and said, "Dear son, you go, escorted by a thousand attendants, and invite the Buddha."
The courtier Kāludāyī, who was born on the same day as the Buddha, replied, "Your Majesty, if I am allowed to ordain as a monk like the ministers and attendants who went before, I shall invite the Buddha." Then King Suddhodana gave him broad permission, saying, "Dear son, after doing whatever you wish, strive and endeavor only so that I may see my son, the Buddha." Kāludāyī accepted, saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," and taking the King's message, he went to the city of Rājagaha escorted by a thousand attendants. He stood at the edge of the assembly while the Buddha was preaching, listened to the Dhamma, and along with his retinue...
499:
...of a thousand attendants, he reached the Fruit of Arahantship and was established in the state of an Ehi Bhikkhu.
Thereafter, the Elder Kāludāyī reflected: "It is now the winter season, and it is not yet the proper time for the Buddha to travel to the city of Kapilavatthu; it is still too cold. When the spring arrives and the forests are in full bloom, and the whole earth is green and covered with fresh grass and plants in a delightful manner, then it will be the right time to travel to the royal city." He waited for the spring, and when the full moon of Phagguna arrived, realizing it was the proper time to travel, he praised the virtues of the journey for the Buddha to travel to Kapilavatthu with sixty verses (as recorded in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, starting from page 30). (Please refer back to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, page 30).
The Buddha reflected, "Udāyī praises the virtues of the journey exceptionally; this is indeed the time to go to the city of Kapilavatthu." Accompanied by twenty thousand Arahant elders, he set out on a steady journey (aturita-desacārī), traveling without haste. The Venerable Kāludāyī, knowing that the Buddha had set out on the journey, thought, "It is proper to inform King Suddhodana," and flying into the sky, he appeared clearly at the golden palace of King Suddhodana. As soon as the King saw the Elder, he was filled with joy...
500:
...and having him sit on a royal throne worthy only of holy ones, he offered the Elder a bowl full of alms-food and curries prepared for himself. When the Venerable Kāludāyī received the food and made a sign as if to depart, King Suddhodana said, "Dear son, please sit and eat right here." The Elder replied, "Great King, I shall eat only when I reach the presence of the Buddha." King Suddhodana then asked, "Dear son, where is the Buddha now?" The Elder replied, "Great King, the Buddha, escorted by twenty thousand Arahants, has now set out on a journey to see you, Great King." King Suddhodana then requested, "Dear son, please eat the alms-food now offered right here in this golden palace, and until my son, the Buddha, arrives at this city of Kapilavatthu, please take alms-food from the golden palace and offer it to him."
After the Elder had finished his meal, he took the alms-food brought for the Buddha and preached a sermon. Even before the King had seen the Buddha, the Elder inspired all the relatives, kin, and ministers in King Suddhodana's palace with radiant faith and devotion toward the Buddha. While everyone was watching, he tossed the alms-bowl into the sky, flew up himself, and taking the food, offered it into the hand of the Buddha. The Buddha partook of that food.
501:
The Elder brought alms-food from the golden palace of King Suddhodana every single day and offered it to the Buddha, who was traveling the sixty-yojana journey at the rate of one yojana per day on a steady journey. (This is the present-day story for receiving the title of Etadagga).
## (C) Receiving the Distinguished Title of Etadagga
Later, on one occasion, the Buddha, while in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, reflected: "This monk Kāludāyī is one who has inspired radiant faith and devotion in all my relatives living in the golden palace of my father, King Suddhodana." He then praised the Venerable Kāludāyī, saying:
"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kulappasādakānaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷudāyī — Monks, among my disciple monks who inspire faith in their families toward me, the monk Kāludāyī is the foremost, the most excellent."
Thus, he placed him in the foremost position—the rank of Etadagga—in the category of "Kulappasādaka," those who inspire faith in their families.
This is the account of the Venerable Kāludāyī.
