## (33) The Account of the Venerable Bākula
## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration
This Bodhisatta, the Venerable Bākula, was reborn into a Brahmin family one asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons ago, before the appearance of the Buddha Anomadassī. When he reached adulthood...
502:
...he mastered the three Vedas. Finding no essence in those Vedic texts, he reflected, "I shall seek the welfare of the world beyond." He became an ascetic at the foot of a mountain, and having attained the five superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), he spent his time delighting in the entry into meditative absorptions (jhāna).
At that time, the Bodhisatta Anomadassī attained the Golden Wisdom of Omniscience and became a true Buddha in the three worlds. Escorted by a company of Noble Saṅgha, he traveled on a journey. The ascetic, the future Bākula, heard the news that "The Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—has appeared in the world." He went to the presence of the Buddha Anomadassī and listened to the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, he took refuge in the Triple Gem, but being unable to abandon his hermitage at the foot of the mountain, he continued to live there as an ascetic. He frequently went to pay homage to the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma.
One day, a wind ailment (vātābādha) arose in the body of the Buddha Anomadassī. When the ascetic came to pay homage, he heard the news that "The Buddha is unwell." He asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the illness?" When he was told, "It is a wind ailment in the stomach," the ascetic thought, "This is a good opportunity for me to perform a meritorious deed." He went to the foot of the mountain, prepared various medicines, and handed them to the attendant...
503:
...monk, saying, "Venerable Sir, please offer this medicine to the Buddha." As soon as the Buddha partook of that medicine, the wind ailment in his stomach was completely pacified and cured. When the Buddha was restored to health, the ascetic went to his presence and made an aspiration, saying, "Venerable Sir, through my medicine, Your health has been restored. By the result of this meritorious deed, in whatever life I am born in Saṃsāra, may I never have even a moment's illness, not even for the duration of a single milking of a cow." This was the special meritorious deed performed by the future Bākula in that life.
## Aspiration for the Etadagga Title in Freedom from Illness
When that future Bākula passed away from that life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm. For a long duration of one asankheyya, he wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī. Seeing the Buddha place a certain monk in the foremost position—the rank of Etadagga—in the category of being free from illness, he performed great meritorious deeds (in the same manner as the great disciples mentioned before) and made an aspiration for that foremost rank of being free from illness, the Appābādha Etadagga. The Buddha also gave him the prophecy (byākarana).
504:
## Another Life as an Ascetic Providing Medical Treatment

That noble son, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Ninety-one aeons before this present world-cycle, prior to the appearance of the Buddha Vipassī, he was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī. As in his previous lives, he became an ascetic, attained the jhānas, and lived peacefully at the foot of a mountain.

When the Bodhisatta Vipassī attained Supreme Enlightenment and became a true Buddha in the three worlds, he resided in the Khema Deer Park near the royal capital of Bandhumatī, accompanied by six million eight hundred thousand (6,800,000) monks, while providing spiritual guidance to his father, King Bandhuma.

At that time, this noble ascetic, the future Venerable Bākula, heard that a Buddha had appeared in the world. He went to the Buddha’s presence, listened to the Dhamma, and took refuge in the Triple Gem. However, unable to renounce his life as an ascetic, he continued to live in his hermitage at the foot of the mountain, though he frequently visited to attend to and serve the Buddha.

Then one day, poisonous plants bloomed in the Himavanta. Due to the touch of the wind blowing from those poisonous plants and flowers, all the monks (except for the Buddha and the two Chief Disciples) were afflicted with severe headaches. When the noble ascetic came to serve the Buddha, he saw the monks lying down with their heads covered.
505:
Seeing them, he asked, "Venerable sirs, what kind of illness has befallen the Saṅgha of monks?" When they replied, "Friend ascetic, the Saṅgha is suffering from an affliction caused by the pollen of poisonous grass," the noble ascetic thought, "This is the right time for me to personally perform service (veyyāvacca) and accumulate merit." Using his own powers, he collected and prepared various medicines and offered them to the Saṅgha. Just by inhaling the scent of that medicine, the illness of all the monks was instantly cured and ceased.

## Renovating an Old Monastery

That noble ascetic lived out his lifespan in the human world, and after passing away, he was reborn in the Brahma realm. For ninety-one aeons, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the era of Buddha Kassapa’s Dispensation, he was born as a noble son in the city of Bārāṇasī. One day, while managing his household, he thought, "My house is weak. I shall go to the border regions, bring back timber, and build a new house." He went to the border regions with carpenters. Along the way, he saw a large, dilapidated monastery complex and reflected, "Let the matter of building my new house wait. A house will not follow me through saṃsāra. If I am to do anything, I should first perform a meritorious deed that will follow me closely throughout saṃsāra."

Reflecting thus, he had the carpenters he brought with him fetch timber from the forest,
506:
and at that old monastery complex, he had them build a new Uposatha hall, a new refectory, a new fire room, a new cloister walkway, a new steam room, a new storehouse (kappiya-kuṭī), a new latrine, and a new infirmary (ārogyasālā), which he then offered to the Saṅgha. He also prepared and offered all kinds of medicines, including those for eating, drinking, and inhaling, for the use of the Saṅgha.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That noble son, the future Venerable Bākula, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans for an incalculable interval between Buddhas (the vast period between Buddha Kassapa and our Buddha). Before our Buddha appeared, he was conceived in the womb of the wife of a wealthy treasurer in the city of Kosambī. From the day of his conception, that treasurer’s house reached the pinnacle of gains and the pinnacle of good reputation and fame. After the noble son was born, his mother, the treasurer’s wife, reflected, "My son is one of great merit who has performed extraordinary deeds. As long as my son lives a long life free from illness, he will be a son who provides us with wealth and prosperity. On the day of birth, children who bathe in the great Yamunā River live long and remain free from illness." Thus, she had the child sent with great ceremony to bathe in the Yamunā River. (According to the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, he was sent to wash his head and play in the river on the fifth day after birth).
507:
While the nurse was playing with the child in the Yamunā River, dipping him in and out of the water, a large fish saw the child and thought, "This object is my food." Opening its mouth, it approached the child. The nurse, terrified, abandoned the child and fled, and the large fish swallowed him.

Because the child was one of great merit, he did not suffer but felt as if he had entered a bedchamber and was lying down. (While an ordinary child would have died upon being swallowed by a fish, this child was destined to become the Arahant Bākula. By the power of the fruit of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) that was to arise in his continuum, the child did not die and remained safe. This type of psychic power is called ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi). Due to the child's power, the large fish felt intense heat as if it had swallowed a red-hot iron ball. It swam with great speed for thirty yojanas and was caught in the net of a fisherman living in Bārāṇasī. Generally, when large fish are caught in a net, they only die when intentionally killed; however, due to the child's power, this fish died on its own as soon as it was taken out of the net, without being struck or beaten. Furthermore, while fishermen usually cut large fish into pieces before selling them, due to the child's influence, they did not cut this fish but carried it whole on a pole, wandering through the city saying, "We will only sell this for a thousand pieces of silver."
508:
No one was able to buy it. In that city of Bārāṇasī, there was a treasurer’s family with a fortune of eighty crores who had no children. When the fishermen reached the door of that treasurer’s house, the household members asked the price of the fish and bought it for a thousand pieces of silver. Although the treasurer’s wife did not usually prepare fish or meat herself, on that day, by the power of the child, she herself placed the fish on a cutting block to cut and cook it. While other women usually cut fish from the belly, the treasurer’s wife cut the fish from the back. Upon doing so, she saw the golden-colored child in the fish's belly. Overjoyed, she cried out, "I have obtained a son from the belly of a fish!" She embraced the child and went to her husband, the treasurer. The treasurer immediately had the news proclaimed throughout the city by beat of drum, then took the child to the King of Bārāṇasī and said, "Your Majesty, I have obtained a child from the belly of a fish. What should we do?" The King of Bārāṇasī replied, "This child, who could live safely and without injury in a fish's belly, is certainly one of great merit. You, Treasurer, should raise and care for this child yourself."

## Being Named Bākula

The biological parents in the Kosambī treasurer’s house heard the news that "a child was obtained from a fish's belly in a treasurer’s house in Bārāṇasī."
509:
The biological parents, the treasurer of Kosambī and his wife, traveled to Bārāṇasī. Upon arriving, when the biological mother saw the child (her own son) adorned with ornaments and playing happily, she praised him, saying, "This child is very delightful," and declared that he was her son. Then, the two treasurers' wives disputed over whose son he was:

(The Nurturing Mother):
"This child is my son."

(The Birth Mother):
"Where did you obtain this son?"

(The Nurturing Mother):
"I obtained him from the belly of a fish."

(The Birth Mother):
"If that is so, this child is not your son; he is my son."

(The Nurturing Mother):
"Where did you obtain this son?"

(The Birth Mother):
"I carried this son in my womb for ten months and gave birth to him. After he was born, while I was letting my son bathe and play in the Yamunā River, a large fish swallowed him."

(The Nurturing Mother):
"Another fish must have swallowed your son. As for this child, I truly obtained him from the belly of a fish."
510:
In this manner, the two treasurers' wives—the birth mother and the nurturing mother—disputed over the child and both went to the palace to seek a judgment from the King of Bārāṇasī.

The King of Bārāṇasī decided: "Since this Kosambī treasurer’s wife carried him in her womb for ten months, I cannot judge that she is not the mother. Since those who buy a fish do not usually buy it after the entrails and liver have been removed—meaning it is customary to buy it along with its contents—and since he was obtained from the belly of that fish, I cannot judge that this Bārāṇasī treasurer’s wife is not the mother. This child is a biological son (atraja) to the Kosambī treasurer’s wife and a given son (dinnaka) to the Bārāṇasī treasurer’s wife. Therefore, let the child be the heir to both households—the Kosambī treasurer’s house and the Bārāṇasī treasurer’s house." From that time on, both households reached the pinnacle of gains and the pinnacle of good reputation and fame. Because he was raised in comfort by two families, they named the child "Bākula Kumāra" (the young nobleman Bākula).

## The Luxury of the Young Nobleman Bākula

When the young nobleman Bākula reached the age of maturity, his parents in both Kosambī and Bārāṇasī had three palaces built for him in each city. They provided many dancers and attendants to serve and entertain him. The young nobleman Bākula lived for four months in one city and four months in the other. The young nobleman Bākula—
511:
After living and enjoying the wealth of a merchant in one city for four months, he had a large pavilion built on joined boats. In that pavilion, the merchant's son Bākula, along with dancers and female attendants, was conveyed and sent to another city with great ceremony. The merchant's son Bākula, enjoying great merchant wealth, arrived at the other city only after four months.

The dancers and female attendants residing in that other city, thinking, "The noble merchant's son will arrive at the halfway point in two months' time," went to meet him halfway. They surrounded, entertained, and cared for the merchant's son Bākula, bringing him to their city within two months. The dancers and female attendants from the city who had accompanied him had to return to their own city from the halfway point. In the city he reached, the merchant's son Bākula lived enjoying merchant wealth for four months, and then departed for the other city in the same manner. In this way, the merchant's son Bākula lived happily, enjoying immense merchant wealth, until he reached the full age of eighty years.

## The Wealthy Youth Bākula Ordaining and Becoming an Arahant

When the merchant's son Bākula reached the full age of eighty, our Bodhisatta attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and became the Buddha in the three realms. After preaching the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he gradually traveled on a journey.
512:
He arrived at the city of Kosambī. (According to the Majjhima-bhāṇaka elders, he arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī.) When the merchant Bākula heard the news that "The Buddha has arrived at our city," being urged by his past meritorious deeds (adhikāra), he took many perfumes and flowers, went to the presence of the Buddha, and listened to the Dhamma. Great faith (saddhā) arose in him, and he entered the Order as a monk. That Venerable Bākula remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days, and at dawn on the eighth day, he became an Arahant possessing the analytical insights (Paṭisambhidā-patta).

At that time, the dancers and female attendants who had served and entertained Venerable Bākula during his lay life in the two cities of Vārāṇasī and Kosambī returned to their parents' homes. While living in those homes, they sewed robes and sent them as offerings to Venerable Bākula. For half a month (one pakkhā), the Great Elder used the robes sent and offered by the residents of Kosambī. For the other half of the month, he used the robes sent and offered by the residents of Vārāṇasī. In this way, he used the robes offered by the residents of the two cities alternately for half a month each. In this manner, whenever excellent requisites appeared in the two cities of Vārāṇasī and Kosambī, they were sent and offered only to Venerable Bākula.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

While Venerable Bākula lived as a householder for eighty years, not even for the duration of picking up a piece of solid perfume
513:
or a piece of scented wood with two fingers to smell it, did any illness ever occur. In his eightieth year, he peacefully entered monkhood. Even after becoming a monk, Venerable Bākula never had the slightest illness, nor was there ever any deficiency in the four requisites. Therefore, the Buddha, in the assembly of the Dhamma where he praised the Noble Saṅgha with Etadagga titles at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, spoke in praise of Venerable Bākula:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ appābādhānaṃ yadidaṃ bākulo."
"Monks, among my disciple monks who are free from illness, the monk Bākula is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha placed him in the foremost position—the Etadagga title—in the category of "Appābādha" (being free from illness).

## The Marvels of Venerable Bākula

In this regard, I shall further extract and present the marvels of Venerable Bākula from the Bākula Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa:

At one time, while Venerable Bākula was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha, the naked ascetic Kassapa (Acela Kassapa), who was a friend of Venerable Bākula in his past lay life, came to Venerable Bākula. After exchanging pleasantries and sitting in a suitable place, he asked Venerable Bākula, "Friend Bākula, how long has it been since you ordained?" Venerable Bākula replied, "Friend, it has been eighty years since I ordained."
514: When he replied thus, Acela Kassapa asked Venerable Bākula rudely, like a false monk outside the Sasana, "In these eighty years, how many times have you engaged in sexual intercourse?" Then, Venerable Bākula spoke of his own marvels in the following manner: (1) "Friend Kassapa, you should not ask me so rudely, 'Friend Bākula, in these eighty years, how many times have you engaged in sexual intercourse?' Friend Kassapa, you should only ask me, 'Friend Bākula, in these eighty years, how many times has a perception associated with sensual pleasure (kāmasaññā) arisen in your mind?' Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained (at this time, Venerable Bākula was 160 years old and had 80 years of monkhood). In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—not once has a perception of sensual pleasure (kāmasaññā) arisen in me." (That not even a single perception of sensual pleasure arose in eighty years is one of the marvels of Venerable Bākula). (2-3) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—not once has a perception of ill-will (byāpādasaññā) or a perception of cruelty (vihiṃsāsaññā) arisen in me." (That a perception of ill-will never arose is one marvel, and that a perception of cruelty never arose is another marvel).
515: (4) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—not once has a sensual thought (kāmavitakka) arisen in me." (That a sensual thought never once occurred is also a marvel). (5-6) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—not once has a thought of ill-will (byāpādavitakka) or a thought of cruelty (vihiṃsāvitakka) arisen in me." (That a thought of ill-will never once occurred is one marvel, and that a thought of cruelty never once occurred is another marvel). (7) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—I have never delighted in nor accepted a robe offered by lay donors (who were not relatives)." (That he never once delighted in or accepted a robe from non-relative donors is also a marvel). (8) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—I have never once cut a robe (cloth intended for a robe) with a knife." (That he never cut one is also a marvel). (9-33) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons: I have never once sewn a robe with a needle; (p) I have never once dyed a robe with dye;
516: I have never once sewn a Kathina robe; I have never once participated in or arranged the sewing of robes for fellow monks; I have never once delighted in a meal to which I was invited by a lay donor; The thought, 'It would be good if some donor would invite me,' has never once arisen in me; I have never once sat inside a house or under the eaves of a house in a village; I have never once eaten a meal inside a village; I have never once looked at a woman with the sign of femininity; I have never once preached the Dhamma to a woman, not even a verse of four lines; (It is permissible to preach the Dhamma to a woman in five or six words; if a question is asked, it is permissible to answer even with a thousand verses. However, the Elder did not do so even though it was allowable. Indeed, this work of preaching is mostly the duty of monks who frequent the houses of donors (kulūpaka). This is to be specially noted). I have never once approached or gone to a nunnery; (In this case too, it is permissible to go to a nunnery to inquire after the sick; however, the Elder did not do so even though it was allowable. It is the same in all matters).
517: I have never preached the Dhamma to a nun (bhikkhunī); I have never preached the Dhamma to a female trainee (sikkhamānā); I have never preached the Dhamma to a female novice (sāmaṇerī); I have never acted as a preceptor (upajjhāya) to ordain a novice; I have never acted as a preceptor to ordain a monk; I have never given dependence (nissaya) to even a single monk; I have never had a novice attend to me (i.e., I have never accepted the service or care of a novice); I have never bathed in a bathhouse; I have never bathed by rubbing the body with bathing powder (soap powder); I have never asked a fellow monk to massage my body (meaning, I have never ordered any fellow monk, 'Please massage my body'); Not even for the duration of a single milking of a cow has any illness occurred in my body; I have never had to consume even a piece of medicine as small as a portion of a gallnut (meaning, I have never had to eat even a small piece of gallnut as medicine for health); I have never slept leaning against a backrest; I have never slept lying down on a bed. (This is also a marvel). (34) "Friend Kassapa, it has been eighty years since I ordained. In these eighty years—eighty rainy seasons—I—"
518:
I have never spent the rains in a village monastery. (This staying in forest monasteries for as long as his monkhood is another marvel of the Elder Bākula).

(35) "Friend Kassapa, after I became a monk, I was one with defilements (a worldling monk) for only seven days, eating the alms-food of the country. Then, on the eighth day, the fruition of Arahantship became manifest in me." (This too is a marvel of Venerable Bākula).

(Upon hearing these marvels of Venerable Bākula, Acela Kassapa requested to be ordained in this Dispensation. Venerable Bākula did not act as the preceptor (upajjhāya) himself, but arranged for another suitable Elder to be the preceptor and supported Acela Kassapa in attaining monkhood.

Thereafter, Venerable Kassapa practiced the Dhamma with great diligence and soon reached the fruition of Arahantship, becoming an Arahant).

(36) Later, on one occasion, Venerable Bākula (aged one hundred and sixty) took the key and went from cell to cell, saying, "Venerables, come; Venerables, come; today my Parinibbāna will take place." (This ability to announce and invite others is another marvel of Venerable Bākula).

(37) After Venerable Bākula had thus invited the Saṅgha, and when the Saṅgha of fellow practitioners had assembled—
519:
—he reflected: "While alive, I have never been a burden to any other monk; I have not given responsibility for my bodily needs to even a single other monk. Now, when I attain Parinibbāna, let this body of mine not be a burden or a cause for concern to the Saṅgha of fellow practitioners." He then entered the fire-element meditation (tejokasina-jhāna) and, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, attained Parinibbāna. Immediately upon his Parinibbāna, the fire element arose from his body and consumed it, so that the skin, flesh, and blood were exhausted, leaving only relics the color of jasmine buds. (This is another marvel of Venerable Bākula).

This is the account of Venerable Bākula.

## (34) The Account of Venerable Sobhita

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Venerable Sobhita was a man of good family in the time of Padumuttara Buddha in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī. Having come of age, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost (etadagga) position among those who recollect past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). He performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position. Padumuttara Buddha then gave him a prophecy.
520:
## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That man of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, without falling into the four lower realms, wandered through the worlds of devas and humans. In the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī. The youth was named Sobhita.

Later, Sobhita the youth heard the Buddha's Dhamma, gained faith, and entered the monkhood. Through the practice of Vipassanā, he attained Arahantship and became exceptionally proficient in the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

## (c) Attaining the Foremost Title

Five hundred aeons ago, this Venerable Sobhita had ordained in a non-Buddhist sect and attained the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-catuttha-jhāna) which is detached from perception (saññā-virāga). Dying without losing his jhāna, he was reborn in the Asaññasatta (unconscious) realm. He remained there for the full lifespan of five hundred aeons. When those five hundred aeons ended, he became the youth Sobhita in this human world. Having ordained in this liberating Dispensation and practiced Vipassanā, he became a Tevijja Arahant, endowed with the three knowledges (pubbenivāsa, dibbacakkhu, āsavakkhaya).

One day, while recollecting his past sequence of aggregates, he saw the rebirth (paṭisandhi) of this final life, but then saw only the death (cuti) of the third life back. (He did not see the second life, which was in the Asaññasatta realm).
521:
(The knowledge of recollecting past lives, though it takes death and rebirth as its object, can only grasp them in connection with the sequence of mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) which have the relation of proximity (anantara-paccaya). Therefore, he did not see the previous second life in the Asaññasatta realm, which consists only of matter (rūpa). — From Sārattha-ṭီkā 2, 297).

Then, being unable to recollect with his past-life knowledge the unconscious (asaññasatta) existence between this final life and the third life back, he deduced: "For beings wandering in Saṃsāra, there is no time when aggregates do not occur; only those born in the Asaññasatta realm exist without mind for as long as five hundred aeons. Therefore, I must certainly have been born in the Asaññasatta realm for the duration of five hundred aeons between this life and the third life." Thus, he grasped that Asaññasatta existence by way of inference.

Such recollection of the Asaññasatta existence, where there are no mental aggregates, can be performed perfectly only by Buddhas. Thus, Venerable Sobhita's recollection of the Asaññasatta existence by way of inference was a difficult feat, like hitting one tip of a hair with another tip of a hair, or like showing footprints in the trackless sky. Therefore, when the Buddha held the assembly to confer the foremost titles based on this event, he said of Venerable Sobhita:

"Monks, among my monk disciples who recollect past lives, Sobhita is the foremost."
522:
Thus praising him, the Buddha placed him in the foremost (etadagga) position as "one who has attained the recollection of past lives" (pubbenivāsalābhī).

(The details of Venerable Sobhita's knowledge of past lives should be noted from the Vinaya Pārājika, the end of the Vinītavatthu of the fourth Pārājika, along with its Commentary and Sub-commentary).

This is the account of Venerable Sobhita.

**********

## (35) The Account of Venerable Upāli

## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Venerable Upāli was a man of good family in Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who are bearers of the Vinaya. He performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position. The Buddha gave him a prophecy.

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That man of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the worlds of devas and humans. In the era of this Buddha's Dispensation, he was born into a barber family and was named Upāli. When he came of age, he was the one who trimmed the hair and beards and adorned the six Sakyan princes: Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Kimbila, Bhagu, Ānanda, and Devadatta. While the Buddha was staying in the Anupiya mango grove near the town of Anupiya—
523:
—he ordained together with those six princes who had come to the forest to enter the monkhood. (The details of their ordination can be found in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 19, starting from page 145).

After becoming a monk, Venerable Upāli heard the Dhamma from the Buddha and requested: "Venerable Sir, please grant me permission to live in a forest monastery." The Buddha said: "Dear son, if you live in the forest, only the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura), the work of meditation, will progress. But if you live near me, both the duty of insight and the duty of books (gantha-dhura), the study of the scriptures, will be fulfilled." Venerable Upāli joyfully accepted the Buddha's words and, while practicing Vipassanā, soon attained Arahantship. Thereafter, the Buddha himself taught and transmitted the entire Vinaya Piṭaka to Venerable Upāli.

## (c) Attaining the Foremost Title

After Venerable Upāli had become proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka, he answered and decided three cases in accordance with the Buddha's intention, comparing them with the Buddha's Omniscience: (1) the Bhārukacchaka case, (2) the Ajjuka case, and (3) the Kumārakassapa case. (Among these, the Kumārakassapa case can be reviewed in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 6, Therāpadāna 28, the account of Venerable Kumārakassapa, pages 417-418).
524:
I shall briefly describe the remaining two cases:

## The Bhārukacchaka Case

A monk from Bhārukaccha dreamt that he had sexual intercourse with his former wife. Because of this dream, he thought, "I am no longer a monk; I shall return to lay life." While traveling to his home in Bhārukaccha, he met Venerable Upāli and reported the matter to him. Venerable Upāli said, "Friend, an offense cannot be committed through a dream." (This story appears in the Vinaya Pārājika Pali, page 49; Burmese translation, page 53). Bhārukaccha is a seaport.

Since dreaming is not a ground for an offense, even though the Buddha had not decided such a case before, Venerable Upāli boldly decided that there was "no offense" by using the method of inference (nayaggāha) from the rule that an offense is not committed by the emission of semen in a dream.

The Buddha, hearing of this, said: "Monks, Upāli has answered well. Just as one might show footprints in the trackless sky, so has the monk Upāli answered this problem well," and he gave his approval (Sādhu).

## The Ajjuka Case

Once, in the city of Vesālī, Venerable Ajjuka had two lay supporters, a son and a nephew...
525:
525
That donor said to Venerable Ajjuka, “Venerable Sir, between these two youths, please tell the location of this hoard of wealth to the one who has faith and devotion to the Triple Gem.” After giving this instruction, the donor passed away.

At that time, since the donor’s nephew was the one who had faith and devotion to the Triple Gem, Venerable Ajjuka told the location of the hoard of wealth to that nephew. That youth used the wealth for trade and commerce, making the fortune stable and also performing acts of charity.

Then, the donor’s son asked Venerable Ānanda, “Venerable Ānanda, (between a son and a nephew) who is the heir of the father? Is it the son who is the heir, or is it the nephew who is the heir?” When Venerable Ānanda replied, “Layman, the son is the heir of the father,” the son said, “Venerable Sir, Venerable Ajjuka has directed our family wealth to our cousin (the father’s nephew).” At that time, without investigating the matter thoroughly, Venerable Ānanda suddenly remarked, “Layman, if that is the case, Venerable Ajjuka is no longer a monk.”

Then, Venerable Ajjuka said to Venerable Ānanda, “Friend Ānanda, please give me a formal decision.” At that time, Venerable Upāli took the side of Venerable Ajjuka. (In this matter, it should be specially noted that Venerable Upāli did not take Venerable Ajjuka’s side out of favoritism;
526:
526
rather, he took Venerable Ajjuka’s side because he knew well that no offense had been committed, and he did so to support a conscientious person and to uphold the Vinaya.)

Then, Venerable Upāli asked Venerable Ānanda, “Friend Ānanda, if a monk is instructed by the owner of wealth to tell the location of that wealth to a certain person, and he tells that person, what offense does that monk commit?” Venerable Ānanda replied, “Venerable Sir, he commits no offense; he does not even commit a minor offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa).” Then Venerable Upāli explained to Venerable Ānanda, “Friend Ānanda, this Venerable Ajjuka was instructed by the owner of the wealth to direct the location of the hoard to a certain person, and thus he directed it to the nephew. Friend Ānanda, Venerable Ajjuka is without offense; he is innocent.” Thus, he delivered a bold and decisive judgment. The Blessed One, hearing of this matter, praised him by saying, “Bhikkhus, the monk Upāli has decided and answered well,” and gave him his approval (Sādhu). (Furthermore, the Apadāna of this Venerable Upāli is very inspiring. One should look for and appreciate the Pali and meaning of that Upāli-apadāna in the Chiddapidhānanī text by the Most Venerable Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw.)

In this way, the Blessed One gave his approval for each decision and, making those three decisions the occasion, later, in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, he addressed Venerable Upāli:
527:
527
“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ upāli — Monks, among my monk disciples who uphold the Vinaya, Upāli is the foremost.”

Thus, praising him, he placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “Vinayadhara — one who upholds the Vinaya Pitaka.”

This is the account of Venerable Upāli.
**********
## (36) The Story of Venerable Nandaka
## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration
This future Venerable Nandaka was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha’s discourse, he saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “Bhikkhunovāda — exhorting the bhikkhunīs.” He performed great meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that position. The Buddha also granted him a prophecy (byādika).

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That youth performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this present era when the Buddha appeared, he was born into a good family in the city of Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Buddha’s discourse, gained faith, and entered the monkhood in the Dispensation.
528:
528
By practicing Vipassanā meditation, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship and became an Arahant. That Venerable Nandaka was proficient and skilled in the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā). When the fourfold assembly came into his presence, he was known as “Dhamma-preacher Venerable Nandaka” because he was able to preach the Dhamma by captivating the minds of all.

When a conflict arose between the Koliyans and the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu over the water of the Rohiṇī River, the Blessed One quenched the fire of enmity by giving them the cool water of the Dhamma. Consequently, 250 Sakyan princes from each side left their households and were ordained as monks. When those five hundred Sakyan monks became dissatisfied and unhappy in the Dispensation, the Buddha took them to Lake Kuṇāla. By preaching the Kuṇāla Jātaka there, he realized that those monks had developed spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He then preached the Four Noble Truths and established them in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Later, in the Mahāvana forest, he preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta and established those five hundred monks in the Fruit of Arahantship. (The details of this account should be reviewed in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 22, starting from page 388.)

The former wives of those five hundred Sakyan Arahants of the Mahāsamaya said, “What shall we do in this palace now?” All of them, being of one mind, went to the Great Foster-Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and, with her as their leader,
529:
529
they went to the Blessed One at the Mahāvana forest in the city of Vesālī. The Great Foster-Mother requested the Blessed One to allow women to become bhikkhunīs in this Dispensation. When the Buddha permitted the Bhikkhunī Sāsana, the Great Foster-Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī became a bhikkhunī by accepting the eight heavy rules (garudhamma-paṭiggahaṇa-upasampadā). Those five hundred Sakyan princesses attained the status of bhikkhunīs through ordination by one side (ekato-upasampanna), as there was no Bhikkhunī Saṅgha at that time, but only the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Notably, in the life immediately preceding this one, all five hundred of those Sakyan princesses had been the five hundred queens when Venerable Nandaka was a king.

At that time, the Blessed One issued a decree that “monks must exhort the bhikkhunīs.” When it was Venerable Nandaka’s turn, he perceived that those five hundred bhikkhunīs had been his attendant queens in a past life. He reflected, “If another monk who possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives sees me sitting in the midst of these five hundred bhikkhunīs, preaching the Dhamma with various similes and reasons, he might look at this past event and say disparagingly, ‘Venerable Nandaka has not yet given up his harem; Venerable Nandaka looks quite grand surrounded by a group of concubines.’” Because of this reflection, he did not go himself but sent another monk in his place to exhort the bhikkhunīs.

In particular, those five hundred bhikkhunīs greatly longed for and desired only the exhortation of Venerable Nandaka.
530:
530
For this reason, the Blessed One said to Venerable Nandaka, “When your turn arrives, do not send another monk, but go yourself and exhort the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha.” Venerable Nandaka, unable to refuse the Buddha’s words, when his turn arrived on the fourteenth-day Uposatha, gave an exhortation to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. He established all five hundred of those Sakyan princesses in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) through a discourse on the six sense bases (āyatana). He caused them to become Noble Ones (Ariyas) who are Stream-enterers.

Those five hundred bhikkhunīs were delighted and satisfied with Venerable Nandaka’s discourse. They went to the Blessed One and reported the supramundane attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry they had achieved. The Blessed One further considered, “By whose preaching will these bhikkhunīs reach the higher Paths and Fruits?” He then perceived, “If they hear the very same discourse preached by Venerable Nandaka on that first day, all five hundred bhikkhunīs will reach the Fruit of Arahantship.” Thus, on the next day, he sent them again to listen to the Dhamma from Venerable Nandaka. On that second day, those five hundred bhikkhunīs heard the same discourse that Venerable Nandaka had preached on the first day, and all five hundred reached the Fruit of Arahantship.

On that day, when those five hundred bhikkhunīs came to pay respects to the Blessed One, he, knowing the benefit of the discourse preached by Venerable Nandaka, remarked, “Yesterday, the monk Nandaka’s
531:
531
discourse was like the full moon appearing on the fourteenth day; today, the monk Nandaka’s discourse is like the full moon appearing on the fifteenth day (the full moon day).” Thus, he gave his approval (Sādhu) to Venerable Nandaka. (The details of these events should be studied in the Nandakovāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, Uparipaṇṇāsa.)

## (c) Attaining the Foremost Title
Making that very event the occasion, the Blessed One later, in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, addressed Venerable Nandaka:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunovādakānaṃ yadidaṃ nandako — Monks, among my monk disciples who exhort the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka is the foremost.”

Thus, praising him, he placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of “Bhikkhunovādaka — one who exhorts the bhikkhunīs.”

This is the account of Venerable Nandaka.
**********
## (37) The Story of Venerable Nanda
## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration
This future Venerable Nanda was also born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position—
532:
532
Among those who are "Indriyesu guttadvāra = monks who guard the doors of their senses," he saw one being placed in the foremost position (Etadagga). Having performed meritorious deeds of great service (adhikāra), he made an aspiration for that very position. The Buddha also granted him a prophecy (byādika).

## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
That noble son, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his lives and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, was born in this final existence (pacchima bhava) in the royal city of Kapilavatthu as the son of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the stepmother of the Buddha. (Two or three days after Queen Mahāmāyā Devī gave birth to the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the younger sister of Māyā Devī and stepmother of the Bodhisatta, gave birth to Prince Nanda. Regarding the account of Prince Nanda's ordination, one should refer back to the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume III, Chapter 1, starting from page 129).

On the third day of the Buddha's first visit to the royal city of Kapilavatthu after his Enlightenment, He ordained his younger brother, Prince Nanda. (The detailed account has been mentioned previously).

From the day he became a monk, Venerable Nanda lived only remembering the words sent by his sister (fiancée) Janapadakalyāṇī: "O Lord, please return quickly." When he remembered those words, it was as if Janapadakalyāṇī was standing right beside him. Venerable Nanda, being oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati) with the Dispensation (Sāsana),
533:
533
...fled from the Nigrodhārāma monastery to a place slightly outside. At that time, for Venerable Nanda, even if he had passed only a single bush or a cluster of trees, it seemed as if the Buddha was standing right in front of him. Then, Venerable Nanda, like a cock's feather thrown into a fire, shrank back and returned to his own dwelling in the monastery.

Then the Buddha reflected: "The monk Nanda is living very heedlessly; he is unable to dispel his dissatisfaction with the Dispensation. It is proper that I act to bring peace to Nanda's mind." Having considered this, He said to Venerable Nanda, "Come, dear Nanda, let us go on a journey to the celestial realm."

Venerable Nanda replied, "Exalted Buddha, how can I go to the celestial realm, a place that can only be reached by those with psychic powers? I cannot go, Bhante."

The Buddha encouraged him, saying, "Dear Nanda, just resolve your mind to go to the celestial realm. If you resolve to go, you will reach the celestial realm and see the celestial objects."

(This account is from the Anguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, pages 244-245. Hereafter, I shall describe the account of Venerable Nanda based on the Udāna Pali and its Commentary).

After the Buddha had spoken thus, He thought, "I shall quench the lust (rāga) arising in Nanda's continuum by a skillful means (upāya)," and then He took Venerable Nanda...
534:
534
...as if taking him by the arm, and by His psychic power, He led him towards the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. (Before going directly to the celestial realm), on the way, He showed him an old female monkey in a burnt field, perched on a burnt tree stump, whose ears, nose, and tail were singed by fire, looking ragged and extremely shriveled with age. After showing this, He proceeded to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

(In this matter: If the Buddha had only intended for Venerable Nanda to see the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, or merely for him to enter it, He could have shown it to him while sitting in the Jetavana monastery, as He did when performing the miracle of world-revelation (loka-vivaraṇa), or He could have sent Nanda alone to the celestial realm by His power.

However, the Buddha wanted to show him that old monkey on the way so that Venerable Nanda could easily realize that a human body is inferior, loathsome, and disgusting compared to a celestial body. He also wanted to show him the glory and luxury of the celestial world vividly. Only by showing him in this way would Nanda gain the benefit of being particularly delighted in practicing the noble life (brahmacariya) of the Threefold Training for the sake of celestial bliss. Therefore, it should be specifically noted that the Buddha personally took Venerable Nanda and went to the celestial realm).

Thus, the Buddha took Venerable Nanda to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Upon reaching there, He showed him five hundred nymphs (celestial maidens) with feet the color of a pigeon's feet, who had come to entertain Sakka, the King of Devas, and who were standing there after paying homage to the Buddha.
535:
535
After showing them to Venerable Nanda, the Buddha and Venerable Nanda had the following dialogue:

(The Buddha)
"Nanda, do you see these five hundred nymphs with feet the color of a pigeon's feet?"

(Venerable Nanda)
"I see them, Bhante."

(The Buddha)
"Nanda, what do you think of the question I am about to ask? You may answer as you please. Between the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī and these five hundred nymphs with feet the color of a pigeon's feet, who is more beautiful, more sightly, and more pleasing?"

(Venerable Nanda)
"Bhante, compared to these five hundred nymphs, the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī is like that old female monkey with the mangled ears and nose (whom we saw on the way). She does not even count as a woman; she does not reach even a fraction of their beauty, she is not comparable. Indeed, these five hundred nymphs are far more beautiful, more sightly, and more pleasing."

(The Buddha)
"Nanda, delight in the Dispensation! Nanda, delight in the Dispensation! I guarantee (take responsibility) for your obtaining these five hundred nymphs with feet the color of a pigeon's feet." (Meaning: "If you, dear Nanda, delight in the Dispensation and practice the Dhamma, I guarantee that you will obtain these five hundred nymphs.")

(Venerable Nanda)
"Bhante, if the Buddha can guarantee that I will obtain these five hundred nymphs...
536:
536
...with feet the color of a pigeon's feet, I shall delight in the Dispensation under the Buddha."

After this agreement was made, the Buddha, in an instant, as if taking Venerable Nanda by the arm, vanished from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and reappeared in the Jetavana monastery.

(In this matter: One might ask why the Buddha showed nymphs to Venerable Nanda, who was being oppressed by lust (rāga). The answer is: He showed the nymphs to easily remove the defilements (kilesa) existing in Nanda's continuum. To clarify further: Just as a skilled physician, wishing to easily treat a patient whose humors—phlegm, bile, and wind—are aggravated, first uses oil treatments to soften and loosen the humors before easily removing them with emetics and purgatives; even so, the Great Physician, the Buddha, who is peerlessly skilled in disciplining those to be tamed, gave the patient Venerable Nanda the "softening medicine" of celestial objects to loosen the aggravated humor of lust. This was because He wished to completely remove the humors of defilements with the emetic and purgative of the Noble Path (Ariya Magga). This should be specifically noted.

Furthermore, one might ask why the Buddha, while desiring for Venerable Nanda to live the noble life of the Dispensation, gave a guarantee for him to live with nymphs, which is a non-celibate life (abrahmacariya-vāsa). The answer is: The lustful defilement that had long and firmly settled on the object of Janapadakalyāṇī could only be easily abandoned if it were shifted to a new object, the nymphs.
537:
537
Therefore, He gave the guarantee because it would allow for an easy renunciation. (In the Buddha's gradual instruction (ānupubbī-kathā), the fact that He preached the talk on heaven (sagga-kathā) serves as evidence for this meaning. From Udāna Commentary, 154-155).

From the time he reached the Jetavana monastery, Venerable Nanda practiced the monk's Dhamma day and night for the sake of obtaining the nymphs. Then the Buddha said to the monks, "Monks, you should go around and speak in various places near Nanda's meditation dwelling, saying: 'It is said that a certain monk is practicing the monk's Dhamma restlessly because he wants to obtain nymphs, having made the Buddha his guarantor.'"

The monks agreed, "Very well, Bhante," and within earshot of Venerable Nanda, they teased and ridiculed him, saying, "It is said that Venerable Nanda is practicing the noble life because he wants nymphs. It is said that the Buddha has guaranteed that Venerable Nanda will obtain five hundred nymphs with feet the color of a pigeon's feet. Venerable Nanda is indeed a hireling (bhataka)! Venerable Nanda is indeed one who has been bought (upakkītaka)!"

Hearing these words, Venerable Nanda thought, "These monks are not talking about someone else; they are talking about me. My conduct is indeed improper!" and "Because of my lack of restraint over the senses, I have to endure such shameful ridicule from my fellow monks. I shall now well-subdue and guard those senses." With this thought, from that time on, in the east, west, south, north, above, below, and across,
538:
Whenever he wished to look at the directions or intermediate directions, he practiced the supreme practice of sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara-paṭipatti) by constantly maintaining mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) to prevent the arising of unwholesome states such as greed and hatred. While striving diligently in the monk's practice, he soon exhausted the taints (āsavas) and attained the state of an Arahant.

At that time, a Brahma who was an Arahant came to the presence of the Buddha at midnight and reported the good news that Venerable Nanda had become an Arahant. Immediately after the Brahma's report, the knowledge that 'The monk Nanda has realized the fruit of Arahantship' clearly arose in the Buddha's mind as He reflected on it.

## Releasing and Being Released from the Guarantee

When Venerable Nanda was teased and mocked by his fellow monks, he felt great spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: 'Having ordained in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, I have made the Buddha a guarantor for the sake of obtaining celestial nymphs. I have indeed committed a heavy matter.' Feeling great shame and fear (hiri-ottappa), he practiced the monk's Dhamma incessantly and attained the fruit of Arahantship. After that, he thought, 'I shall release the Buddha from that guarantee/responsibility.' Having thought so, when morning came, Venerable Nanda went to the Buddha, paid homage, sat in a suitable place, and said: 'Venerable Sir, regarding the five hundred dove-footed nymphs for whom the Buddha stood as guarantor...'
539:
...for me to obtain, the Buddha stood as a guarantor. Venerable Sir, I now release the Exalted One from that guarantee.'

Then the Buddha said to Venerable Nanda: 'Dear Nanda, I too have already known with my mind, encompassing your mind, that "the monk Nanda has realized the fruit of Arahantship." Moreover, a Brahma has also come and reported that you have reached the fruit of Arahantship. Dear Nanda, from the very moment your mind was liberated from the taints without clinging (i.e., when you attained Arahantship), I was already released from that guarantee. (Immediately after your mind was freed from the taints, I was naturally released from that guarantee; there is no need for you to specially release me.)'

Having said this, because the Buddha clearly saw the meaning of being entirely unshaken by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as pleasure and pain, since all taints had been exhausted in Venerable Nanda, He was greatly satisfied and joyful, and uttered this inspired verse (Udāna):

Yassa nittiṇṇo paṅko,
maddito kāmakaṇṭako.
Mohakkhayaṃ anuppatto,
sukhadukkhesu na vedhatī sa bhikkhu.

Yassa = In which Noble One. Paṅko = the deep mire of saṃsāra.
540:
Nittiṇṇo = has been crossed over by building the bridge of the Noble Path directly to the shore of Nibbāna. Yassa = In which Noble One. Kāmakaṇṭako = the thorn of sensual craving (kilesa-kāma) which pierces beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—unbearably. Maddito = has been crushed and destroyed without a trace by the staff of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). Yo = Which Noble One. Mohakkhayaṃ = Nibbāna, the fruit of Arahantship where delusion is exhausted. Anuppatto = has reached by following the four stages of Path-knowledge. Sa bhikkhu = That monk who has become an Arahant, having broken the thick mass of the darkness of defilements. Sukhadukkhesu = due to the eight worldly conditions such as pleasure and pain. Na vedhati = does not tremble or fluctuate with an unsteady mind like worldlings (puthujjana).

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At another time, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery, He praised Venerable Nanda in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha:

'Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ yadidaṃ nando = Monks, among my disciple monks who guard the doors of the sense-faculties, Nanda is the foremost.'

Thus, He placed him in the position of Etadagga (foremost) in 'indriyesu guttadvāratā' (guarding the doors of the sense-faculties).
541:
(In this regard: Other disciple monks of the Buddha also guard their sense-faculties. However, Venerable Nanda was exceptional; if he wished to look at any of the ten directions, he would only do so after reflecting with the four types of clear comprehension (sampajañña): clear comprehension of purpose (satthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Indeed, that Venerable Nanda thought, 'Because I did not guard my sense-faculties, I fell into abnormality such as dissatisfaction in the Dispensation; I shall now restrain this lack of sense-control excessively.' Thus, he renewed his efforts, possessed strong hiri and ottappa, and because he had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) for the sake of sense-restraint since a hundred thousand aeons ago, he reached the pinnacle of excellence in guarding them. He would look at all directions without letting go of the four types of clear comprehension. Therefore, it should be noted that the Buddha placed only Venerable Nanda in the foremost position of Etadagga in 'indriyesu guttadvāratā'.)

This is the story of Venerable Nanda.

**********

## (38) Story of Venerable Mahākappina

## (a) Past Aspiration of the Elder

This Great Being, the future Venerable Mahākappina, was a man of good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. One day, while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Buddha declare a certain monk foremost (Etadagga) in the category of 'bhikkhu-ovādaka' (one who exhorts and teaches monks amazingly).
542:
Having performed meritorious deeds, he made an aspiration for that position of Etadagga as a bhikkhu-ovādaka. Padumuttara Buddha also gave him the prophecy that his aspiration would be fulfilled. (The Aṅguttara Commentary only briefly mentions his good deeds during the time of Kassapa Buddha and details his final life. In this Mahābuddhavaṃsa, to inspire faith in the readers, I shall first describe his meritorious deeds during the intervening period as found in the Dhammapada Commentary.)

## Life as the Head of Weavers

That future Venerable Mahākappina, having performed meritorious deeds throughout that life, passed away and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In one life, he became the head of weavers in a large weavers' village near the city of Bārāṇasī. At that time, one thousand Paccekabuddhas used to live in the Himalayas for eight months (four months of winter and four months of summer) and stay in the districts during the four months of the rainy season.

Once, those Paccekabuddhas descended from the sky near Bārāṇasī and sent eight Paccekabuddhas to the King of Bārāṇasī, instructing them: 'Go to the King and ask for manual labor (hatthakamma) to build a monastery.' Specifically, it was the time when the King of Bārāṇasī was about to celebrate the plowing festival (vappamaṅgala).
543:
As soon as the King of Bārāṇasī heard the news that 'the Noble Paccekabuddhas have arrived,' he went out immediately without delay. After inquiring about the reason for their visit, he said: 'Venerable Sirs, today there is no opportunity to build a monastery. Tomorrow we have our plowing festival. Therefore, please let us build it on the third day from today.' After saying this, he entered the palace without inviting the Paccekabuddhas for alms the next day.

The Paccekabuddhas thought, 'Let us go elsewhere,' and departed from the royal palace. At that moment, the wife of the head weaver, who was going to Bārāṇasī for some business, saw the Paccekabuddhas. She paid homage with respect and devotion and asked: 'Venerable Sirs, why are you traveling at an unusual time?' The Paccekabuddhas explained the situation from the beginning. Hearing this, the weaver's wife, who was endowed with both faith and wisdom, invited them: 'Venerable Sirs, please accept my alms tomorrow out of compassion.' When the Paccekabuddhas said, 'Sister, we Paccekabuddhas are many,' she asked, 'How many are there, Venerable Sirs?' The Paccekabuddhas replied, 'There are about a thousand.' Then the woman said, 'Venerable Sirs, in this weavers' village, there are a thousand weaver households. Each household will provide for one Paccekabuddha...'
544:
“I will provide the alms-food; please accept and delight in only the alms-food I invite you to, Venerable Sirs. I myself will lead the construction of a monastery for your residence as well,” she stated clearly. The Paccekabuddhas accepted and delighted in the woman's invitation.

That woman, the wife of the chief weaver, entered the village and proclaimed, “O brothers and mothers, I have seen and invited one thousand Paccekabuddhas. Arrange places for the Venerable Ones to reside. Prepare gruel, alms-food, and so on.” Then, she had a pavilion built in the middle of the village and seats arranged. The next day, after seating the one thousand Paccekabuddhas in their respective places, she served them with excellent hard and soft food. When the meal was finished, she brought all the women living in the village and, together with them, paid homage to the Paccekabuddhas, saying, “Venerable Sirs, please grant us the promise to stay for the three months of the rainy season (Vassa).” After receiving the promise from the Paccekabuddhas, she again proclaimed in the village, “O brothers and mothers, let one man from each house take an axe, a hatchet, and so on, enter the forest to bring timber, and I wish to have monasteries built for the Paccekabuddhas to reside in.”

Upon hearing the woman's call, the people of the weaver village, each person—
545:
—built one thousand leaf-roofed huts, including night quarters and day quarters, one for each person. They took responsibility, saying, “I will serve with respect, I will serve with respect,” as their faith increased, and they served respectfully throughout the three months of the rainy season. When the rainy season ended, the wife of the chief weaver encouraged them, saying, “O brothers and mothers, prepare cloth for robes for the Paccekabuddhas who have completed their residence for the rainy season in your respective huts.” She had them offer robes worth one thousand pieces of currency to each Paccekabuddha. After the rainy season ended and the robes were offered, the Paccekabuddhas gave a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), made aspirations, and departed.

## Life as a Chief Treasurer

All the people living in the weaver village performed meritorious deeds, and when they passed away from that life, they were reborn as groups of devas and devīs in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. After enjoying heavenly bliss in Tāvatiṃsa, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were reborn in the houses of treasurers (seṭṭhis) in the city of Bārāṇasī. The chief weaver became the son of the head treasurer, and his wife also became the daughter of a head treasurer. When all those women reached the age of maturity and had to go to their husbands' houses, they went to the houses of those respective sons of treasurers, just as in their previous life as weavers.
546:
One day, when a proclamation was made to hear a sermon at the monastery where Kassapa Buddha was residing, all those treasurers heard the news that “The Buddha will preach the Dhamma” and went to the monastery together with their wives to listen to the sermon. At the very moment they entered the monastery grounds, a heavy rain fell. Other people who had monks or novices as relatives ran to the precincts (pariveṇas) where those relatives resided to take shelter from the rain.

However, those one thousand treasurer couples, because they had no such relatives among the monks or novices, did not dare to enter any precinct and had to stand in the middle of the monastery grounds, getting soaked by the rain. Then, the head treasurer said to the other treasurers, “O friends, look at our state of being without a refuge and in disorder. If one is a person of good birth, one should feel ashamed by this much.” When the other treasurers asked, “Sir, what meritorious deed should our group perform?” the head treasurer consulted and suggested, “Because we have no place of intimacy, we have come to such disorder. Let us all pool our wealth and build a precinct.” When all the other treasurers agreed, saying, “Very well, sir,” the head treasurer contributed one thousand pieces of currency, the other treasurers contributed five hundred each, and their wives contributed two hundred and fifty each. Those one thousand treasurer families pooled their wealth—
547:
—and began to build a large monastery precinct for Kassapa Buddha to reside in, surrounded by one thousand pinnacled buildings (pāsādas). Because the new project was very large and the initially collected wealth was insufficient, they again contributed half of their previous donations. In this way, when the monastery precinct was completed, they held a dedication ceremony, offering a great alms-giving (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by Kassapa Buddha, and they prepared robes to be offered to twenty thousand Arahants.

## The Extraordinary Devotion of the Chief Treasurer's Wife

In particular, the wife of the head treasurer did not act exactly like the others but, relying on her own wisdom, thought, “I will worship the Buddha by doing something superior and more excellent than others.” She brought a cloth for a robe worth one thousand pieces of currency, which had a golden-yellow hue like the Anojā flower, along with a basket of Anojā flowers. When the discourse of appreciation for the monastery was being given, she worshipped Kassapa Buddha with the Anojā flowers, placed the set of robe-cloth at the feet of the Buddha, and—

“Venerable Sir, in whatever life I am born in Saṃsāra, may my body have a golden-yellow hue like this Anojā flower.
548:
May my name also be known only as Anojā.”

She made this prayer and aspiration. The Buddha also gave the blessing of appreciation, saying, “Evaṃ hotu—May it be as you have now prayed.”

## (c) Becoming Monks in the Final Life

All those people performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives, and when they passed away from that life, they were reborn in the deva realm. In the time when this current Buddha appeared, they passed away from the deva realm. The head treasurer became a prince named Mahākappina in the royal palace of the city of Kukkutavatī, and when he reached maturity, he became King Mahākappina. The other treasurers were reborn in the families of ministers. The wife of the head treasurer became a Madda princess in the royal palace of the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom. Because her complexion was golden-yellow like the Anojā flower, she was named “Anojā” according to her previous prayer.

When Princess Anojā reached maturity, she went to the palace of King Mahākappina and became the chief queen, Anojā Devī. The other treasurers' wives were also reborn in the families of ministers, and when they reached maturity, they became the wives of their former lords, the sons of the ministers, according to their previous karmic connection. All of them enjoyed splendor equal to that of King Mahākappina. The way they enjoyed it was: when King Mahākappina wore full regalia and traveled by elephant, those one thousand ministers also traveled by elephant just like the King.
549:
When the King traveled by horse or by chariot, those one thousand ministers also traveled by horse or by chariot just like the King. Thus, those one thousand virtuous people enjoyed splendor together solely due to the power of the meritorious deeds they had performed together.

## The King Sending Messengers for News

King Mahākappina had five noble horses: (1) the horse named Bala, (2) the horse named Balavāhana, (3) the horse named Puppha, (4) the horse named Pupphavāhana, and (5) the horse named Supatta. Among these five noble horses, the King himself rode the horse named Supatta, and he assigned the other four noble horses to messengers to bring news. The King would feed those four messenger heroes excellent rice and food early in the morning and command them, “Friends, go and travel for two or three yojanas around the capital of Kukkutavatī. If you hear the good news that the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—has appeared in the world, you must bring that news of happiness to me quickly.” He sent the messenger heroes to the four directions every day. Those messenger heroes would each go out from the four city gates, travel for three yojanas, and listen for news, but they would return to the city without receiving the news that the Triple Gem had appeared.
550:
## Hearing the News of the Triple Gem

Then one day, King Mahākappina, riding his noble steed named Supatta and accompanied by a thousand ministers, went out to the royal gardens. Seeing five hundred merchants entering the city looking weary from their journey, he thought, "These merchants are exhausted from travel. Surely, I shall hear some good news from them." Expecting this, he summoned the merchants and asked, "Friends, from where have you come?" The merchants replied, "Your Majesty, there is a city named Sāvatthī, one hundred and twenty yojanas from this royal city of Kukkutavatī. We have come from that city of Sāvatthī." When they said this, the King asked further, "Friends, has any extraordinary news or special event occurred in your city of Sāvatthī?" The merchants replied, "Your Majesty, there is no other special news to report. However, the Blessed Buddha has appeared in our city of Sāvatthī."

At that moment, the King’s entire body was suffused with the five kinds of joy (pīti). Unable to take note of anything else, he let a moment pass and then asked, "Friends, what news did you just report?" The merchants replied again, "Your Majesty, the Blessed Buddha has appeared in the world." The King let time pass in the same way a second and third time. On the fourth time, he asked, "Friends, what news did you just report?" and...
551:
...the merchants replied once more as before, "Your Majesty, the Blessed Buddha has appeared in the world." Then King Mahākappina said, "Friends, because you have brought me the news that the Blessed Buddha has appeared, I grant you a reward of one hundred thousand coins."

Having said this, the King asked again, "Is there any other special news?" The merchants replied, "There is, Your Majesty. The Treasure of the Dhamma has appeared in the world." Upon hearing this news, the King again let time pass three times as before. On the fourth time, when the merchants said, "The Treasure of the Dhamma has appeared in the world," he said, "Friends, because you have brought me the news that the Treasure of the Dhamma has appeared, I grant you a reward of one hundred thousand coins."

Then the King asked again, "Friends, is there any other special news?" The merchants replied, "There is, Your Majesty. The Treasure of the Saṅgha has appeared in the world." Upon hearing this news, the King again let time pass three times as before. On the fourth time, as soon as the merchants spoke even a part of the word "Saṅgha," he said, "Friends, because you have brought me the news that the Treasure of the Saṅgha has appeared, I grant you a reward of one hundred thousand coins."
552:
## King Mahākappina's Renunciation

After saying this, King Mahākappina looked at his thousand ministers and asked, "Friends, what will you do?" When the ministers asked, "Your Majesty, what will you do?", King Mahākappina replied, "Friends, because I have heard the news that the Treasure of the Buddha has appeared, the Treasure of the Dhamma has appeared, and the Treasure of the Saṅgha has appeared, I shall not return to the golden palace. From this very spot, I shall go forth intending to reach the Blessed Buddha and become a monk in his presence." The ministers also replied in unison, "Your Majesty, we too shall become monks together with you."

King Mahākappina had a message inscribed on a gold plate and said to the merchants, "Friends, Queen Anojā will grant you a reward of three hundred thousand coins on my behalf. The specific message is this: You must tell Queen Anojā, 'The King has relinquished all his royal wealth, power, and glory to you, O Queen. Please enjoy the royal sovereignty happily as you wish.' If Queen Anojā asks you, 'Where is the King?', you must tell her, 'He has departed to become a monk, intending to reach the Blessed Buddha.'" Having given this verbal message, he entrusted the gold plate to the merchants and sent them away. The ministers also sent similar messages to their own wives.
553:
After sending the merchants away, the King, riding his noble steed Supatta and accompanied by his thousand ministers, departed for the forest at that very moment.

## The Buddha Waiting in Readiness

On the day King Mahākappina was to renounce the world, the Blessed Buddha surveyed the world of sentient beings and saw King Mahākappina together with his thousand ministers. He reflected, "This King Mahākappina, having heard the good news of the appearance of the Triple Gem from the merchants and having honored their news with three hundred thousand coins, has abandoned his royal sovereignty. Accompanied by a thousand ministers, he will set out tomorrow to become a monk, intending to reach me. This King Mahākappina, along with his thousand ministers, will become Arahants endowed with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). I shall go to welcome King Mahākappina." Having reflected thus, the next day, like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) welcoming a minor village head, the Buddha himself took his bowl and robes and traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas to welcome him. He sat at the foot of a banyan tree at the landing of the river named Candabhāgā, emitting the six-colored rays.

## King Mahākappina Crossing the Three Rivers

As King Mahākappina was traveling through the forest, each riding their own horse along with the thousand ministers, they reached a river and he asked, "What is the name of this river?" When the ministers replied, "Your Majesty, this river is named Aparacchā,"...
554:
...he asked again, "Friends, what is the size of this Aparacchā river?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, the size of this river is one gāvuta in depth and two gāvutas in width." The King then asked, "Are there any boats or rafts on the bank of this river?" When the ministers replied, "There are none, Your Majesty," the King thought:

"Even while we are searching for boats and rafts, the phenomenon of birth (jāti) is carrying us toward aging (jarā), and aging is delivering us toward death (maraṇa). I am one who is free from doubt and have truly come forth for the sake of the Triple Gem. For me, by the power of those Triple Gems, let this water not act like water."

Reflecting on the virtues of the Triple Gem and meditating on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati) starting with "Itipi so Bhagavā Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho...", he recited:

"The Buddha has indeed crossed the stream of existence, reached the end of the world, and is the Knower. By this word of truth, may my journey be successful."

[Verse Meaning:] The Buddha, known as the Omniscient Buddha, the Supreme One of the world, has indeed truly crossed the vast waters of the three realms of existence to reach the shore of Nibbāna. Or—having crossed over, he has reached the end of the world with a pure heart. He is the Knower who has clearly and distinctly understood all phenomena.
555:
By this auspicious word of truth, may my journey—the act of going to the presence of the Buddha to become a monk—be fulfilled and completed without danger or hindrance. Reciting this verse repeatedly, he crossed the expanse of water two gāvutas wide together with his thousand ministers and their thousand Sindh horses. The Sindh horses ran as if on a stone slab; not even a drop of clear water moistened the tips of their hooves.

After crossing the Aparacchā river and continuing his journey, King Mahākappina encountered a second river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, it is named Nīlavāhinī." The King asked again, "Friends, what is the size of this Nīlavāhinī river?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, the size of this Nīlavāhinī river is half a yojana in both depth and width." (The rest is the same as before). The King meditated on the Recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati) starting with "Svākkhāto Bhagavatā Dhammo..." and recited:

"If the Path leads to peace, and Liberation is the ultimate happiness, by this word of truth, may my journey be successful."

[Verse Meaning:] The fourfold Noble Path, the supramundane Dhamma, can indeed truly lead to Nibbāna. And the noble Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is to be attained through the Noble Path...
556:
...is indeed ultimate happiness. By this auspicious word of truth, may my journey—the act of going to the presence of the Buddha to become a monk—be fulfilled and completed without danger or hindrance. Reciting this verse repeatedly, he crossed the expanse of water half a yojana wide together with his thousand ministers and their thousand Sindh horses. As before, the Sindh horses ran as if on a stone slab, and not even a drop of clear water moistened the tips of their hooves.

After crossing the Nīlavāhinī river and continuing his journey, King Mahākappina encountered a third river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, it is named Candabhāgā." The King asked again, "Friends, what is the size of this Candabhāgā river?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, the size of this Candabhāgā river is one yojana in both depth and width." (The rest is the same as before). Regarding this Candabhāgā river, the King meditated on the Recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati) starting with "Suppaṭipanno Bhagavato Sāvakasangho..." and recited:

"The Saṅgha has indeed crossed the wilderness, the incomparable field of merit. By this word of truth, may my journey be successful."

[Verse Meaning:] The Noble Saṅgha of the ultimate sense has indeed truly crossed the difficult journey of Saṃsāra...
557:
...has crossed over to the other shore in an amazing way. *Anuttaro* = peerless and most noble. *Puññakkhetto* = a true field of merit, the field where seeds of merit are sown. *Etena saccavajjena* = By this word of truth, this auspicious speech. *Me* = of me, named Mahākappina. *Gamanam* = my journeying to the presence of the Exalted One to become a monk. *Samijjhatu* = may it be accomplished and fulfilled without danger or hindrance.”

Reciting this verse repeatedly, he crossed the expanse of water, one league wide, together with his retinue of one thousand ministers and one thousand Sindh horses. Just as before, the Sindh horses galloped as if on a stone slab, and not even a drop of clear water moistened the tips of their hooves. (These three verses regarding King Mahākappina crossing the three rivers are extracted from the Mahākappina Thera Apadāna Pali).

## Meeting the Buddha and Ordaining

As soon as the King crossed the Candabhāgā River and proceeded, he beheld with wonder the six-colored rays of the Buddha emanating and radiating from the person of the Exalted One, who was residing at the foot of a banyan tree. At that time, the entire banyan tree—its trunk, branches, twigs, and leaves—shone brilliantly like pure gold. Then the King reflected truthfully: “This radiance is not that of the moon, nor of the sun. It is not the radiance of a deva, Māra, nāga, or garuḍa. Surely, the Great Sage of the Gotama lineage, having seen that I have come to ordain in his honor, must have come here.”
558:
At that very moment, King Mahākappina descended from his horse's back, bowed his body, and followed the direction of the radiating rays. Approaching the Exalted One, he entered within the Buddha's aura, like one submerged in a sea of realgar and orpiment. Having paid respectful homage to the Buddha, he sat down in a suitable place along with his thousand ministers. The Exalted One preached to King Mahākappina the gradual discourse, the noble path leading to the attainment of the Paths and Fruits: (1) *Dānakathā* = discourse on generosity, (2) *Sīlakathā* = discourse on virtue, (3) *Saggakathā* = discourse on the heavenly realms, (4) *Maggakathā* = discourse on the practice of the path leading to the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. At the conclusion of the teaching, King Mahākappina, together with his thousand ministers, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpattiphala*).

Then, they all rose from their seats and requested for ordination as monks. The Exalted One, considering whether miraculous (*iddhimaya*) bowls and robes would appear for these noble sons, knew: “These noble sons once offered a thousand sets of robes to a thousand Paccekabuddhas. Not only that, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, they also offered twenty thousand sets of robes to twenty thousand Arahant elders. For these noble sons, the arrival of miraculous bowls and robes to their persons is no wonder; they will arrive easily.”
559:
