Extending his right hand, he gave the "Ehi Bhikkhu" invitation, saying: "Etha bhikkhavo—Come, monks; receive the state of novice and monkhood that you have requested. The Dhamma has been well-preached by me. Practice the noble conduct of the three trainings with diligence to make an end of suffering." As soon as he gave the "Ehi Bhikkhu" invitation, King Mahākappina and the thousand ministers were instantly adorned with supernaturally created requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra), each in its proper place. Like Great Elders of sixty years' standing (who are eighty years of age), their lay appearance vanished, and they attained monkhood. They ascended into the sky, descended again, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down.

## The Merchants Going to Queen Anojā

Those merchants from Sāvatthī also went to the Kukkuṭavatī golden palace. They had the Queen informed that they were sent by the King. When Queen Anojā-devī gave permission, saying, "Let them come," they entered the golden palace, paid respectful homage to the Queen, and stood in a suitable place. Then, the Queen and the merchants questioned and answered each other as follows:

(The Queen)
"Friends, for what reason have you come to this golden palace?"

(The merchants)
"Noble Queen, the King has sent us to you."
560:
“He said to grant us rewards of three hundred thousand coins.”

(The Queen)
“Friends, you speak of a very large amount. What service have you rendered to the King? For what favor did the King, with a clear mind, command that such a reward be given to you?”

(The Merchants)
“Your Majesty, we have not rendered any other service to the King. In truth, we reported a piece of special news to the King. Therefore, the King was pleased and commanded that this reward of three hundred thousand coins be given to us.”

(The Queen)
“Friends, can you also tell that special news to me?”

(The Merchants)
“We can tell you, Your Majesty.”

(The Queen)
“Friends, if so, please tell me.”

(The Merchants)
“Your Majesty, the Buddha Jewel has appeared in the world.”

As soon as the Queen heard this news, like the King, her whole body was suffused with the five kinds of joy (*pīti*). For three times, she could not register anything else, but on the fourth time, upon hearing even a part of the word “Buddha Jewel,” she asked: “Friends, for this word ‘Buddha Jewel,’ how much reward did the King give you?”
561:
When the merchants replied, “Your Majesty, he gave us a reward of one hundred thousand coins,” she said: “Friends, although you have heard such rare and wonderful news, the King’s gift of only one hundred thousand coins is not worthy of the value of the news. As for me, I give you three hundred thousand coins as my humble gift. What other special news did you report to the King?” The merchants then reported the news of the appearance of the Dhamma Jewel and the news of the appearance of the Saṅgha Jewel in succession. Just as before, the Queen’s body was suffused with the five kinds of joy, and for three times she could not register anything, but on the fourth time, upon hearing even a part of the words “Dhamma” and “Saṅgha,” she gave rewards of three hundred thousand coins for each. Thus, the merchants received a total reward of one million two hundred thousand (1,200,000) coins—three hundred thousand from the King and nine hundred thousand from the Queen.

After that, the Queen asked the merchants, “Friends, where is the King now?” The merchants replied, “Your Majesty, he has gone forth into the forest, saying, ‘I shall ordain in honor of the Exalted One.’” The Queen then asked, “What other message did the King leave for me?” The merchants, as instructed by the King, replied:
562:
"Great Queen, the King has renounced and handed over all his royal wealth and sovereign power to you. May the Great Queen enjoy and use the royal wealth as you wish," they reported. Again, the Queen asked the merchants, "Friends, where are the thousand ministers now?" The merchants replied as they had seen, "Great Queen, the ministers have also followed, saying, 'We too shall ordain together with the King.'"

## Queen Anojā Consults with the Ministers' Wives
## and Renounces the World

Queen Anojādevī summoned the wives of the thousand ministers and consulted with them, saying:

(The Queen)
"Friends, your husbands, the ministers, have followed the King, saying, 'We shall ordain together with the King.' What will you do, ladies?"

(The Wives)
"Great Queen, what message did those ministers leave for us?"

(The Queen)
"Your husbands, those ministers, have renounced and handed over all their wealth to you. They said you should enjoy and use the wealth as you wish."

(The Wives)
"Great Queen, what then will you do?"
563:
(The Queen)
“Ladies, my lord King Mahākappina, upon hearing the news of the appearance of the Triple Gem, even while standing on the road, honored the Triple Gem with three hundred thousand coins. He then abandoned the royal wealth like a glob of spit and has already gone forth to the forest, saying, ‘I shall ordain.’ As for me, having heard the good news of the appearance of the Triple Gem, I have honored the Triple Gem with nine hundred thousand coins. This royal wealth is not something that can cause suffering only to the King; it can also cause suffering to me. What wise person would crouch down to catch with their mouth the spit that the King has spat out? I will not. I have no need for royal wealth; I do not want it. I, too, shall go to the presence of the Exalted One to ordain in his honor.”

(The Wives)
“Your Majesty, we too shall ordain together with you.”

(The Queen)
“It is good, ladies, if you are able.”

(The Wives)
“We are able, Your Majesty.”

Then the Queen said, “Very well, ladies. If so, let us go.” She ordered a thousand chariots to be prepared, mounted a chariot, and together with those thousand wives, departed from the city. On the way, they encountered the first river which King Mahākappina and his ministers had crossed.
564:
Asking in the same manner as before and learning all the facts, she said, "Look for and seek the path the King has crossed." When they reported back, "O Queen, we do not see even the footprints of the Sindh horses," the Queen thought, "My lord, the Great King Kappina, must have gone forth into the homeless life dedicated to the Triple Gem, and crossed this river by making an Act of Truth. I, too, have gone forth dedicated to the Triple Gem. By the power of the Triple Gem, let this river water not act like water." Reflecting on the virtues of the Triple Gem, she ordered the thousand chariots to be driven onto the surface of the river. At that time, the surface of the water became like a slab of stone. Not even the rims of the chariot wheels were moistened by the water. In this same manner, she crossed the remaining two rivers just as the King had done. (This portion is extracted from the Dhammapada Commentary; what follows will be written according to the explanation in the Anguttara Commentary, Vol. 1): 

As soon as Queen Anojā crossed the third river, the Candabhāgā, she saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a banyan tree. The Blessed One reflected, "If these women see their lords and husbands, desire and lust will arise, which would create an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits. They would not be able to listen to the Dhamma directly." Thus, He performed a feat of psychic power so that they could not see each other. All those women climbed up from the bank of the Candabhāgā River, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. The Blessed One...
565:
He preached the Dhamma to those women. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and saw their own lords and husbands. As soon as the Buddha thought, "Let Uppalavaṇṇā Therī come," the Therī arrived, ordained all the women, and took them to the nunnery. The Buddha, accompanied by the thousand monks, traveled through the air to the Jetavana monastery.

## Preaching the Dhammapada Verse
## Concerning Ven. Mahākappina

Thereafter, when Ven. Mahākappina reached the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) through the practice of monastic Dhamma, and knowing that his task as a monk had reached its pinnacle and was completed, he did not strive to preach to the thousand resident disciples near him. Instead, spending his time in the bliss of the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti), whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in a secluded place, he constantly uttered the inspired word: "Aho sukhaṃ, aho sukhaṃ! = Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" Other monks heard this inspired utterance and misunderstood, saying, "Ven. Kappina is uttering this inspired word while remembering the royal luxury of his kingdom." Later, when those monks reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said, "My son, the famous Ven. Kappina, is uttering this inspired word with the bliss of the Path and the bliss of the Fruit as his object," and He preached this Dhamma verse in the Dhammapada:
566:
Dhammapīti sukhaṃ seti, vippasannena cetasā.
Ariyappavedite dhamme, sadā ramati paṇḍito.

Bhikkhave = O monks, my sons. Dhammapīti = A person who drinks the Dhamma, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, joyfully and fully. Vippasannena cetasā = With a mind that is exceptionally clear and free from defilements. Sukhaṃ = Happily in both body and mind. Seti = Sleeps. (Or) Sukhaṃ seti = Lives happily in the four postures. Paṇḍito = The wise one who contemplates and knows the nature of the body. Ariyappavedite = In the Dhamma preached by the Noble Ones such as the Buddha. Dhamme = In the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). Sadā = At all times, day and night. Ramati = Delights and finds pleasure.

(At the end of the teaching, many people became Noble Ones, such as Stream-enterers. From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, 356.)

## Preaching to the Resident Disciples
## of Ven. Mahākappina

Then one day, the Buddha called the thousand monks (formerly ministers) who were resident disciples of Ven. Mahākappina and asked, "Monks, how is it? Does your teacher preach the Dhamma to you?" The thousand monks replied, "Exalted Buddha, our teacher does not preach the Dhamma to us. Without striving to preach the Dhamma, he remains constantly practicing the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti), which is the cause of living happily in the present life."
567:
He does not give even a word of instruction or advice to any of his disciples, Venerable Sir." Upon hearing this, the Blessed One had Venerable Mahākappina summoned and asked, "Dear Kappina, is it true that you do not give even a word of instruction or advice to your resident disciples?" When Venerable Mahākappina replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Blessed One urged him, saying, "O dear son, who is called a Brahmin because you have discarded evil (bāhitapāpa), do not do this. Do not remain without preaching the Dhamma. From today onwards, dear son, preach the Dhamma to your thousand resident disciple monks."

The Elder accepted the Blessed One's exhortation with great respect, saying, "Very well, Blessed One." In a single session, he preached the Dhamma to the thousand monks and caused all of them to attain the Fruit of Arahantship. (This very achievement was the basis for the Elder receiving the title of Etadagga.)

## (C) Receiving the Title of Etadagga

At a later time, while the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha and was appointing the Elders to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga), He declared regarding Venerable Mahākappina:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhūovādakānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākappino = Monks, among my disciple monks who give exhortation to monks, Mahākappina is the foremost."
568:
Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "those who give exhortation to monks (Bhikkhu-ovādaka)."

This is the account of Venerable Mahākappina.

**********

## (39) The Account of Venerable Sāgata

## (A) The Elder's Past Aspiration

This future Venerable Sāgata was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, he saw the Blessed One appoint a monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those skilled in entering the Tejo-kasiṇa jhāna (fire-device meditation). Having performed great meritorious deeds, he made an aspiration for that foremost position of being skilled in entering the Tejo-kasiṇa jhāna. Buddha Padumuttara then gave him the prophecy.

## (B) Ordination in the Final Life

That gentleman performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born as a young Brahmin named Sāgata in the city of Sāvatthī. Later, upon hearing the Blessed One's Dhamma, faith arose in him, and he entered the Order. He developed the eight mundane meditative attainments (samāpatti) and in those attainments...
569:
...he achieved great mastery. He also attained mastery in the five mundane psychic powers (abhiññā).

## Venerable Sāgata Subduing the Naga

(Extracted from the Surāpāna Sikkhāpada of the Vinaya Pācittiya): One day, while the Blessed One was wandering in the Cetiya country, He arrived at a village named Bhaddavatikā. (The village was named Bhaddavatikā because its fencing was very good). Cowherds, goatherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Blessed One coming from afar and pleaded, "Blessed One, please do not go to the Mango Ferry (Ambatiṭṭha). At the hermitage of the Mango Ferry ascetic, there lives a Naga who is swift, fierce, venomous, and possessed of great power. May that Naga not harm the Blessed One." When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

(Note: A brief summary of the background of the Mango Ferry Naga: At that Mango Ferry, there was once a boatman who made a living by ferrying people. At one time, many travelers had a conflict with him and beat him to death. Because that boatman made an aspiration with a hostile mind, he became a Naga king of great power at that very Mango Ferry.

Because that Naga king had a very hostile mind toward the local people, he used his power to cause rain when it should not rain, and prevented rain when it should rain. Consequently, the crops in that region were not successful. All the people living in the Cetiya country performed annual offerings to appease that danger.
570:
They even built a hut for the Naga to reside in. This is the brief background of the Mango Ferry Naga. From Anguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, page 251).

The Blessed One also went up the bank at that Mango Ferry, surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the intention of staying there for the night. Although the anxious cowherds, goatherds, farmers, and travelers pleaded three times for Him not to go, He remained silent as He already knew the circumstances.

Then, the Blessed One continued His journey and arrived at Bhaddavatikā village, where He stayed. At that time, Venerable Sāgata went to the Mango Ferry ascetic's hermitage, entered the fire-hut where the Naga resided, spread a grass mat, sat down cross-legged, kept his body erect, and remained there with mindfulness directed toward his meditation object.

When the Naga saw Venerable Sāgata enter, it became displeased and emitted smoke. Venerable Sāgata also emitted smoke using his psychic power (iddhividha), surpassing that of the Naga. Then the Naga, unable to control its anger, emitted flames. Venerable Sāgata entered the Tejo-kasiṇa jhāna and emitted flames even greater than those of the Naga.

At that point, the Naga thought, "This monk is indeed very powerful," and crouched at the feet of Venerable Sāgata, saying, "Venerable Sir..."
571:
"I take refuge in you, venerable sir," the Naga King said. The Venerable Sāgata replied, "There is no need to take refuge in me; take refuge only in the Blessed One." The Naga King agreed, saying, "Very well," and became one established in the Refuges. From that time on, he did not harm anyone. He also caused the rain to fall at the proper time. Consequently, the crops were fully abundant. (This passage is from the Manorathapūraṇī, Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 252).

Thereafter, the Venerable Sāgata, having successfully disciplined the Naga, arrived at the village of Bhaddavatikā where the Blessed One was staying.

## Continuing the Journey towards Kosambī

Then, the Blessed One stayed in the village of Bhaddavatikā as long as there were those to be disciplined and taught, and then set out on a wandering journey to Kosambī. The lay devotees of Kosambī had already heard the news that "Venerable Sāgata fought and conquered the Naga that lived at the Mango Ferry." As the Blessed One wandered by stages, he arrived at Kosambī. Then, the lay devotees of Kosambī went out to welcome the Blessed One. They approached Venerable Sāgata, paid homage to him, and stood at a respectful distance, saying, "Venerable sir, what material thing is difficult for you to obtain? What would you like? What material thing should we prepare for you?"
572:
When this was asked, the Chabbaggī monks (the group of six) intervened and said to the lay devotees of Kosambī, "Lay followers, a clear liquor called Kāpotika, which has a reddish color like a pigeon's foot, is difficult for monks to obtain. It is also something they like. Prepare that liquor."

(Here is a brief background of the Chabbaggī monks: Six young friends from Sāvatthī—(1-2) Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, (3-4) Mettiya and Bhumajaka, and (5-6) Assaji and Punabbhasuka—consulted together, saying, "Friends, in this world, farming and such are very difficult. Come, friends, let us ordain as monks. If we ordain, it would be proper to do so under a prominent person where we can decide matters of importance ourselves." Having agreed, they ordained under the two Chief Disciples.

After these monks had reached five years of seniority (vassa) and had mastered the Mātikā (the codes), they consulted, "Friends, in the countryside, food is sometimes plentiful and sometimes scarce. Therefore, let us not all six stay in one place, but let us divide and stay in three locations."

Then they instructed (1) Paṇḍuka and (2) Lohitaka: "Friends, Sāvatthī is a great city where five million seven hundred thousand (5,700,000) households reside. It is the royal capital where taxes are paid from the Kāsī and Kosala regions, adorned with eighty thousand (80,000) villages. Friends, you should build monastery compounds in the prominent areas of Sāvatthī, plant mango, jackfruit, and coconut trees, and support and attract lay devotees with flowers and fruits. Ordain their sons and strive to increase our following."
573:
They instructed (3) Mettiya and (4) Bhumajaka: "Friends, Rājagaha is a great city where one hundred and eighty million (180,000,000) people reside. It is the royal capital where taxes are paid from the Aṅga and Magadha regions, which are three hundred yojanas wide and adorned with eighty thousand (80,000) villages. Friends, you should build monastery compounds in the prominent areas and good locations of Rājagaha, plant mango, jackfruit, and coconut trees, and support and attract lay devotees with flowers and fruits. Ordain the sons of good families and strive to increase our following."

They instructed (5) Assaji and (6) Punabbhasuka: "Friends, the Kīṭāgiri region is a great district where the three types of crops flourish because of the abundant rains in both the monsoon and winter seasons. Friends, you should build monastery compounds in the prominent areas and good locations of that Kīṭāgiri region, plant mango, jackfruit, and coconut trees, and support and attract lay devotees with flowers and fruits. Ordain the sons of good families and strive to increase our following."

Those six leading monks acted exactly as they had planned. Among those three groups of monks, each faction had five hundred monks as followers. Thus, including the six leading monks, the Chabbaggī group consisted of over fifteen hundred (1,500) monks. (Because of the six leading monks, this group is called 'Chabbaggī', meaning a group of six).

Among those Chabbaggī monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, along with their five hundred followers, were virtuous individuals (sīlavanta). They also accompanied the Blessed One on his wandering journeys.
574:
Although those monks committed past offenses, they did not violate the training rules that had already been established. However, the monks of the other two factions were all shameless (alajjī). They committed offenses that had not been committed before and also violated the established training rules. This is a brief account of the Chabbaggī monks. (From Samantapāsādikā, Vinaya Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 199).

Following the suggestion of the Chabbaggī monks, the honest lay devotees of Kosambī prepared the clear liquor called Kāpotika in every house. Seeing Venerable Sāgata coming for alms, they said, "Venerable sir, may Venerable Sāgata drink this clear liquor called Kāpotika. Venerable sir, may Venerable Sāgata drink this clear liquor called Kāpotika."

At that time, as the training rule had not yet been established, Venerable Sāgata did not consider it an offense. Because the devotees requested him, he drank a little of the clear Kāpotika liquor at every house. As he was leaving the city, he collapsed at the city gate.

Then, as the Blessed One was leaving the city with many monks, he saw Venerable Sāgata lying at the city gate and said to the monks, "Monks, carry Sāgata away." The monks replied, "Very well, Blessed One," and having accepted the Blessed One's word, they carried Venerable Sāgata to the monastery and laid him down with his head toward the Blessed One. Then, Venerable Sāgata, being extremely intoxicated and completely unconscious, turned around and...
575:
...slept with his feet toward the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One and the monks questioned and answered each other as follows:

(The Buddha)
"Monks, did Sāgata not have respect and deference for me in the past?"

(The Monks)
"He did, Blessed One."

(The Buddha)
"Monks, does Sāgata have respect and deference for me now?"

(The Monks)
"He does not, Blessed One."

(The Buddha)
"Monks, did Sāgata not fight and conquer the Naga that lived at the Mango Ferry?"

(The Monks)
"He did fight and conquer, Blessed One."

(The Buddha)
"Monks, would Sāgata be able to fight and conquer a Naga now?"

(The Monks)
"He would not be able to, Blessed One."

(The Buddha)
"Monks, should one drink that liquor which, when drunk, causes intoxication and loss of consciousness, leading to confusion?"

(The Monks)
"One should not drink it, Blessed One."

The Blessed One continued, "Monks, although he has attained the five higher powers (abhiññā), it is improper, unbefitting, unsuitable, not the behavior of a monk, inappropriate, and should not be done for the monk Sāgata to drink liquor like this. Monks, why has Sāgata drunk liquor? Monks, this act committed by Sāgata does not lead to the faith of those who do not yet have faith..." In this manner, he...
576:
...rebuked and criticized him, and then established this training rule for the monks: "Surāmerayapāne pācittiyaṃ = There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for drinking fermented and distilled liquors." (Extracted from the Surāpāna training rule in the Pācittiya Pali of the Vinaya).

## Venerable Sāgata Becoming an Arahant

The next day, when Venerable Sāgata became sober and regained consciousness, he learned about his mistake. Feeling great shame and dread regarding unwholesome states, he confessed his fault and paid homage to the Blessed One. Filled with great spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) and soon attained the fruit of Arahantship.

## (C) Receiving the Title of Foremost (Etadagga)

At another time, while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery, as he was assigning the various foremost positions (etadagga) to the great elders, he praised Venerable Sāgata, saying:

"Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tejodhātukusalānaṃ yadidaṃ sāgato = Monks, among my disciple monks who are skilled in entering the fire-element meditative absorption (tejodhātu-kasiṇa-jhāna), Sāgata is the foremost."

Thus, he placed him in the highest position—the Etadagga title—in the category of "Tejodhātukusala," meaning one who is skilled in entering the fire-element absorption.

This is the account of Venerable Sāgata Thera.
577:
## (40) About Venerable Rādha Thera
## (a) The Elder's Past Aspiration
(In describing the past aspiration of this Elder, since the Theragāthā Commentary is slightly more detailed than the Aṅguttara Commentary, it will be presented according to the Theragāthā Commentary, Volume I, page 321)—

The Bodhisatta of this Venerable Rādha Thera was born into a noble family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. When he reached the age of discretion, he went to the monastery, approached and paid homage to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place. At that time, he saw the Buddha appointing a certain monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of 'Paṭibhāneyya'—meaning the ability to inspire ever-new insights (paṭibhāna) in the preaching of the Dhamma. Desiring that same rank (ṭhānantara) for himself, he performed a great act of charity. He also performed an extensive and grand worship to the Buddha.

## Another Life as a Nobleman
After making this aspiration to be a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka), that nobleman passed away from that life and accumulated merits in various subsequent existences. During the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was again born into a noble family. When he reached the age of discretion, he one day saw Vipassī Buddha wandering for alms. With a heart overflowing with faith and devotion, he offered very sweet ripe mangoes.
578:
## (b) Ordination in the Final Life
Due to those meritorious deeds, that nobleman was reborn in the celestial realms. After performing merits in successive lives and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, during the time when this Buddha appeared, he became a Brahmin youth named Rādha in the city of Rājagaha. Upon reaching adulthood, he lived as a householder. In his old age, as his wife and children no longer treated him with the same affection and care as before, he thought, "I will spend my remaining time as a monk." He went to the monastery and requested the Elders to ordain him.

However, thinking, "He is a Brahmin who is old, frail, and decrepit; he will not be able to fulfill the major and minor duties," none of the Elders were willing to ordain him.

Because the elderly Brahmin Rādha was old and could not obtain the ordination he desired, he became thin and emaciated, his flesh and blood wasted away, his appearance was ruined, and his complexion became pale like a withered leaf. Furthermore, his body was covered in protruding veins like a spread-out net (jāla). One day, the old Brahmin approached the Buddha, engaged in detailed conversation, and sat in a suitable place. The Buddha, perceiving that the old Brahmin possessed the past merits necessary to attain the Paths and Fruits (Magga-Phala), asked him to start a conversation, "Brahmin, do your wife and children look after you?"

The old Brahmin replied, "O Venerable Gotama, where is there any care from my wife and children? There is none. Because I am an old and aged man, my wife and children have cast me out."
579:
When he had reported this, the Buddha asked the old Brahmin, "Brahmin, if that is the case, is it not suitable for you to ordain?"

## The Quality of Gratitude and Thankfulness of Venerable Sāriputta
The old Brahmin Rādha replied to the Buddha, "O Venerable Gotama, who will ordain me? Because of my old age, none of the Elders are willing to ordain me."

Then, the Buddha asked the monks about the cause of the old Brahmin Rādha's emaciation and ruined appearance. When the monks reported that the Brahmin was emaciated and his appearance was ruined because there was no one to ordain him, the Buddha asked the monks, "Monks, who remembers a favor done by this Brahmin?"

At that time, Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, I remember a favor done by this Brahmin."

When the Buddha asked, "Dear son Sāriputta, how do you remember a favor done by this Brahmin?", Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Exalted Buddha, once while I was wandering for alms in this city of Rājagaha, this Brahmin offered me a single ladleful of alms food. Exalted Buddha, I remember that favor (of offering a single ladleful of alms food) from this Brahmin."

Then the Buddha said, "Sāriputta, well said. Dear son Sāriputta, the virtuous are grateful.
580:
They know how to repay a favor. Dear son Sāriputta, if that is so, you should ordain him as a novice and also give him higher ordination."

Then, Venerable Sāriputta asked the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, how shall I ordain him as a novice and give him higher ordination?" Thereupon, the Buddha, having given a Dhamma discourse based on this question by Venerable Sāriputta, addressed the monks: "Monks, from this day forward, I abolish the higher ordination by the Three Refuges which I previously permitted. Monks, I allow higher ordination by the act of a motion and three proclamations (Ñatticatuttha Kamma). Monks, higher ordination should be given in this way," and He preached the Ñatticatuttha Kammavācā.

(Special Note: After the Buddha attained Enlightenment on the full moon day of Kason in the year 103 of the Great Era, He spent the first rainy season in the Migadāvana forest. At the end of the rainy season, He sent out sixty Arahants to propagate the Sasana. In the early period, the Buddha Himself granted both novice ordination and higher ordination by the Three Refuges to the candidates brought by those missionary Arahant Elders. Later, because all three—the candidate for novice ordination, the candidate for higher ordination, and the missionary Elders—became exhausted (due to traveling long distances), the Buddha permitted the monks themselves to grant novice and higher ordination by the Three Refuges in those various places.

On the full moon day of Pyatho of that year, He arrived at Rājagaha, and on the 1st day of the waxing moon of Tabodwe, the two Chief Disciples along with their followers were ordained. On the seventh day after his ordination,
581:
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna became an Arahant, and on the fifteenth day—the half-month (the full moon day of Tabodwe)—Venerable Sāriputta became an Arahant. The matter of this old Brahmin Rādha's higher ordination occurred within the month between the full moon of Tabodwe and the full moon of Tabaung.

In this matter, a question may arise: "Why did Venerable Sāriputta still ask, 'Exalted Buddha, how shall I ordain him as a novice and give him higher ordination?' specifically for the case of this old Brahmin Rādha, even though he knew that the Buddha had already permitted ordination by the Three Refuges while staying in the Migadāvana forest of Bārāṇasī?"

The answer is: Although the Buddha had permitted the simple higher ordination by the Three Refuges in the beginning when there were not many monks, when He arrived at Rājagaha and the number of monks increased (at that time, there were already over twenty thousand Arahants), He wished to abolish that simple higher ordination by the Three Refuges and permit the more formal higher ordination by the Ñatticatuttha Kammavācā. At that time, knowing the Buddha's intention, Venerable Sāriputta asked, "Exalted Buddha, how (=in what way) shall I ordain him as a novice and give him higher ordination?" Indeed, the disciples of the Buddhas are skilled and proficient in knowing the Buddha's intention, and this Venerable Sāriputta was the most excellent and supreme among the Buddha's disciples. Therefore, it should be concluded that Venerable Sāriputta asked in that manner because he perceived the Buddha's intention.

Furthermore, from the full moon day of Tabaung in the year 103 of the Great Era, the Buddha traveled from Rājagaha to Kapilavatthu for two months at the rate of one yojana per day. After arriving at Kapilavatthu on the full moon day of Kason in the year 104,
582:
on the seventh day, when Prince Rāhula followed Him to ask for his inheritance, the Buddha instructed Venerable Sāriputta to ordain him. At that time as well (even though novice ordination by the Three Refuges had been permitted previously), Venerable Sāriputta, knowing the Buddha's intention, asked: "Kathaṃhaṃ bhante rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājemi = Exalted Buddha, how (=in what way) shall I ordain Prince Rāhula?"

To make it clearer: In the matter of granting ordination, the Buddha had permitted both novice ordination (Pabbajjā) and higher ordination (Upasampadā) by the Three Refuges while staying in the Migadāvana forest of Bārāṇasī. Of these two, when He arrived at Rājagaha and the story of the old Brahmin Rādha arose, He abolished the simple higher ordination by the Three Refuges and permitted higher ordination by the Ñatticatuttha Kammavācā. However, novice ordination by the Three Refuges was neither abolished nor explicitly re-permitted. Therefore, in the future, a doubt might arise in the minds of monks: "This novice ordination was the same as higher ordination in the past; now, should this novice ordination also be performed by Kammavācā like higher ordination, or should it be performed by the Three Refuges as originally?" Knowing this, the Buddha wished to re-confirm the novice ordination by the Three Refuges to make it firm. Therefore, Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, knowing the Buddha's intention, asked: "Kathaṃhaṃ bhante rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājemi = Exalted Buddha, how (=in what way) shall I ordain Prince Rāhula?" so that the Buddha would firmly re-confirm the novice ordination by the Three Refuges. How well he knew the intention! (This is an extract from the Vinaya Mahā-Aṭṭhakathā for special note).
583:
## The Ordination and Attainment of Arahantship by the Brahmin Rādha

The Venerable Sāriputta, placing the command of the Blessed One upon his head, personally acted as the preceptor (upajjhāya) for the elderly Brahmin Rādha, ordaining him as a novice and then as a monk. Afterwards, he reflected: “The Blessed One, with great respect and consideration, commanded me to ordain this elderly Brahmin Rādha. It is not proper for me to look after this elderly monk Rādha with disrespect or negligence; it is only fitting that I look after him with great care.” Having thus considered, he took the Elder Rādha and went to a small village monastery.

In that small village monastery, because he was a newly ordained monk, the Elder Rādha suffered great hardship regarding lodgings and other necessities. His preceptor, the Venerable Sāriputta, favored and supported him by giving him the superior lodgings that he himself received according to seniority. Furthermore, he also gave the Elder Rādha the excellent alms-food that he received according to seniority, while he himself sustained his life with whatever alms he obtained by wandering for food. Through the support of his preceptor, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Elder Rādha obtained suitable lodgings and suitable food. He learned the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Venerable Sāriputta and, through diligent practice, soon attained the fruit of Arahantship; he became an Arahant.

## The Preaching of the Alīnacitta Jātaka

Thereafter, the Venerable Sāriputta took the Elder Rādha and came to pay homage to the Blessed One.
584:
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked the Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, my son, I have entrusted to you the monk Rādha as your resident pupil (nissaya-antevāsika). How is it with that monk Rādha? Is he not weary of the Dispensation?” The Venerable Sāriputta replied: “Venerable Sir, any monk who finds delight in the Dispensation should be exactly like this monk Rādha.”

Subsequently, among the Saṅgha, words of praise concerning the virtues of the Venerable Sāriputta arose: “Friends, the Venerable Sāriputta is indeed one who knows gratitude. He indeed performs acts of gratitude in return.” Hearing this, the Blessed One said to the monks: “Monks, it is not surprising that Sāriputta knows gratitude and performs acts of gratitude in this, his final existence (pacchima-bhava). Even in the distant past, when he was born as a rootless animal (ahetuka-tiracchāna), Sāriputta was one who knew gratitude and performed acts of gratitude.” When the monks asked, “Venerable Sir, at what time was that?” the Blessed One preached the Alīnacitta Jātaka (from the Dukanipāta) regarding the events of the past as follows:

Monks, in the past, five hundred carpenters living at the foot of a mountain used to enter the great forest, cut and hew timber for buildings, construct a large raft, and float it down the river. Then, a certain great elephant, while breaking off a branch with his trunk in an uneven place, stepped with his foot upon a very sharp tree stump as the branch broke.
585:
Because the stump was large, he could not withstand the force of the impact, and the stump pierced his foot, causing the great elephant intense painful feelings (dukkha-vedanā). The great elephant was in such extreme pain that he could no longer continue his journey and had to lie down right there.

After two or three days had passed, the great elephant saw those carpenters passing near him and thought: “By depending on these carpenters, I shall obtain my life.” Thinking thus, he stood up and followed behind the carpenters. When the carpenters looked back and saw the great elephant, they were terrified and ran away. When the carpenters ran in fear, the great elephant stood still; when the carpenters stood still again, he followed them once more.

The wise master carpenter thought: “This elephant follows us when we stand still and stands still when we run. There must be some reason for this behavior.” Then, all the carpenters climbed up various trees and waited for the great elephant to come. The great elephant went to those carpenters, turned his foot that was pierced by the stump, showed it to them, and lay down. At that moment, the thought occurred to the carpenters: “Friends, this elephant follows us because he is unwell, and for no other reason.”
586:
Having gained this understanding, they went near the great elephant and looked. Seeing the large stump-splinter pierced into the sole of his foot, they realized the truth: “This elephant followed us because of this pierced splinter.” They then used a sharp adze to cut around the edge of the stump, tied it firmly with a rope, and pulled it out. Afterwards, they squeezed the wound on the great elephant's sole to remove the pus and blood, washed it with a decoction, and applied medicines they knew. Before long, they treated and cared for him until he was restored to his natural well-being.

After the great elephant had recovered, he thought: “These carpenters have been very kind to me. It is only proper that I be one who knows their gratitude and repays it.” He then went to his own place in the forest and brought back his young son, an auspicious white elephant of the Gandha breed, whose body was pure white. When the carpenters saw the young white elephant, they were very delighted, thinking: “Our great elephant has brought his son too.” Then the great elephant thought: “If I remain in this place, the carpenters will not know the reason for my coming.” Thus, he departed from the place where he stood.

The young white elephant followed closely behind his father. Knowing that his son was following, the great elephant gave a vocal signal for him to turn back. Hearing his father's voice, the young white elephant turned back and went to the carpenters. Only then did the carpenters realize: “This great elephant must have come to give his young white elephant son to us.”
587:
Knowing this, they addressed the young white elephant: “There is nothing for you to do with us; go back only to your father,” and they gave him leave to go. Although the great elephant's son returned to him three times, the father sent him back each time to the carpenters. From that time on, the carpenters kept the young white elephant with them and nurtured him. At mealtime, each carpenter gave a morsel of rice to the young white elephant; thus, the food for the young white elephant was as abundant as needed. The young white elephant would bring all the timber that the carpenters had cut and hewn in the forest, transporting it from the forest and piling it up in an open clearing. In this way, he also performed other acts of service for the carpenters.

(In the Aṅguttara Commentary, the Alīnacitta Jātaka is mentioned only this far, enough to illustrate the Venerable Sāriputta’s nature of knowing gratitude. The Jātaka, however, is not yet finished. I shall continue to present a summary.)

(Continuation of the Alīnacitta Jātaka): From that time on, the young white elephant followed the words of the carpenters, accepted their discipline, and performed all kinds of work. The carpenters also raised the young white elephant by giving him a morsel of rice every day. When the work was finished, the young white elephant would go down to the river, bathe, and play in the water before returning. The young children of the carpenters would also play with the young elephant both in the water and on land, holding onto his trunk and other parts.
588:
Notably, noble elephants, noble horses, and noble men do not void excrement or urine in the water. Therefore, the young white elephant also did not void excrement or urine in the river, but only outside, away from the river.

One day, heavy rain fell upstream from the city of Vārāṇasī, where the young white elephant lived. At that time, a piece of dried dung that the young white elephant had voided outside the river was carried into the river by the rainwater and, floating down, got caught in a bush at a landing place in the city of Vārāṇasī. Then, the King’s elephant trainers brought five hundred elephants to the riverbank, saying, “Let us bathe the elephants.” Having caught the scent of the noble white elephant’s dung, not a single elephant dared to go down into the river; all the elephants raised their tails and prepared to flee. The trainers told this matter to the elephant physicians. The elephant physicians, thinking, “There must be some danger in the water,” had the water cleared. They found the noble elephant’s dung stuck in the bush and realized: “This dung is the root cause of these elephants’ attempt to flee.” They had a large jar brought, filled it with water, and had the noble elephant’s dung kneaded into the water. They then had it poured over the bodies of the five hundred elephants. The bodies of the elephants became very fragrant. Only then did the elephants go down into the river and bathe.
589:
The elephant physicians reported this matter to the King and suggested: “Your Majesty, it would be proper to search for that noble elephant and bring him to the golden palace.” The King went up the river with a fleet of boats and reached the forest at the foot of the mountain where the carpenters lived. While playing in the water at the riverbank, the young white elephant heard the sound of drums, ran, and stood near the carpenters. The carpenters welcomed the King and politely asked: “Your Majesty, if you desire timber, why did you come yourself? Would it not have been proper to send a messenger to have it delivered?” The King replied: “Carpenters, I have not come for the sake of obtaining timber. Indeed, I have come for the sake of obtaining this young white elephant that is with you.” The carpenters then gave their permission, saying: “Your Majesty, if that is the case, have him taken as you desire and proceed.”

The young white elephant did not wish to go; even though the elephant trainers tried to capture and pull him, he stood firm. Then the King asked the trainers: “Trainers, what does the white elephant wish to have done?” The trainers replied: “Your Majesty, the white elephant wishes for the feeding fee to be paid to the carpenters.” The King said, “Very well,” and had one hundred thousand coins (kahāpaṇas) piled up near each of the six points: the four legs, the trunk, and the tail of the white elephant.
590:
590
Even with this amount (six hundred thousand pieces of money), the white elephant still did not follow. Therefore, the King had a set of clothes given to each of the carpenters, a set of garments to each of their wives, and a complete set of children's accessories to the elephant's playmates. Only after these were given did the white elephant follow the King, looking back repeatedly at the carpenters, their wives, and his playmates.

When the King arrived at the city with the white elephant, he had the city and the elephant stable decorated. He led the white elephant in a clockwise procession around the city and brought him into the stable. After adorning him with all the elephantine ornaments, the King performed the auspicious consecration (Abhiseka), made him the state elephant, and placed him in the position of a friend. He granted half of the kingdom's wealth to the white elephant and treated him with honors and ceremonies equal to his own. From the time the white elephant arrived, the sovereignty over the entire island of Jambudīpa came into the hands of the King of Vārāṇasī.

After some time had passed in this manner, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen (Aggadevi Mahesī) of the King of Vārāṇasī. When the Queen's pregnancy was mature, the King of Vārāṇasī passed away. If the white elephant were to know that the King had passed away, he would have died of a broken heart on the spot. Therefore, the ministers did not let the white elephant know of the King's death and continued to care for and serve him as before.
591:
591
In particular, having heard that the King of Vārāṇasī had passed away and that "the city of Vārāṇasī is without a king," a neighboring King of the Kosala kingdom arrived with a large army and besieged the city. The citizens of Vārāṇasī sent a message to the King of Kosala, saying: "Our King's Chief Queen is now in an advanced stage of pregnancy. The experts in body marks and signs (aṅgavijjā) and physiognomists have predicted that she will give birth to a son on the seventh day from today. If the Queen gives birth to a son, we will not surrender the country on the seventh day but will instead give battle. Please wait for this duration (seven days)." The King of Kosala agreed, saying, "Very well."

On the seventh day, the Queen gave birth to a son. On the day the prince was named, he was called "Prince Alīnacitta" because he was born to uplift the undaunted hearts of all the citizens. (Alīnacitta means the prince who causes an undaunted mind to arise).

Specifically, from the day the prince was born, the citizens of Vārāṇasī fought against the King of Kosala. However, because there was no king to lead the battle, even though the soldiers were numerous, their morale gradually declined and wavered as they continued to fight. The ministers reported this to the Queen, saying, "O Queen, if we continue in this way...
592:
592
...and the morale of the soldiers continues to decline, we fear we will lose the war. We wish to make a special request: the King's friend, the Auspicious White Elephant, does not yet know that our King has passed away, that a son has been born, or that the King of Kosala has come to wage war against our country. Shall we let the Auspicious White Elephant know these facts?" The Queen agreed, saying, "Very well." She dressed her son, laid him on a white rug, descended from the palace, and, surrounded by the ministers, went to the elephant stable. She placed the Bodhisatta prince at the feet of the white elephant and said, "O Lord White Elephant, your friend has passed away. We did not inform you because we feared you would die of a broken heart. This prince is the son of your friend. Now, the King of Kosala has come, besieged the city, and is at war with your friend's son. The soldiers' morale is declining. If you, Lord Elephant, wish to kill your friend's son, then kill him. Or, if you wish to take the kingship and give it to this prince, then give it."

Then, the white elephant caressed the Bodhisatta (the young Prince Alīnacitta) with his trunk, embraced and lifted him up, placed him on his frontal globes (uṅkīna), and wept bitterly. He then lowered the Bodhisatta from his head, placed him back in the Queen's hands, and roared, "I shall capture the King of Kosala alive!" and emerged from the stable. Then the ministers...
593:
593
...put the armor and trappings on the white elephant, opened the city gates, and, surrounding the white elephant, marched out of the city. After leaving the city, the white elephant let out a heron-like cry (trumpeted), causing the masses to flee in terror. He broke through the enemy king's ranks, seized the enemy King of Kosala by his topknot, and brought him back to be laid at the feet of the young Bodhisatta Prince Alīnacitta. He restrained his own soldiers who were rising up to kill that king and admonished him, saying, "O King of Kosala, from now on, do not be heedless. Do not think, 'The prince is just a small child,'" and then released him.

From that time on, the sovereignty over the entire island of Jambudīpa came into the hands of the Bodhisatta Prince Alīnacitta. No other enemy dared to rise up. When the Bodhisatta was seven years old, he received the royal consecration and became the king known as Alīnacitta. He ruled righteously and, at the end of his life, passed away to the heavenly realm.

(Note: This original Alīnacitta Jātaka was first preached by the Buddha concerning a monk who had given up his persistence. Later, when the story of Venerable Rādha arose, it was preached again to highlight the quality of gratitude and thankfulness of Venerable Sāriputta, up to the point where the father elephant gave his young white elephant calf to the carpenters).

The Blessed One, having brought forth this past account, preached these two verses upon becoming the Buddha:
594:
594
(1) Relying on Alīnacitta, the great army was delighted.
It captured the King of Kosala alive, who was dissatisfied with his own army.

O Bhikkhus! Relying on me, the Great Being named Alīnacitta, the large army of the Vārāṇasī side was joyful and enthusiastic. They were able to capture the enemy King of Kosala alive—a king who, driven by excessive greed, was not satisfied with his own kingdom and power—through the strength of the white elephant.

(2) Thus, a monk who is well-supported, who has aroused energy,
Developing wholesome states for the sake of attaining security from bondage,
Should gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.

In the same way, a Bhikkhu—a wise one who perceives the dangers of Saṃsāra and the nature of the aggregates—who is endowed with the support of a good friend (kalyāṇa-mitta) such as the Buddha or a noble disciple, and who possesses renewed and repeated energy, should develop the faultless Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma through the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) in order to swiftly reach Nibbāna, the state of security from the four yokes (yoga). By doing so, he should gradually reach the Fruit of Arahatship, which is the total destruction of the ten fetters and all unwholesome states, through the sequence of the four Path Knowledges (Magga-ñāṇa).
595:
595
...he should reach the destination as intended.

Thus, the Blessed One crowned the discourse with the Deathless Nibbāna and then further explained the Four Noble Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, the monk who had given up his persistence was established in the Fruit of Arahatship. At that time, the mother became Queen Mahāmāyā, the father became King Suddhodana, the white elephant who secured the kingdom became the monk who had given up his persistence, the father elephant became Venerable Sāriputta, the neighboring King of Kosala became Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and Prince Alīnacitta became I, the Buddha. Thus he identified the Jātaka. This is the Alīnacitta Jātaka from the Duka Nipāta.

The Blessed One, having brought forth and preached this Alīnacitta Jātaka, showed that even in the past, the Venerable Sāriputta was one who knew gratitude. Furthermore, concerning Venerable Rādha, the Blessed One preached the (2) Rādha Saṃyutta, adorned with 4 chapters (vaggas) and 46 discourses (suttas), in the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Moreover, when Venerable Sāriputta brought Venerable Rādha, who had reached the Fruit of Arahatship, to the presence of the Blessed One and sat down after paying homage, the Blessed One asked Venerable Sāriputta: "Dear Sāriputta, is your resident pupil (antevāsika)...
596:
596
...the monk Rādha, easy to admonish?" Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Bhante, the monk Rādha is very easy to admonish. If any fault is pointed out to him, he never gets angry." The Blessed One then asked, "Dear Sāriputta, if you could get such pupils who are easy to admonish, how many would you like to have?" Venerable Sāriputta replied, "Bhante, if I could get pupils as easy to admonish as this monk Rādha, I would like to have many of them."

Later, when the monks were praising the quality of gratitude and thankfulness of Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One preached the aforementioned Alīnacitta Jātaka to illustrate Sāriputta's gratitude even in his life as an animal. Then, concerning Venerable Rādha, he said: "Bhikkhus, one who has become a monk should be easy to admonish like this monk Rādha. When teachers point out faults and give admonition, one should not get angry. One should regard the teacher who gives advice and instruction as one who points out a pot of gold or silver." Wishing to connect the discourse and preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

One should follow a wise person,
Who points out faults and gives reproof,
As if they were a revealer of treasures.
One should associate with such a sage.
For one associating with such a person,
It is better, never worse.
597:
“Bhikkhave = O monks. Nidhīnaṃ = Like one who points out a hidden treasure. Pavattāraṃ viya = Like one who speaks with a desire for another's benefit. Vajjadassinaṃ = One who scrutinizes and points out faults for the sake of one's benefit. Yaṃ = Which wise teacher. Passe = Passeyya = If one should encounter through the support of past wholesome kamma. Niggahavādiṃ = One who is accustomed to rebuking and restraining according to the fault. Medhāviṃ = One who possesses the wisdom of the essence of Dhamma (dhammojapññā) and penetrates all truths. Tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ = Such a noble and wise teacher. Bhaje = Bhajeyya = One should associate with day and night. Tādisaṃ = For one who associates with such a noble and wise teacher. Bhajamānassa = For the one who associates constantly. Seyyo = Only excellence and progress, which are highly praised. Hoti = Occur. Pāpiyo = Decline and inferiority. Na hoti = Do not occur.”

At the conclusion of the sermon, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. (Dhammapada Commentary 1, page 346).

## (c) Receiving the Foremost (Etadagga) Title

At another time, when the Buddha was appointing the Elders to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga), He addressed Elder Rādha:

“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭibhāneyyakānaṃ yadidaṃ rādho = Monks, among my disciple monks who inspire the inspiration of Dhamma teaching (dhamma-desanā-paṭibhāna),”
598:
“Rādha is the foremost.”

Thus, the Buddha praised him and placed him in the foremost position (Etadagga) as “Paṭibhāneyyaka = the one who inspires the Buddha’s inspiration and wisdom in preaching the Dhamma.”

(In this matter: Based on Elder Rādha’s insight and his great faith (saddhā) in the Dhamma, new and further wisdom and inspiration for preaching the Dhamma arose within the Buddha’s own continuum. This point should be understood by subtly observing the last six suttas of the first chapter of the Rādha Saṃyutta and the entire fourth chapter of the Rādha Saṃyutta. Therefore, Elder Rādha became the recipient of the foremost title of Paṭibhāneyyaka—the one who inspires the Buddha’s wisdom and inspiration in Dhamma teaching. The grammatical derivation is: Paṭibhānaṃ janentīti paṭibhāneyyakā. Ye = Those disciples who. Paṭibhānaṃ = The Buddha’s inspiration and wisdom in preaching the Dhamma. Janenti = Cause to arise. Iti tasmā = Therefore. Te = Those disciples. Paṭibhāneyyakā = Are called Paṭibhāneyyaka. Paṭibhāneyyakā = Disciples who cause the Buddha’s inspiration and wisdom in Dhamma teaching to arise. This is how the definition should be constructed.)

This is the account of Elder Rādha.
