## (41) The Account of Elder Mogharāja

(I shall present the account of this Elder Mogharāja by extracting it from the Aṅguttara Commentary, the Suttanipāta Commentary, and the commentary on the Pārāyanavagga.)

## (a) The Elder’s Past Aspiration

This Bodhisatta, the future Elder Mogharāja, was a youth of good family in the royal city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara.
599:
Later, while listening to the Buddha’s Dhamma, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the foremost position (Etadagga) among those who wear coarse robes (lūkhacīvaradhārī)—robes made of rags that are poor in terms of fabric, thread, and dye. Having performed meritorious deeds of great significance (adhikāra), he made an aspiration for that same position of being the foremost among those who wear coarse rag-robes. The Buddha Padumuttara also granted him a prophecy (byādika).

## His Life as the Great Minister of King Kaṭṭhavāhana

That youth of good family performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Long before the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he was born into a family of ministers in the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. Upon reaching maturity, he served King Kaṭṭhavāhana and attained the rank of Great Minister.

Detailed account of King Kaṭṭhavāhana (from Suttanipāta Commentary 2): In the past (before the appearance of Buddha Kassapa), there was a master carpenter in the city of Bārāṇasī who was second to none in his master's craft of carpentry. That master had sixteen chief disciples, and each chief disciple had one thousand subordinate disciples. Thus, a total of 16,017 masters and disciples lived and earned their livelihood depending on the city of Bārāṇasī in this manner:
600:
They would go near the forests and mountains, fell trees, and saw them into timber. In those forest areas, they would complete the construction of various wooden goods and furniture for palaces and mansions. They would then build large rafts to carry these goods down the Ganges River to the city of Bārāṇasī. If the King of Bārāṇasī desired them, they would assemble and build for him a single-story palace... (up to)... a seven-story palace. If the King did not desire them, they would sell them to others and live by supporting their wives and children.

## The Master Builds a Garuda-shaped Mechanical Flying Vehicle

Then one day, the master carpenter thought, “I cannot live by the work of a carpenter or architect forever. Indeed, when I grow old and frail, it will be very difficult to perform this carpentry work.” Considering this, he said to his disciples, “Lads, bring light wood such as that from the cluster fig tree (udumbara) which is pithless and light.” The disciples agreed and brought the light wood. With that wood, the master made a large Garuda figure, entered inside it, and installed mechanical engines. When the Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicle was finished, the master started the engine and, riding the vehicle, went to the forest where his disciples were working. The Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicle flew into the sky like a living King of Garudas, traveled above the forest, and descended in front of the disciples.
601:
Then the master said to his disciples, “Lads, by building such Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicles, we can take the kingship of the entire island of Jambudīpa. Lads, you too should build these Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicles. Let us take kingship and live; earning a living by carpentry is difficult.” He gave this advice and encouragement. The disciples built the Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicles as instructed by the master and informed him of their completion. Then, when the master consulted them, asking, “Lads, which country shall we take?” the disciples replied in unison, “Master, let us take the city of Bārāṇasī.” At that time, the master said, “Lads, it is not suitable. Do not favor the idea of taking Bārāṇasī. Indeed, if we take Bārāṇasī, we will not escape being called 'Carpenter King,' 'Carpenter Crown Prince,' 'Carpenter Prince,' or 'Carpenter Minister,' and so forth. The island of Jambudīpa is very vast; let us go elsewhere.” Thus he advised them, and all agreed.

## Becoming King Kaṭṭhavāhana

Thereafter, the 16,017 masters and disciples, together with their wives and children, each rode their respective Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicles. Having prepared and armed themselves with weapons, they drove the vehicles toward the Himalayas. They entered a city near the Himalayas and gathered at the royal palace itself.
602:
Those masters and disciples took over the kingship in that city and, having performed the royal consecration (rājābhisheka) for the master carpenter, they raised him to kingship. Because that king was the owner of the Garuda-shaped mechanical flying vehicle made of wood (kaṭṭha), he became famous as “King Kaṭṭhavāhana.” Because it was conquered and ruled by King Kaṭṭhavāhana, that country and city also became known as the country and city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. King Kaṭṭhavāhana, the Crown Prince, and the sixteen chief disciples who were appointed to the rank of Great Ministers were all righteous kings and ministers (dhammika) who followed and practiced the Dhamma. Since the entire realm of Kaṭṭhavāhana was honored and protected by the King through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), it was very prosperous, abundant, and free from dangers and calamities. The citizens and inhabitants of the districts said, “We have obtained a good and noble king; we have obtained a very noble royal retinue,” and they greatly relied on and cherished the King and his ministers and troops.

## Becoming Allies with the King of Bārāṇasī

One day, merchants from the Middle Country (Bārāṇasī) brought goods for sale and came to the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. They brought gifts and met with King Kaṭṭhavāhana. When the King asked, “Lads, where have you come from?” the merchants replied, “We have come from the city of Bārāṇasī, Your Majesty.” King Kaṭṭhavāhana asked about all the situations and events in Bārāṇasī and then said, “Lads, please act and manage so that your King of Bārāṇasī and we may become friends (allies).”
603:
The merchants agreed, saying, “Very well.” King Kaṭṭhavāhana provided those merchants from Bārāṇasī with provisions, accommodation, and all necessary assistance. When it was time for the merchants to return, he spoke respectfully once more about his desire to be allies and sent them off.

When those merchants reached their home in Bārāṇasī, they reported the matter to the King of Bārāṇasī. Upon hearing this, the King of Bārāṇasī was delighted and had a drum beaten to announce, “From this day forward, merchants coming from the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana are granted exemption from taxes.” He made the decision, “Let King Kaṭṭhavāhana be my friend and ally.” Thus, both kings became “unseen great friends” (adiṭṭhamahāmitta)—friends who were very fond of each other without having ever met. King Kaṭṭhavāhana also had a drum beaten in his city to announce, “From this day forward, merchants coming from the city of Bārāṇasī are granted exemption from taxes. All necessary assistance, such as provisions and accommodation for those merchants from Bārāṇasī, must be provided from the royal treasury.”

Subsequently, the King of Bārāṇasī sent a royal message to King Kaṭṭhavāhana, saying, “If any wonderful things worthy of seeing or hearing should arise in your districts, we would like you to arrange for us to have the opportunity to see and hear them as well.” King Kaṭṭhavāhana likewise sent a friendly royal message to the King of Bārāṇasī.
604:
## The Exchange of Gifts

While these two kings lived according to their mutual promise, on one occasion, King Kaṭṭhavāhana came into possession of extremely soft blankets (kambala) that shone brilliantly like the radiance of the rising sun. Upon seeing these blankets, King Kaṭṭhavāhana said, "I will send these to my friend, the King of Bārāṇasī." He then had ivory carvers carve eight ivory caskets and placed the blankets inside them. He then had lacquer workers decorate the outside of the caskets to resemble lacquer balls. These eight lacquer balls were then placed in a chest, wrapped with very soft cloth, and sealed with the royal seal. He dispatched his ministers, saying, "Present these to the King of Bārāṇasī." Furthermore, he sent a message saying, "I wish my friend, the King of Bārāṇasī, to open and view this gift in the middle of the royal city, surrounded by his assembly of ministers."

The ministers went and presented the gift to the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī read the message, gathered his ministers, and in the royal courtyard in the middle of the city, he broke the royal seal, removed the wrapping cloth, and opened the chest. Seeing the eight lacquer balls, he thought, "My friend Kaṭṭhavāhana has sent me lacquer balls as a gift, as if I were a young child who delights in playing with such things." Feeling displeased and with a fallen countenance, he struck one of the lacquer balls against his royal throne. At that moment, the lacquer fell away...
605:
...and the ivory casket opened, splitting into two parts, the lid and the base. Inside the casket, the King of Bārāṇasī saw the kambala blanket. He then opened the remaining seven caskets and looked; in all of them, he found similar blankets. Each blanket was sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width. When the blankets were spread out, the entire royal courtyard shimmered and glowed as if reflecting the light of the sun.

Seeing this, the multitude of people snapped their fingers in amazement. They also performed the act of throwing their turbans into the air. They were delighted and satisfied, saying, "Our King's unseen friend (adiṭṭhasahāya), King Kaṭṭhavāhana, has sent such a magnificent gift. It is truly fitting and proper to maintain a great friendship with such a person."

## Returning the Gift

The King of Bārāṇasī summoned the appraisers and had them value each blanket. All of them were found to be of inestimable value. Then, the King of Bārāṇasī reflected, "One who sends a return gift should send a gift that is superior and more noble than the gift first received. My friend King Kaṭṭhavāhana has sent me blankets of priceless value. What kind of return gift should I send to my friend King Kaṭṭhavāhana?"
606:
At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa had appeared prominently among the three types of beings and was residing in the city of Bārāṇasī. Then, the thought occurred to the King of Bārāṇasī: "In this world, there is no other treasure superior to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Well then, I shall send to my friend King Kaṭṭhavāhana the good news of the appearance of the Triple Gem in the world as a return gift." Having made this decision, he wrote:

"Buddho loke samuppanno, hitāya sabbapāṇinaṃ.
Dhammo loke samuppanno, sukhāya sabbapāṇinaṃ.
Saṅgho loke samuppanno, puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ."

"O friend King Kaṭṭhavāhana! The Buddha, known as the Omniscient One, the Supreme One of the world, has appeared in this world where we live, like the sun rising over the eastern mountain, for the benefit and welfare of all living beings.

In this world where we live, the Dhamma—consisting of the ten aspects: the Path, the Fruit, Nibbāna, and the Dhamma-groups—has appeared like the sun rising over the eastern mountain, for the happiness of all living beings in the three realms: human, celestial, and Nibbāna.

In this world where we live, the Saṅgha—the Noble Saṅgha in the ultimate sense, who are the incomparable field of merit for sowing the seeds of wholesome deeds—..."
607:
...has appeared like the sun rising over the eastern mountain."

He had this verse (consisting of six lines) and also the practice (paṭipatti) starting from the fulfillment of a monk's virtue up to the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) inscribed on a golden plate with vermilion. He then had that golden plate placed (1) first into a casket adorned with the seven kinds of gems. (2) Then, he had that seven-gemmed casket placed into an emerald casket. (3) He had that emerald casket placed into a masāragalla gem casket. (4) He had that casket placed into a ruby casket. (5) He had that ruby casket placed into a gold casket. (6) He had that gold casket placed into a silver casket. (7) He had that silver casket placed into an ivory casket. (8) He had that ivory casket placed into a casket made of heartwood or sandalwood. He placed that sandalwood casket into a chest, wrapped the chest with soft cloth, and had it sealed with the royal seal.

Then, he had a royal elephant in rut adorned with golden ornaments, covered with a golden net, and a golden flag hoisted upon it. He had a throne placed upon the elephant, and the gift chest was set upon the throne. Under the shade of a white umbrella, with offerings of all kinds of perfumes and flowers, and with various kinds of music, drumming, and singing, he had the road cleared and decorated all the way to the border of his kingdom of Kāsi. The King of Bārāṇasī himself supervised the dispatch of the gifts. Not only that, the King of Bārāṇasī, while remaining at his own border...
608:
...sent messages and the gifts to the neighboring kings, saying, "In this same manner, you, the kings of these realms, shall make offerings and pass this treasure-gift along from one to another." Hearing the words of the message, those neighboring kings came to meet the gift on the way and escorted it with great ceremony to the border of the kingdom of Kaṭṭhavāhana.

King Kaṭṭhavāhana, having heard the good news of the arrival of the royal treasure-gift, went to meet it on the way. He honored it in the same manner and brought it into his capital. He gathered his ministers and the townspeople, and in the royal courtyard before the assembly, he removed the wrapping cloth and opened the chest. Inside the chest, he found the sandalwood casket. He then opened the eight caskets one by one in succession. He found and read the inscription on the golden plate about the appearance of the Triple Gem and the practice of the Path. He was filled with joy and satisfaction, thinking, "Oh, my friend the King of Bārāṇasī has sent a supreme gift, a treasure that is extremely difficult to obtain even in hundreds of thousands of aeons." He reflected, "We have now heard the extraordinary news, never heard before, that 'the Buddha has appeared in the world.' It would be wonderful if I could go and behold the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma." He then asked his ministers, "Friends, the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—have appeared in the world. What do you think should be done?" The sixteen ministers replied, "Great King...
609:
...may Your Majesty remain here in this city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. We shall go and investigate to know the news of what has happened." They all spoke in unison.

## The Ministers Go to Investigate

Then, the sixteen chief ministers, who had a total of sixteen thousand followers, respectfully paid homage to King Kaṭṭhavāhana and said, "Great King, if it is true that the Buddha has appeared in the world, there will be no opportunity for us to see Your Majesty again (meaning they would ordain). If the Buddha has not appeared, we shall return to Your Majesty." Having said this, they departed from the kingdom.

In particular, the minister who was the biological nephew of King Kaṭṭhavāhana (his sister's son) paid homage to the King last and said, "I shall also depart." The King gave him a special instruction, saying, "Dear son, once you know that the Buddha has appeared in that Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), come back and inform me." The nephew minister accepted, saying, "Very well," and departed.

Those sixteen chief ministers, along with their sixteen thousand followers, traveled by forced marches, sleeping only one night at each place along the way, and arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī. Specifically, even before those ministers reached Bārāṇasī...
610:
Kassapa Buddha had already entered Parinibbāna. The ministers entered the monastery and asked, "Who is the Buddha? Where does the Buddha live now?" and as they wandered through the entire monastery, they met the great Elder disciples and asked them about it.

The great Elder disciples told the ministers, "The Buddha has entered Parinibbāna." The ministers wept and said, "Oh, though we have traveled a long distance, we did not even get to pay homage to the Buddha," and they further asked the Elders, "Venerable sirs, are there any instructions or advice left that were given by the Buddha?" The Elders replied, "Lay disciples, yes, there are. You must be established in the Three Refuges, observe the Five Precepts, practice the Eight-fact Uposatha, give alms, and (if you are able) ordain as monks yourselves." Upon hearing this, all the ministers, except for one who was a nephew, ordained together with their followers.

## King Kaṭṭhavāhana Passing Away
## After Performing Meritorious Deeds for Life

The minister who was the nephew brought back the Paribhoga-dhātu (relics of use) or Paribhoga-cetiya from the great Elder disciples and returned to the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana. The Paribhoga-dhātu or Paribhoga-cetiya refers to the Bodhi tree, the alms-bowl, the robes, the water-filter, and so on, which were used by the Buddha.
611:
The minister who was the nephew returned to the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana, bringing with him a paribhoga-cetiya—the water-strainer used by the Buddha—along with an Elder who was a bearer of the Sutta, Vinaya, and Abhidhamma.

When the minister eventually reached the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana, he informed the King, "Great King, my uncle, it is true that a Buddha appeared in the world. It is also true that He has now entered Parinibbāna." He then relayed the instructions and exhortations granted by the Buddha, just as the Great Elders had told him.

King Kaṭṭhavāhana attended upon the Elder who was a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, listened to the Dhamma, and built a monastery for the noble Elder to reside in. He enshrined the water-strainer brought by his nephew in a cetiya, planted and venerated a new Bodhi tree, and remained constantly established in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. On Uposatha days, he observed the Eightfold Uposatha and performed meritorious deeds such as dāna. After living out his full lifespan, he was reborn in a celestial realm of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara deva-loka).

The sixteen chief disciple-ministers, along with their retinue of sixteen thousand, also became monks, developed and practiced the Dhamma, and upon their passing—even as worldlings (puthujjanas)—they were reborn as the attendant deities of the celestial King Kaṭṭhavāhana. (It should be noted that among these sixteen chief disciples, the Bodhisatta who was to become the Venerable Mogharāja was included as one of the chief disciple-ministers who became a monk).
612:
## (b) Ordination in the Final Life

That group of teacher and disciples spent an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period of one Buddha-interval in the celestial realm. They passed away from the celestial realm even before our Buddha appeared. The teacher was reborn as the son of the chaplain (purohita) to King Mahākosala, the father of King Pasenadi Kosala, and was named Bāvarī. This Brahmin Bāvarī was endowed with three of the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa). He was also a master who had reached the completion of the three Vedas. When his father, the chaplain, passed away, the Brahmin Bāvarī received the position of chaplain to King Mahākosala.

The remaining sixteen thousand and sixteen disciples were also reborn into Brahmin families in the city of Sāvatthī. Among those sixteen thousand and sixteen:

"Ajita, Tissa-metteyya,
Puṇṇaka, and Mettagū,
Dhotaka, and Upasīva,
Nanda, and Hemaka,
Todeyya, and Kappa, both,
Jatukaṇṇī the wise,
Bhadrāvudha, and Udaya,
and the Brahmin Posāla,
Mogharāja the intelligent,
and Piṅgiya the Great Sage."

According to these verses (found in Khuddaka Nikāya 1, pages 431-432), (1) the youth Ajita, (2) the youth Tissa-metteyya, (3) the youth Puṇṇaka, (4) the youth Mettagū, (5) the youth Dhotaka, (6) the youth Upasīva, (7) the youth Nanda, (8) the youth Hemaka, (9) the youth Todeyya,
613:
(10) Kappa the youth, (11) Jatukaṇṇī the youth, (12) Bhadrāvudha the youth, (13) Udaya the youth, (14) Posāla the youth, (15) Mogharāja the youth, (16) Piṅgiya the youth—these sixteen great disciples studied the arts and sciences under the teacher Bāvarī. The remaining sixteen thousand (16,000) disciples studied under these sixteen great disciples, one thousand under each. Thus, all these 16,017 teachers and disciples were reunited in this final existence. (Among the sixteen great disciples mentioned, it should be noted in advance that No. 15, Mogharāja the youth, would later become Ven. Mogharāja).

## The Chaplain Bāvarī and His Disciples
## Ordaining as Hermit Ascetics

After King Mahākosala passed away, his son, King Pasenadi Kosala, was consecrated as king. The great chaplain Bāvarī continued to be the chaplain during the reign of King Pasenadi Kosala. King Pasenadi Kosala, in addition to the wealth given by his father King Mahākosala, also offered and honored the chaplain Bāvarī with much other wealth during his own reign. Indeed, King Pasenadi Kosala had studied the arts and sciences under the teacher Bāvarī when he was young. (Therefore, since Bāvarī was both the mentor and the chaplain of King Pasenadi Kosala, the King gave him additional wealth beyond what King Mahākosala had originally given).
614:
One day, the teacher Bāvarī went to a secluded place and reflected on the essence of his Vedic knowledge. Finding no essence that would be of benefit in the afterlife, he thought, "I shall become an ascetic and seek the essence for the afterlife." He then went to King Pasenadi Kosala and said, "Noble King, I shall become an ascetic."

King Kosala tried to dissuade him, saying, "Teacher, when you are here, it is as if my royal father were still standing firm. Please do not become a monk." However, urged by the power of his perfections (pāramī), the teacher Bāvarī insisted, "Noble King, it is not proper for me to remain. I shall certainly become an ascetic."

King Pasenadi Kosala, unable to prevent him, finally pleaded, "Teacher, if that is the case, I would like you to reside and practice as an ascetic in the royal garden, where I may easily come to see and meet you at any time, day or night." The teacher, together with his sixteen chief disciples and their sixteen thousand young followers, became ascetics and resided in King Kosala's garden. King Kosala supported them with the four requisites and regularly visited the teacher day and night.

Then one day, the disciples unanimously suggested to the teacher, "Teacher, living near the city involves many impediments (palibodha). Teacher, let us go to a place where there is no coming and going of people.
615:
Living in a place far from towns and villages is of great benefit to ascetics." The teacher agreed, saying, "Very well," and informed King Kosala of this. After King Kosala had tried to dissuade them three times without success, he gave them two hundred thousand coins and commanded two ministers, "You must build hermitages in the place where the ascetics wish to reside."

The great teacher-ascetic Bāvarī, surrounded by his sixteen thousand and sixteen disciple-ascetics and receiving the support and care of the ministers, headed south from the city of Sāvatthī. As they traveled, they found a place between the two kingdoms of Assaka and Aḷaka, which were outside the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa). There, where the great Godhāvarī River divided into two branches, was an island three leagues wide, covered in a forest of brushwood—a place where in ancient times great teacher-ascetics like Sarabhaṅga had resided. The ascetic Bāvarī told the ministers, "This place was the residence of ancient ascetics and is suitable for monks."

To acquire the land, the ministers offered one hundred thousand coins to King Assaka and one hundred thousand coins to King Aḷaka. Those two kings gladly granted not only that three-league area but an additional two leagues, making a total of five leagues. The two ministers who had come from Sāvatthī had hermitages and a monastery (ārāma) built there.
616:
They brought additional wealth from Sāvatthī, established a great alms-hall, and then returned (this is according to the Sutta Nipāta Commentary). (According to the Aṅguttara Commentary) One day after the ministers had built the hermitage and returned, a man came to pay respects to the ascetics and, with their permission, built his house and lived on the land belonging to the ascetics. Seeing this man living there, a hundred other families also built a hundred houses and lived in that place. In this way, because of the hermit teacher Bāvarī, the large village grew and prospered day by day. The hermit teacher Bāvarī, along with his disciples, lived happily in that large village by collecting alms and sometimes by seeking and consuming forest fruits.

## Bāvarī Giving a Great Alms-offering
## of One Hundred Thousand Coins Annually

In that village (gocaragāma), an annual tax of one hundred thousand coins was generated from farming and other activities. The wealthy men of the village took those one hundred thousand coins of tax revenue to King Assaka and said, "May the King accept and be pleased with this tax money." King Assaka refused, saying, "I do not wish to accept or be pleased with these one hundred thousand coins of tax. Send them only to the teacher Bāvarī." When the wealthy men brought the one hundred thousand coins to Bāvarī, he asked, "For what purpose have you brought these coins?" The wealthy men replied, "Venerable teacher, it is for the sake of our living, eating, and working happily on the land belonging to you, our teachers."
617:
617
“We have brought this to offer as a return of gratitude,” they replied. The great teacher Bāvarī said, “If I desired gold and silver, I would not have renounced a great mass of wealth to become an ascetic. It is because I do not desire gold and silver that I renounced such great wealth and became an ascetic. Take your wealth and go.” When he spoke these words of refusal, the householders pleaded, “We will not take back the wealth that we have already offered to the Venerable One. Indeed, we will bring one hundred thousand coins in this manner every year. We wish for the teacher to accept these coins and perform acts of charity.” In the end, unable to refuse, the ascetic teacher Bāvarī accepted the one hundred thousand coins and performed the act of donating them to the lonely, the poor, travelers, and beggars every year. The good news of the great teacher’s annual donation of one hundred thousand coins spread and became famous throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa.

## A Deceitful Brahmin Comes to Threaten
Thus, the great teacher Bāvarī continued to give great donations every year. One year, after completing the great donation, he left the village and entered his hermitage. He lay down, reflecting joyfully on his donation, thinking, “I have successfully performed the great donation.” At that moment, in the Brahmin village of Dunniwiṭṭha in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, the wife of a deceitful Brahmin, who was a descendant of the lineage of Jūjaka Brahmin, repeatedly pointed out his faults and scolded him, saying, “The great Brahmin Bāvarī...
618:
618
...is giving a great donation. Go to that place of donation and bring back gold and silver.” Because he was scolded and blamed by the Brahmin woman, the deceitful Brahmin could no longer stay and went to the great teacher Bāvarī. He arrived at the time mentioned before (when the great teacher Bāvarī was joyfully reflecting on his donation).

Upon arrival, the deceitful Brahmin begged loudly, saying, “O Brahmin Bāvarī, give me a gift! O Brahmin Bāvarī, give me a gift!” Bāvarī replied, “O Brahmin, you have arrived late, at an improper time. I have already given to the recipients who arrived. Now, I have no more coins.” The deceitful Brahmin then insisted, “O Brahmin Bāvarī, I do not desire many coins. For one like you who gives such a great donation, it is impossible to be without coins. Give me five hundred coins.” Again, Bāvarī spoke reasonably, “O Brahmin, I do not have five hundred coins either. You will receive them when the next time for donation arrives.” The deceitful Brahmin then spoke angrily, “Must I wait for the time you give donations?” He then took cow dung, red flowers, and dabba grass, went quickly to the door of Bāvarī’s hermitage, smeared the ground with cow dung, scattered the red flowers, and spread the dabba grass. Then, he washed his left foot with water from a pitcher, walked seven steps...
619:
619
...massaged his feet, and with his lips trembling as if reciting a mantra, he uttered this curse in verse:

“Sace me yācamānassa, bhavaṃ nānuwadassati.
Sattame diwase tuyhaṃ, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.”

“If, when I am asking, your honor (Bāvarī) does not give me five hundred coins, on the seventh day from today, may your head split into seven pieces.”

After he recited this curse, the great teacher Bāvarī thought, “The words of this Brahmin might sometimes be true,” and he lay on his bed in great anxiety. While he was there at midnight, a deity (the guardian deity of the hermitage), who had been Bāvarī’s mother in a previous life, saw her son’s grief and approached him, saying:

“Na so muddhaṃ pajānāti, kuhako so dhanatthiko.
Muddhani muddhāpāte wā, ñāṇaṃ tassa na wijjati.”

“Dear Bāvarī, that Brahmin does not know the Dhamma called 'the head' (muddha). He is a deceitful Brahmin who only desires your wealth. He has no knowledge regarding 'the head' or 'the splitting of the head' (muddhādhipāta).”
620:
620
Thus she explained. Then, the great teacher Bāvarī pleaded with the deity who was his former mother, “O mother deity, if you know the Dhamma called 'the head' and the Dhamma called 'the splitting of the head' which can split that head, please preach and answer me. Let us hear those words of Dhamma preached by you.” (The relevant verses should be noted from the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi, page 430). The deity replied, “Dear Bāvarī, I also do not know or see these two Dhammas. I have no knowledge of these two Dhammas. Knowledge regarding 'the head' and 'the splitting of the head' exists only with the Buddhas.” When she said this, Bāvarī pleaded again, “If you do not know, who then knows these two Dhammas? Please point out that person to me.” The deity answered that the Sammāsambuddha, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds, knows. As soon as Bāvarī heard the word 'Buddha,' his sorrow vanished, and he was filled with great joy. He asked, “Where is the Blessed One residing now?” The deity replied that the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in the city of Sāvatthī.

At dawn the next morning, the great teacher Bāvarī called his sixteen chief disciples...
621:
621
...all sixteen of them, and said, “O young men, a Buddha has appeared in the world! Go quickly and investigate whether he is truly a Buddha, and then return and tell me. I will follow to the presence of the Blessed One. However, because I am very old, it is difficult to know the danger to my life. Go to the presence of the Buddha and ask questions in this manner.” He then fully taught them how to ask the questions called “Muddhaphālana” (or “Muddhādhipāta”), which consisted of seven points. (This will be explained later).

(Note: The Buddha appeared eight years after the great teacher Bāvarī began residing in the hermitage on the banks of the Godhāvarī River. — From Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā 2, page 297).

Then, the great teacher Bāvarī reflected, “All sixteen of these chief disciples of mine are wise. If they hear the Dhamma of the Buddha and reach the summit of their monkly duties, they may return to me, or they may not.” He then gave a special instruction to his nephew, the youth named Piṅgiya, “O nephew Piṅgiya, you should certainly return to me. Preach to me again the supramundane virtues you attain.”

Then, sixteen thousand disciple ascetics, with the youth Ajita as their leader and head, together with the sixteen chief disciples, paid respects to the teacher Bāvarī and set out from the hermitage toward the north.
622:
622
(Those ascetics traveled through the city of Māhissati in the realm of King Aḷaka, Ujjeni, Gonaddha, Vedisa, Pawana, Kosambī, Sāketa, Sāvatthī, Setawya, Kapilavatthu, Kusinārā, Pāwā, Bhoga, Vesālī, and Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha—passing through these cities one by one over a journey of many leagues).

In every place those ascetics reached, people asked, “Venerable sirs, where are you going?” They replied, “We are going to the presence of the Blessed One to ask questions.” Thus, people from various places gathered and followed them. By the time they reached Sāketa from Kosambī, the assembly was six leagues long. At that time, the Blessed One reflected, “The ascetics who are disciples of Bāvarī are coming, increasing the crowd of people. Their faculties (indriya) are not yet mature, and this city of Sāvatthī is not a suitable (sappāya) place for them. Indeed, the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya in the kingdom of Magadha is the suitable place for them. If I preach the Dhamma there, the realization of the Four Noble Truths and liberation will occur for the multitude. If those ascetics enter all the cities and come, they will arrive with a very large crowd.” Considering this, the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, preceded them from Sāvatthī toward Rājagaha.

Those ascetics also reached Sāvatthī, entered the Jetavana Monastery, and searched, asking, “Who is the Blessed One? Where is the Blessed One...
623:
623
...residing now?” While searching, they reached the vicinity of the Gandhakuti. When they saw the Buddha’s footprint (which the Blessed One had resolved to leave for them to see), they recited this verse:

“Rattassa hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhawe,
Duṭṭhassa hoti awakaḍḍhitaṃ padaṃ.
Mūḷhassa hoti sahasānupīḷitaṃ,
Wiwaṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ padaṃ.”

“The footprint of one full of lust is hollow in the middle.
The footprint of one full of hatred is as if dragged behind.
The footprint of one full of delusion is as if pressed down by the toes and heels.
This footprint we see now is the footprint of the All-Knowing Buddha, who has destroyed and opened the roof of defilements.”

Based on this verse, they decisively recognized, “The owner of this footprint is the All-Knowing Buddha.”

The Blessed One also entered the cities of Setawya, Kapilavatthu, and others in order, increasing the crowd, and arrived at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya in Rājagaha, Magadha. At the very moment they made that decision, the ascetics left Sāvatthī, entered all the cities such as Setawya and Kapilavatthu, and eventually arrived at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya in Rājagaha, Magadha.

(Pāsāṇaka Cetiya refers to a shrine that existed on a large stone slab in ancient times before the Buddha appeared. When the Blessed One appeared, the donors...)
624:
A monastery was built and donated to the Dispensation. This monastery would be known by its ancient name, "Pāsāṇaka Cetiya."

At that Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, Sakka, the King of Devas, had pre-created a great Dhamma pavilion. The ascetics followed the Buddha, traveling by night the distance meant for the morning, and by morning the distance meant for the night. When they heard that "The Buddha is staying at this Pāsāṇaka Cetiya monastery," they were filled with extreme joy, like a thirsty person finding cool water, like a merchant obtaining a great profit, or like a weary traveler finding shade. They rushed up the hill to the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya monastery.

At that time, the Buddha, surrounded by a group of monks, was preaching the Dhamma to them like a lion roaring in the forest. The youth Ajita (the chief disciple ascetic) saw the Buddha sitting in the Dhamma pavilion, preaching the Dhamma, looking as beautiful as the sun or the full moon, adorned with the six-colored rays and the major and minor marks. When the Buddha spoke welcoming words such as, "O ascetics, how is it? Can you endure the weather?", Ajita replied in detail, "O Venerable Gotama, we can endure the weather." Being very joyful, he stood in a suitable place and, as instructed by his teacher Bāvarī, asked mentally (without speaking):

"Tell us his age, tell us his clan along with his marks.
Tell us his mastery of the mantras; how many does the Brahmin teach?"
625:
(Referring only in the mind): (1) Tell us the age of our teacher, (2) Tell us the clan of our teacher along with (3) the Marks of a Great Man he possesses, (4) Tell us of our teacher's mastery of the Vedas, (5) How many students does our teacher, the Brahmin, himself teach?

(The teacher Bāvarī had taught this question verse to the youth Ajita and instructed him: "Keep this question verse in your mind and ask it. If he is truly a Buddha, he will verbally answer what you have asked mentally." Accordingly, Ajita, the chief disciple, kept this verse in his mind and asked these five questions.)

Then the Buddha, wishing to answer the five questions asked mentally by the youth Ajita, said:

"His age is one hundred and twenty years; his clan is Bāvarī.
Three marks are on his body; he is a master of the three Vedas.
In the marks and the Itihāsa, along with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha,
He teaches five hundred; he has reached perfection in his own Dhamma."

(1) Dear Ajita, your teacher's age is one hundred and twenty years. (2) Your teacher is Bāvarī by clan. (3) On the body of your teacher Bāvarī, there are three Marks of a Great Man. (4) Your teacher...
626:
Brahmin Bāvarī is a master of the three Vedas, and also a master of the Marks of a Great Man, the Itihāsa (Purāṇas), along with the Nighaṇḍu (Lexicon) and Keṭubha (Poetics). (5) Your teacher Brahmin Bāvarī, being a master of his own Vedas, himself teaches five hundred students, even those who are lazy or of dull intellect.

The Buddha answered these two verses verbally and brilliantly.

Then, regarding the third answer which stated, "There are three Marks of a Great Man," the youth Ajita wished for a clear explanation of their specific characteristics. He again asked mentally:

"O Best of Men, reveal the details of the marks of Bāvarī.
O Cutter of Doubts, let us not have any doubt."

Cutter of Doubts = O Buddha, who can remove and cut off the doubts of humans, devas, and brahmas. Best of Men = O Buddha, who is supreme among men. Of Bāvarī = Of our teacher, the Brahmin Bāvarī. Of the marks = Of the three marks that are beautiful and present on his body. Details = Please reveal the specific characteristics and details that should be known. Us = In us.
627:
Doubting = Let there be no doubt or hesitation.

Thus he asked again. Then the Buddha, speaking with his golden voice, said to the youth Ajita:

"He covers his face with his tongue; between his eyebrows is the Uṇṇā.
His male organ is enclosed in a sheath; know this, O youth."

O youth named Ajita... (1) With his tongue, he can cover his entire face (referring to the mark of the Long Tongue). (2) Between his eyebrows, there is a tuft of hair called Uṇṇā (referring to the mark of the White Tuft of Hair). (3) His male organ is enclosed in a sheath like that of a Chaddanta elephant (referring to the mark of the Sheathed Male Organ). O youth named Ajita, know the three marks in this way.

The Buddha answered precisely in this manner. At that time, the entire assembly of people (extending twelve leagues), hearing the answers to the questions without hearing any questions being asked, were filled with joy. They raised their joined palms and said in amazement, "Who asked these questions mentally? Was it a Deva? Was it a Brahma?
628:
Was it Sakka, the husband of Sujā? To whom is the Buddha giving these answers?"

Thus, after hearing the answers to the five questions, the youth Ajita wished to ask two more questions and asked mentally:

"Bāvarī asks about the 'Head' and the 'Splitting of the Head.'
O Blessed One, explain that; O Seer, remove our doubt."

O Seer = O Buddha, who has sought and attained special qualities such as the aggregate of virtue. Our teacher Bāvarī asks about the 'Head' (6) and the 'Splitting of the Head' (7) with the desire to know. O Blessed One, please explain these two things, the Head and the Splitting of the Head, out of compassion. Please remove our doubt with the wheel of your teaching.

The Buddha, speaking with his golden voice, answered what Ajita had asked mentally:

"Know that Ignorance is the 'Head'; Knowledge is the 'Splitting of the Head,'
Associated with faith, mindfulness, concentration, desire, and energy."

O youth named Ajita... (6) Know that Ignorance (avijjā), which covers the Four Noble Truths, is the 'Head' of the beginningless...
629:
Saṃsāra. (7) Knowledge (vijjā), specifically the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, which is associated with faith, mindfulness, concentration, desire, and energy, is the 'Splitting of the Head' that can split the head of Ignorance.

The Buddha answered precisely in this manner. Then the youth (ascetic) Ajita was extremely joyful. Placing his black antelope skin over his left shoulder, he bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and said:

"The Brahmin Bāvarī, O Venerable One,
Together with his disciples, O Worthy One,
With an uplifted and joyful heart,
Pays homage at your feet, O One with Vision."

O Worthy One = O Buddha, who has ended all suffering. O One with Vision = O Buddha, the supreme of the world who possesses the five types of eyes. The Brahmin named Bāvarī, our teacher, with an uplifted and joyful heart, together with more than sixteen thousand disciple ascetics, pays homage at your lotus-like feet.

He shouted this verse, paying homage joyfully on behalf of both the teacher and all the disciples. The Buddha, also...
630:
Out of great loving-kindness and compassion for the youth (ascetic) Ajita, said:

"May the Brahmin Bāvarī be happy,
Together with his disciples.
And may you also be happy;
Live for a long time, O youth."

O youth named Ajita, may your teacher Brahmin Bāvarī be happy in both body and mind, together with his more than sixteen thousand disciples. And may you, Ajita, also be happy in both body and mind. May you live for a long time, for the duration of a lifespan. (After giving this blessing, he continued):

"Whether for Bāvarī or for yourself,
Ask any doubt you have in your mind,
Since the opportunity is given,
Ask whatever you wish."

O youth named Ajita, whatever question or doubt you have in your mind, whether it is for your teacher Brahmin Bāvarī or for yourself, or for all of your group of teacher and disciples—since I have given you the opportunity out of compassion, ask whatever you wish to know by using your wisdom without hesitation.
631:
The Buddha then made the invitation known as the Sabbaññupavāraṇā, the invitation of the Omniscient One, by saying, "Ask whatever you wish."

When the Buddha thus invited and gave permission to ask questions, all those ascetics sat down from where they were standing, and each raising their hands in reverent salutation, the youth Ajita was the first to ask a question. The Buddha answered the question, culminating the discourse in the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). At the conclusion of the teaching, the youth Ajita, along with his one thousand disciples, established themselves in the Fruit of Arahantship. Many thousands of others in the audience also attained the Paths and Fruits. Simultaneously with reaching the Fruit of Arahantship, the Venerable Ajita and his thousand disciples received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination; their ascetic appearance vanished, and they appeared adorned with miraculous requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra) like great elders of sixty years' standing, and they sat down worshiping the Buddha with joined palms. (The same manner applies to the other chief disciples when they questioned the Buddha. The details of how the questions were asked and how the Buddha answered should be noted in order from the Myanmar translation of the Sutta Nipāta, starting from page 410. In this text, however, only the account of the Venerable Mogharāja and the later account of the teacher Bāvarī will be presented for clarity.)—

After the youth Ajita had first asked his questions, the other chief disciples mentioned earlier asked their desired questions in succession. To every question asked, the Buddha gave clear answers and delivered the Dhamma. At the conclusion of each set of questions and answers, the chief disciple who questioned, along with
632:
his one thousand resident disciples (antevāsika), became Arahants and received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination.

In particular, among those sixteen chief disciples, the youth Mogharāja was one who was stubborn with pride (māna), thinking, "I am wiser than all of them." In Mogharāja's mind, the thought occurred: "This youth Ajita is the eldest among all the chief disciples; it is not proper for me to ask questions before him." Out of respect for Ajita, he did not ask first. After Ajita had finished, Mogharāja, as the second chief disciple, attempted to ask the Buddha a question.

The Buddha, considering that "The youth Mogharāja is stubborn with pride. His wisdom is not yet mature; it is proper to restrain his pride first," stopped him by saying, "Mogharāja, wait a while; let others ask their questions first." When restrained by the Buddha, Mogharāja thought, "For so long, I have lived wandering about, thinking there is no one wiser than I. But Buddhas do not speak without knowing; the Buddha must surely see some fault in my questioning," and he remained silent.

After 1. Ajita, 2. Tissa-metteyya, 3. Puṇṇaka, 4. Mettagū, 5. Dhotaka, 6. Upasīva, 7. Nanda, and 8. Hemaka had asked their questions, Mogharāja could not remain without asking and tried again. The Buddha, seeing that Mogharāja's spiritual faculties (indriya) were still not mature, restrained him as before.
633:
The Buddha restrained him again. Mogharāja remained silent once more. After 9. Todeyya, 10. Kappa, 11. Jatukaṇṇī, 12. Bhadrāvudha, 13. Udaya, and 14. Posāla had asked their questions, Mogharāja thought, "I cannot by any means accept being the Saṅghanavaka (the most junior in the Saṅgha)," and he became the fifteenth questioner to ask the Buddha. At this time, Mogharāja's spiritual faculties were mature, and the Buddha answered his question. The manner of their questioning and answering is as follows:

(Mogharāja:)
Dvāhaṃ sakkaṃ apucchissaṃ,
Na me vyākāsi cakkhumā.
Yāvatatiyañca devīsi,
Vyākarotīti me sutaṃ.

"I, the one named Mogharāja, have already asked the Buddha, the Sakyan Prince, twice—once after Ajita had finished, and once after Hemaka had finished. The Buddha, the Lord of the World who possesses the five eyes (Cakkhumā), did not answer me but restrained me. However, I have heard even while living on the banks of the Godhāvarī that if the Great Sage (Devīsi) is asked up to three times by one desiring to know, he will answer out of compassion."
634:
Ayaṃ loko paro loko,
Brahmaloko sadevako.
Diṭṭhiṃ te nābhijānāti,
Gotamassa yasassino.

"This world of humans, the other worlds beyond, and the Brahma world together with the devas (meaning all beings including humans, devas, and Brahmas)—none of them truly know the view of You, the Venerable Gotama, who possesses great fame and a vast following."

Evaṃ abhikkantadassāviṃ, atthi pañhena āgamaṃ.
Kathaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passati.

"Thus, I have come before the Buddha, who possesses such excellent and delightful vision (or who can penetrate and see the inclinations, dispositions, destinations, and futures of all beings), with a desire to ask a profound question. How should one look upon the world (the world of conditioned things, both animate and inanimate) so that the King of Death (Maccurāja) does not see them?"
635:
(The essence of the question is: How must one view the world of conditioned things to reach the Path and Fruit of Arahantship and thereby escape from death?)

When the youth Mogharāja had thus praised the Buddha with three verses and asked his question in the latter half of the final verse, the Buddha replied:

Suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu,
Mogharāja sadā sato.
Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca,
Evaṃ maccutaro siyā.
Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ,
Maccurājā na passati.

"Mogharāja, always be mindful (sato) both day and night. By uprooting and discarding the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi)—the wrong view that takes the five aggregates to be a 'soul' or 'I'—look upon the world of conditioned things as empty (suññato), realizing it is merely conditioned phenomena that do not follow one's will. By looking upon it in this way, one may transcend death. The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this manner."
636:
The Buddha taught this verse as the answer to the question.

(The meaning is that by discarding the view of self (attadiṭṭhi or sakkāyadiṭṭhi), one must view the collection of conditioned things as non-self (anatta) and as empty (suñña). By frequently viewing it thus, one transcends death. Since reaching the Fruit of Arahantship means transcending death, the statement 'transcends death' fulfills the teaching of 'reaching the Fruit of Arahantship.' Therefore, this verse taught by the Buddha is a discourse culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship.)

At the conclusion of this teaching culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship, the youth Mogharāja, like the previous chief disciples, reached the Fruit of Arahantship along with his one thousand resident disciples and received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Many thousands in the audience also attained liberation through the Paths and Fruits.

## (c) Receiving the Title of Etadagga
From the time he became an 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monk, this noble Arahant Mogharāja was accustomed to wearing only robes that were: (1) Vattha-lūkha = coarse and inferior in the quality of the cloth; (2) Sutta-lūkha = coarse and scarce in the quality of the thread used to sew the robes; and (3) Rajana-lūkha = coarse and inferior in the quality of the dye, being dyed with just enough to be considered allowable. Therefore, at a later time while residing at the Jetavana monastery, when the Buddha was appointing the great elders to their respective foremost positions (Etadagga), He declared of the Venerable Mogharāja:
637:
“Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ yadidaṃ mogharājā”

"Monks, among my disciple monks who are accustomed to wearing robes that are coarse and inferior in three ways, the monk Mogharāja is the foremost."

Thus, the Buddha praised him and appointed him to the foremost position (Etadagga) in the category of "Lūkhacīvaradhara"—those who wear coarse and inferior robes.

This is the account of the Venerable Mogharāja.

## Appendix
## About the Teacher Bāvarī
Among the sixteen chief disciples of the teacher Bāvarī, fifteen disciples from the youth Ajita to the youth Mogharāja had asked their questions and reached the Fruit of Arahantship along with their respective one thousand resident disciples, each becoming an 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monk. At the end, the youth Piṅgiya, who was the biological nephew of the teacher Bāvarī and was one hundred and twenty (120) years old, being the sixteenth and final person, addressed the Buddha:

Jiṇṇohamasmi abalo vītaṇṇo,
Nettā na suddhā savanaṃ na phāsu.
Māhaṃ nassaṃ momuho antarāva,
Ācikkha dhammaṃ yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ.
Jātijarāya idha vippahānaṃ.

"I am old, weak, and my complexion is faded. My eyes are not clear, and my hearing is not good. Let me not perish while still confused in the midst of life. Tell me the Dhamma that I may understand, for the abandoning of birth and aging in this very life."
638:
638
"Bhante, I, Pingiya, am aged, weak, and my youthful complexion has faded. My eyes are not clear; my hearing is not good. May I not perish in the midst of delusion before I have realized the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One. Please, out of compassion, teach me the Dhamma to abandon birth and aging, that I may realize it here at the feet of the King of Dhamma."

Thus he pleaded. Because the youth Pingiya was one who was attached to his own body, he spoke with such emphasis on his physical condition. Therefore, the Blessed One, in order to dispel the youth Pingiya's attachment to the body (especially to materiality/form), spoke this verse:

"Seeing people being tormented because of forms,
Heedless people are oppressed by forms.
Therefore, Pingiya, being diligent,
Abandon form for the sake of non-rebirth."
639:
639
"Dear Pingiya, those heedless people who are forgetful and lack mindfulness are oppressed by the forms you delight in, being tormented by the ninety-six kinds of diseases and ailments until their appearance is ruined. Therefore, dear Pingiya, having clearly seen those many heedless people who suffer and worry because of the afflictions of disease due to having this form, and those who are intensely tormented by the thirty-two fates and so on because of materiality—having seen this with your own eyes, you should hold fast to the practice of diligence (appamāda). For the sake of not being reborn in a new existence, abandon materiality (or rather, abandon the craving and greed that clings to materiality) without leaving even the root of latent tendencies (anusaya)."

The Buddha preached this verse. (In this context, since reaching the fruit of Arahantship means one is not reborn in a new existence, by the phrase "for the sake of non-rebirth," the Blessed One preached the practice leading all the way to Arahantship). Although he heard the practice leading to Arahantship preached by the Blessed One, because the youth Pingiya was old and weak, he was not yet able to attain the special Dhamma of the Path and Fruit, and so he spoke again:
640:
640
"The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions,
Above and below—these are the ten directions.
There is nothing in the world unseen, unheard, unsensed,
Or unknown by you.
Please teach me the Dhamma that I may realize,
The abandoning of birth and aging here."

"Bhante, Supreme One of the Three Worlds, in this human world, in the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—in these ten directions—there is truly not a single thing that is unseen, unheard, unsensed by the nose, tongue, or body, or unknown by the mind of the Blessed One. Therefore, please, out of compassion, teach me the Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna, so that I may realize the abandoning of birth and aging here at the feet of the King of Dhamma."

Thus he praised the Blessed One and pleaded again for the preaching of the Dhamma. At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to show the youth Pingiya the practice leading to Arahantship, said:
641:
641
"Seeing humans overwhelmed by craving,
Tormented and oppressed by aging.
Therefore, Pingiya, being diligent,
Abandon craving for the sake of non-rebirth."

"Dear Pingiya, you see with your own eyes the multitude of humans who are oppressed, overwhelmed, and destroyed by craving, and who live in the heat of suffering such as birth, being severely tormented by the decay of old age. Therefore, dear Pingiya, holding fast to the practice of diligence (appamāda) by striving day and night without interruption in wholesome deeds, abandon the threefold craving—sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—through the abandonment of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) without leaving even the root of latent tendencies, for the sake of not being reborn in a new existence."

The Buddha preached this verse of Dhamma. At the conclusion of this verse, which was preached with Arahantship as its climax, the Venerable Pingiya was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala); he became an Anāgāmī Ariya. However, while listening to the Dhamma, the Venerable Pingiya repeatedly thought, "My uncle, the great teacher Bāvarī, does not have the opportunity to hear such a Dhamma preached with such diverse and brilliant analytical insight (paṭibhāna)." Because his mind was distracted by affection for his uncle, he was unable to reach the fruit of Arahantship. His disciples, the one thousand ascetics, however, reached the fruit of Arahantship and became Arahants.
642:
After becoming Anāgāmīs and Arahant Noble Ones, all the teachers and disciples became Ehi Bhikkhu monks who were adorned with miraculously created requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra).

[The collection of Dhamma teachings consisting of questions asked by these sixteen great disciples of Bāvarī and the answers given by the Buddha were recited and categorized by the Elders who performed the Council as individual suttas, such as the Ajita Sutta. These sixteen suttas, together with the introductory verses (vatthugāthā), are called the "Pārāyana Sutta" because they lead to Nibbāna, which is the other shore of Saṃsāra. (Pāra = to Nibbāna + ayana = teachings that can lead one through.)]

When the Buddha finished preaching the Pārāyana Sutta, sixteen thousand and sixteen (16,016) ascetics (only the ascetic Piṅgiya reached the Fruit of Non-returning, while all others) reached the Fruit of Arahantship. The remaining 140,000,000 devas and humans also realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

When the great Dhamma assembly ended, the people who had come from various places to hear the Dhamma appeared in their own villages and towns by the power of the Buddha—that is, they arrived there automatically. The Buddha, surrounded by thousands of monks (except for Ven. Piṅgiya), returned to Sāvatthī.

## Ven. Piṅgiya Preaching the Dhamma
## Again to the Teacher Bāvarī

Ven. Piṅgiya, having paid homage to the Buddha, said, "Exalted Buddha, I have an uncle, Bāvarī, in the world..."
643:
643
While the great teacher Bāvarī was sitting and watching the path, he saw the Venerable Pingiya from afar, arriving in the form of a monk without his ascetic requisites, and he concluded, "The Blessed One has indeed appeared in the world." When the Venerable Pingiya arrived at the hermitage, Bāvarī asked, "How is it, Pingiya? Has the Blessed One appeared in the world?" The Venerable Pingiya replied, "Yes, Brahmin, the Blessed One has appeared in the world. Residing at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya monastery, he has preached the Dhamma to us. I shall preach that Dhamma to you again." When he said this, the great teacher Bāvarī, together with his five hundred young disciples, paid great honor to the Venerable Pingiya and prepared a seat for him. Sitting there, the Venerable Pingiya preached the fifteen verses of the Dhamma known as the "Pārāyanānugīti" to the great teacher Bāvarī. (The Pali verses can be studied starting from page 449 of the Sutta Nipāta Pali, Volume 1. In this work, only the Burmese translation will be presented in easy-to-understand language.)
644:
644
(1) The Venerable Pingiya spoke thus:
"I shall preach the Pārāyana Sutta as taught by the Blessed One. The Blessed One, who is free from the stains of defilements, whose wisdom is as vast as the earth, who has emerged from sensual pleasures, who is free from defilements, and who is an Arahant, has preached the Dhamma exactly as he has seen and known it through the Knowledge of Enlightenment of the Truths (Sacca-abhisambodha-ñāṇa) and Unshared Knowledge (Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). Why would that Blessed One speak any false word? He would not."

(2) "I shall now preach to you the words of Dhamma concerning the virtues of the Blessed One, who has abandoned the stain of delusion (moha), and has also abandoned the evil qualities of pride (māna) and ingratitude (makkha)."

(3) "Brahmin, the Blessed One has dispelled the darkness of defilements. He possesses the eye of wisdom that sees all around. He has reached the end of the world and has transcended all existences. He is free from taints (āsavas) and has abandoned all suffering. He truly bears the name 'Buddha'. O Brahmin, I have served that Blessed One."

(4) "Brahmin, just as a bird leaves a repulsive forest with little fruit and dwells in a forest with much fruit, even so, I have left those of little vision and knowledge, like a swan reaching a great lake..."
645:
645
I have arrived in the presence of the Buddha, who is like a vast body of water of wisdom.

(5) "Brahmin, in the past, before the appearance of the Buddha Gotama, those teachers who told me their doctrines saying, 'It was like this, it will be like this,' all that they said was mere hearsay. All those doctrines only served to increase the three kinds of unwholesome thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire.

(6) "Brahmin, that Blessed One of the Gotama lineage whom I have served is peerless. He dwells having destroyed the darkness of defilements. He is radiant in his own person and also provides the light of wisdom for those to be tamed. My teacher, the Blessed One of the Gotama lineage, possesses the banner of wisdom. He has wisdom as vast as the great earth.

(7) "Brahmin, that teacher of mine, the Blessed One, taught me the Dhamma that is to be realized by oneself, is immediate in its results, is the end of craving, and is free from danger. There is no comparison or simile that can be found for my teacher, the Blessed One."

(8-9) (At that time, the elder teacher Bavari spoke and questioned the Venerable Piṅgiya again thus:) "Piṅgiya, if your teacher, the Blessed One, taught you the Dhamma that is to be realized by oneself, is immediate in its results, is the end of craving, and is free from danger—
646:
646
—if you say there is no comparison or simile for your teacher, the Blessed One, and that your teacher, the Blessed One, possesses the banner of wisdom and wisdom as vast as the great earth, then why do you stay away from him even for a moment? (If your teacher, the Blessed One, is as endowed with virtues as you praise him to be, you should not remain apart from such a teacher even for a moment. Why then do you now remain apart? Thus he spoke, rebuking his own nephew.)

(10-11) (Then, the Venerable Piṅgiya, showing that he did not remain apart from the Buddha in his mind, replied to the elder teacher Bavari as follows:) "Brahmin, that teacher of mine, the Blessed One, taught me the Dhamma that is to be realized by oneself, is immediate in its results, is the end of craving, and is free from the danger of defilements. There is no comparison or simile for my teacher, the Blessed One. I do not stay away even for a moment from my teacher, the Blessed One, who possesses the banner of wisdom and wisdom as vast as the great earth. (The words of Venerable Piṅgiya do not end here.)

(12) "Brahmin, I see that teacher of mine, the Blessed One, with my mind day and night, without negligence, just as if seeing him with physical eyes. I spend the night constantly worshipping that teacher of mine, the Blessed One.
647:
647
Therefore, I consider and know that I do not stay away from him even for a moment.

(13) "Brahmin, my faith (saddhā), my joy (pīti), my mind (citta), and my mindfulness (sati)—these do not depart from the teaching (sāsana) of my teacher, the Buddha Gotama. In whatever direction my teacher, the Blessed One, who has wisdom as vast as the great earth, travels, I am one who is always inclined towards that direction with my mind.

(14) "Brahmin, it is only because I am old and my strength is failing that my body cannot go to where the teacher, the Blessed One, resides. I am always going to where my teacher, the Blessed One, is by means of the movement of my thoughts. Indeed, my mind is constantly joined with the place where my teacher, the Blessed One, resides.

(15) "Brahmin, I used to drift along, wallowing in the mire of sensual desire, moving from one teacher-island to another. O Brahmin, while I was thus drifting in the current of wrong views, I have now seen my teacher, the Blessed One, at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya monastery, who has crossed over the flood (ogha) of saṃsāra and is free from taints (āsava)."

(In this exchange between the uncle and nephew, the Venerable Piṅgiya, being an Ariya monk, addressed his uncle simply as "Brahmin" as befits a monk. The elder teacher Bavari, being the biological uncle, addressed him as "Piṅgiya" as he always had. This should not be regarded as being rude.)
648:
648
## The Buddha Preaching by Emitting Rays
At the end of the fifteenth verse mentioned here, the Blessed One, knowing that the faculties (indriya)—faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—of the Venerable Piṅgiya and his uncle, the elder teacher Bavari, were mature, emitted a golden ray (pīta-rasmi) that was bright and shining, while remaining at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī (just as a large electric spotlight is shone at a cinema or theater). While the Venerable Piṅgiya was praising the virtues of the Blessed One to his uncle Bavari, he saw that ray and looked at it attentively, wondering, "What is this?" He then saw the Blessed One as if he were standing upright right in front of him, and said to Bavari in amazement, "Look, the Blessed One has arrived!"

Then the elder teacher Bavari also rose from his seat and stood with his palms joined. The Blessed One, increasing and spreading the rays, showed himself clearly to Bavari. Knowing what would be suitable for both the uncle and the nephew, he addressed the Venerable Piṅgiya:

"Just as Vakkali, Bhadrāvudha,
And Āḷavi-Gotama released their faith,
In the same way, you too, Piṅgiya, release your faith;
You shall go to the far shore beyond the realm of death."
649:
649
"Dear Piṅgiya, just as the monk Vakkali, the monk Bhadrāvudha (who is among the sixteen chief disciples of Bavari), and the monk Āḷavi-Gotama reached the goal of Arahantship by releasing their faith, in the same way, you, dear son, should also release your faith, directing it towards Nibbāna. When you have thus released it, by undertaking the practice of Insight (Vipassanā), you, dear son, shall reach the far shore of Nibbāna, beyond the realm of death, attaining the fruit of Arahantship with analytical insight (paṭibhāna-arahatta-phala)."

He preached this verse of Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Venerable Piṅgiya attained the fruit of Arahantship, and the elder teacher Bavari attained the fruit of Non-Returner (Anāgāmi). The five hundred young disciples of the elder teacher Bavari became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna).

Now, because the Venerable Piṅgiya wished to clearly express his faith and devotion, he recited these three verses:

"I am even more delighted,
Having heard the words of the Sage.
The Buddha has removed the veil,
He is free from taints and possesses analytical insight. (1)"
650:
650
"Having known the supreme ones among the gods,
He knows everything, the high and the low.
The Teacher who puts an end to questions
For those who claim to be free from doubt. (2)"

"Venerable Sir, I, the disciple known as Piṅgiya, having heard the words of the Dhamma spoken by the Great Sage, the peerless Buddha, am increasingly delighted with faith. You have broken and opened the roof of the three-fold cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). You are free from the thorns of defilements and possess the wisdom of analytical insight (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-paññā).

"The Blessed One, the Supreme in the world, who puts an end to all questions and problems, and who is the Teacher of those who, while still having the thorns of doubt (vicikicchā), falsely claim to be teachers free from doubt—having known with higher knowledge (abhiññā) the Ariyas who are Visuddhidevas (gods by purity), being superior to and more noble than conventional gods (sammuti-deva) and gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), has understood the entirety of the Dhamma in its two aspects: the noble and the base, which lead to the state of a Visuddhideva."
651:
651
"That which is unshakeable and unalterable,
To which there is no comparison anywhere.
I shall certainly go there; of this I have no doubt.
Regard me as one whose mind is thus dedicated."

"O Sage, who has clearly understood all phenomena, I, the disciple known as Piṅgiya, shall certainly reach that Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), for which there is no comparison anywhere, and which is entirely without movement or instability, and entirely without change or destruction. In this certain arrival at the Nibbāna element without remainder, there is not even a slight doubt for me, the disciple known as Piṅgiya. Venerable Sir, please regard me as one whose mind is dedicated to the peaceful Nibbāna through the three-fold vehicle, with faith as the forerunner, up to the fruit of Arahantship, just as the Buddha instructed: 'In the same way, you too, release your faith.'"

This is the supplementary account of the elder teacher Bavari.
